# INTRODUCTION

The U.S. Department of Agriculture proposes to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule) (66 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B (2001)), which prohibits road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas on National Forest System lands, with limited exceptions. Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule is intended to return decision making for these activities to local officials, in conjunction with Forest-level land management planning. The 2001 Roadless Rule applies to approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System (NFS) lands, including in Alaska.

Accompanying the Proposed Rule, which is published in the Federal Register, and an environmental impact statement, the Forest Service has prepared this draft ‘framework programmatic’ biological assessment in compliance with the Endangered Species Act. This draft biological assessment discloses the potential effects to ESA-listed resources under the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service jurisdiction that would result from rescinding the proposed 2001 Roadless Rule. An additional biological assessment has been prepared to assess effects to ESA-listed resources under National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, National Marine Fisheries Services (NFMS) jurisdiction. The Forest Service is requesting framework consultation and conferencing and commits to consulting on any future projects in the action area that may affect ESA-listed species or designated critical habitats.

All documents, including the proposed rule and other supporting information, may be found on the following website: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/planning/roadless.

## Roadless Rule History

Throughout its history, the Forest Service has managed undeveloped areas to conserve their unique characteristics. After passage of the Wilderness Act of 1964 (Pub. L. 88-577), management of these areas, commonly known as “roadless areas,” became the focus of national attention when the Forest Service initiated a review to determine their suitability for inclusion in the National Wilderness Preservation System, known as the Roadless Area Review and Evaluation (RARE) I (1973) and RARE II (1977). In the decades following the inventory, roadless area management continued to be controversial in land management planning and project proposals to harvest timber, build roads, or otherwise develop these areas. In 1999, President Clinton directed the Forest Service to undertake a public process to “provide appropriate long-term protection for most or all of these currently inventoried ‘roadless’ areas...”, initiating the rule-making process. In 2001, the Forest Service issued the Roadless Area Conservation Rule establishing a national-level rule to maintain the values of inventoried roadless areas, limit their development, and address the history of controversy.

The 2001 Roadless Rule prohibited road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting on inventoried roadless areas (IRAs) on 58.5 million acres, or 31 percent, of National Forest System lands (defined in 36 CFR 294.11 (2001) identified in the set of maps contained in the 2001 Final EIS). The Rule provided for certain limited exceptions, including for forest stewardship purposes, public health and safety, reserved or outstanding rights, existing or renewed mineral leases, and realignment to prevent resource damage or address safety hazards (36 CFR 294.12 and 294.13 (2001)).

In the promulgation of the 2001 Roadless Rule, the Forest Service found that the Rule’s prohibitions on road construction and timber harvest were not likely to adversely affect threatened or endangered species or adversely modify designated or critical habitat; were not likely to jeopardize proposed species or adversely modify proposed critical habitat; and may beneficially affect threatened, endangered, and proposed species and critical habitat (USFS 2000c).  The Services concurred with the determination (66 FR 9 3271).

## Inventoried Roadless Areas

Today, inventoried roadless areas total approximately 58.2 million<sup>1</sup> acres, or about 30 percent of all National Forest System lands. The 2001 Roadless Rule applies to approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands, including about 9.3 million acres within the Tongass National Forest. The 44.7 million acres exclude approximately 9.3 million acres in Idaho and 4.2 million acres in Colorado, which are under state specific roadless rules. Current areas are reflected on national maps at the Forest Service Roadless Area website (https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/planning/roadless)<sup>2</sup> .

More than 95 percent of IRAs managed under the 2001 Roadless Rule (outside of Colorado and Idaho) are in ten Western states (from largest inventoried roadless area acreage to smallest): Alaska, Montana, California, Utah, Wyoming, Nevada, Washington, Oregon, New Mexico, and Arizona. In the West, IRAs were typically 5,000 acres or greater. Some roadless areas are less than 5,000 acres—either because they are adjacent to Congressionally designated wilderness or in the eastern U.S. (east of the 100th meridian). While they are referred to as “roadless”, because of the history of their inventory and designation, there are thousands of miles of existing roads within lands designated under the 2001 Roadless Rule, including National Forest System roads as well as roads of other ownerships. Additionally decommissioned roads and unauthorized routes that are not part of the official system or records may exist.

# PURPOSE AND NEED

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA or Department) is proposing to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule), which established broad prohibitions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting within inventoried roadless areas on National Forest System lands. The intent of this proposed action is to reduce regulatory burden and return decision-making for the management of inventoried roadless areas to the land management planning process at the individual national forest level. Rescission of the nationallevel prohibitions provides responsible officials with flexibility to better guide management of National Forest System lands and respond to changing local resource conditions. The Forest and

Rangeland Renewable Resources Planning Act of 1974, as amended by the National Forest Management Act of 1976, the 2012 National Forest System Land Management Planning Rule (2012 Planning Rule), and the associated land management planning processes and plans are the appropriate and effective mechanisms to guide sustainable, integrated management of the resources within the plan areas in the context of the broader landscape, giving due consideration to the relative values of the various resources in particular areas. For additional discussion on the purpose and need please refer to the Final Rule.

# CONSULTATION HISTORY

July 8, 2025 – The ESA compliance team is stood up for the Roadless Rule Rescission.

August 21, 2025 – The ESA compliance team decided to conduct a programmatic analysis for the rule rescission despite all future activities being required to conduct project-level ESA consultation.

August 29, 2025 – The Forest Service confirms a full analysis is preferred for this action given the history of the 2001 Roadless Rule.

November 21, 2025 – The analytical data needed to conduct exposure analyses is completed. December 24, 2025 – Preliminary draft BA submitted to the Services to begin technical assistance.

# DESCRIPTION OF THE ACTION

The proposed action described below is a “framework programmatic action” as defined in 50 CFR 402.02, where the framework programmatic action only establishes a framework for the development of specific future action(s) but does not authorize any future action(s). The effects to listed species and designated critical habitat of future actions that are subsequently authorized, funded, or carried out would be addressed in subsequent section 7 consultations. While this is a ‘framework programmatic action’, it does not provide a new framework. Instead, the proposed rule would remove the Roadless Area Conservation Rule regulation/prohibitions from the broader existing legal framework in which the Forest Service plans, authorizes, and implements activities. The programmatic effects are evaluated based on the legal framework that would remain in place, focusing on the effects of the removal of the prohibitions on roads construction and timber harvest (see Legal Framework, below).

Under the proposed rulemaking, the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule prohibiting activities in inventoried roadless areas would be rescinded (also referred to as ‘repealed’). This action would eliminate the national prohibitions set forth in the 2001 Roadless Rule – road construction, reconstruction, and timber harvest may be authorized within inventoried roadless areas, where they are consistent with land management plans, or other statutory and regulatory requirements. In addition, the proposed rule would remove the national “inventoried roadless area” designation from the 44.7 acres million acres of National Forest System lands currently designated as inventoried roadless areas under the 2001 Roadless Rule<sup>3</sup> .

Management of lands formerly managed as inventoried roadless areas would be governed by applicable land management plan direction alongside other relevant law, regulation, and policy. Some land management plans include components that restrict timber harvest or road building to meet other management objectives or legal requirements, such as to protect sensitive areas, to provide for primitive recreation opportunities, or to provide wildlife habitat. The proposed rescission of the Roadless Rule would not alter this existing land management plan direction.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule does not authorize, fund, or carry out future forest management activities that could occur in these areas. All future site-specific project decisions, including those to authorize road construction, reconstruction, and timber harvesting, must be consistent with land management plans. Any proposed actions must undergo environmental review, including National Environmental Policy Act compliance prior to a decision. Project decisions must comply with applicable Federal and State laws, such as the Clean Water Act, the Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, National Historic Preservation Act, and the Wilderness Act, as well as provisions for government-to-government consultation with Tribes and Alaska Native Corporations.

In addition, the proposed rule would not compel the amendment or revision of any land management plan. While the rulemaking would not require such changes, plans may be amended in any manner whatsoever and are revised periodically (16 U.S.C. 1604(f)). Local responsible officials would continue to have discretion to initiate land management plan amendment or revise, as deemed necessary. A determination to amend or revise a land management plan is based on a variety of factors. Any future administrative changes, amendments, or revisions to land management plans would comply with NFMA and planning regulations (36 CFR 219 and the planning directives at FSM 1920 and FSH 1909.12), which includes substantive requirements to provide for species biodiversity, recovery of threatened and endangered species, and ecological conditions to provide viable populations of species of conservation concern. To the degree that a land management plan could change in the future, the effects of such a change would be attributed to and analyzed as part of the decision-making for that action.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule does not constrain or alter the statutory requirement of sections 7(a)(1) through section 7(a)(4) of the Endangered Species Act. All future activities in currently inventoried roadless areas will require compliance with the ESA prior to implementation.

> 3 The 9.3 million acres of inventoried roadless area within the Tongass National Forest would be included in the 44.7 million acres no longer managed according to the 2001 Roadless Rule. Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule does not affect state-level roadless rules that exist in Colorado and Idaho, nor does it preclude the development of state-led roadless efforts in the future.

# ANALYTICAL METHODS

## Action Area Determination

There are 44.7 million acres of IRAs subject to the 2001 Roadless Rule, although only ~40 million acres are included in the action area where the proposed rulemaking could result in changes to future management activities. In this assessment, the term “action area” and “affected environment” are used interchangeably.

The action area for the proposed Roadless Rule Rescission was defined by removing nonNational Forest System lands, wilderness, wilderness study areas, and wild portions of wild and scenic rivers from Inventoried Roadless Areas managed under the 2001 Roadless Rule (resulting in ~40 million acres of action area) as potential future management of these areas would not be affected by the proposed rulemaking.

More specifically, review of the geospatial data found that 44.3 million acres of these are on National Forest System lands, meaning about 0.4 million acres of lands have had land ownership change since the 2001 Roadless Rule or there may be vertical integration problems (mapping errors) between the inventoried roadless data and official land ownership boundary data<sup>4</sup> .

In addition, over 4 million acres are within Congressionally-designated wilderness<sup>5</sup> , wilderness study areas<sup>6</sup> , and wild segments of wild and scenic rivers<sup>7</sup> . These statutory designations have more restrictive and more permanent mandates than the 2001 Roadless Rule. Therefore, changes in management activities in these areas under any alternative are highly unlikely and not reasonably certain to occur. The Forest Service did not arbitrarily buffer the action area to account for the possibility that some stressors such as noise and dust may extend beyond the IRA boundary. At the national scale, it is not reasonably certain that a majority of stressors associated with a single action may extend beyond the boundary of the IRAs, with the exception of sedimentation being carried downstream. Stressors such as noise and dust are expected to be minimally impactful where they occur, whereas sedimentation from proposed activities is

Outside of the action area (i.e., outside IRAs) there are no prohibitions to road construction or timber harvest such that these activities could have already been occurring, suggesting a buffer to include these areas may not be prudent. The fourth circuit court has defended that the action area for a programmatic action need not include areas outside of the relevant administrative boundary because the programmatic action does not authorize any specific activity and extension beyond those borders would be largely speculative. (Case 1:24-cv-00118-MR-WC).

For impacts considerations for aquatic species, downstream portions of aquatic habitats were included in the action area for up to 2 miles, to capture the most likely locations where sedimentation may be an issue. Instream work has been shown to cause turbidity that is generally not detectable more than half a mile downstream (see the Sedimentation section of the Fish discussion for more details). While activities on land can lead to increased sedimentation entering surface waters, best management practices will reduce these sediment loads. Although sediment transport is dependent on stream flow and particle size, a 2-mile downstream buffer is expected to capture a majority of the reasonably certain effects from sedimentation that would potentially occur with the future actions (indirect effects). Although storm events may cause sediment plumes that travel more than 2 miles downstream, these events are often short in duration, unpredictable, and not a result of forest management. This downstream buffer distance is similar or longer than most aquatic effect analyses have required from consultations on timber and road construction activities in the west. National grasslands and forests in Idaho and Colorado are not included in the action area because roadless areas in these states are managed under state-specific roadless rules, which are not affected by rescission of the national roadless rule.

## Legal Framework for Future Projects<sup>8</sup>

As stated under the description of the action, the proposed rulemaking does not authorize any site-specific actions, however, it does remove prohibitions on certain actions such that they are reasonably certain to be proposed in some of these areas in the future (see also “Scope” below). Under the proposed rulemaking, all future projects that authorize road construction and timber harvest within the action area must still be consistent with all federal laws, including, Endangered Species Act (ESA), National Forest Management Act (NFMA) of 1976, National Environmental Policy Act, and, Clean Water Act, and must comply with the relevant land management plan. To ensure compliance with these laws and plans, during project-level environmental review and decision-making, the Forest Service includes project design measures that minimize<sup>9</sup> adverse effects to species and their habitats.

> 8 Not all inclusive.

> 9 Apply pre-project planning, best available technology, management practices, and scientific knowledge to

> reduce the magnitude, extent and/or duration of impacts.

### Endangered Species Act

The Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA) the primary U.S. law protecting imperiled species and their habitats from extinction. Under Section 7 of the ESA, federal agencies must ensure actions they authorize, fund, or carry out, such as permits, construction, or resource management, do not jeopardize listed species or adversely modify critical habitats. Agencies must consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) or National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) if a project "may affect" protected species. Typically, ESA consultations include design measures that minimize adverse effects to ESA listed species and their designated critical habitats. Per the ESA, federal agencies are not allowed to jeopardize the continued existence of ESA listed species and destroy or adversely modify critical habitat. Because there is no way to predict where projects will occur and all future projects that occur in the affected environment will undergo ESA Section 7 consultation, this analysis will be high level effects that may be expected for actions proposed under this Environmental Assessment. In some cases, previous consultation effects to species and critical habitats for similar actions were utilized to determine effects.

### National Forest Management Act

NFMA requires “guidelines for land management plans developed to achieve the goals of the Program which…provide for diversity of plant and animal communities based on the suitability and capability of the specific land area in order to meet overall multiple-use objectives, and within the multiple-use objectives of a land management plan adopted pursuant to this section, provide, where appropriate, to the degree practicable, for steps to be taken to preserve the diversity of tree species similar to that existing in the region controlled by the plan.”  NFMA is implemented through either the 2012 planning rule or the 1982 planning rule.

A primary purpose of the 2012 Planning Rule (planning rule) is to promote the ecological integrity of national forests and grasslands and other National Forest System administrative units. Ecological integrity – a substantive requirement of the planning rule – is designed to support Ecological Sustainability (36 CFR 219.8), Diversity of Plant and Animal Communities (36 CFR 219.9), and Multiple Uses (36 CFR 219.10). Similarly, the 1982 planning rule dictates “Fish and wildlife habitat shall be managed to maintain viable populations of existing native and desired non-native vertebrate species in the planning area. For planning purposes, a viable population shall be regarded as one which has the estimated numbers and distribution of reproductive individuals to insure its continued existence is well distributed in the planning area. In order to insure that viable populations will be maintained, habitat must be provided to support, at least, a minimum number of reproductive individuals and that habitat must be well distributed so that those individuals can interact with others in the planning area” and that “Forest planning shall provide for diversity of plant and animal communities and tree species consistent with the overall multiple-use objectives of the planning area. Such diversity shall be considered throughout the planning process. Inventories shall include quantitative data making possible the evaluation of diversity in terms of its prior and present condition. For each planning alternative, the interdisciplinary team shall consider how diversity will be affected by various mixes of resource outputs and uses, including proposed management practices. (Refer to Sec. 219.27(g).)”

All forest and grassland management plans, regardless of which planning rule they follow, must be consulted on under the Endangered Species Act.

#### _Aquatic Species Conservation Strategies_

Specific to aquatic species habitat, NFMA mandates that U.S. Forest Service protect streams, streambanks, shorelines, lakes, and wetlands from detrimental changes in water temperature, sediment deposits, and blocked watercourses during timber harvesting and management. It requires, through land management plans, that soil and water resources are not irreversibly damaged, often by establishing riparian management areas and utilizing Best Management Practices (BMPs). Further, individual land management plans contain standards and guides for aquatic management zones, some in the form of Aquatic Conservation Strategies (ACS) (such as the Northwest Forest Plan (USFS and USBLM 1994b), PacFish (USFS 1995a), and InFish (USFS 1995b)). Aquatic conservation strategies and land management plans standards and guides are designed to move the aquatic management zones to desired ecological conditions.

Aquatic conservation strategies use an ecosystem approach to management of riparian and aquatic habitats and were designed to (1) protect watersheds that had good-quality habitat and strong fish populations at the time they were drafted, and (2) halt further declines in watershed condition and restore ecological processes that create and maintain favorable conditions in aquatic ecosystems in degraded ecosystems (FEMAT 1993). The long-term goal (100+ years) is to develop a network of functioning watersheds that supports populations of fish and other aquatic and riparian-dependent organisms (such as the Northwest Forest Plan (USFS and USBLM 1994b), PacFish (USFS 1995a), and InFish (USFS 1995b)). Aquatic conservation strategies are based on preserving and restoring key ecological processes, including the natural disturbance regimes (USFS and USBLM 1994b) that create and maintain habitat for native aquatic and riparian-dependent organisms, and it recognizes that periodic natural disturbances may be required to sustain ecological productivity. As a result, aquatic conservation strategies do not expect all watersheds to be in favorable condition (highly productive for the same aquatic organisms) at any point in time, nor does it expect that any watershed will remain in a certain condition through time. The primary objective of aquatic conservation strategies is to maintain and restore the distribution, diversity, and complexity of watershed-level features and processes to which aquatic and riparian species are uniquely adapted. Aquatic conservation strategies were also designed to develop a strategy to guide management of aquatic ecosystems on federal lands, where amended, that would meet potential ESA requirements (Reeves et al. 2018). Aquatic conservation strategies were expected to make significant contributions to the recovery of the ESA-listed fish by increasing the quantity and quality of freshwater habitat for Pacific salmon and protecting and enhancing habitats of other species (Reeves et al. 2006, FEMAT 1993).

### Best Management Practices (Clean Water Act)

Forest Service National Best Management Practices for Water Quality Management on National Forest System Lands (USFS 2012a) was developed to improve agency performance and accountability in managing water quality consistent with the Federal Clean Water Act (CWA) and State water quality programs. Current Forest Service policy directs compliance with required CWA permits and State regulations and requires the use of BMPs to control nonpoint source pollution to meet applicable water quality standards and other CWA requirements. The National BMP program document provides consistency among Forest Service administrative units to efficiently administer the program and demonstrate improvements in performance and accountability at multiple scales. The National BMP Program consists of four main components: (1) a set of National Core BMPs, (2) a set of standardized monitoring protocols to evaluate implementation and effectiveness of those BMPs, (3) a data management and reporting structure, and (4) corresponding national direction.

Relationship Between the 2001 Roadless Rule and Land Management Planning

Administration of each national forest and grassland is directed by a land management plan, along with numerous land management laws, regulations, policies, and agency directives. A land management plan provides a framework for future site-specific project analysis and decision making. Land management plans are developed, amended, and revised under the National Forest Management Act and the 2012 Planning Rule at 36 CFR 219. All land management plans must conform to existing laws and regulations. Laws and regulations take precedence over management direction in the land management plans. When new or changed laws or regulations create conflicts with land management plan content, plans are administratively changed as needed to conform to new statutory and regulatory requirements (36 CFR 219.1(f) and 219.13(c)).

The 2001 Roadless Rule did not amend, revise, or compel amendment or revision of any land management plans (36 CFR 294.14(b) (2001); 66 FR 3273); however, the Roadless Rule supersedes individual land management plans where a provision of the rule is more restrictive than a plan. Similarly, for some areas, the plans may contain plan components that are more restrictive than the 2001 Roadless Rule.  Under the 2012 Planning Rule, inventoried roadless areas are treated as a type of designated area,<sup>10</sup> with the option to also identify these areas as unique geographic areas or management areas in the plans. Plans may also include additional plan components for inventoried roadless areas if they are compatible with the restrictions of the applicable roadless rule. Within land management plans, inventoried roadless areas currently overlap other management areas or geographic areas, such as core habitats, research natural areas, alpine areas, or areas managed for backcountry recreation where there are expected to be low levels of development, including timber harvest and road construction.

Current land management-plans often include plan direction and components that identify where timber management and road construction may or may not be allowed. Example management

> 36 CFR 219.9 Designated area. An area or feature identified and managed to maintain its unique special character or purpose. Some categories of designated areas may be designated only by statute and some categories may be established administratively in the land management planning process or by other administrative processes of the Federal executive branch. Examples of statutorily designated areas are national heritage areas, national recreational areas, national scenic trails, wild and scenic rivers, wilderness areas, and wilderness study areas. Examples of administratively designated areas are experimental forests, research natural areas, scenic byways, botanical areas, and significant caves.

> Management area. A land area identified within the planning area that has the same set of applicable plan components. A management area does not have to be spatially contiguous

areas where timber management or road construction may be limited include recommended wilderness, research natural areas, or backcountry management areas. Some plans include plan components with direction specific to IRAs.

A national review of plan components in management areas overlapping the potentially affected environment was completed to identify where plans do or do not further restrict timber harvest and road construction activities. There is much variation between individual land management plans and Regions reflecting differences in local conditions, age of the plans, and changes in planning policies over time. Overall, within potentially affected IRAs, land management plan components:

- Further restrict (do not allow or generally do not allow) road construction on 21.8 million acres (54.5 percent of the potentially affected IRAs), and

- Further restrict (do not allow or generally do not allow) timber harvest on 26.7 million acres (66.5 percent of the potentially affected IRAs).

Note that this information is intended for programmatic analysis purposes, actual implementation of any activities would be subject to local interpretation of the land management plans based on unique local conditions, which would also include numerous considerations of forest-wide or habitat related forest plan direction also to likely be limiting on where timber management and road construction would be allowed or proposed.

### Consideration of Existing Protections

Species-specific conservation measures and design criteria were considered on an individual basis for certain species. Conservation measures largely come from forest plans but might also originate from regional strategies and previous consultations. These measures were reviewed and analyzed to determine if they affected the standard determinations made based on the procedures described above. Species-specific measures associated with forest plans typically apply to any location on that forest that is inhabited by the species unless otherwise stated. Species-specific measures from forest plans and other approved strategy documents are mandatory in nature unless otherwise stated.

## Scope

The following describes how the agency drew a reasonable and manageable line in consideration of effects of the proposed action that are reasonably certain to occur, and those that may extend outside the geographical territory of the proposal or might materialize later in time.

In general, it is reasonably likely activities with potential for beneficial or adverse environmental effects could occur within or near inventoried roadless areas following the proposed rulemaking. However, the rulemaking would not compel, require, or authorize any site-specific activities. Therefore, site-specific locations and amounts of activities that could occur in the future under the alternatives are uncertain. Any future decisions on these activities are greatly influenced by factors beyond the proposed rulemaking such as local decision-making through land management plans and projects, local industry capacity, agency budget allocations and resources, and other regulations and policies. Site-specific effects can be meaningfully measured and evaluated at the project and activity stage and are evaluated during the project-level ESA Section 7 consultation process. In addition, some of the potential adverse effects described could be reduced or mitigated at the project level, through complying with policy, following land management plan direction, implementing best management practices, or developing projectspecific design criteria. Protections/requirements that reduce impacts are noted throughout this analysis.

The analysis focuses on the difference where (what locations) activities, particularly road construction and timber harvest, are more or less reasonably likely to occur within inventoried roadless areas, and the resulting effects to listed species. Estimates of areas where activities could occur, were prepared for effects analysis purposes – they do not reflect proposed or planned activity areas. The stressors associated with these activities were assumed to potentially occur when species would be present and affected as the timing of future activities is not known.

The geographic extent of the environmental effects analysis focuses on activities with a close causal relationship to the rulemaking. Changes to regulations remain in place until additional rulemaking or Congressional action. Short- and long-term reasonably likely to occur environmental impacts of the rulemaking are considered.

The short-term potential for road construction and timber harvest or related activities and associated effects is more predictable and reasonably likely to occur. Within the potentially affected environment the following areas are more likely to have activities or impacts, in the short term (5 years):

- areas where activities are allowed under existing land management plans (see environmental baseline below);

- areas with a greater management priority or ‘need’ (ex. high risk firesheds and areas affected by insect and disease or other disturbances);

- areas that are more feasible or economical for equipment and workers to access (more operable); and,

- areas with high product potential/economic viability for timber production to support management objectives.

In the longer term (up to 20 years and beyond), the extent of activities is more uncertain. Still, it is reasonable to expect a greater proportion of the potentially effected environment could be impacted by activities over time. Factors affecting long term change include natural events such as storms and wildfires, local decision-making through projects and land management plan amendments/revisions, national policy changes, technological changes, industry and economic changes, etc. Areas that are least likely for development in the short term (currently restricted, less developed, etc.) could be impacted by change, in the longer term. However, given the long causal chain and distance from the action proposed, predicting the specific amounts is too speculative.

The Roadless Rule prohibited road construction and timber harvest (with exemptions) but did not directly restrict other activities. Rescinding the Roadless Rule increases the likelihood of timber and road construction activities occurring within the boundary of previously designated IRAs. However, removing the prohibitions on road construction in IRAs may increase accessibility and therefore increase use of the land for purposes other than timber harvest. These activities are speculative, not reasonably certain to occur, and would require a lengthy causal chain to tie to the proposed rescission of the Roadless Rule. As such, only timber and road construction activities are considered in this analysis.

### Road Construction

**Road construction**<sup>**11**</sup> **or road reconstruction**<sup>**12**</sup> **or road maintenance**<sup>**13**</sup> may be associated with timber harvest or other forest vegetation management (fuels reduction, thinning, etc.), private or special uses, existing rights, minerals and energy exploration<sup>14</sup> , watershed restoration, habitat improvement, and recreation development. Aside from timber harvest, these activities are currently allowed under the 2001 Roadless Rule (see environmental baseline section).

The objective of the NFS transportation system is to provide the minimal mileage road system needed for safe and efficient travel, and for administration, utilization and protection of NFS lands. Any new roads would be designed and maintained in a way that would minimize negative effects on water quality, soil stability, and wildlife habitat. The decision to construct a new, permanent road that would become part of the NFS road system would be made as part of transportation planning associated with planned resource management activities and use of NFS lands. Proposals for new roads related to development and the associated environmental effects would be considered through project-level planning. If future decisions authorize it, modifications to the transportation network would follow law, regulation and policy found at 16 USC 1608, FSM/FSH 7700, relevant State and Federal statutes such as the Clean Water Act, NEPA, and Endangered Species Act, and national forest land management plans. Implementation of these policies can minimize, but not eliminate, some adverse environmental effects.

Timber harvest activities would likely generate the highest need for permanent and temporary roads on the landscape. New roads will not be required for some timber activities. For example, it’s assumed timber related activities within 0.5 miles of existing roads where terrain slopes are 40 percent or less, would less likely require the development of new, permanent roads (11.3 million acres or 28.3 percent of the affected environment). Conversely, where timber activities are occurring beyond 0.5 miles of existing roads, some construction of new temporary and permanent roads would be more likely<sup>15</sup> . New projects would not automatically be approved as

### Timber Harvest

**Vegetation and Forest Management** include commercial timber harvest<sup>17</sup> and non-commercial timber treatments<sup>18</sup> and are completed for multiple resource objectives, including but not limited to timber production, fuels reduction, public health and safety, forest health improvement, watershed improvement, and wildlife habitat improvement. Land management plans must ensure: (1) Timber harvest is only allowed in areas that will not be irreversibly damaged, where cutting units can be visually blended into the terrain, where streams, wetlands, riparian areas, and water bodies are protected; (2) Timber harvest does not exceed sustained yield and is not designated solely to maximize outputs; and, (3) Harvested areas must be regenerated within 5 years. Any project activity, including timber harvest, must be consistent with land management plans. The 2012 Planning Rule provides further direction for forest management activities including timber harvest and non-commercial treatments. These plans include plan components (desired conditions, goals, objectives, standards, and guidelines) and identify areas suitable and not suitable for timber production to maintain sustained yield levels, identify maximum harvest levels on suitable lands (allowable sale quantity or sustained yield limit), and allow, prohibit, or limit timber harvest to protect resources.

Timber harvest effects are the same and not dependent on the resource objective; therefore, the deconstruction table (Table 1) only includes a basic timber harvest activity. Silvicultural prescriptions are utilized to meet direction within individual land management plans. Timber sales and other removals of forest products support agency strategic objectives to foster resilient, adaptive ecosystems, mitigate wildfire risk, and strengthen communities (USFS 2015). Table 1 was developed to cover all types of timber harvest and silvicultural prescriptions covered by the Roadless Rule Rescission. Other Activities Potentially Involving Road Construction or Tree Cutting

#### **Access to National Forest System Lands and Special Use Authorizations**

Access to the National Forest System (NFS) lands come in many forms from general usage by members of the public that do not require permits in most cases, to lands and special use authorization uses that are allowed through Land Management Plans and require a special use permit or similar legal instrument. Special use authorizations are needed for activities on or occupancy of National Forest System Lands including water transmission/storage, utilities, research, military training, communication uses, agriculture, pipelines, organized recreation events, ski areas, road access and much more. Pre-existing uses and those related to reserved or outstanding rights for access, occupancy, and use of NFS lands were not affected by the 2001 Roadless Rule. The continuation, re-issuance, or renewal of existing special use authorizations for activities in inventoried roadless areas is not prohibited by the 2001 Roadless Rule. Any future or additional special use authorizations would be reactive in nature to respond to public and customer requests. Under the proposed rulemaking, it is reasonably certain to occur that there would be an increase in new proposals for uses involving road construction or reconstruction that benefit the public or provide access to non-Federal lands within or adjacent to IRAs, as well as requests for expansion of existing uses (for example, additional access routes or improved road quality). An authorization is issued only after being evaluated and having passed through screening criteria (36 CFR 251.54), including compliance with the applicable land management plan and environmental analysis processes. Under the proposed action, new special use proposals would be evaluated on their own merits and no longer be rejected outright due to prohibitions for road construction or reconstruction. Requests for and approval of road construction-related authorizations are most likely to occur in areas that are ‘operable’ and where current land management plans allow these activities. For the purposes of this assessment, road construction is considered but future activities requiring a special use permit are outside the scope of this analysis and will be consulted on at the time of permit application.

#### **Minerals Exploration and Development**

Mineral and energy exploration and development occur within inventoried roadless areas (though to a lesser degree than other NFS lands) and would continue where there are existing rights or permits/leases/authorizations. Road construction, reconstruction, and tree cutting for locatable (gold, silver, copper, lead, zinc, etc.) mineral exploration and development is considered a right of access as provided by the General Mining Law and the 2001 Roadless Rule’s exceptions (36 CFR 294.12(b)(3); 36 CFR 294.13(b)(2)). Changes may occur for leasable minerals exploration and development (primarily oil and gas and coal). Any new, modified or renewed leases would continue to be managed under existing laws and regulations governing oil and gas and coal, including project specific environmental review documents and compliance with other relevant law, regulation, and policy prior to leasing. For new leases or modifications of leases, construction or reconstruction of roads that are reasonable and necessary for development of existing energy or mineral leases, for access to new or existing energy or mineral leases, and for access to associated product conveyance lines could be allowed as necessary in accordance with the terms of the lease, where they are consistent with land management plans or other laws and policy requirements. In addition, the 2001 Roadless Rule and IRA boundary would not apply or be considered in any future analyses for the modification of existing leases. However, in a site-specific leasing analysis, a no surface occupancy stipulation may still be applied to protect surface resources. For example, to prevent excessive erosion on steep slopes, a no surface occupancy may still be applied to the Federal lease. The Forest Service is not proposing to extend this consultation to include future minerals exploration and development. Future mineral exploration and development will require standalone consultation to comply with the Endangered Species Act.

## Species Lists

Threatened, endangered, and proposed species and their designated or proposed critical habitat were compiled from existing consultation documents for species under NMFS’s jurisdiction. A shapefile of IRA boundaries by administrative unit were imported into IPaC to compile the list of species under FWS’s jurisdiction. Both species lists were reviewed by regional FS staff and species that do not actually occur on NFS lands were removed. Species lists were sent to the Services in September and October 2025 for review. Where appropriate, species were grouped taxonomically to facilitate discussing the effects to a large number of species and critical habitats. Species of high public interest and forest species known to be severely impacted by timber harvest and road construction are often discussed separately from taxonomic groupings.

## Data Collection and Use

We acquired species occurrence data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) and Natural Resource Manager (NRM) using R and ArcGIS Pro, respectively. The databases do not differentiate between DPSes of vertebrate species listed under the ESA, which causes potential inflation of exposure to these entities. The data is managed in such a way that occasionally species occurrences occur in locations where the entity is not listed or protected by the ESA; however, the FS does not believe these discrepancies have altered the conclusions provided.

A custom exposure analysis is performed for some species known to be impacted by roads and timber activities and where national data could support such analyses. Where custom analyses are performed, they will be documented in either the administrative record or in the taxonomic sections below. While the potential for inflated exposure is possible the FS does not believe it would significantly affect the determinations made. These data discrepancies will also be addressed during project-level consultation. We processed GBIF data using three Python scripts to unzip the downloaded GBIF folders and join relevant data (e.g., NLCD, basic ownership, Roadless Rule Affected Environments), filter to ESA sensitive species, and summarize the data into region-wide csv files. For Forest Service Alaska Region (Region 10), we separated the GBIF data from the conterminous United States (CONUS) data and ran a separate Python script due to available NLCD data (2024 Annual NLCD data for CONUS and the 2016 NLCD Alaska data for Region 10). We designated NRM data features using ArcGIS Pro’s ArcPy as either inside or outside of Roadless Rule Affected Environments in National Forest land. We then determined each feature’s NLCD value and class using pixel count majorities in R, joined relevant data (e.g., basic ownership and Roadless Rule Affected Environments), created Forest Service region-wide summaries, and exported them as an excel workbook. Species occurrence data are opportunistic and do not represent the results of exhaustive structured species surveys nor do they include negative occurrence data. Additionally, for mobile species, an observation of an individual in a specific location does not mean that that location is occupied by resident individuals- some of these observations could have been of transient individuals.

Exposure was determined by comparing species occurrence data with roadless area operability (as defined in the Environmental Baseline section below) and categorized as high, moderate, and low likelihood of exposure. Low exposure was determined for species that had no occurrences in IRAs. Medium exposure was determined for species with less than 50% of occurrences in IRAs. High exposure was determined for species that had greater than 50% of occurrences in IRAs. Where there was no occurrence data the exposure was classified as unknown. Exposure estimates were performed in a manner to err on the side of likely exposure. Existing protections afforded by land management plans and other documents/decisions were also reviewed to determine how they may affect the determinations for each species, particularly if effects to the species were determined to be highly impactful. The response of species was derived from published scientific literature and previous consultations. Together, exposure and response were used to make the determinations: No effect (NE), Not likely to adversely affect (NLAA), and likely to adversely affect (LAA).

|||Exposure||
|---|---|---|---|
||Low or unknown|Medium or unknown|High|
|Response is impactful|NLAA or LAA|LAA|LAA|
|Response is minimal|NE or NLAA|NLAA or LAA|LAA|

Where available information indicated a less impactful determination was warranted compared to the general determinations a less impactful determination was made. Where information is lacking the Forest Service erred on the side of making the more impactful determination.

The exposure of critical habitat to stressors associated with road construction and timber activities was performed by comparing the overlap of critical habitat with the action area categorized by operability. Where overlap occurred, the physical and biological features of the critical habitat were assessed to determine whether the stressors associated with road construction and timber harvest could be expected to adversely affect those PBFs and the functionality of the critical habitat. Determinations for critical habitat were either no effect, not likely to adversely affect, or likely to adversely affect. Where information was lacking the Forest Service erred on the side of making the more impactful determination.

# ENVIRONMENTAL BASELINE

This section briefly describes the status of inventoried roadless areas that may be affected (Roadless Affected Environment or Environmental Baseline). There are approximately 40 million acres of IRAs managed under 2001 Roadless Rule<sup>19</sup> within the action area. Additional information on the status of the action area is available in the environmental impact statement for the roadless rule rescission.

## Land Management Plans and Operability

A national review of plan components in management areas overlapping the potentially affected environment was completed to identify where plans do or do not further restrict timber harvest and road construction activities<sup>20</sup> . There is much variation between individual land management plans and Regions reflecting differences in local conditions, age of the plans, and changes in planning policies over time. Current land management-plans include plan direction and components that identify where timber management and road construction uses may or may not be allowed (Table 3). Example management area types where timber management or road construction may be limited include recommended wilderness, research natural areas, or backcountry management areas are administrative land management planning designations that limit active management.

- Across the Roadless Affected Environment, land management plan components generally allow timber harvest across 13.4 million acres (33.4% of NFS land within the Roadless Affected Environment). [36% not allowed, 26.8 generally not allowed (with some exceptions)].

- Across the Roadless Affected Environment, land management plan components generally allow road construction across 18.2 million acres (45.5% of NFS land within the Roadless Affected Environment).

This analysis is directed at actions that are reasonably likely to occur in the remaining acres of inventoried roadless areas where road construction and reconstruction or timber harvest would be most likely to occur under current land management plans. A nationwide geospatial analysis was used to estimate potential operability, or the capability of mechanized treatment or activities, in each area based on slope, distance from roads, site productivity, and statutory restrictions (Table 2):

- Likely Operable: Less than 0.5 miles from a road, on slopes less than 40%, are productive for restocking (greater than 20 cubic feet/acre/year), are potentially forested, and have no statutory restrictions from timber harvest.

- Likely Operable but Complex: Less than 0.5 miles from a road and on slopes between 40% and 70% or between 0.5 miles and one mile from a road and on slopes less than 70%. These areas have the same productivity for restocking as likely operable areas, are potentially forested, and no statutory restrictions from timber harvest.

> 19 Current areas are reflected on national maps at the Forest Service Roadless Area website: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing- <u>land/planning/roadless</u>

> 20 Note that this national level review is currently undergoing quality control and Regional/local vetting and the data presented will be updated in the final BA.

- Likely Not Operable: Include slopes over 70%, further than one mile from a road or areas over one mile from a road and less than 70% percent slope. These areas have low productivity, are potentially forested, and no statutory restrictions from timber harvest.

The affected environment’s overlap with hydrologic unit codes (HUC) is presented in Table 4. Within the Tongass National Forest 9.3 million acres of inventoried roadless area managed under the 2001 Roadless Rule, or about 56 percent of the Forest. Approximately 9.2 million acres of these are in the affected environment (on National Forest System lands and outside of wilderness, wilderness study area and wild river segments). Operability analysis excluded portions of the action area that were not forested.

## General Characteristics of the Affected Environment

Roadless Rule prohibitions do not mean no activities occur in Inventoried Roadless Areas. Activities that are ongoing and permissible, if not restricted by land management plans or other law, regulation, and policy include, but are not limited to:

- Access for reserved or outstanding rights/existing rights for minerals,

- Continuation of existing land use authorizations (ex. utilities, recreation special uses, private access, easements, etc.),

- Road maintenance on existing roads,

- Motorized and non-motorized trail construction or maintenance,

- Hunting, fishing, hiking, camping, and other recreational uses,

- Use of a motorized vehicle on a trail open to motorized use,

- Mountain biking on a trail open to mechanized use,

- Prescribed burning, and

- Livestock grazing.

The 2001 Roadless Rule prohibition on road construction and reconstruction in IRAs did not affect already existing access, occupancy, and use rights. These rights include those that exist by law, treaty, or by other authority. They include, but are not limited to, the right to provide reasonable access across NFS lands to private property, mining claims for locatable minerals under the 1872 Mining Law, and land uses protected by Native American treaty rights. These rights include, but are not limited to, rights of access provided in the ANILCA (Public Law 96487), and recognized highway rights-of-way granted over NFS lands under Revised Statute 2477 (Public Law 94-579). The most common type of access pursued in conjunction with these two prominent statues is motorized road access. Land use authorizations and rights-of-way existing prior to the 2001 Roadless Rule are ongoing and part of baseline conditions.

While they are referred to as “roadless”, because of the decades between inventory and designation, there are thousands of miles of existing roads within lands designated under the 2001 Roadless Rule, including National Forest System roads as well as roads of other ownerships. Additionally decommissioned roads and unauthorized routes that are not part of the official system or records may exist.

Between 1984 and 2024, wildfire burned 20.5% of potentially affected IRAs (or 29.9% of potentially affected IRAs outside of Alaska). Of these, 4.2% (1.7 million acres) were high severity wildfire and 5.2% (2.1 million acres) were moderate severity wildfire. Nationally, wildfire hazards are commonly characterized using the Wildfire Hazard Potential (WHP) index, which integrates burn probability and potential fire intensity. Across potentially affected IRAs outside of Alaska, 42 percent of lands are classified as high or very high Wildfire Hazard Potential, indicating a high potential for intense wildfire under severe weather conditions. Regional values range from 5 percent in the Eastern Region to 60 percent in the Pacific Southwest Region. Within potentially affected IRAs 9.8 million acres (24 percent) overlap with Healthy Forests Restoration Act Wildland Urban Interface. Within the potentially affected environment 5.9 million acres (14.8 percent) overlap with Community Wildfire Risk Reduction Zones (CWRRZ). Nearly all CWRRZ within the potentially affected environment occurs within the transition zone (within the 1.5‑mile buffer surrounding building clusters).

## 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule Implementation

The 2001 Roadless Rule provided that the Responsible Official may grant certain limited exceptions to the road construction and timber harvest prohibitions, including for forest stewardship purposes, public health and safety, reserved or outstanding rights, existing or renewed mineral leases, and realignment of roads to prevent resource damage or address safety hazards (36 CFR 294.12(b) and 294.13(b) (2001)). It also provided exceptions to the timber harvest prohibitions for generally small diameter tree cutting to improve habitat for threatened, endangered, or sensitive species or to maintain or restore ecosystem characteristics and where it maintains or enhances one or more of the roadless characteristics, or when the activity is incidental to activities not otherwise prohibited (36 CFR 294.13(b) (2001)). The rule states that use of the timber harvest exceptions would be expected to be infrequent. Amid legal challenges to the 2001 Roadless Rule and to provide for consistent application, exceptions for specific activities in IRAs were reviewed and authorized by the Secretary and Forest Service Chief until 2012. In 2012, certain exceptions were delegated to the applicable regional forester. In 2018 all exceptions were delegated to the regional foresters, and some exceptions for public health and safety or small diameter tree cutting<sup>21</sup> may be further delegated to responsible officials. Approval of exceptions generally requires review documentation, including maps and justification.

Regional forester approval of exceptions under the 2001 Roadless Rule has been limited, and the majority have been for stewardship purposes. There is no national-level tracking of the review, approval, or implementation of 2001 Roadless Rule exceptions, though the Washington Office has recommended that Responsible Officials document reviews and approvals. Regional level tracking of review and approvals between 2018 and 2025 shows about 188 documented projects were granted exceptions. About 10 percent involved road related activities and 96 percent involved tree cutting (some involved both road and tree cutting activities). Since 2018, the majority were related to maintaining and restoring ecosystem characteristics. Eight exceptions approved tree cutting for the explicit purpose of “improving threatened, endangered, or sensitive species habitat,” although some of the exceptions outside of this category may have served multiple purposes, such as providing benefits to species habitat. This information does not include responsible official reviews or approvals below the regional forester level<sup>22</sup> , so it is not possible to list all exceptions that were granted with existing data sources.

> 21 Regional foresters and deputy regional foresters must retain sole authority for exceptions under §294.12(b)(3)-(7) and

> §294.13(b)(4) (2001).

> 22 Similarly, the Agency does not track when requests for exceptions were abandoned or not approved.

The best available information on activities that have been implemented within IRAs over the last decade comes from the Forest Service Activity Tracking System (FACTS). This data shows an average of 500 acres per year of timber harvest and a total of 1.8 million acres of hazardous fuels reduction within IRAs managed under the 2001 Roadless Rule. More than half of the hazardous fuels reduction was from wildfire use, which is reported when acres burned by wildfire are determined to meet land management planning objectives in the post-fire assessment. An additional 25 percent of the hazardous fuels reduction was from prescribed burning activities for reducing fuel hazards and as resource management treatments. Best available records of permanent road construction indicate that approximately 60 miles of roads were built within inventoried roadless areas after 2013.

Use of the available exceptions has been limited in scope and inconsistent. This is due in part to rigorous project-level analysis requirements and associated reviews and approvals needed to demonstrate consistency with Roadless Rule requirements, as well the rule’s intent for infrequent use.

# STATUS OF THE SPECIES AND CRITICAL HABITAT

Given the near-national scope of the project and large number of ESA-listed resources it is not prudent to include a description of the status of every species and critical habitat in the action area.  Given the large geographic scope of the action the status of the species in the action area is essentially the same as the status of the species overall, which is managed and published by the Fish and Wildlife Service online or in a number of species review documents held by the Services.  During early coordination the FWS indicated development of a species status section for this project would not be prudent or efficient.  As such, no species status section is included. For information on the current status of each species see the Fish and Wildlife Service’s ECOS website.

# EFFECTS ANALYSES

A discussion of effects on taxonomic groups is below. Where necessary for species of high interest, effects discussions are provided at the species level.

## Mammals

The potential impacts of the proposed action are diverse as listed mammalian species in the action area include large carnivores, small herbivores, ungulates, and marine mammals in disparate portions of the United States and its territories. As such, we have provided evaluations for each species separately, with narrow exceptions for subspecies whose evaluations depend on similar literature. The mammal group includes 32 total species including 22 endangered, 8 threatened, and 2 experimental populations of mammals (Table 5).

### Marine Mammals

#### _West Indian Manatee_

The West Indian Manatee, which is a general name for two distinct subspecies, the Florida manatee ( _Trichechus manatus latirostris_ ) and the Antillean manatee ( _Trichechus manatus manatus_ ), has a complex listing history beginning with the listing of the Florida manatee (32 FR 4001) as endangered under the Endangered Species Preservation Act of 1966. An amendment added the Antillean manatee to the listing (35 FR 18319). These subspecies were subsequently grandfathered into listing under the ESA as the West Indian manatee. In 2017, the West Indian manatee was reclassified as threatened (82 FR 16668), however there is currently a proposed rule to list the two entities separately with the Florida manatee receiving threatened status and the Antillean manatee receiving endangered status (90 FR 3131).

Trends for the Florida manatee were stable or increasing in all 4 management units until recent unusual mortality events (UME) that affect the Atlantic Management Unit. The demographic impact of the Atlantic mortality unit that began in December 2020 was not known as of the 2024 SSA (USFWS 2024a). The Antillean manatee in Puerto Rico is thought to be stable, although survey data is a few years old and deaths caused by watercraft are thought to be increasing (USFWS 2024b).

The listed entity, West Indian manatee is found in both Florida and Puerto Rico. Manatees inhabit coastal waters and lakes and spend time in both fresh and salt water. Manatees in Florida are reliant on springs and other sites where water temperatures exceed a specific threshold. Both species are dependent on seagrass food sources. Critical habitat for the Florida manatee was designated in 1976 (41 FR 41914). In 2024, revisions to critical habitat for the Florida manatee and designation of critical habitat for the Antillean manatee were proposed (89 FR 78134). None of the current West Indian manatee critical habitat overlaps with an inventoried roadless area affected by the proposed action. In the NRM and GBIF databases, there are no observations of West Indian Manatee in inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action, and only 36 observations of them at all on USFS lands. It is difficult to draw conclusions from this data, so we conducted a supplementary analysis overlapping the USFWS range for the species (USFWS 2026a) with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action. There were no points of intersection. Florida Manatees are known to occur in waterbodies in Ocala National Forest (1999 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a), and there are two inventoried roadless areas within this forest one of which (Alexander Springs Creek) abuts a stream below a spring site. The true impacts of any potential future activities in that roadless area would be more accurately assessed by surveys of that creek. Proposed Antillean Manatee critical habitat includes coastal habitat in Puerto Rico, some of which is downstream from waterbodies originating in El Yunque National Park, which contains multiple inventoried roadless areas which could be affected by the proposed action.

#### Effects of Roads

Sedimentation from roads can affect seagrass growth, an important food source for manatees (USFWS 2024b). The consequences of seagrass quality on manatee forage and health are detailed in multiple sources (USFWS 2024b, Hieb et al. 2021). Manatees frequent waterbodies used by human recreationists, if road development led to increased recreation this could cause increased disturbance to manatees from human presence (USFWS 2024a). This is more of a concern for the Florida manatee which has an inventoried roadless area right next to a spring site visited by recreationists.

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Timber harvest can affect sedimentation of nearby waterbodies, thus affecting water quality in manatee habitat. Sedimentation can also affect the growth of seagrasses, a critical food source for manatees (USFWS 2024b). The consequences of seagrass quality on manatee forage and health are detailed in multiple sources (USFWS 2024bean, Hiep et al. 2021).

#### Existing Protections

The 1999 Land Management Plan for Forests in Florida provides two guidelines with respect to manatees. They are to 1) “Restrict the construction of boating facilities to areas where their construction and subsequent use will not adversely affect manatees” and 2) “Restrict activities that degrade manatee habitat.” There is no mention of the manatees in the El Yunque Forest Plan.

The physical and biological features identified as critical for Florida manatee habitat in the 2024 proposed critical habitat are as follows:

“(1) Areas of water warmed by natural processes (e.g., spring discharges, passive thermal basins) that have either:

(a) Reliable thermal quality throughout the winter (i.e., having at least a medium thermal quality as defined by the Florida Manatee WWHAP (Valade et al. 2020, pp. 25–32)), which consists of water temperatures that stay at or above:

- (i) 72 degrees Fahrenheit (°F) (22 degrees Celsius (°C)) during mild weather,

(ii) 68 °F (20 °C) during cold weather, and

(iii) 64 °F (18 °C) during severe cold weather; or

- (b) Established manatee use throughout the winter each year (see the Florida Manatee WWHAP (Valade et al. 2020, pp. 25–32)).

- (2) Areas supporting submerged, emergent, or floating aquatic vegetation within 18.6 miles (30 kilometers) of:

(a) The natural warm-water sources described in paragraph (1), above; or

- (b) Other established winter manatee aggregation areas (i.e., power plants with established manatee use.” (89 FR 78134)

None of the 2024 proposed Florida manatee critical habitat overlaps with an inventoried roadless area affected by the proposed action. There is one small roadless area that is upstream of manatee critical habitat in the Ocala National Forest.

Although forest streams occur upstream of the critical habitat designated in Florida, the downstream distance suggests effects from sedimentation will be greatly reduced as sediment settles out of the stream as it progresses toward the ocean.  Further, very little of the action area is upstream of designated critical habitat in Florida.  Inland activities are not expected to produce so much sediment that the critical habitat will be permanently impacted.  A such, the FS has determined West Indian manatee critical habitat in Florida will not be affected.

For the Antillean manatee elements of critical habitat were defined as “nearshore marine waters with at least two of the following resources within a 3-mile (5-kilometer) radius:

- (1) Freshwater sources, such as streams and wastewater outfalls;

- (2) Seagrass in waters less than 43 ft (13 m) deep; and

- (3) Calm waters, such as shallow bays and coves, with water depths less than 9.8 ft (3 m) and wave heights less than 0.98 ft (0.3 m).” (89 FR 78134)

None of the 2024 proposed Antillean manatee critical habitat overlaps with an inventoried roadless area affected by the proposed action, however there are large tracts of inventoried roadless areas that are upstream of critical manatee habitat in El Yunque National Forest. It is possible that sedimentation in these streams from actions that become more likely with the rescission of the roadless rule could affect seagrass in critical manatee habitat.

Although forest streams occur upstream of the critical habitat designated off the coast of Puerto Rico, the distance is greater than 5 stream miles, suggesting effects from sedimentation will be greatly reduced as sediment settles out of the stream as it progresses toward the ocean. Any sediment reaching the ocean will settle and be redistributed over time. Inland activities are not expected to produce so much sediment that the coastal environment will be permanently impacted. A such, the FS has determined West Indian manatee critical habitat off the coast of Puerto Rico will not be affected.

#### Effects Determination

Given the low likelihood of exposure to activities that may occur in the action area following rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule and that the Forests of Florida land management plan contains direction to restrict activities that degrade manatee habitat, the Forest Service has determined rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule is not likely to adversely affect the West Indian Manatee because the likelihood of effects to this species are so low as to be discountable. Effects to the subpopulation in the coastal waters of Puerto Rico are far enough removed from the inland waters of El Yunque NF that the Forest Service has made a separate determination of No Effect for that population. Should the Caribbean population of West Indian Manatee be listed as a separate entity in the future, this determination will apply. The Forest Service has determined the proposed activity will have No Effect on West Indian manatee critical habitat.

### Bats

#### _Ozark big-eared bat_

The Ozark big-eared bat ( _Corynorhinus townsendii ingens_ ), a subspecies of Townsend’s bigeared-bat, is an insectivorous bat that was listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 1979 (44 FR 69206). Current conservation actions are informed by a recovery plan (USFWS 1995a) and a 5-year review (USFWS 2020a). As of 2020, population trends in seven maternity colonies and nine hibernacula were mixed, with most displaying stable trends, several declining, and a few increasing (USFWS 2020a). However, the methods used for both maternity counts and hibernacula surveys are variable and contribute to substantial uncertainty in trend estimates (USFWS 2020a). Ozark big-eared bats are at risk of extinction due to their small population size, limited distribution, and vulnerability to human disturbance (USFWS 1995a, USFWS 2020a).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

Ozark big-eared bats are currently found in Oklahoma and Arkansas, and historically they also inhabited Missouri. They hibernate and roost year-round in caves and karst habitats that are surrounded by oak-hickory hardwood forests (USFWS 1995a). They forage for insects, and especially moths, near trees and in stream- and forest-edge habitats (USFWS 1995a, Clark et al. 1993). The greatest threat to Ozark big-eared bats is human disturbance of caves, especially during the maternity and hibernation periods (USFWS 1995a). No designated critical habitat currently exists for Ozark big-eared bats (44 FR 69206), but many stakeholders engage in habitat conservation efforts on both public and private land.

There are several inventoried roadless areas (IRAs) on the Ozark-St. Francis National Forest. Although road construction or reconstruction is allowed on more than half of this IRA acreage, there are also some areas where it is not currently allowed (USFS 2000a). As such, rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule could eventually lead to more road and timber development in areas near Ozark big-eared bat habitat. There is only one observation of the species in inventoried roadless areas and it occurred on lands classified as operable, suggesting this species has potentially high likelihood of exposure to at least a few individuals, although it is extremely difficult to draw conclusions from such a limited sample size. As such we conducted a supplementary analysis intersecting the USFWS range with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action and found that approximately 0.004% of the current range is in the proposed action area.

Additional bat habitat is located on both public and private land. The Ozark Plateau National Wildlife Refuge was created to conserve habitat for threatened and endangered species including the Ozark big-eared bat, and it is accessible by permit only to protect the bats (USFWS 2025a). Key conservation easements have also been implemented on private land, including two separate 40-acre tracts purchased by the Cherokee Nation for bat cave habitat protection (USFWS 1995a).

#### Effects of Roads

The specific effects of roads on Ozark big-eared bat population trends have not been explicitly quantified to date. This may be due in part to the fact that big-eared bats have relatively lowintensity echolocation calls which are often not well recorded by detectors which makes researching them challenging (Loeb et al. 2011). However, given that human disturbance to caves is a major threat to population persistence (USFWS 1995a, USFWS 2020a), the increased access that roads can provide to caves is a concern. For example, in another bat species, a maternity colony decline was thought to be the result of increased recreation by cavers after a road was paved (USFWS 1995a).

If new roads must be constructed near Ozark big-eared bat habitat, then installing gates and signage that deter cave access without impeding bats is an effective measure that can help mitigate negative effects (USFWS 2020a). Many stakeholders have contributed to successful cave gating efforts for Ozark big-eared bat protection on both public and private lands (USFWS 2020a). On the Ozark Plateau National Wildlife Refuge, which was created in part to protect cave habitat, proposed management alternatives included avoiding new road development, closing caves to the public, building and repairing cave gates, and posting signs prohibiting entry (78 FR 9410).

Although published studies are unavailable, it is reasonable to assume that roads could lead to increases in direct mortalities from vehicle collisions. Road construction could also impact bat habitat including nearby caves, which is a documented concern for another _Corynorhinus_ bat (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2019f). Although not specific to roads, human disturbance is known to be a major threat to Ozark big-eared bat populations (USFWS 2020a).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Research on the effects of timber production activities on Ozark big-eared bat populations has been limited to date, so impacts remain uncertain. The 1995 Revised Recovery Plan noted that there had been a loss of caves and foraging habitat used by Ozark big-eared bats due to various types of development, including timber development (USFWS 1995a). This Plan also noted that since human disturbance is the main threat to the species, protecting caves and foraging habitat from all types of development is a key recovery strategy (USFWS 1995a). However, the 2020 Five-Year Review acknowledged that timber thinning, planting, and prescribed burns can be important parts of habitat enhancement and restoration (USFWS 2020a).

More recently, a study conducted in Arkansas’ Ozark National Forest investigated the effects of prescribed fire and mechanical thinning treatments on Ozark big-eared bat foraging behavior and prey availability (Marsh 2023). This research suggested that prescribed burning and mechanical thinning may benefit Ozark big-eared bat prey availability and foraging because bat prey was higher in areas with open canopies and more groundcover (Marsh 2023). However, the authors noted that study design challenges and forest complexity made it difficult to draw strong conclusions about the bats’ relative use of burned and thinned habitats (Marsh 2023).

In contrast, a previous review of _Corynorhinus_ (the genus encompassing Ozark big-eared bats) foraging behavior found that preferred moth prey were typically captured in areas of mature timber and avoided open habitats, but that _Corynorhinus_ bats made decisions about where to forage based on forest structure, not solely based on prey availability (Loeb et al. 2011). This review showed that the bats selected forest corridors and edges which may make it easier for them to glean prey (Loeb et al. 2011) which may have different implications for forest management than if maximizing prey availability was the primary management concern. Additional research found that moths were more abundant in poletimber stands, riparian areas, and upland forests, and suggested that using forest management to maintain habitat heterogeneity around roosts may benefit bats (Dodd et al. 2008).

Although the specific effects of timber production on Ozark big-eared bat populations remains uncertain, the 2005 Ozark-St. Francis Forest Plan limits the cutting of overstory vegetation, road construction, and prescribed burning within 200 feet of colony sites (USFS 2025a). Given the bats’ sensitivity to human disturbance, it is reasonable to assume that any timber harvest or forest management activities would typically use design features to limit short-term disturbance while offering compelling evidence of future benefits to habitat.

#### Existing Protections

The USDA Forest Service manages important habitat for these bats on the Ozark-St. Francis National Forest in Arkansas (2005 land management plan, USFS 2025a) and there are some existing protections for these bats in the Forest’s Plan.
