For example, the Ozark-St. Francis Forest Plan specifies a forest-wide standard designed to protect habitat which states, “A 200-foot buffer of undisturbed forest will be maintained around […] Ozark big-eared bat maternity sites, bachelor sites, or winter colony sites. Prohibited activities within this buffer include cutting of overstory vegetation; construction of roads, trails, or wildlife openings or development of pastures; and prescribed burning…” (2005 land management plan, USFS 2025a).

#### Effects Determination

Given the low degree of overlap of the proposed action with the species’ range, we expect the potential for exposure to be low. Although the Ozark-St. Francis NF forest plan provides protections for this species, given the high degree of sensitivity of the species to human disturbance, we have determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect Ozark bigeared bats.

#### _Virginia big-eared bat_

The Virginia big-eared bat ( _Corynorhinus townsendii virginianus_ ), a subspecies of Townsend’s big-eared bat, is an insectivorous bat that was listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 1979 (44 FR 69206). Current conservation actions are informed by a recovery plan (USFWS 2024c) and a 5-year review (USFWS 2019a). As of 2019, the range-wide population of Virginia big-eared bats was thought to have increased by 28-30 percent since 2008, with an estimated 19,574 bats in hibernacula and 11,778 in maternity sites (USFWS 2019a). However, some populations and regions experienced declines (USFWS 2019a). There are four geographically distinct management units of this subspecies that do not intermix and that each contribute to the genetic diversity, adaptive capacity, and distribution of the subspecies (USFWS 2024c). As such, maintaining healthy populations across all four of these management units is important. However, Virginia big-eared bats are very sensitive to human disturbance so their small population size and low genetic variability are causes for concern (USFWS 2019a).

#### Exposure to the proposed action area and proposed actions

Virginia big-eared bats are currently found in West Virginia, Virginia, Kentucky, North Carolina, and Tennessee; historically, they were also found in Pennsylvania (USFWS 2024c). They hibernate, roost, breed, and raise their young in caves and cave-like areas such as abandoned mines and rock crevices (USFWS 2024c). They forage primarily for moths in forested habitats that are interspersed with open fields, cliff lines, rock outcroppings, riparian areas, and water features (USFWS 2024c).

Critical habitat for Virginia big-eared bats was designated at the time of initial listing under the Endangered Species Act and encompasses five caves in West Virginia (44 FR 69206). These caves were designated as critical habitat because they contain precise conditions that support Virginia big-eared bat populations, and any actions that affect these caves’ temperature, structure, humidity, air flow, or disturbance are specified as actions that could adversely affect the critical habitat (44 FR 69206). Other important caves have since been identified, of which some are considered protected, and some of which are not (USFWS 2019a).

The USDA Forest Service manages federal land across the subspecies’ range that provides important habitat for Virginia big-eared bats. The Monongahela, George Washington, Jefferson, Cherokee, Daniel Boone, Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests all contain critical habitat for the subspecies. There are currently inventoried roadless areas on all of these Forests except for the Daniel Boone National Forest (USFS 2000a).

There are only 12 acres of critical habitat in inventoried roadless areas, which is approximately 2% of total critical habitat. Of these 12 acres, all are classified in habitat that is considered operable. There are no observations of the species in inventoried roadless areas, which could be due to low sampling effort (there are only 38 observations of the species in the NRM and GBIF database), the rarity of the species, or other factors. As such, no conclusions about the relative vulnerability of the species to potential development from the proposed action can be drawn from this occurrence data. Given this we ran a supplemental analysis that intersected the USFWS range for this species (USFWS 2026a) with inventoried roadless affected by the proposed action. The result was approximately 1.7%.

#### Effects of Roads

The effects of roads on Virginia big-eared bat populations are generally negative (USFWS 2019a, USFWS 2024c). Based on concern about the increasing threats posed by barriers to movement, the latest recovery plan amendment identified a new recovery action: “Within each [recovery unit], avoid and/or minimize barriers to movement and sources of direct mortality to [Virginia big-eared bats] (e.g., roads,…)” (USFWS 2024c). Since roosts in caves are in separate places from foraging habitats, there is concern that roads cause fragmentation by separating discrete habitat areas (USFWS 2019a). Further contributing to this concern, evidence suggests that Virginia big-eared bats avoid crossing major roads when foraging (Weber et al. 2016).

Roads can also damage Virginia big-eared bat habitat. In West Virginia and North Carolina, road development and widening was proposed within the Virginia big-eared bat’s range, and there was concern that this activity would lead to a loss or alteration of important cave and mine habitat or reduce foraging success (USFWS 2019a, Weber et al. 2016). Additionally, since human development is increasing in North Carolina, there is concern that associated road widening, road development, human access, and increased predation from domesticated cats could be detrimental (USFWS 2019a). Although it is plausible that larger roads could have a larger effect on bat habitat, even small roads have caused direct mortalities of Virginia big-eared bats (USFWS 2019a). There is also concern that roads could contribute to reduced reproductive success which could contribute to population declines (USFWS 2019a).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

The specific effects of timber production on Virginia big-eared bat populations are uncertain, but there are likely tradeoffs between the potential negative effects of disturbance and the potential benefits of certain forest management activities on bat habitat. Biologists have long voiced concerns about the effects of timber harvesting on Virginia big-eared bat habitat (Adam et al. 1994), but some research suggests that Virginia big-eared bats populations may be able to tolerate some timber harvest if a diversity and abundance of local plants are retained to ensure adequate levels of prey (Loeb et al. 2011). A review of _Corynorhinus_ (the genus encompassing Virginia big-eared bats) foraging behavior found that prey were typically captured in areas of mature timber and avoided open habitats (Loeb et al. 2011). These bats select forest corridors and edges (Loeb et al. 2011), and they do not forage in areas that have been clearcut (USFWS 2019a). As such, selective logging may be a useful strategy for maintaining Lepidopteran moth prey levels (USFWS 2019a).

#### Existing Protections

Land management plans for the Monongahela (2011), George Washington (2014), Jefferson (2004), Cherokee (2004), and Daniel Boone (2004) National Forests all contain standards that protect Virginia big-eared bat habitat within a short distance of known bat colonies (typically either within 200 feet or within ¼ mile; USFS 2025a). The 2023 Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests land management plan mentions that the presence (or absence) of Virgina big-eared bats needs to be documented on the forest (USFS 2025a).

#### Critical Habitat

“The Service has concluded that five caves in West Virginia should be designated as Critical Habitat for the Virginia big-eared bat. Because of precise conditions of physical structure, temperature, and humidity, these caves are suitable for use by the species as sites for hibernation and reproduction. The species has a limited range and is highly susceptible to changes in its habitat. Even minor disturbance or physical changes in the caves occupied may result in extinction. Therefore, these caves are essential for its conservation. The physical and biological features of its habitat are such as to require special management considerations and protection.” (44 FR 69206)

There are only 12 acres of critical habitat in inventoried roadless areas, which is approximately 2% of total critical habitat. Of these 12 acres, all are classified in habitat that is considered operable. Despite minimal overlap, given minor disturbances to habitat can have a profound effect on the species we have determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect critical habitat for this species.

#### Effects Determination

Given the available data for assessing occurrence of the species, we are assigning the species an exposure level of high”. Given the species’ sensitivity to human disturbance, we have determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect this species and its designated critical habitat.

#### _Mexican long-nosed bat_

The Mexican long-nosed bat ( _Leptonycteris nivalis_ , also known as the greater long-nosed bat) is a migratory, mostly-nectivorous bat that was listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 1988 (53 FR 38456). Conservation actions are informed by a recovery implementation strategy (USFWS 2024d), a recovery plan (USFWS 2024eand a species status assessment (USFWS 2018a).

The Mexican long-nosed bat is considered a single population (Pourshoushtari and Ammerman 2020) that is composed of several subpopulations associated with different roosting sites (USFWS 2018a). The current population size of Mexican long-nosed bats is uncertain, in part due to the species’ migratory behavior (USFWS 2018a). However, most of the 11 recentlymonitored roosting sites (of ~30 known roosts) support fewer than 2,000 individuals, and the two known roosts in the United States support 500-3,000 individuals (Texas) and 500-7,000 individuals (New Mexico) (USFWS 2018a). The greatest threats facing Mexican long-nosed bats are the reduced availability of roosting sites, a lack of connectivity among their foraging habitat, and human disturbances to their roosting sites (USFWS 2018a, USFWS 2024e).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

In the United States portion of their range, Mexican long-nosed bats are primarily located in New Mexico and Texas (USFWS 2018a), but they were also recently documented in Arizona (Bat Conservation International 2025). They hibernate and roost in caves, abandoned mines, and cavities on cliff faces (USFWS 2018a). They forage in agave- and desert-scrub woodlands where they primarily feed on agave, cactus pollen, and insects (USFWS 2024e). These bats rely heavily on a “nectar corridor” (Burke et al. 2019) created by flowering plants, especially agave, during their migrations (USFWS 2018a).

At present, there is no designated critical habitat for this species, but the known roosts in the United States portion of their range are on protected land that is part of Big Bend National Park (NPS 2004) and a Bureau of Land Management Wilderness Protected Area (USFWS 2018a). Potential connectivity habitat may also exist on National Forests and Grasslands in New Mexico and Texas, although agave is only mentioned in the land management plans for the Cibola (2022) and Coronado (2018) National Forests (USFS 2025a) and the Mexican long-nosed bat is only listed as present in the 2018 land management plan for the Coronado National Forest (USFS 2025a). There are three occurrence records for the species in inventoried roadless areas in NRM and GBIF databases and none of them occur in operable areas, however given the low sample size and the opportunistic nature of many detections in these data sources the relative exposure of the species to the proposed action cannot be determined using these data. We ran a supplementary analysis overlaying the USFWS range for the species with inventoried roadless and found that approximately 0.005% of the species’ range occurs in the proposed action area.

Additionally, other stakeholders including non-governmental organizations and states are engaged in improving habitat for Mexican long-nosed bats. For example, in New Mexico where these bats are a “species of greatest conservation need” (NMDW 2025a), partners are monitoring and improving a large patch of agave to serve as habitat for long-nosed bats on a state-managed Wildlife Management Area that is adjacent to the Gila National Forest (NMDW 2025b).

Effects of Roads

The effects of roads on Mexican long-nosed bat populations are unknown. However, due to this bat species’ long-distance migratory movements and the existing challenges posed by fragmentation of important food resources such as agave (USFWS 2018a), it is feasible that new road construction could further fragment habitat and cause additional challenges for the species. At present, there are some inventoried roadless areas that do not allow road construction or reconstruction on the Coronado National Forest and close to the southern border with Mexico (USFS 2000a). It is uncertain whether the proposed action would lead to an increase in road construction in this area, but both Mexican long-nosed bats and important agave species are documented on the Coronado National Forest, meaning that some impacts to bat habitat could be possible (2018 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a).

Similarly, since Mexican long-nosed bats are sensitive to human disturbance (USFWS 2018a), roads could negatively affect the species by increasing recreation levels around important caves, which could exacerbate the existing challenge posed by all-terrain vehicle disturbance (USFWS 2018a). Since these bats are sensitive to noise (USFWS 2024e), it would be important to ensure that road construction did not contribute to noise at roosts. Lastly, it is theoretically possible that roads could cause mortalities from collisions as well since this has been documented in other bat species.

The effects of timber production on Mexican long-nosed bat populations are unknown. It is also unclear how much of the species’ range on National Forests would be suitable for timber production. However, it is worth noting that deforestation around caves was thought to be enough of a concern for the species that it merited monitoring around at least one cave in Mexico (USFWS 2018a). If timber harvest were to impact agave connectivity or areas around important caves and bat roosts, then it is reasonable to assume that this might have a negative effect on the species.

#### Existing protections

Plans for National Forests in New Mexico and Texas (with the exception of the Lincoln and Gila National Forests) contain standards and guidelines designed to protect general bat habitat, such as caves (1986 Lincoln NF, 1986 Gila NF, 1996 Texas NFs, 2020 Coronado NF, 2022 Carson NF, and 2022 Cibola NF land management plans, available at USFS 2025a).

#### Effects Determination

Given the low overlap between the species’ range and inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action we are assigning an exposure level of low. However, given its sensitivity to human disturbance we have determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species **.**

#### _Gray bat_

The gray bat ( _Myotis grisescens_ ) is an insectivorous bat that was listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 1976 (41 FR 17736). Conservation actions are informed by a recovery plan (USFWS 1982) and a five-year review (USFWS 2025b). As of 2021, the rangewide gray bat population was considered stable (USFWS 2025b). The 2021 winter survey estimated approximately 4.9 million gray bats present within 15 major hibernacula as compared to 5.3 million bats estimated during the 2019 winter survey (USFWS 2025b). Experts determined that these counts are within the margin of error due to the challenges of counting hundreds of thousands of bats at a time (USFWS 2025b).

At present, the major threats to gray bats include human disturbance and destruction of roosting sites, cave flooding due to natural or human causes, pesticide contamination and siltation of waterways near bat habitat (which can affect their insect prey), deforestation along waterways where the bats forage, wind turbine interactions, and white-nose syndrome (USFWS 1982, USFWS 2025b).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

Gray bats are currently found in Alabama, Arkansas, Kentucky, Missouri, and Tennessee; they were also documented in Florida as recently as 2011 (USFWS 2025b). They may rarely occur in parts of Georgia, Kansas, Indiana, Illinois, Oklahoma, Mississippi, Virginia, and North Carolina (USFWS 1982). Year-round, they hibernate and roost in limestone karst habitats such as caves, sinkholes, and springs, and their habitat is very closely tied to areas around these caves (USFWS 1982). Many bats migrate seasonally between maternity caves and hibernacula (USFWS 1982).

They tend to forage over and around bodies of water where they rely in part on access to mayflies, and they prefer deep, vertical caves that occur near rivers (USFWS 1982, USFWS 2025b). Approximately 98% of the species occurs in only 15 hibernacula (USFWS 2025b), putting them at an elevated risk of extirpation. Although there is not a specific subpopulation structure of gray bats, there is some genetic variation between eastern and western groups which should be considered as part of species and habitat management (Holliday et al. 2023).

There is not currently any federally designated critical habitat for gray bats, but some key habitat elements are protected in other ways. For example, three National Wildlife Refuges in Alabama were specifically established to protect gray bat habitat (USFWS 2025c, USFWS 2025d, USFWS 2025e), and there are some habitat protections on National Forests across their range (see below). In the NRM and GBIF databases, there are 3 occurrences of the species in potentially affected IRAs out of 250 records on NFS lands. All of these occurrence records occur in areas that are operable. Given the potential bias in opportunistic datasets like this, we also conducted a supplementary analysis overlaying the species’ USFWS range with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action. The overlap was approximately 0.004%. Given the importance of a limited number of hibernacula to the species, we visually inspected the locations of 15 caves highlighted in the 2021 SSA as being important to the species relative to inventoried roadless areas. This visual inspection did not identify areas of potential overlap. Project level analyses should also conduct evaluations of potential impacts to maternity and other colony locations.

#### Effects of Roads

The specific effects of roads on gray bat populations are unknown, but evidence suggests that the effects of roads on this species are probably mixed, with some benefits and some negative effects. Gray bats use roads during flight, so the development of rural roads may serve as flight corridors to foraging areas (Jackson et al. 2023). Gray bats have also been documented roosting under bridges when caves are unavailable (in North Carolina, Etchison & Weber 2020) as well as during migration (in Arkansas, Sasse 2019), meaning that road infrastructure could be an important alternate source of roosting habitat.

However, roads likely also have negative implications for gray bats. Roads can provide access to caves that are otherwise inaccessible, increasing human disturbance, although roads and caves can be gated to prevent human entry (USFWS 2025b). In theory, road construction could also impact roosting and foraging habitat or otherwise disturb bats, as well as cause mortalities from vehicle collisions. Recent research mapped particularly high-use areas of gray bat habitat as occurring in north-central Arkansas, central Missouri, north-central and north-eastern Tennessee, south-central Kentucky, and northeastern Alabama (Nagel et al. 2024), indicating that new road development in these areas may need special consideration to mitigate any negative impacts on gray bats and their habitat.

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

The specific effects of timber production on gray bat populations are unknown, but based on gray bat behavior and the impacts of timber production on other similar species, it is plausible that the effects of timber harvest might be negative. Gray bats – and particularly young bats – rely on forests for cover, and deforestation in areas near caves and waterways used for foraging is listed as a threat to the species (USFWS 1982, USFWS 2025b). Gray bats have also been documented using daytime tree roosts during migration periods (Samoray et al. 2020), but more research is needed to understand gray bat reliance on forests since trees were not considered to be roosting habitat previously (USFWS 2025b). Experts suggest that any activities that could affect foraging habitat (which includes forested areas near waterways) within 25 kilometers of gray bat caves should be carefully considered to protect bat habitat, particularly given the context that “substantial areas of habitat have been destroyed or degraded by clearing…” (USFWS 1982).

#### Existing Protections

Gray bats inhabit several National Forests that are managed by the USDA Forest Service where they benefit from some habitat protections. On the Ozark-St. Francis National Forest in Arkansas, a 200-foot buffer of undisturbed forest must be maintained around gray bat maternity and hibernation colonies where overstory cutting, road construction, pasture development, and prescribed burning are prohibited (2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). On the Shawnee National Forest in Illinois, seismic testing cannot be conducted within 2.5 miles of gray bat hibernacula during the hibernation season, smoke effects on gray bat hibernacula must be considered when responding to wildland fire or conducting prescribed fire, and no prescribed burns may be conducted in upland or bottomland forests during specific spring-summer seasons to protect maternity roosts (2006 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). On the Hoosier National Forest in Indiana, known gray bat hibernacula are surrounded by a ¼ mile buffer where new construction is prohibited, caves containing gray bats may be considered for access restrictions, and at least 70% of forest canopy cover should be maintained within a onemile radius of gray bat hibernacula. Additionally, “timber harvest should be restricted to singletree and group selection within this zone,” but vegetation management can be implemented to maintain or improve bat habitat (2006 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a).

On the Cherokee National Forest in Tennessee and Georgia, consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is conducted for any project that is proposed within 20 miles of known gray bat maternity sites if the project is anticipated to affect canopy cover in riparian corridors or along forested lakeshores (2004 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Additionally, a ¼ mile buffer of undisturbed forest is maintained around maternity and hibernation colony sites where overstory cutting, prescribed burning, road construction, and prescribed burning are prohibited (2006 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Although gray bats are not currently documented in Texas, National Forests and Grasslands in this state restrict the use of aerially-applied herbicides within 300 feet of gray bat habitat and ground-applied herbicides within 60 feet of gray bat habitat (1996 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a).

#### Effects Determination

Given the proportion of the species’ range that overlaps with inventoried roadless areas and the absence of an indication that major hibernacula occur in inventoried roadless, the FS has determined that the exposure of the species to the proposed action is low. This could be revised should better spatial evaluations of maternity and other colony locations suggest overlap with the proposed action area. Despite existing protections, given the sensitivity of the species to human disturbance the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species.

#### _Northern long-eared bat_

The northern long-eared bat ( _Myotis septentrionalis_ ) is an insectivorous bat that was listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 2023 (88 FR 4908) after initially being listed as threatened in 2015 (80 FR 17974). Conservation actions are informed by a Species Status Assessment (USFWS 2022a).

As of 2023, the northern long-eared bat has been experiencing precipitous declines across most of its range, due in large part to white-nose syndrome (88 FR 4908). There are no range-wide population estimates for this species, but both winter and summer surveys conducted across the range show evidence of dramatic decline over the last two decades (88 FR 4908). At present, the major threat to northern long-eared bats is the spread of white-nose syndrome, but other stressors include habitat loss, wind energy development, and changes in climate patterns (88 FR 4908, USFWS 2022a).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

There is no federally designated critical habitat for the northern long-eared bat (88 FR 4908). These bats currently inhabit 37 states, ranging from Montana and Wyoming in the West to Maine in the northeast to Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana in the southeast (88 FR 4908). In the eastern portion of the range, these bats were widely distributed prior to the arrival of white-nose syndrome, but since then, they are generally rare with documented extinctions of hibernacula across the range (88 FR 4908).

In the winter, northern long-eared bats primarily hibernate in caves and mines with stable, cool temperatures, but they have also been documented hibernating in tunnels and bunkers, or more rarely in sewers and aqueducts or other similar areas when caves and mines are not present (88 FR 4908). In the summer, northern long-eared bats roost in tree cavities, tree crevices, and under the bark of both live and dead trees, as well as occasionally in caves, mines, and human structures like barns and utility poles (88 FR 4908). Although these bats do not seem to select particular tree species, in some areas, they frequently choose shade-tolerant, deciduous hardwoods, particularly for maternity colonies (as opposed to males roosting alone) (88 FR 4908). In other areas, they may opt for a higher proportion of dead conifers or live trees with dead branches and other visible signs of decay (88 FR 4908). Females may roost in more open areas than males which may provide solar radiation or aid bats learning to fly, and roost tree diameter is highly variable (88 FR 4908). Northern long-eared bats forage in forests, typically between the understory and the canopy, although they occasionally forage near water, along roads, or in small clearings (88 FR 4908). They generally do not use larger forest openings or clearings (88 FR 4908).

Given the broad range of northern long-eared bats, they have been documented on many National Forests and Grasslands across the country. In the bats’ listing decision, 18 different National Forests and Grasslands were mentioned by name as being places that northern longeared bats were found (88 FR 4908). As such, it is likely that public lands managed by the USDA Forest Service are important sources of habitat and monitoring effort for these bats. In the GBIF and NRM databases there are 66 occurrences of the species in inventoried roadless areas potentially affected by the proposed action, all but one of which occur in operable or operable but complex areas. This leads to an assessment of “high” exposure to the proposed action given the analytical framework defined for this BA. However, given the sources of biases inherent in opportunistic datasets, we also conducted an analysis overlaying the total USFWS species range with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action and found an overlap of 0.004%.

#### Effects of Roads

The specific effects of roads on northern long-eared bats are likely mixed. These bats are known to forage over small roads, and some research has suggested that they use road corridors more than expected, making use of skid trails for travel and foraging habitat within areas that experienced timber harvest (Owen et al. 2003). However, other research has suggested the opposite, indicating that northern long-eared bats are less likely to be present in corridors and edge habitats and that their occupancy is positively associated with the distance from the nearest road (Hyzy et al. 2020). In general, there is consensus that these bats prefer intact forests of mixed types that contain small gaps (i.e., forest trails, small roads) over clear cuts (USFWS 2022a), indicating that bigger roads with more open space likely contribute to habitat fragmentation. Like other bat species, roads also present the risk of increased disturbance to bats (particularly via increased access to caves and hibernacula) as well as mortality from collisions.

#### Effects of Timber/Vegetation Management

The specific effects of timber production on northern long-eared bat populations and habitat are likely mixed, but given these bats’ reliance on trees for both roosting and foraging habitat, forest management likely has both benefits and risks depending on how it is conducted. According to the species’ listing decision, the benefits of timber harvest could include maintaining or increasing suitable roosting and foraging habitat, whereas the negative impacts could include bat death (88 FR 4908).

Forest conversion to other landcover types is listed as a cause of habitat destruction in the listing decision for northern long-eared bats (88 FR 4908). Forest conversion can make it more difficult for bats to find roosting and foraging habitats, and it may require them to travel farther between roosting and foraging habitats due to the fragmentation of travel corridors (88 FR 4908). This is of particular concern in the areas of the bat’s range where forest is already fragmented (88 FR 4908).

Evidence suggests that this bat species prefers intact forest over fragmented forest patches (88 FR 4908), including mixed-type forests with small gaps (i.e., forest trails, small roads) rather than clearcuts (USFWS 2022a). One study suggested that these bats selected water, areas that were historically thinned, and patch cuts over other habitats, and they generally avoided larger openings such as clearcuts (Divoll et al. 2022). Similarly, another study suggested that partial timber harvests that leave a closed canopy could improve foraging habitat (Owen et al. 2003).

At the same time, some research has indicated that northern long-eared bats continue to roost in areas that have been harvested or thinned (88 FR 4908), and that timber harvest openings did not negatively impact northern long-eared bats’ use of roosts (Bergeson et al. 2021). Other authors found that silvicultural practices could support northern long-eared bat habitat and stated, “use of patch cuts or selective logging practices could allow for the retention of large-diameter snags, while also providing regenerating forest (Lacki and Schwierjohann 2001).”

Ultimately, as stated in the listing decision, “Impacts to northern long-eared bats from forest management would be expected to vary depending on the timing of removal, location (within or outside northern long-eared bat home range), and extent of removal (88 FR 4908).”

#### Existing Protections

Many states and National Forests protect habitat for various bat species, including other treeroosting bats that have similar habitat needs as the northern long-eared bat, such as the Indiana bat (87 FR 56381). For example, some caves are restricted or gated to protect Indiana bats and other bat habitat, and all known hibernacula within USDA Forest Service’s Rocky Mountain Region (Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, South Dakota) are closed during the winter to reduce the risk of transmitting white-nose syndrome (87 FR 56381).

Since the northern long-eared bat was listed under the Endangered Species Act relatively recently, it is not mentioned by name in many Forest Plans for National Forests and Grasslands that are managed by the USDA Service. However, since the northern long-eared bat’s range overlaps with the Indiana bat in several southeastern states, it benefits from the habitat protections offered by several National Forests and Grasslands (e.g., 2004 Daniel Boone NF, 2005 Ouachita NF, 2005 Ozark-St. Francis NF, 2006 Hoosier NF, 2006 Shawnee NF, 2011 Monongahela NF, and 2023 Nantahala and Pisgah NFs land management plans, available at USFS 2025a). Despite these protections, it is possible that northern long-eared bats could benefit from greater protections in the more northern portions of its range, although most forest plans do have general protections to safeguard cave habitats for sensitive bats in general.

#### Effects Determination

In the GBIF and NRM databases there are 66 occurrences of the species in inventoried roadless areas potentially affected by the proposed action, all but one of which occur in operable or operable but complex areas. This leads to an assessment of “high” exposure to the proposed action given the analytical framework defined for this BA. However, we note that inventoried roadless areas constitute only 0.004% of the species range. Given this exposure and the sensitivity of the species to human disturbance the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species **.**

#### _Indiana bat_

The Indiana bat ( _Myotis sodalis_ ) is an insectivorous bat that was originally listed as being at risk of extinction under the Endangered Species Preservation Act in 1966 (32 FR 4001) and is now listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act. Critical habitat was designated for Indiana bats in 1976 and 1977 (41 FR 41914, 42 FR 47840) and was upheld after a petition to expand it in 2007 was found to be not warranted (72 FR 9917). Current conservation actions are informed by a recovery plan (USFWS 2007a) and a five-year review (USFWS 2019b). Indiana bat conservation benefits from a greater depth of research and monitoring information than many other bat species, including a database containing records of all known hibernacula and a biennial, range-wide population estimation system (USFWS 2019b).

The species experienced a substantial decline from the 1980s until 2003, after which there was a four-year reprieve followed by another decline that has extended to the present day, due in part to the range-wide effects of white-nose syndrome (USFWS 2019b). As of 2019, the range-wide population is estimated to be 537,297 bats (USFWS 2019b). Historical records indicate that the range used to be broader and abundance used to be higher (USFWS 2019b).

Historically, the main range-wide threats to Indiana bats were habitat loss and degradation, forest fragmentation, human disturbance, and environmental contaminants. More recently, additional threats have included white-nose syndrome, invasive species, and wind turbines (USFWS 2019b).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

Indiana bats currently occur in 19 states in the eastern United States, ranging from Arkansas and Alabama in the south to Oklahoma, Illinois, Missouri in the Midwest, and to Connecticut and Vermont in the northeast (USFWS 2019b). Designated critical habitat for Indiana bats encompasses one mine in Illinois, two caves in Indiana, two caves in Kentucky, five caves and one mine in Missouri, one cave in Tennessee, and one cave in West Virginia (41 FR 41914). These sites were designated as critical habitat because at the time of the rulemaking, 75% of the known Indiana bat population hibernated in these caves and mines (41 FR 41914).

Indiana bats hibernate over the winter in caves and mines, and in the summer, they forage in forested areas (USFWS 2019b). The bats may either stay close to their hibernacula (especially males and nonreproductive females) or migrate hundreds of miles to summer habitat (especially reproductive females) (USFWS 2007a). In the summer, reproductive females often roost in tree crevices and under the bark of both live and dead trees, choosing primarily dead trees with dried bark or occasionally live trees with naturally peeling bark like shagbark and shellbark hickory (USFWS 2007a). Maternity colonies are formed in roost trees as well, and there is some (albeit mixed) evidence that roost trees tend to be larger-diameter trees that receive some sunlight (USFWS 2007a).

In 2005, around 90% of the species hibernated in five states (Indiana, Missouri, Kentucky, Illinois, and New York) and 72% of the species hibernated in just 10 hibernacula (USFWS 2007a).

Of the critical habitat designated for this species, 0.31% of it occurs in inventoried roadless areas potentially affected by the proposed action. 74% of such habitat is classified as operable or operable but complex. Of occurrence records in NRM and GBIF, there are 15 observations of bats in inventoried roadless areas potentially affected by the proposed action with all of them occurring in operable or operable but complex areas. Given the small sample size and known potential for bias in opportunistic sampling, we conducted a supplemental analysis overlaying the USFWS species’ range with inventoried roadless and found that approximately 0.003% of the range is in inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action.

Roads pose risks to Indiana bats and their habitats, but they may offer some benefits as well. Caves (which serve as hibernacula for bats) are very sensitive to changes on the land’s surface, especially from a drainage perspective (USFWS 2007a). Road construction and urban development can contribute to increased stormwater runoff and siltation which can enter caves, increase flood risk, and lead to contamination from pesticides and other chemicals (USFWS 2007a). For this reason, experts suggest that forest buffers should be maintained between roads and hibernacula to stabilize soils and reduce erosion and sedimentation issues within these caves (USFWS 2007a).

Roads can also contribute to mortality risk and increased human disturbance. At least one record exists of an Indiana bat being killed by a vehicle collision, and while this may not pose a major threat to the population, it may be worth considering if new roads are being developed. (USFWS 2007a). There is also concern that roads can provide recreational access to caves that would otherwise be inaccessible, although this concern can be mitigated by gating, fencing, blocking, or removing roads and caves to restrict access (USFWS 2007a).

Despite these risks, roads may provide some habitat for Indiana bats that would otherwise be unavailable. These bats have been documented roosting in bridges (USFWS 2019b) and hibernating in a railroad tunnel (USFWS 2007a). In areas without waterways, Indiana bats may be attracted to road ruts that fill with water, although water features are plentiful throughout much of their range (USFWS 2007a).

In general, Indiana bats forage and roost in forest openings created by downfall, riparian areas, or road and trail edges (USFWS 2007a). For this reason, corridors produced by roads may be useful if they are wooded. However, Indiana bats avoid large open areas, meaning that larger roads may fragment their habitat (although they have been documented crossing highways) (USFWS 2007a).

Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Timber production can pose risks to Indiana bats and their habitat, but it is likely that silvicultural treatments and forest management can also be used to benefit their habitat. According to the Indiana bat recovery plan (which contains detailed information about the impacts of forest management), “Quality habitat around hibernacula is very important to roosting and foraging Indiana bats […] adjacent and nearby forests typically need some special management to ensure that a continual supply of roost trees and foraging habitat are maintained and to avoid the potential for take occurring during timber harvests or prescribed burns (USFWS 2007a).” In general, retaining buffers of intact forest around hibernacula can reduce the risk of flooding, contaminant runoff, stormwater runoff, siltation, and temperature or humidity change that can occur during logging, land clearing and other land uses. (USFWS 2007a, USFWS 2019b).

If timber production and forest management is designed to maintain small, forested openings, this may benefit Indiana bats. When foraging, Indiana bats use small regeneration openings over a large area (Divoll et al. 2022), and they may be most active at harvest edges and in adjacent forests (Caldwell et al. 2019). As such, maintaining a heterogenous forest structure may support these bats along with other species (Divoll et al. 2022). Importantly, Indiana bats avoid traveling through large open areas, meaning that large-scale clearing could fragment their habitat. Deforestation was one of the initial identified causes of decline (USFWS 2019b), and the loss of forest habitat connectivity was added as a threat later (USFWS 2007a). Maintaining wooded areas and small forest openings is important to reduce fragmentation for this species.

It is also important for forest management activities to protect roost trees. Indiana bat deaths and injuries have been recorded because of the inadvertent felling of roost trees, but this can be minimized by retaining snags, preserving potential roost trees, and avoiding cutting trees when bats are occupying their summer range (USFWS 2007a). Similarly, restricting the cutting of firewood to downed trees (rather than standing dead trees) near hibernacula may help to protect potential Indiana bat habitat. Other work suggests that managing some forest elements to develop older-growth characteristics, developing a plan to ensure that live trees can develop into snags, and using two-age shelterwood cuts that retain plenty of live trees and snags may be beneficial (USFWS 2007a).

#### Existing Protections

Indiana bats inhabit several National Forests that are managed by the USDA Forest Service where they benefit from habitat protections. On some Forests, protections are minimal to moderate. For example, on the Shawnee National Forest in Illinois, seismic testing cannot be conducted within 2.5 miles of Indiana bat hibernacula during the hibernation season, smoke effects on gray bat hibernacula must be considered when responding to wildland fire or conducting prescribed fire, and no prescribed burns may be conducted in upland or bottomland forests during specific spring-summer seasons to protect maternity roosts (2006 land

management plan, available at USFS 2025a). On the Ouachita National Forest in Arkansas and Oklahoma, a cave gate must be maintained, ground-disturbing projects and prescribed burns proposed within 2 miles of a hibernaculum must be evaluated to determine their effects on bats, and bat surveys must be conducted prior to roof, bridge, mine, or well modifications (2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). On the Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests in North Carolina, hibernation, foraging, roosting, and maternity habitat must be maintained (2023 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Additionally, despite Indiana bats’ presumed absence in Texas, National Forests and Grasslands in the state must restrict the use of aerially applied herbicides within 300 feet of Indiana bat habitat and ground-applied herbicides within 60 feet of Indiana bat habitat (1996 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a).

In contrast, four National Forests in Indiana, Arkansas, Kentucky, and West Virginia have more extensive management direction related to Indiana bat habitat. The land management plan for the Hoosier National Forest in Indiana contains multiple pages of guidelines that specify hibernaculum protection zones, canopy cover goals during timber harvest, prescribed fire restrictions, forest composition goals in roosting habitat that specific tree DBH, species, and density, and firewood and snag cutting restrictions, among others (2006 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). The land management plan for the Ozark-St. Francis National Forest in Arkansas contains a similar level of detail and provides guidance on tree thinning, improving roosting and foraging conditions, retaining potential roost trees of specific DBHs and densities during salvage logging, maintaining specific overstory densities around hibernacula, and restricting road construction, certain agricultural allotments, and pest management near hibernacula (2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Similarly, the land management plans for the Monongahela National Forest in West Virginia (2011 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a) and the Daniel Boone National Forest in Kentucky (2004 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a) contain multiple standards and guidelines related to habitat maintenance, silvicultural prescriptions, and mining.

#### Critical Habitat

Of the critical habitat designated for this species, 0.31% of it occurs in inventoried roadless areas potentially affected by the proposed action. 74% of such habitat is classified as operable or operable but complex. There are no PCEs for this species. Given that small amount of overlap of critical habitat with the action area (<1%) and the existing protections discussed above, the FS has determined the proposed action is not likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species.

#### Effects Determination

While there are only 15 occurrence records of the species in inventoried roadless areas, all of them occur in operable or operable but complex. Additionally, even though only a small portion of the total range intersects with inventoried roadless, there is inventoried roadless in the species’ critical habitat which encompasses sensitive hibernacula.  Based on these data, the FS has assigned an exposure level of high to the proposed action. Given this exposure and the sensitivity of the species to human disturbance the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species.  Given that small amount of overlap of critical habitat with the action area (<1%) and the existing protections discussed above, the FS has determined the proposed action is not likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species.

#### _Tricolored bat_

The tricolored bat ( _Perimyotis subflavus_ ) is a broadly distributed, insectivorous bat that was proposed for listing as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 2022 (87 FR 56381). The tricolored bat is also listed as endangered under Canada’s Species At Risk Act (COSEWIC 2013) and has additional protections in several U.S. states (87 FR 56381). Conservation actions in the United States are informed by a species Status Assessment (USFWS 2021a).

As of 2021, the tricolored bat population is in danger of extinction throughout its range (87 FR 56381). Both the species’ abundance and range have contracted, and these reductions have likely impacted genetic diversity, exacerbating its vulnerability (USFWS 2021a). The major threat to the tricolored bat is white-nose syndrome which has caused populations declines of 90-100% across 59% of the species’ range (87 FR 56381). Other threats include changes to climate patterns, mortality from wind turbines, human disturbance during hibernation, and habitat loss (87 FR 56381).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

The tricolored bat is a wide-ranging bat that is found across 39 states (87 FR 56381) spanning the midwestern and eastern United States, extending as far west as Colorado and Wyoming and ranging into parts of central America to the south and Canada to the north. Tricolored bats hibernate over winters in caves, abandoned mines, and road-associated culverts (in areas where caves and mines are unavailable, 87 FR 56381). They disperse between winter hibernacula and summer roosting habitat, and they engage in migrations of up to 150 miles (USFWS 2021a).

During spring, summer, and fall, tricolored bats forage near water and in forested habitats where they roost in trees (USFWS 2021a). They tend to select tree roosts in the live and dead foliage of deciduous hardwoods, but they also roost in Spanish moss, lichen, pine needles, and human structures (e.g., barns, roofs, bridges, tunnels, and road-associated culverts) (87 FR 56381). There is no federally designated critical habitat for this species (87 FR 56381).

Of records in the NRM and GBIF databases, there are 13 records of the species in inventoried roadless areas, of which 69% occurred in areas that were operable or operable but complex. Given the wide range of this species, we also conducted an analysis overlaying the USFWS range map (USFWS 2026a) with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action.  The result was approximately a 0.002% overlap.

#### Effects of Roads

The specific effects of roads on tricolored bat populations and habitat are unknown, but it is likely that roads can create both benefits and risks. Like many bats, tricolored bats are sensitive to disturbance, meaning that the increased human access to caves that is possible from roads could be detrimental. However, gating caves can be an effective way of reducing disturbance to hibernating bats (USFWS 2021a). Additionally, it is possible that roads can contribute to mortalities from vehicle collisions as documented in other bats.

That said, roads offer important habitat elements to bats in some portions of their range. In the southern United States where climate conditions are subtropical and there is an absence of cold winters, many tricolored bats hibernate in road-associated culverts when caves and mines are sparse (USFWS 2021a). In fact, road-associated culverts comprise the majority of winter hibernacula in Mississippi, Georgia, and Louisiana (USFWS 2021a). These culverts are likely an important habitat element for tricolored bats, particularly because there is some evidence suggesting that bats overwintering in culverts may be less susceptible to white-nose syndrome because they experience shorter torpor bouts and forage intermittently year-round (USFWS 2021a).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

The specific effects of timber production on tricolored bat populations and habitat are mixed and likely depend on the circumstance. However, given tricolored bats’ reliance on trees for both roosting and foraging habitat, forest management activities likely have both benefits and risks for bats and their habitats depending on how they are conducted.

Forest removal and conversion is listed as a cause of habitat loss in the proposed listing decision for tricolored bats, and there is concern that this could become a greater issue in the future (87 FR 56381). Forest removal can make it more difficult for bats to find roosting and foraging habitats, and it may require them to travel farther between roosting and foraging habitats due to the fragmentation of travel corridors (87 FR 56381, USFWS 2021a). The loss of roosts, foraging habitat, the need to expend more energy can all reduce survival and reproductive success (USFWS 2021a). Forest removal is particularly risky in areas where forested areas are already fragmented because there is a higher chance of losing connectivity or removing roost trees (USFWS 2021a).

If conducted with consideration for tricolored bat habitat needs, forest management can likely benefit the bats by improving roosting and foraging habitat. Tricolored bats likely benefit from forest management that prioritizes retaining mature forests and well-connected corridors (USFWS 2021a) along with large-diameter snags and allowing for roost-tree regeneration (87 FR 56381). Making forests more heterogeneous in terms of forest type, age, and structure may also benefit tree-roosting bats (87 FR 56381). Studies have also shown that tricolored bats were more active in areas that were harvested 3 years prior (Silvis et al. 2016) and at harvest edges (Caldwell et al. 2019). The timing of timber harvest and forest management activities is important to consider as well. Due to their reliance on trees for roosting, tree removal when bats are active can cause injuries or death (87 FR 56381). For this reason, some states conduct forest management in the winter within bat home ranges to protect them (USFWS 2021a).

#### Existing Protections

Many states and National Forests protect habitat for various bat species, including other treeroosting bats that have similar habitat needs as the tricolored bat, such as the Indiana bat (87 FR 56381). For example, some caves are restricted or gated to protect Indiana bats and other bat habitat, and all known hibernacula within USDA Forest Service’s Rocky Mountain Region (Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, South Dakota) are closed during the winter to reduce the risk of transmitting white-nose syndrome (87 FR 56381).

Since the tricolored bat was proposed for listing under the Endangered Species Act relatively recently, it is not mentioned by name in many Forest Plans for National Forests and Grasslands that are managed by the USDA Service. However, since the tricolored bat’s range overlaps with the Indiana bat in several southeastern states, it benefits from the habitat protections offered by several National Forests and Grasslands (e.g., 2004 Daniel Boone NF, 2005 Ouachita NF, 2005 Ozark-St. Francis NF, 2006 Hoosier NF, 2006 Shawnee NF, 2011 Monongahela NF, and 2023 Nantahala and Pisgah NFs land management plans, available at USFS 2025a). Despite these protections, it is possible that tricolored bats could benefit from greater protections in other regions since the tricolored bat’s range is much greater than the Indiana bat’s range.

#### Effects Determination

While there are only 13 records of the species in inventoried roadless areas in the NRM and GBIF databases, 69% of them occur in areas that are operable or operable but complex. Given this, we are assigning them an exposure level of “high.” However, note that only approximately 0.002% of the range occurs in inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action. Given this exposure and the sensitivity of the species to human disturbance the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species.

### Ungulates

_Peninsular bighorn sheep and Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep_

The Peninsular bighorn sheep ( _Ovis canadensis nelsonii)_ and Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep _(Ovis canadensis sierrae)_ are both listed as endangered.

The Peninsular bighorn sheep was listed in 1998 (63 FR 13134). Since 2008 it has been recognized as a distinct population segment of desert bighorn sheep (74 FR 17288). The most recent status review for this DPS was completed in 2020. It found that the DPS has been generally increasing since listing, but that sparse data since 2011 limits knowledge of the species currently (USFWS 2020b). In 2024 the population was estimated at 742 [95% CI: 656-829] individuals- there may have been a decline in the population between 2016 and 2022 associated with drought (CADFW 2025).

The Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep was listed in 2000 (65 FR 20–30). It is recognized as a subspecies of bighorn sheep (73 FR 45534). In 2023 the total population was estimated to be about 350 individuals (USFWS 2024f). This represents a steep decline after approximately 50% of adults were lost in the harsh winter of 2022-2023.  This population also faced a steep decline after a harsh winter in 2016-2017 (USFWS 2024f). Small population size is one of the threats that contributes to the species’ current status (USFWS 2024f)- it also faces the challenge of having fragmented subpopulations across its range.

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action

Both the Peninsular bighorn sheep and the Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep live in the mountains of California.

The Peninsular bighorn sheep DPS lives in the Colorado Desert of Southern California.  They can be found in the Peninsular Mountain Ranges from the San Jacinto Mountains south to the border with Mexico (USFWS 2011a) and additional range for the subspecies extend into Mexico. They typically inhabit relatively low elevation habitat for bighorn sheep <4,600 ft.  While sheep habitat is typically steep slopes with low levels of vegetation they will also use more gentle terrain (USFWS 2011a). Critical habitat was designated for the DPS in 2009 (74 FR 17288), but no critical habitat overlaps with IRAs in the proposed action area. While critical habitat does not overlap with IRAs in the proposed action, the San Bernadino National Forest Plan (2005 land management plan Part B, available at USFS 2025a) reports that there over 5,000 acres of key peninsular bighorn sheep habitat in and near the Pyramid Peak Inventoried Roadless Area.  Bighorn sheep habitat is also found in the Cactus Springs A and B Inventoried Roadless Areas (2005 land management plan Part B, available at USFS 2025a) which abut the Santa Rosa Wilderness. The NRM and GBIF databases had very limited observations of this DPS, so we used the USFWS range map (USFWS 2026a) to evaluate the exposure of the species to the proposed action. Approximately 1% of the DPS’s range overlaps with inventoried roadless areas in the proposed action area.

The Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep lives in Eastern California in the Sierras within Tuolumne, Mono, Fresno, Inyo, and Tulare counties (73 FR 45534). Best sheep habitat is open, for visibility, and on steep rocky slopes (USFWS 2008a). While they avoid dense forest, they will use open woodlands (USFWS 2008a). They can be found across a wide range of elevations, typically selecting high alpine habitat >10,000 ft in the summer, but using areas down to ~4,000 ft in the winter (73 FR 45534). Critical habitat for the species was designated in 2008 (73 FR 45534) and approximately 2.6% of it is within an IRA affected by the proposed action, with 15% of that habitat in areas that are designated as operable or operable but complex. There are only 13 observations of Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep in IRAs in the NRM and GBIF database. As such it is not possible to use these data to draw conclusions about their relative exposure areas that may be more likely to be altered by the proposed action. We ran a supplemental analysis intersecting the USFWS range map (USFWS 2026a) for this species with inventoried roadless areas in the proposed action area. The overlap was approximately 8.2%. The majority of herd units have some portion of their habitat overlapping or immediately adjacent to IRAs.

Effects of Roads

Vehicle strikes on roads have led to the deaths of both Sierra Nevada and Peninsular Bighorn sheep. While there are not extensive road networks in Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep habitat, several mortalities have been reported on roads in Lee Vining Canyon on several occasions (listing decision). Road networks are more extensive in Peninsular sheep habitat and both highways and county roads have led to mortality from strikes (USFWS 2011a).

There are some data from Peninsular Bighorn sheep to suggest that road avoidance behavior may fragment bighorn sheep habitat. Roads or traffic on roads may make sheep, especially ewes (Rubin et al. 1998) reluctant to cross roads. There are several sheep subpopulations whose home ranges are delineated by roads (USFWS 2011a). There are also fairly detailed accounts of sheep behavior near the Dunn Road within the Santa Rosa Mountains. While this road, which was built illegally, was actively used by humans, sheep appeared to stay 1.5-3 km east of it. Because of this avoidance behavior, authorities closed the road and sheep have since started using habitat to the west of it (USFWS 2011a). Another study suggested that on days of high recreational vehicle traffic in Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, sheep reduced use of waterholes by as much as 50% (Jorgenson 1974 as cited in USFWS 2011a). Similarly, a study reported that noise from motorcycles also deterred sheep from using waterholes Olech (1979). The effect of roads on sheep may be sex specific, a study in Peninsular sheep showed that a greater proportion of males were more likely to cross roads than females, but that this difference in propensity occurred during periods of segregation between the sexes and not aggregation (Bleich et al. 2016). The same study found that on an annual basis, sheep showed no difference in their likelihood to cross a two-lane paved road with ~100 vehicle daily traffic volume versus a dirt road that received ~ 1 vehicle a day (Bleich et al. 2016). While habituation to roads may occur as shown in a study in Desert Sheep in Utah, most sheep avoid road corridors and road corridors cause a loss in habitat (Papouchis et al. 2001).

Given that vehicle noise appears to disturb bighorn sheep, it is perhaps not surprising that bighorn sheep may also be impacted by human recreation, which could increase in IRAs affected by rule rescission. There are several examples reported in the Peninsular Bighorn sheep species status assessment that suggests sheep avoid trails when being used by humans and that closing trails to humans leads sheep to return to habitat near trails (USFWS 2011a). The recovery plan calls for prevention of infrastructure (including roads) and activities (increased use of offroad vehicle areas) that may serve as barriers to sheep movement. Data from Desert bighorn sheep in Utah suggests that sheep have a particularly strong behavioral response to hikers, fleeing well over half the time (Papouchis et al. 2001). Another study from Utah found that Desert bighorn sheep spent less time grazing and were more vigilant in an area of high human use compared to low human use (Sproat et al. 2020).There are fewer data specifically addressing the response of Sierra Nevada Bighorn sheep to recreation, although the critical habitat designation notes the need to better understand this relationship. The sensitivity of other bighorn sheep subspecies to human recreation suggests there is a similar potential for disturbance during exposure.

Increased risk of wildfire caused by human ignitions could also affect Bighorn sheep. Severe wildfires, which may be more likely due to long term fire suppression policies, are thought to degrade sheep habitat, at least temporarily. This may be especially true in habitat types used by sheep that are not well adapted to fire disturbance, such as the Sonoran scrub used by the Peninsular sheep (USFWS 2000a). For Peninsular sheep, catastrophic fire is thought to be a higher risk at the lower elevation sites where invasive plant cover has increased (USFWS 2011a).

Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Commercial timber harvest is not discussed in listing decisions and status assessments for either sheep species. However, other vegetation management and removal activities do have the potential to affect them. Evaluations for both sheep species suggest that fire suppression has degraded sheep habitat. Specifically expanding dense vegetative cover is thought to reduce visibility for sheep and provide cover for mountain lions, which are a predator of sheep and have a big impact on population numbers (74 FR 17288, Gammons et al. 2025). The 2011 Species Status assessment for Peninsular Sheep identified several areas where habitat conversion due to fire suppression was thought to have reduced bighorn sheep habitat (USFWS 2011a). Therefore, vegetation management activities that reduce dense cover and provide greater visibility for sheep may benefit these two species if it reduces predation by mountain lions (74 FR 17288). Fire mitigation activities, such as prescribed fire or other vegetation management practices, may create habitat that are used by desert bighorn sheep (Holl et al. 2012: Bleich et al. 2019). For example, a population in the San Rafael mountains used recently burned chapparal habitat for forage (Holl et al. 2012;). A recent review suggested that prescribed fire has the potential to be especially beneficial for sheep habitat may be especially important for chaparral habitat in the Southwestern United States (Whiting et al. 2023).

The literature on Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep is more limited but suggests a similar pattern. Greene et al. 2012 documented an improvement in winter sheep forage after a natural fire. Mountain lion predation is also a primary cause of mortality for Sierra Nevada sheep (Gammons et al. 2025) and improved visibility in burned areas may also be attractive to this subspecies. The authors recommend more research is needed to evaluate whether prescribed fire or other vegetation management activities confer similar benefits to natural fire. In study of Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep, authors found that the timing of vegetation recovery after prescribed fire, which can be affected by weather conditions, had a strong impact on whether fire benefitted forage (Clapp and Beck 2016).

The San Bernadino Forest Plan has some specific directives for Peninsular Bighorn sheep. Specifically, the desired conditions in the Santa Rosa and San Jacinto Mountains National Monument region of the forest include the enhancement of all habitat for TES species. The “program” for this region states that “Enhancement of wildlife habitat for threatened, endangered, proposed, candidate, and sensitive species (such as the Peninsular Ranges bighorn sheep) will be emphasized in all management activities” and specifically emphases that “The habitat linkage from the Santa Rosa Mountains into the Anza Borrego State Park for Peninsular Range bighorn sheep will be maintained.” The Inyo National Forest has desired conditions specific to Sierra Nevada Bighorn sheep, and the guideline that the forest should “manage recreation, or other disturbances, where research has found it to cause Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep to avoid important habitat as described in the Sierra Nevada Bighorn Sheep Recovery Plan or other guidance from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service” (USFS 2025a).

#### Critical Habitat

For the Peninsular Bighorn sheep, critical habitat was designated for the DPS in 2009 (74 FR 17288), but no critical habitat overlaps with IRAs in the proposed action area. As such we do not discuss PCEs and we have determined the proposed action will have no effect on critical habitat for this species **.**

For the Sierra Nevada Bighorn sheep, critical habitat was designated in 2008 (73 FR 45534) and approximately 2.6% of it is within an IRA affected by the proposed action, with 15% of that habitat in areas that are designated as operable or operable but complex. The PCEs for this species habitat are:

- “(1) Non-forested habitats or forest openings within the Sierra Nevada from 4,000 ft (1,219 m) to 14,500 ft (4,420 m) in elevation with steep (greater than or equal to 60 percent slope), rocky slopes that provide for foraging, mating, lambing, predator avoidance, and bedding and allow for seasonal elevational movements between these areas.

- (2) Presence of a variety of forage plants as indicated by the presence of grasses (e.g., _Achnanthera_ spp.; _Elymus_ spp.) and browse (e.g., _Ribes_ spp.; _Artemisia_ spp., _Purshia_ spp.) in winter, and grasses, browse, sedges (e.g., _Carex_ spp.) and forbs (e.g., _Eriogonum_ spp.) in summer.

- (3) Presence of granite rock outcroppings containing minerals such as sodium, calcium, iron, and phosphorus that could be used as salt licks/mineral licks in order to meet nutritional needs.”

Given that there is critical habitat in inventoried roadless areas, even though it is a small amount, we have defined the exposure level as medium. Given that the PCEs for the species are unlikely to be modified by roads and sheep habitat is high elevation and steep we have determined the proposed action is not likely to adversely affect critical habitat for this species because the effects are discountable.

The exposure of the Peninsular Bighorn sheep to the proposed action is low. However, given that the species is sensitive to roads and human activities associated with roads, we have determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species.

The exposure of the Sierra Nevada Bighorn sheep to the proposed action is medium because even though a decent portion of their range overlaps with the proposed action it is not a landscape that is conducive to road construction. Given that this species is sensitive to roads and human activities associated with roads, we have determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species.

#### _Southern mountain caribou DPS_

The southern mountain caribou distinct population segment (DPS) of woodland caribou _(Rangifer tarandus caribou)_ is a transboundary (United States and Canada) caribou population that is listed as endangered by both the Endangered Species Act (ESA) (84 FR 52598) and the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC) (COSEWIC 2014). For the portion of the range in the United States, critical habitat for this DPS was originally designated in 2012 (77 FR 71042) and then reaffirmed in the 2019 listing decision (84 FR 52598), and a recovery plan outline was published in 2019 (USFWS 2019c). During that same year, the last female southern mountain caribou known to be present in the United States was captured in Idaho and moved to a captive breeding facility in Canada (USFWS 2023a), marking the extirpation of the subpopulation that inhabited remote areas of northeast Washington and northwest Idaho (WDFW 2025).

The southern mountain caribou DPS was estimated to encompass 1,356 adults in 2014, reflecting a decline of 27% since 2002 and a decline of 45% in the previous three generations (COSEWIC 2014). The DPS consists of 17 subpopulations, of which at least two have been extirpated, and most of the other extant populations in Canada are very small (COSEWIC 2014). As of 2019, the southern mountain caribou DPS is thought to be in an accelerating state of decline (84 FR 52598). A main driver of southern mountain caribou DPS decline is predation by gray wolves, bears, and mountain lions resulting from habitat fragmentation (COSEWIC 2014) due to roads and human disturbance. When old-growth caribou habitat is fragmented, the early-seral vegetation that grows after disturbance supports moose and deer that were not previously present, in turn supporting a greater number of predators that then use caribou as secondary prey (Wittmer et al. 2007, Seip 1992). For this reason, one of the stated goals of the Mountain Caribou Recovery Implementation Plan is to “protect [5,436,320 ac] of caribou habitat from logging and road building” (84 FR 52598).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

Southern mountain caribou are strongly associated with old-growth forests (Apps et al. 2001). In particular, they inhabit high-elevation Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir forests and western red cedar and western hemlock at low elevations (Apps et al. 2001). They use different habitat types seasonally, including lower elevations with green vegetation (spring), high-elevation areas (during calving for females), valley bottoms and low slopes (early winter), and upper slopes and ridgetops (late winter) (Apps et al. 2001, 84 FR 52598). This caribou DPS is adapted to living in areas with deep snow, and their winter diet is composed almost entirely of arboreal lichens, meaning that they require large intact areas of old forest (which support hair lichens in the overstory, Goward et al. 2024) and steep mountainous terrain to achieve their nutritional needs. However, maintaining intact areas of habitat in the areas surrounding these steep old-forest areas is also very important for population abundance (Lochhead et al. 2022) because caribou benefit from access to large areas of mature forest so they can space out from other competing ungulates and their shared predators (Seip 1992).

Critical habitat for this species encompasses 30,010 acres in the northeast corner of Washington and the northwest corner of Idaho (77 FR 71042). The entirety of this designated critical habitat occurs on federal land that is managed by the USDA Forest Service (77 FR 71042). The critical habitat is located on the Idaho Panhandle National Forest (IPNF), which encompasses portions of Idaho, Montana, and Washington, and the Colville National Forest (CNF) in Washington (77 FR 71042). Both the IPNF and the CNF contain inventoried roadless areas (USFS 2000a). Approximately 4.4% of critical habitat for the species is in a potentially affected IRA, and of that habitat 82% is classified as being in areas that are operable or operable but complex. There are no observations of the species in NRM or GBIF, making these datasets unsuitable for drawing conclusions about the relative exposure of the species to the proposed action. We ran a supplemental analysis overlaying the USFWS range map (USFWS 2026a) for this species with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action to further evaluate exposure and the overlap was approximately 7.8%.

#### Effects of Roads

A large body of research has demonstrated that roads and other linear features can cause caribou, their competitors (moose, deer, and elk), and their shared predators to modify their space use (Dickie et al. 2023) with ramifications for caribou demographic rates (Serrouya et al. 2017) and population declines (Wittmer et al. 2007). Competitor ungulates and predators can use roads to access parts of caribou range that were previously inaccessible to them (Dickie et al. 2020). This can lead to increased predation on caribou populations and depressed population growth.

Additionally, a recent study provided evidence that roads in both currently used (“core”) and surrounding (“matrix”) habitat were negatively associated with caribou abundance. The research predicts that for every 1% increase in roads in the matrix habitat, there will be a 42% decline in southern mountain caribou abundance (Lochhead et al. 2022). This is concerning for a DPS that is already characterized by small, isolated subpopulations with limited interbreeding (COSEWIC 2014, 84 FR 52598).

Roads also create opportunities for more human disturbance in areas that were previously less accessible (84 FR 52598). Human recreation activities, especially winter activities like backcountry skiing, heli-skiing, cat-skiing, and snowmobiling, are known to affect caribou behavior (84 FR 52598), and many of these activities make use of existing roads and require road maintenance.

Finally, roads are a source of direct mortality for caribou. Highways have led to several fatal collisions (84 FR 52598) which can have a major effect on already-small subpopulations. To address these concerns, the Forest Service has been working to mitigate threats from roads within caribou critical habitat by avoiding road construction through mature forest when possible and by emphasizing road closure and habitat mitigation (USFWS 2019c).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

In general, timber harvest is associated with negative effects on southern mountain caribou. Caribou avoid areas where timber was recently harvested, and they abandon areas that experienced high levels of harvest (Smith et al. 2000, Stevenson et al. 2025). For example, timber harvest and other anthropogenic disturbances in low-elevation portions of seasonal habitat were associated with a shift from migratory to resident behavior in one population of southern mountain caribou which ultimately corresponded with a decrease in survival rates (Williams et al. 2021). Further, a study that compared the effects of timber harvest on caribou to the effects of wildfire found that caribou are far “more likely to shift, abandon, or contract their range in response to timber harvest than in response to wildfire” and that caribou population declines are stronger in response to timber harvest than wildfire as well, possibly due to timber-associated roadbuilding (Stevenson et al. 2025).

Timber production contributes to habitat fragmentation and loss via conversion to younger forest that leads to increased ungulate presence, increased predation, and then population decline (COSEWIC 2014, 84 FR 52598, Wittmer et al. 2007, Lochhead et al. 2022). To address this concern, recommendations for forest management in mountain caribou habitat include retaining upper-elevation mature forest at specific age levels, using partial cutting and uneven-aged silvicultural methods, and retaining mature forest corridors and mature forest remnants within cutblocks (Seip 1998).

Negative effects of salvage logging after insect outbreaks have been documented in some caribou populations, although results depend on the population and the season (Labadie et al. 2021, Griffin et al. 2025). One population of central mountain caribou whose habitat experienced a pine beetle outbreak avoided areas that experienced higher timber harvest and fire density (Griffin et al. 2025). These caribou also increased their avoidance of timber harvest as it became more prevalent on the landscape (Griffin et al. 2025). Similarly, a population of boreal caribou experienced increased mortality after a spruce budworm outbreak led to more deciduous vegetation, more moose, and more wolf predation that was eventually exacerbated by salvage logging (Labadie et al. 2021).

#### Existing Protections

Both the IPNF and CNF Forest Plans contain provisions to protect woodland caribou habitat. The IPNF Forest Plan emphasizes connectivity with habitat in Canada, low levels of disturbance, reducing disturbance in seasonal habitats during key times, and management activities in seasonal habitat that are aimed to steer vegetation toward target stand conditions (2015 IPNF land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). This plan also incorporates a court-ordered snowmobile closure that restricts access and trail grooming and incorporates a protected caribou travel corridor (84 FR 52598). Similarly, the CNF Forest Plan restricts over-the-snow vehicle use to designated routes within the caribou recovery area and emphasizes disturbance reduction and vegetation management to ensure the availability of preferred lichens for forage (2019 CNF land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Both the IPNF and the CNF contain inventoried roadless areas (USFS 2000a).

#### Critical Habitat

Designated critical habitat for the United States portion of the southern mountain caribou DPS’ range includes five elements: 1) mature hemlock/western red cedar and subalpine fir/Engelmann spruce forests above 5,000 feet in elevation, 2) ridgetops and basins above 6,000 feet in elevation, 3) the presence of arboreal hair lichens, 4) high-elevation areas with shallow slopes, meadows, and flowering plants, and 5) corridors connecting the habitats described above (77 FR 71042). This designated critical habitat encompasses 30,010 acres in the northeast corner of Washington and the northwest corner of Idaho (77 FR 71042).
