Approximately 4.4% of critical habitat for the species is in a potentially affected IRA, and of that habitat 82% is classified as being in areas that are operable or operable but complex. Given that 82% of critical habitat in inventoried roadless areas is in operable or operable but complex environments we are assigning an exposure level of “high” for critical habitat. Given this exposure and that a number of the PBFs for this species’ critical habitat may be affected by road and timber activities, the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species.

#### Effects Determination

The exposure level of the Southern Mountain Caribou DPS to the proposed action is high given the overlap of the proposed action with its range. Given the importance of mature forest to the species, the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species. Given exposure and the requirement for mature forest, the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species.

### Small Rodents

#### _Utah Prairie Dog_

The Utah Prairie dog _(Cynomys parvidens)_ was listed as threatened in 1973 (38 FR 14678) and was uplisted to endangered (76 FR 36053) in 2011. There is considerable variability in the estimated population size, and although the overall long-term trend is for stability or potentially an increase in population numbers, the range-wide count of animals was noticeably lower in 2020 than it was in 2016. These are the data available in the most recent species status assessment (USFWS 2021b). Plague is one of the most important threats to the species (USFWS 2021b).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

Currently the Utah Prairie Dog only occurs in southwestern Utah (USFWS 2021b) where it lives in semiarid shrub-steppe and grassland habitats and build burrows in well-drained soils (76 FR 36053). This distribution represents a retraction from its historical range which extended further north (USFWS 2021b). It is thought to be present on the Dixie, Fishlake, and Manti-la Sal National Forests. There are 28 observations of the Utah Prairie dog in inventoried roadless areas that may be affected by the proposed actions in the NRM and GBIF databases. Of these, only 4% are in areas that are potentially operable or operable but complex.  Given the opportunistic nature of sampling from these data sources, we also conducted an analysis overlaying the USFWS range for this species (USFWS 2026a) with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action to evaluate the consistency of these two approaches. The overlap is approximately 12.3%. There is no designated critical habitat for the Utah prairie dog.

#### Effects of Roads

Utah prairie dogs can be killed by vehicle strikes on roads (76 FR 36053). Additionally, the use of off-highway vehicles and the creation of trails by these vehicles by recreationists can cause habitat loss for the species and potentially extirpation of colonies (76 FR 36053). At the time of the 2011 listing decision, the USFWS concluded that “Road construction, off-highway vehicle (OHV) use, and recreation may have effects to individuals or colonies that occur adjacent to the roadways, trails, or play areas; however, these are localized areas and do not result in population level effects" (76 FR 36053).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

The 2011 listing decision and the 2021 species status assessment do not address the impacts of timber harvest on this species, which is perhaps not surprising given the species’ habitat association.

#### Existing Protections

The Dixie National Forest Plan has the goal of maintaining or enhancing prairie dog habitat (1986 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Similarly, the Fishlake National Forest Plan states that “it will also meet the habitat requirements of the Utah prairie dog recovery plan” (1986 land management plan, available at USFS 2025aa). The Manti-La Sal National Forest plan does not contain specific direction for the species (USFS 2025a).

#### Effects Determination

Given that 12.3% of the species’ range overlaps with inventoried roadless areas, the FS has determined that the exposure of the species to the proposed action is high. There is potential for individual impacts to survival due to road construction and road usage. Therefore, the FS has determined that the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species.

#### _Carolina Northern Flying Squirrel_

The Carolina northern flying squirrel _(Glaucomys sabrinus coloratus)_ was listed as endangered in 1985 (50 FR 26666). The 2022 Species Status Assessment noted that some data in a preliminary occupancy analysis suggests that populations in 7/10 management units for the subspecies were stable, but that a number of methodological limitations limited the strength of conclusions from this data (USFWS 2022b). The recent assessment notes that many of the populations of this subspecies are isolated and that some have only a little high-quality habitat (USFWS 2022b).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and the Proposed Actions

The Carolina northern flying squirrel is a subspecies occurring at the southern extent of the range of the northern flying squirrel in the Southern Appalachians in North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. They are present on the Cherokee, George Washington and Jefferson, Nantahala, and Pisgah National Forests and all of these forests have inventoried roadless areas that could be affected by the proposed action. Spruce fir forests are thought to be especially important for foraging (USFWS 2013a) and hardwood stands with yellow birch are thought to be important for denning (USFWS 2013a). The subspecies is thought to primarily occur above 4,500 ft, although more recent work has demonstrated use in the 4,000-4,500 ft elevational band (USFWS 2022b). Analyses of vegetation on the Cherokee, Nantahala, and Pisgah National Forests show that large portions of the forest that used to be spruce-fir are now uncharacteristic vegetation types (USFWS 2022b). Habitat fragmentation from logging is thought to have played a role in their decline (50 FR 26999).

There is no critical habitat for this subspecies. There are no records of this subspecies in the NRM and GBIF databases. As such, it is not possible to use these data for an assessment of the potential impact of the proposed action on this species. We conducted a supplementary analysis overlapping the USFWS range map (USFWS 2026a) for this species with inventoried roadless affected by the proposed action. Approximately 6% of the species’ range is in the proposed action area.

#### Effects of Roads

Roads can create a barrier to movement for this subspecies. For example, the Cherohala Skyway was a barrier to dispersal within the Unicoi Mountains GRA when it was constructed, even though it was a two-lane rural scenic byway with relatively low traffic volume (Kelly et al. 2013). Researchers suggest that even roads of this size create a large enough gap to impede traverse by gliding, and that squirrels were averse to crossing the road by foot as evidenced by the absence of significant roadkill data for the subspecies across its range (Weigl et al. 2002 in Kelly et al. 2013). In this specific instance, red spruce have been planted and artificial crossing structures have been installed (USFWS 2022b; Kelly et al. 2013) to improve connectivity, but the example illustrates how road construction can affect movement behavior and gene flow within the subspecies.

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

According to the 2022 5-year review, “significant areas [of squirrel habitat] are still suffering from legacy effects of past disturbances and land use (e.g., industrial logging in the late 1800s/early 1900s), and work is needed to properly restore and manage lands to help recover the species." Several national forests where the species occurs currently have uncharacteristic vegetation types. Restoration of spruce-fir habitat is identified as a need for this species (USFWS 2022b). The 5-year review also notes that “while there is the potential for timber harvesting in Carolina northern flying squirrel habitat, these areas are largely avoided, and any harvest would likely be small in scale and undertaken for the purpose of restoration” (USFWS 2022b). Vegetation management activities that restore this spruce-fir type, when properly designed, could be beneficial for the species.

Having “sufficient ecological data and timber management data ... to assure future protection and management” of the Carolina northern flying squirrel is a requirement for recovery (USFWS 2022b). As of the assessment in 2022, studies explicitly evaluating the impact of different timber management practices on the subspecies had not been conducted (USFWS 2022b).

#### Existing Protections

The Cherokee National Forest plan lists the management objective of “Provide high quality northern hardwood/spruce fir habitats; improve habitat connectivity where possible” for this subspecies (2004 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). The Nantahala- Pisgah National Forest Plan includes the desired condition that “habitat components at finer scales provide for wildlife occupancy, are present in sufficient amounts, and distributed across all ecozones. For example...smaller live or dead trees with crevices provide critical nesting and roosting habitat for flying squirrels and bats” (2024 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Additionally, the forest should “Maintain species presence within currently occupied habitat" on the forest and offers the goal of “Emphasize restoration of spruce-fir habitat for the Carolina northern flying squirrel and maintain the health and resiliency of this forest type in the face of climate change” (2024 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). The Jefferson National Forest Plan also has objectives specific to the recovery of the subspecies (2004 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a).

The assessment of the 2013 5-year review was that while it “appears” that “sufficient habitat for population maintenance is maintained” but it is “unclear if sufficient habitat is being managed for expansion or to allow for habitat corridors that connect GRAS” (USFWS 2013a).

#### Effects Determination

Given that 6% of this species’ range is affected by the proposed action is affected by the proposed action we have assigned an exposure level of high. Additionally, given the species’ dependence on specific forest types, the negative impacts of habitat loss, and the negative impact of roads on connectivity the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species.

#### _San Bernardino Merriam’s kangaroo rat_

San Bernardino Merriam’s kangaroo rat ( _Dipodomys merriami parvus_ ) is a granivorous subspecies of the Merriam’s kangaroo rat that was listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 1998 (63 FR 51005). At the time of listing, the subspecies’ historical range had contracted by 95% due to human development including agricultural conversion, urbanization, and industrial development (63 FR 51005).

At present, range-wide estimates of population trends and occupancy are not available (USFWS 2023b). However, ongoing human-caused threats to the subspecies include habitat destruction and loss, fragmentation from gravel mining operations, urbanization, off-highway vehicle use, and flood control projects (63 FR 51005). Some populations of San Bernardino kangaroo rats are also threatened by changes in stream flow patterns and related vegetation changes (63 FR 51005).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

Critical habitat for the San Bernardino kangaroo rat was originally designated in 2002 and then revised in 2008 (73 FR 61936). Approximately 7,779 acres across five units are designated as critical habitat in San Bernardino and Riverside counties of California, including multiple locations (specific creeks and washes) on the San Bernardino National Forest (73 FR 61936; 2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Approximately 6% of critical habitat is in inventoried roadless areas, and, of that, 35% of it is within areas that are operable or operable but complex.

San Bernardino kangaroo rats inhabit alluvial habitats and adjacent upland areas with low vegetation cover and sandy soils that enable them to dig shallow burrows, such as flood plains and alluvial fans (63 FR 51005). This type of area typically contains gravel, rock, sand, silt, and clay that is deposited by moving water (73 FR 61936). Areas near rivers that experience flooding every few years to maintain lower vegetation cover tend to support higher densities of San Bernardino kangaroo rats (63 FR 51005). Due to the changing vegetation and soil patterns, not all alluvial scrub habitat is appropriate for this subspecies at any given time since they use more open areas with low shrub canopy cover (63 FR 51005). Alluvial sage scrub is a “distinct and rare plant community that dominates major outwash fans at the mouths of canyons along the coastal side of the San Gabriel, San Bernardino, and San Jacinto mountains and some smaller floodplain and riverine areas of southern California” (73 FR 61936). Maintaining habitat connectivity between the stream and the upland alluvial terraces is important for supporting San Bernardino kangaroo rat populations (USFWS 2024g, USFWS 2024h).

San Bernardino kangaroo rats have occasionally been documented in areas that have occasionally been altered by humans such as the edges of orchards, vineyards that are inactive, and areas of wildland-urban interface that are near occupied alluvial habitat (73 FR 61936). Although these are not areas of high-quality habitat, these individuals may serve an important role in recolonizing after flooding or other dynamic events within the primary habitat (73 FR 61936).

There are no records of the species in the NRM or GBIF databases, making it impossible to use these data sources to evaluate the exposure of the species to the proposed action. As such we ran a supplementary analysis overlaying the USFWS range map (USFWS 2026a) for the species with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action.  The overlap was approximately 7.2%.

#### Effects of Roads

The specific effects of roads on San Bernardino kangaroo rats are generally negative. This species cannot use areas of compacted soil due to its weak forelegs and the need for looser soil that enables burrowing (73 FR 61936), meaning that road construction fragments existing habitat. Urbanization, development, and associated road construction is a major threat across the entirety of the subspecies’ range due to the increasing human population in the surrounding areas (73 FR 61936). Sand and gravel mining is a particular concern for this subspecies’ habitat due to the way it alters soil composition (73 FR 61936), and mining access roads could also pose challenges. Additionally, off-road vehicle use has been noted as a concern due to the way it can damage kangaroo rat burrows, soil structure, and the surrounding vegetation (73 FR 61936).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

The specific effects of timber production on San Bernardino kangaroo rats are likely negligible. The species inhabits alluvial fans with low shrub canopy cover, and especially areas that flood periodically (73 FR 61936). It is unlikely that timber harvest would occur within the subspecies’ habitat, and neither timber harvesting nor forest management are mentioned in the Species Status Assessment (USFWS 2023b).

#### Existing Protections

San Bernardino kangaroo rats and some of their designated critical habitat are located on the USDA Forest Service’s San Bernardino National Forest (2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). The land and resource management plan for the San Bernardino National Forest was revised in 2005 and incorporates multiple provisions intended to benefit this subspecies’ habitat (73 FR 61936; 2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). However, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service opted to designate critical habitat on these lands in addition to the provisions outlined in this plan since the habitat contains elements that are “essential to [San Bernardino kangaroo rat] conservation” (73 FR 61936).

#### Critical Habitat Determination

The primary constituent elements of critical habitat for this species are as follows:

- “(1) Alluvial fans, washes, and associated floodplain areas containing soils consisting predominately of sand, loamy sand, sandy loam, and loam, which provide burrowing habitat necessary for sheltering and rearing offspring, storing food in surface caches, and movement between occupied patches;

- (2) Upland areas adjacent to alluvial fans, washes, and associated floodplain areas containing alluvial sage scrub habitat and associated vegetation, such as coastal sage scrub and chamise chaparral, with up to approximately 50 percent canopy cover providing protection from predators, while leaving bare ground and open areas necessary for foraging and movement of this subspecies; and

- (3) Upland areas adjacent to alluvial fans, washes, and associated floodplain areas, which may include marginal habitat such as alluvial sage scrub with greater than 50 percent canopy cover with patches of suitable soils (PCE 1) that support individuals for repopulation of wash areas following flood events. These areas may include agricultural lands, areas of inactive aggregate mining activities, and urban/wildland interfaces.”  (73 FR 61936)

Given that approximately 6% of critical habitat is in inventoried roadless areas, and of that 35% of it is within areas that are operable or operable but complex the exposure of the habitat to the proposed action is high. Given that roads, soil compaction, and vegetation trampling or removal may adversely affect critical habitat the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect critical habitat for this species **.**

#### Effects Determination

Given that 7.2% of the species’ range intersects with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action exposure is high. Given the potential for roads and OHV use to damage soils and vegetation the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species. Given that roads, soil compaction, and vegetation trampling or removal may adversely affect critical habitat the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect critical habitat for this species **.**

#### _Stephens’ kangaroo rat_

Stephens’ kangaroo rat ( _Dipodomys stephensi_ ) is a nocturnal mammal that was listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 1988 after experiencing extensive habitat loss and degradation that yielded small, isolated populations (53 FR 38465). More recently, the species was downlisted to threatened in 2022 due to a reduction in extinction risk, and a “4(d) rule” that prohibits intentional take and specifies exceptions was published (87 FR 8967). Current habitat loss, fragmentation, and population isolation were noted as reasons that the species should be reclassified as threatened, as well as the ongoing effects of past habitat fragmentation (87 FR 8967). The current range-wide population trend and density is unknown due to incomplete surveys, challenges of detecting the animals, and natural year-to-year population fluctuations (87 FR 8967).

As of the time of downlisting, experts concluded that “the Stephens’ kangaroo rat continues to occur in suitable habitat in seemly stable populations across its range” (87 FR 8967). Conservation actions are informed by a draft recovery plan (USFWS 1997) and a five-year review (USFWS 2025f).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

Critical habitat has not been designated for Stephens’ kangaroo rats (53 FR 38465). Populations occur in three geographic regions of southern California (53 FR 38465). Historically, they likely inhabited a broader range, but they were slowly confined to a smaller area as urban and agricultural development in the region expanded (53 FR 38465). They inhabit open scrublands and grasslands with herbaceous annuals that are native to California (53 FR 38465, 87 FR 8967). They are found in areas with slightly disturbed or plowed soil and flat or rolling terrain (53 FR 38465). They live in underground burrows and come to the surface to forage at night (53 FR 38465), occupying patchy areas of habitat containing burrow entrances and connecting paths (87 FR 8967). They may prefer plant communities that are maintained by disturbances like fire, grazing, and agriculture that do not have dense grass or high cover of non-native grasses (USFWS 2025f).

There are only 6 records of the species in the NRM and GBIF databases, none of which occur in inventoried roadless areas. Given the paucity of records for this species and the potential for sampling bias, the relative exposure of this species to the proposed action cannot be assessed with these data. We ran a custom analysis overlaying habitat for the species (Conservation Biology Institute 2019) with inventoried roadless areas.  Less than 0.001% of modelled habitat overlapped with the proposed action area.

#### Effects of Roads

The specific effects of roads on Stephens’ kangaroo rats are uncertain, but it is plausible that they could have detrimental effects. This species does not use areas of compacted soil (53 FR 38465), meaning that road construction could fragment existing habitat. Additionally, off-road vehicle use has been noted as a concern due to the risk of vegetation destruction, soil and burrow compaction, and collisions (53 FR 38465, USFWS 1997). For this reason, the recovery plan notes that habitat blocks without roads and that are inaccessible to people are more appropriate for Stephens’ kangaroo rat conservation efforts (USFWS 1997).

However, under certain circumstances, the species may be able to colonize areas that have been modified for agriculture, grazing, clearing, and roads (USFWS 1997). Stephens’ kangaroo rats are frequently found near disturbed areas including dirt roads (USFWS 1997).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

The specific effects of timber production on Stephens’ kangaroo rats are negligible. The species inhabits a small area of habitat that is dominated by grasslands, scrub, and some shrublands. It is unlikely that timber harvest would occur within the species’ habitat.

#### Existing Protections

The majority of Stephens’ kangaroo rat’s range occurs on private land (53 FR 38465). However, the USDA Forest Service manages the Cleveland National Forest which contains suitable habitat for Stephens’ kangaroo rat (2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a) and which may provide connectivity habitat to other areas (USFWS 1997). The Cleveland National Forest Plan does not contain specific standards and guidelines related to this species; rather, it tiers to the Recovery Plan (2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Other federally managed land is also an important component of the species’ habitat, including several military bases and areas under the Bureau of Land Management’s jurisdiction (53 FR 38465). At least two major habitat conservation efforts have been implemented within the species’ range, and the military installations within the range have also developed natural resources management plans and are engaged in habitat conservation efforts (87 FR 8967).

#### Species Effects Determination

Given that the overlap of modelled habitat for this species and inventoried roadless areas is extremely low the FS has determined the proposed action is not likely to adversely affect this species because the effects are so unlikely as to be discountable.

#### _Peñasco Least Chipmunk_

The Peñasco Least Chipmunk ( _Neotamias minimus atristriatus_ ) was listed as Endangered effective as of January 9. 2025. The Peñasco least chipmunk is a disjunct subspecies at the southernmost extent of least chipmunks, historically found in the Sacramento and White Mountains of New Mexico. In the Sacramento Mountains, it occupied canyon-bottom meadows and open ponderosa pine forests between 2,103–2,438 m (6,900–8,000 ft), while in the White Mountains it occurred in high-elevation (>3,109 m/10,200 ft) Thurber’s fescue grasslands with rock outcrops.

The Peñasco least chipmunk population is currently restricted to a small portion of the White Mountains within Lincoln National Forest, New Mexico. The 2024 Species Status Assessment (SSA) prepared by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service concluded that the subspecies persists at extremely low abundance, with the best available data indicating fewer than 50 individuals remain (USFWS 2024i). The population is confined to a single, isolated habitat patch, representing a significant contraction from its historical range. Genetic diversity is presumed to be severely reduced, increasing the risk of inbreeding depression and limiting adaptive potential. The SSA determined that the population has experienced a long-term decline with no evidence of recovery or expansion. Surveys and monitoring efforts have consistently documented low detection rates, suggesting that the subspecies is at imminent risk of extirpation. The decline is attributed to multiple interacting stressors, including habitat degradation, disturbance and fragmentation, predation and alteration of weather.

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and the Proposed Action

The Peñasco least chipmunk ( _Neotamias minimus atristriatus_ ) had critical habitat designated simultaneously with the Endangered listing date effective January 2025 (89 FR 99656). The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service listed the subspecies as endangered and concurrently designated approximately 4,386 acres (1,774 hectares) of critical habitat in Lincoln County, New Mexico, within the Lincoln National Forest. This designation encompasses the chipmunk’s remaining occupied range and is intended to protect native meadow and ponderosa pine forest habitats essential for survival. One of the smallest chipmunks, the Peñasco least chipmunk uses mature conifers to provide shade and protection from overhead predators as it forages on seeds and flowers in meadows and other openings in subalpine forests. All of the designated critical habitat for the Peñasco least chipmunk (100%) is on federal lands, specifically within the Lincoln National Forest managed by the U.S. Forest Service. However, there are no roadless areas in the affected environment in this critical habitat.

#### Effects of Roads

The 2024 Species Status Assessment did not identify roads as a primary driver of decline compared to grazing, ski resort operations, feral hogs, drought, and wildfire (USFWS 2024i). There are no documented cases of direct mortality from vehicle strikes in this species however, roads may contribute to habitat fragmentation, disturbance, and reduced connectivity in the chipmunk’s already restricted range. Road construction and maintenance can degrade native meadow and ponderosa pine understory habitats, increase edge effects, and facilitate human access that elevates predation and competition pressures. Roads also act as barriers to dispersal, further isolating the small population and limiting gene flow. Studies of small mammals in western forests have shown that road networks reduce movement across landscapes, increase mortality risk from vehicles, and alter predator–prey dynamics by providing travel corridors for predators. Research on chipmunks and other sciurids indicates sensitivity to habitat fragmentation, with reduced occupancy in areas near roads and disturbed corridors.

The 2024 Species Status Assessment did not identify timber harvest or logging as a primary driver of the species decline (USFWS 2024i). However, timber harvest activities can negatively affect the chipmunk’s habitat by reducing old growth ponderosa pine stands and associated native grassland understory that historically supported the subspecies in the Sacramento Mountains. Logging can fragment meadows and forest openings, alter canopy structure, and diminish the parklike understory conditions that provide food and cover. Increased human access associated with timber harvest may further exacerbate disturbance and predation risks. While not highlighted as a major threat, timber harvest can contribute to habitat degradation and reduced resiliency, compounding the species’ vulnerability given its already small population size and restricted distribution.

#### Existing Protections

Because all designated habitat occurs on U.S. Forest Service lands, habitat will also be subject to management guidelines under the Lincoln National Forest Land Management plan (1986) and amendments (USFS 2025a). At the state level, the New Mexico Department of Game and Fish recognizes the subspecies as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need, providing additional monitoring and coordination with federal agencies.

#### Critical Habitat Determination

Given that no critical habitat overlaps with the proposed action area the Forest Service has determined there will be No Effect to designated critical habitat for this species.

#### Effects Determination

Exposure data on species occurrence are insufficient for assessment so we will assume potential exposure. However, given the limited spatial extent of the population and that area does not overlap with the affected environment exposure is likely low. As the impacts of roads or timber on this species are mostly indirect and not identified as major stressors, combined with low exposure to the affected environment, we determine that the proposed action is not likely to adversely affect this species.

#### _Mount Graham Red Squirrel_

The Mount Graham red squirrel _(Tamiasciurus fremonti grahamensis)_ was listed as endangered subspecies in 1987 (52 FR 20994). The results from a census in 2023 suggest that there were 144 individuals (USFWS 2024j). This is a decline from the 200-300 squirrels that were documented consistently from 2000-2016, but an improvement from the 35 individuals that were estimated following the 2017 Frye Fire, which burned much of the squirrel’s habitat (Merrick et al. 2021; USFWS 2024j). Midden surveys suggest that the species had previously experienced a decline in the mid-1990s to early 2000s associated with loss of spruce-fir habitat from wildfires and fire suppression activities (USFWS 2011b). The Mount Graham squirrel is genetically distinct and isolated from other red squirrels and the dramatic decline in population after the Frye fire suggests a recent population bottleneck (USFWS 2024j).

Exposure to the Proposed Action and the Proposed Action Area

The Mount Graham squirrel lives in a very restricted habitat in the Pinaleño Mountains of southeastern Arizona (52 FR 20994) in the Safford Ranger District of the Coronado National Forest. It occurs in mature mixed conifer and spruce-fir forest above 8,000 feet and requires full forest canopy cover (USFWS 2011b). The 2024 SSA reported that due to widespread habitat loss there are currently about 6,400 acres of squirrel habitat remaining, 34 of which is spruce-fir forest. Critical habitat for the squirrel was designated in 1990 (55 FR 425) and approximately 41% of it occurs in IRAs and of that critical habitat, 76% of it is classified as operable or operable but complex.

Our initial evaluation of squirrel occurrence records (in NRM and GBIF) was not informative because there are only 2 observations of the species in this dataset. However, given the extensive overlap of designated CH there are likely more individuals present within the action area. We ran a custom analysis overlaying squirrel habitat (USGS 2018) with the footprint of inventoried roadless areas and the Frye Fire to evaluate potential exposure. The proportion of total squirrel habitat (pre-fire) that overlapped with the proposed action was ~ 16.3%.  However, approximately 77% of modeled squirrel habitat burned in the Frye Fire. If roadless areas were to be affected by the proposed action, the total proportion of squirrel habitat affected by the Frye Fire or inventoried roadless areas is ~82.2%. Of the habitat that was not in the Frye Fire footprint, approximately 22.8% is inventoried roadless. This analysis does not consider burn severity and the potential for squirrel habitat to remain within the Frye Fire footprint.

#### Effects of Roads

Roads have the potential to impact Mount Graham red squirrels through direct mortality, loss of habitat, and behavioral avoidance. There is no systematic data collection of direct mortality, however 14 road-killed squirrels have been reported incidentally between 1987 and the early 2020s (USFWS 2024j). Openings created by roads may also increase vulnerability of squirrels to avian predators (Chen and Koprowski 2016a).

Squirrels avoid crossing roads (Chen and Koprowski 2016a) and move more quickly while crossing than immediately before or after (Chen and Koprowski 2016b). Interestingly probability of crossing was not related to traffic volume, but gaps in tree cover (<50%) created by roads, may lead to crossing avoidance (Chen & Koprowski 2016a). Squirrel occupancy of middens exposed to higher levels of traffic noise was also lower than middens in quieter environments (Chen and Koprowski 2015). This avoidance may be particularly impactful during reproduction as squirrels cross roads more often during the mating season and when there are larger number of mates on the opposite side of the road (Chen and Koprowski 2016a). Squirrels may also be negatively impacted if roads lead to increased human caused wildfires that cause habitat loss.

Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

While Mount Graham red squirrels are negatively affected by tree removal, they are also negatively affected by loss of habitat from high severity wildfire. Tree removal from selective thinning, harvest, or prescribed burning can result in loss of habitat, food resources, and protection from aerial predators (USFWS 2024j).

However, high severity fires can also severely impact red squirrels. In the Nuttall-Gibson Complex Fire 35% of marked squirrels within the burn perimeter were never relocated and 75% of middens within the perimeter were destroyed (Koprowski et al. 2006). 31% of surviving squirrels within the burn perimeter abandoned middens within 2 weeks of the fire- all were within areas with intensive crown fire (Koprowski et al. 2006). In the days following the Frye Fire, squirrel survivorship was lower than expected, potentially due to increased avian predation (Merrick et al. 2021). 31% of squirrel habitat was lost in the 2017 Frye Fire, and substantial amounts of habitat was lost from other disturbance events prior to that (Merrick et al. 2021).

These data suggest that Mount Graham red squirrels may benefit from carefully planned forest management approaches that reduce the risk of high intensity wildfire, while maintaining sufficient canopy cover.

#### Existing Protections

The Arizona-Idaho Conservation Act of 1989 and the Coronado National Forest land management plan are important vehicles for the conservation of Mount Graham red squirrels. The conservation act established the Mount Graham Astrophysical and Biological Research Area, which is ~2,900 acres of land encompassing an astrological observatory and the Mount Graham Red Squirrel Refugium, which focuses on research for red squirrels and spruce-fir.

The Coronado National Forest land management plan has several components that address conservation of Mount Graham Red Squirrels (available at USFS 2025a). It identifies that a desired condition for the biological research area is habitat for the red squirrel and that “management activities do not degrade these special habitats.” The standard for this area is that “within habitat for the Mount Graham red squirrel, no new recreational residence or developed recreation areas will be established” and guidelines advise that red squirrel habitat needs “should supersede the needs of all other species of plants and animals”, that hiking levels should not negatively impact individual squirrels or their habitat, and that vegetation treatments “should be designed and implemented to avoid disturbance of ... squirrel middens.” Another standard for a forest treatment objective states that “vegetation treatments should be designed to create stand conditions that enhance cone production of white fir, corkbark fir, Engelmann spruce, and Douglas-fir in order to provide a reliable Mount Graham red squirrel food source.”

#### Critical Habitat Determination

Critical habitat for the squirrel was designated in 1990 (55 FR 425). When critical habitat was designated, it was determined that selected areas “contain major concentrations of the Mount Graham red squirrel, and the habitat necessary to its survival, including cover, food sources, nest sites, and midden sites. The winter survival of the red squirrel depends primarily on the availability of seeds of cones stored in middens. Therefore, an environment in which the middencached cones will stay cool and moist, and be prevented from opening and losing their seeds, is of critical importance. Such an environment is most often found in dense, shady forest above 10,000 feet (3,048 meters) and at lower elevations on north-facing slopes or in protected pockets and small basins (Spicer et al. 1985).”

Approximately 41% of squirrel critical habitat occurs in IRAs and of that critical habitat, 76% of it is classified as operable or operable but complex. Given that a large portion of the habitat is exposed to the proposed action, the exposure level is high. Given the importance of cones and shady forest for critical habitat, the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species **.**

#### Effects Determination

A considerable proportion of pre-fire and post-fire squirrel habitat that is inventoried roadless. Given the impacts of roads on squirrels and the importance of forested vegetation, the Forest Service has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species. Given overlap and the importance of cones and shady forest for critical habitat, the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species **.**

#### _New Mexico meadow jumping mouse_

The New Mexico meadow jumping mouse _(Zapus hudsonius luteus)_ is a subspecies of jumping mice that was listed as endangered in 2014 (79 FR 33119). The approximate population size has not been measured directly (USFWS 2020c). Habitat loss is the major threat facing the subspecies. As its habitat is currently quite fragmented and is likely to become more so, lack of connectivity is a threat to their persistence. The viability of the subspecies was described as compromised in the near term at the time of listing (79 FR 33119).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

This subspecies is found in Arizona, New Mexico and small portions of Colorado. It has specific habitat requirements, thriving in tall and dense herbaceous vegetation in riparian habitat corridors with perennial or seasonal flowing water (USFWS 2020c). It also requires nearby upland habitat for foraging and other activities (USFWS 2020c).

The species is thought to occur on the Apache-Sitgreaves, Gila, Lincoln, Rio Grande, San Juan, and Santa Fe National Forests. It might occur on the Comanche National Grassland and Pike and San Isabel National Forest though confirmation is needed.

Critical habitat was designated for the subspecies in 2016 (81 FR 14263). Approximately 0.79% of critical habitat for the subspecies occurs in inventoried roadless areas, of that 28% is considered operable or operable but complex. In the NRM and GBIF databases there are eight occurrences of the subspecies in inventoried roadless areas, of which five occur in operable or operable but complex environments. Given the opportunistic nature of most occurrence data, we conducted a supplementary analysis overlaying the USFWS species range with inventoried roadless affected by the proposed action and found that 1.8% of the species’ range occurred in these areas.

#### Effects of Roads

Roads can have a number of direct and indirect effects on the subspecies. In addition to direct loss of habitat during construction, soil erosion, mowing, and flooding from inappropriately size culverts could all cause habitat loss (USFWS 2020c). Debris flows from small landslides during heavy rain events also have the potential to modify water flow in jumping mouse habitat (USFWS 2020c). Habitat can also become fragmented due to road construction creating a barrier to movement, although there is at least one individual jumping mouse that was observed to cross a gravel road (USFWS 2020c). The potential for sedimentation from dirt roads to influence New Mexico meadow jumping mouse was noted in the listing decision (79 FR 33119), however at the time the Services noted that they did not have data to evaluate this risk.

If human use of riparian habitat increased due to increased road access, this could increase the negative effects of dispersed camping, OHV use, and dispersed hiking on jumping mouse habitat (USFWS 2020c).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Timber harvest upstream has the potential to affect the riparian habitats used by this subspecies by modifying waterflows to downstream habitat (USFWS 2020c). Historically this has affected the subspecies in portions of its range (USFWS 2020c).

Fire is considered a threat to the species and the listing decision notes that “following fires, we found that, depending on fire intensity and the subsequent ash and debris flow within stream reaches, New Mexico meadow jumping mouse populations can be significantly affected and likely extirpated, even when 15 km (9 mi) of continuous suitable habitat existed prior to the fire” (79 FR 33119). The 2020 SSA notes that activities to reduce the risk of high severity wildfire in headwaters to jumping mouse habitat may reduce the risk of fire on the species (USFWS 2020c). At the same time prescribed fire, in the wrong place, can be detrimental to the species. At the time of listing, the Services noted that “unauthorized modification or manipulation of riparian habitat, including mowing or prescribed burning of occupied habitats, especially during the active season” would constitute a violation of Section 9 of the ESA (79 FR 33119).

#### Existing Protections

The jumping mouse is mentioned multiple times in the Apache Sitgreaves National Forest Plan and there are components of the forest plan that protect the species. For example, one forest guideline is that “the needs of localized species (e.g., New Mexico meadow jumping mouse, Bebb willow, White Mountains paintbrush) should be considered and provided for during project activities to ensure their limited or specialized habitats are not lost or degraded” (2015 ApacheSitgreaves NFs land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Another desired condition that applies to the whole forest states that “floodplains and adjacent upland areas provide diverse habitat components (e.g., vegetation, debris, logs) as necessary for migration, hibernation, and brumation (extended inactivity) specific to the needs of riparian-obligate species (e.g., New Mexico meadow jumping mouse, Arizona montane vole, narrow-headed gartersnake)” (2015 Apache-Sitgreaves NFs land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). There are no forest plan components specific to the jumping mouse in the Santa Fe Forest Plan (2022 Santa Fe NF land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). This illustrates the variety of existing protection for the jumping mouse in different jurisdictions.

#### Critical Habitat Determination

The primary constituent elements of jumping mouse habitat identified in the critical habitat designation are:

- “1) Riparian communities along rivers and streams, springs and wetlands, or canals and ditches that contain:

- a) Persistent emergent herbaceous wetlands especially characterized by presence of primarily forbs and sedges ( _Carex_ spp. or _Schoenoplectus pungens_ ); or

- b) Scrub-shrub riparian areas that are composed of willows (Salix spp.) or alders (Alnus spp.) with an understory of primarily forbs and sedges; and

- 2) Flowing water that provides saturated soils throughout the New Mexico meadow jumping mouse’s active season that supports tall (average stubble height of herbaceous vegetation of at least 61 cm (24 in)) and dense herbaceous riparian vegetation composed primarily of sedges ( _Carex_ spp. or _Schoenoplectus pungens_ ) and forbs, including, but not limited to one or more of the following associated species: spikerush ( _Eleocharis macrostachya_ ), beaked sedge ( _Carex rostrata_ ), rushes ( _Juncus_ spp. and _Scirpus_ spp.), and numerous species of grasses such as bluegrass ( _Poa_ spp.), slender wheatgrass ( _Elymus trachycaulus_ ), brome ( _Bromus_ spp.), foxtail barley ( _Hordeum jubatum_ ), or Japanese brome ( _Bromus japonicas_ ), and forbs such as water hemlock ( _Circuta douglasii_ ), field mint ( _Mentha arvense_ ), asters ( _Aster_ spp.), or cutleaf coneflower ( _Rudbeckia laciniata_ ); and

- 3) Sufficient areas of 9 to 24 kilometers (5.6 to 15 miles) along a stream, ditch, or canal that contains suitable or restorable habitat to support movements of individual New Mexico meadow jumping mice; and

- 4) Adjacent floodplain and upland areas extending approximately 100 m (330 ft) outward from the boundary between the active water channel and the floodplain (as defined by the bankfull stage of streams) or from the top edge of the ditch or canal.” (81 FR 14264)

Approximately 0.79% of critical habitat for the subspecies occurs in inventoried roadless areas, and of that 28% is considered operable or operable but complex. Given the sensitivity of habitat to any action that alter waterflow, even actions that occur at a distance from the critical habitat itself, the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species, however we do not expect those effects to be widespread **.**

#### Effects Determination

Given that 1.8% of the species’ range occurs in areas affected by the proposed action, the FS has determined that exposure is high. Given the susceptibility of the subspecies to activities that modify waterflow to riparian areas, the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect this species. Given the sensitivity of habitat to any action that alter waterflow, even actions that occur at a distance from the critical habitat itself, the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species, however we do not expect those effects to be widespread **.**

#### _Preble’s meadow jumping mouse_

The Preble’s meadow jumping mouse ( _Zapus hudsonius preblei_ ) (“Preble’s mouse”) was listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act in 1998 (63 FR 26517). In 2001, a rule was published to clarify some circumstances when “take” might be acceptable (e.g., certain agricultural practices, rodent control, structure modifications, and water rights situations, 66 FR 28125). Critical habitat was finalized in 2010 (75 FR 78430), and current conservation actions are informed by a Recovery Plan (USFWS 2018b).

Current population trends are uncertain in Wyoming, and at the time the Recovery Plan was written, it was not clear whether existing survey data were adequate to determine mouse occupancy and distribution in Wyoming (USFWS 2018b). However, the Recovery Plan describes clear population targets within two recovery units and outlines future research and information that would support delisting efforts (USFWS 2018b). The primary threat to the Preble’s mouse is habitat loss and degradation resulting from residential development, commercial development, and agricultural conversion (63 FR 26517).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

The Preble’s mouse inhabits densely vegetated riparian areas of the high plains spanning southeastern Wyoming to south-central Colorado (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2018). This mouse depends on wet grasslands, riparian shrublands, and near-stream habitats (63 FR 26517), inhabiting a relatively restricted area of the landscape that is very closely tied to riparian areas (USFWS 2018b). Areas used by the Preble’s mouse usually have multi-layer canopies of woodland and herbaceous vegetation and high volumes of litter that the mice can use for burrowing and nesting (63 FR 26517). These mice have also been found in irrigation ditches, road ditches, and wetlands near highways, and it is possible that these types of adjacent habitats provide individuals with dispersal opportunities (63 FR 26517).

At the time of listing, the Preble’s mouse inhabited two counties in Wyoming and seven counties in Colorado, but historical records show that its range was previously broader in both states (63 FR 26517). Critical habitat was designated in Colorado in in 2010 (75 FR 78430), but no critical habitat has been designated in Wyoming (USFWS 2018b). The designated critical habitat encompasses 34,935 acres including 411 miles of rivers and streams in seven Colorado counties (75 FR 78430), including on the Arapaho-Roosevelt and the Pike San Isabel National Forests (75 FR 78430).

The Preble’s mouse digs to create nests belowground, is mostly crepuscular or nocturnal, and hibernates in riparian areas from October through May (63 FR 26517, USFWS 2018b). Their specific diet is uncertain, but it likely eats seeds, fruits, fungus, and insects (63 FR 26517). The Preble’s mouse may need an open water source for drinking which could explain its close ties to streams and rivers, and at least one study has indicated that trapping success decreased after a seasonal stream stopped flowing (63 FR 26517).

There are only nine observations of the species in the NRM and GBIF databases in Wyoming, making these data insufficient to draw conclusions about the relative exposure of the species to the proposed action. We ran a supplementary analysis overlaying the USFWS range of the species with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action. The overlap is less than 0.005%.

#### Effects of Roads

The effects of roads on the Preble’s mouse are likely negative. The initial listing decision stated, “Roads, trails, or other linear development through Preble’s [mouse] habitat may act as barriers to movement,” and emphasized that maintaining dispersal corridors between habitat patches is likely important (63 FR 26517). The Recovery Plan also noted that vehicle accidents in riparian areas can pose a risk of fuel and chemical spills that could contaminate important areas of riparian habitat (USFWS 2018b).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

The effects of timber production on the Preble’s mouse would likely be negative if they were to occur within areas surrounding important habitat areas. There is at least one example of commercial timber production being restricted from an area to protect Preble’s mouse habitat (75 FR 78430), but timber production is not listed as a concern in the Recovery Plan (USFWS 2018b). However, given that the Preble’s mouse uses areas with multi-layered vegetation including trees, changes to vegetation structure and ground disturbance in riparian areas are expected to negatively impact Preble’s mouse habitat.

#### Existing Protections

The proposed action overlaps with the Medicine Bow National Forest, which contains standards and guidelines specific to the Preble’s meadow jumping mouse (2003 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). These include guidelines specific to road construction, such as “In suitable habitat within the range of the Preble's meadow jumping mouse, avoid placing new recreation sites, trails or roads within the riparian zone. Existing roads in designated critical habitat will be reviewed for possible closure or Relocation" (2003 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). There are also guidelines about the way that vegetation management actions, such as prescribed fire, can be implemented in the species’ habitat and for surveys for listed species during project planning.

#### Critical Habitat Determination

There is no critical habitat in the proposed action area; therefore, the FS has determined there would be No Effect.

#### Effects Determination

Given that less than 0.005% of the species’ range that intersects with IRAs in the proposed action area, the exposure of the species to the action is low. While there are some potential impacts of roads and timber on this species and its habitat, the Medicine Bow National Forest plan has standards and guidelines that shape how these activities can occur. Given this, the FS has determined the proposed activity is not likely to adversely affect this species.

### Carnivores

#### _Gray wolf_

The gray wolf was first listed throughout the contiguous United States under the Endangered Species Preservation Act of 1969 (38 FR 14678), a predecessor to the ESA. The listing status of gray wolves in the U.S. is complex, with numerous revisions to listable units and their listing status (see Ward 2020 for a review of wolf regulatory history in the U.S.). In February 2024, FWS published a 12-month finding that concluded (1) the Northern Rocky Mountain DPS no longer constitutes a valid listable entity, and (2) that the Western United States is a valid DPS but does not meet the definition of threatened or endangered (89 FR 8391). In August 2025, the finding was partially vacated by a federal judge and FWS was ordered to reconsider the relisting petition for the delisted Northern Rocky Mountain region (NRMR). Currently, gray wolves in the United States (excepting the Mexican wolf subspecies, considered separately below) have one of the four listing statuses depending on geographic region:

1. Delisted due to recovery in the Northern Rocky Mountain region (Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, eastern Washington and Oregon, and a small portion of north-central Utah (74 FR 15123)

2. Nonessential and experimental in Colorado (88 FR 77014)

3. Threatened in Minnesota (43 FR 9607)

4. Endangered in the remainder contiguous states, sometimes referred to as the “44-entity”

Wolves in the western U.S. have generally increased in abundance and expanded in distribution since their reintroduction in the 1990s (USFWS 2023c). According to state wildlife agencies, the per state abundance estimates for delisted populations in 2022 were as follows: Idaho (958), Montana (1,087), Wyoming (338), Washington (inside the NRMR = 159; outside the NRMR 57), and Oregon (inside the NRMR = 140, outside the NRMR 38), and California (18). In the winter of 2021, approximately 2,700 wolves were estimated to be present in the state of Minnesota (MNDNR 2022) and 1,126 in Wisconsin (WIDNR 2023).  Abundance estimates are collected by state agencies using varying methods with different biases and degrees of precision (USFWS 2023c).

Connectivity is considered important to the ability of wolves to recolonize vacant but suitable habitat and maintain demographic resilience. Excepting the Mexican wolf subspecies and the isolated population in Isle Royale National Park, North American gray wolves generally exhibit high levels of genetic diversity and low levels of population differentiation (USFWS 2023c). Range-wide genetic analyses support relatively high rates of effective dispersal and gene flow, suggesting metapopulation dynamics are being maintained under current conditions (USFWS 2023c).

The FWS deems the primary stressor to wolf populations as human-caused mortality, which includes regulated harvest in the NRMR, illegal take outside of the NRMR, and lethal control of wolves depredating livestock (USFWS 2023c). Human-caused mortality was the main factor responsible for decline that led to initial listing and accounts for 60 to 80 percent of total mortalities in the coterminous U.S now (USFWS 2023c, Hill et al. 2022, Morales-González et al. 2025). Determination of how much human-caused mortality can be tolerated without affecting population viability is complex and long-contested in the scientific literature, depending not only on the total mortality rate but also the degree to which mortality is compensatory or additive in nature (see USFWS 2023c for literature review of compensatory dynamics). Other potential stressors to population resiliency include episodic disease outbreaks, inbreeding depression, disease in prey species, and other sources of habitat modification, such as human development and wildfire (USFWS 2023c).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

Gray wolves are habitat generalists that successfully occupy a wide range of environments. The two principal factors limiting their distribution in the U.S. are density of large ungulate prey and human-caused mortality (USFWS 2023c). Accordingly, gray wolf presence is positively correlated with Federal land ownership and forest cover and is negatively correlated with the density of roads and humans (Mladenoff et al. 1995, Carroll et al. 2006, Oakleaf et al. 2006). National forests accounted for approximately 52% of the occupied range for wolves of the western U.S. in 2023 (USFWS 2023c). Large areas of modeled wolf habitat exist that are currently unoccupied or in early stages of recolonization exist that could theoretically support wolves and contribute to range-wide recovery (Carroll et al. 2001, Carroll et al. 2003, Mladenoff and Sickley 1998, van den Bosch et al. 2022). Critical habitat was designated in Minnesota and Isle Royale, Michigan in 1978 (43 FR 9607) but no critical habitat has been designated in the western states. Approximately 1% of the Minnesota critical habitat overlaps with potentially affected IRAs, and of that approximately 89% is in areas classified as operable or operable but complex. Of gray wolf occurrence data in the NRM and GBIF databases, 571 occurrence records occur in IRAs, 59% of them in regions that are operable or operable but complex. Since there are both threatened and endangered wolves, which are not differentiated in the occurrence analysis, we ran analyses overlaying the threatened and endangered ranges with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action. Approximately 0.002% of the Minnesota threatened gray wolf range is affected by the proposed action, whereas approximately 4.2% of the range of the “44entity”(the endangered population) is affected by the proposed action.

#### Effects of Roads

Roads have mixed effects on gray wolves at the individual level. Roads negatively affect wolves by increasing mortality and degrading habitat quality and cause positive effects by increasing hunting efficiency for ungulate prey. At the population level, roads have the potential to inhibit population growth and recolonization of new areas.

#### _Mortality_

Roads expose wolves to human-caused mortality directly through vehicle collisions and indirectly by increasing risk of illegal killings due to more frequent human encounters.

Vehicle strikes contribute to wolf mortality but rank well below other sources of anthropogenic mortality, such as lethal control and illegal killings (Tables S2,S3; Morales-González et al. 2025). In a study of 711 collared wolves (1982-2004) in the NRMR prior to de-listing, 18 wolves (2.5% of all wolves, 5.0% of known mortalities) died from vehicle strikes (Murray et al. 2010). A study of wolves across four National Parks found that vehicle strikes accounted for 5.9% of total mortalities and 9% of human-caused mortalities (Cassidy et al. 2023). In Wisconsin, between 1979 and 2012, vehicle strikes were estimated to account for 13% of mortalities (Treves et al. 2017a). A meta-analysis of mortality data from studies across Europe and North America found that mortalities increase as the density of roads increase (Morales-González et al. 2025). However, none of these mortality studies distinguished between strikes that occurred on paved, high traffic roads and unpaved, secondary or forest roads.

Illegal killing is one of the highest sources of mortality for gray wolves and has the potential to significantly alter population dynamics. In the NRMR prior to delisting, 24% of known mortalities were attributed to illegal killings (Smith et al. 2010). Other studies have found illegal killings accounted for between 5 and 12 percent of the known wolf population in the NRM (Smith et al. 2010, Murray et al. 2010, Ausband et al. 2017, Stenglein et al. 2018). The true rate of illegal killing is almost certainly higher, after also accounting for collared wolves with unknown fates or unknown causes of mortality (Treves et al. 2017b, Liberg et al. 2012, Liberg et al. 2020).

Roads increase susceptibility to illegal killings by acting as points of access for humans that increase their encounter rates with wolves. Multiple studies have found lower rates of illegal killings in areas associated with low road density and low human presence (Fritts et al. 2003, Smith et al. 2010, O’Neil et al. 2017, Simpson et al. 2023) but generally have been challenged to tease apart road access from other confounding factors, such as proximity to livestock, private land, and human settlements. However, a wolf mortality study centered on the Superior National Forest from 1968 to 2018 found that wolves in wilderness areas had fewer mortalities from illegal killings than non-wilderness wolves, providing strong evidence that increased human access from trails and roads was responsible for the difference (Barber-Meyer et al. 2021). In contrast, a meta-analysis of mortality patterns from 21 studies in North America (12 in the conterminous U.S.) found no significant effect of road density on mortality due to illegal killing (Hill et al. 2022). Authors were surprised and suggested this may in part be explained by varying conditions and context-specific effects, such as differing spatial scales and regional densities of roads. As an example of the latter, a study of wolves on the Tongass National Forest found that the rate of wolf harvest (in this case, pooled legal and illegal mortality) increased with density of roads when overall road density was low (<0.9 km/km2) but had no additional effect on harvest rates when road density was higher (Person and Russel 2008).

_Displacement and Inhibition of Recolonization_

Wolves can clearly tolerate living in areas with high road densities and dense human settlement, as evidenced by recolonization of densely populated regions in Europe. Less understood is the degree that long-term occupancy in areas with higher rates of human encounters is sustained by inputs from remote or largely inaccessible regions. Like designated wilderness, roadless areas may act as refugia from human mortality, helping stabilize demography in areas with more development and foster recolonization of suitable but vacant habitat (Mech 1989, Haight et al. 1998, Mladenoff et al. 1999; Person and Russel 2008, Barber-Meyer et al. 2021).

Most studies conducted at broader spatial scales (e.g., home range and larger) agree that wolf occupancy is negatively correlated with road density (Thiel 1985, Mech et al. 1988, Mladenoff et al. 1995).  Construction of new roads could negatively affect gray wolf recovery by slowing or inhibiting recolonization of vacant but suitable areas. A global meta-analysis of data from throughout Eurasia and North America found that reproductive dens and rendezvous sites are located significantly farther from roads than random points (Saztornil et al. 2016). However, this meta-analysis lumped forest roads with highways and other paved roads; when only main roads were considered, the avoidance was stronger, suggesting paved roads were driving much of the global signal. Telemetry studies of recolonizing wolves have shown that new territories are preferentially established in areas with low road density, but that affinity for low road density relaxes as wolves proliferate. For example, analysis of territory locations for 56 recolonizing packs in Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming in the early 2000s found that both overall territories as well as core use areas had a significantly lower density of 2-wheel and 4-wheel drive roads relative to the surrounding environment (Oakleaf et al. 2006). Similarly, in northern Wisconsin and upper Michigan, a telemetry study of 14 packs found that territories mostly consisted of areas with a density of paved and unpaved roads <0.45 km/km2 and no portion of any territory area had a road density >1.0 km/km2 (Mladenoff et al. 1995). Habitat models parameterized with this relationship correctly predicted the location of early re-colonizing packs in Wisconsin (18 of 23; Mladenoff et al. 1999) but failed to predict pack locations in later years when wolves occupied a broader range of habitat type (Mech 2006). Additional analyses encompassing the first 28 years of re-establishment in Wisconsin showed that wolves in marginal habitat—defined as regions with higher road density, lower amounts of federal land, and higher proportions of agricultural land—had lower reproductive output and higher human-caused mortality than habitat with low road density, high proportions of federal land, and low proportions of agriculture  (Simpson et al. 2023). The study, however, did not distinguish the effects of roads relative to land ownership and human use categories.

#### _Habitat degradation_

Wolves, like all wildlife, presumably select for habitat types and landscapes that maximize their fitness. In theory, evaluating how wolves select or avoid roads offers insight into how the presence of roads affects habitat quality for wolves. In practice, evidence shows that the behavioral response of gray wolves to roads is complex and highly contextual, depending on attributes of the road, its surrounding environment, the individual wolf, time of day and year, and the physical scale of inference.

Studies generally agree that roads and other linear features facilitate wolf movements and allow wolves to travel at faster speeds, but the interpretation of this response has varied by context (McKenzie et al. 2012, Zimmerman et al. 2014, Dickie et al. 2017, Dickie et al. 2020). In the boreal forests of Canada, where there is a dense network of logging roads and seismic lines, greater speed allows for longer distances traveled per day (McKenzie et al. 2012, Zimmerman et al. 2014, Dickie et al. 2017, Dickie et al. 2020), which in turn increases search and encounter rates for ungulate prey (Whittington et al. 2011). In this scenario unpaved forest roads may confer a slight fitness advantage to wolves. Yet in areas with a more extensive human footprint, such as near towns or in areas with significant recreation, faster travel has instead been interpreted as a response to increased risk from humans (Dickie et al. 2017, Whittington et al.

2022). In this case, the loss of important "slow state" movements such as resting, foraging, and reproduction, may represent a fitness loss and degradation of habitat quality.

Many studies have demonstrated that wolves use roads frequently (e.g., St-Pierre et al. 2022, Dickie et al. 2017, Dickie et al. 2020, Zimmerman et al. 2014, Muhly et al. 2019). However, the direction and strength of selection for roads within a home range varies widely depending on road characteristics. First, wolves vary their response to roads based on the amount of human use of a given road (Thurber et al. 1994, Bojarska et al. 2020, Dennehy et al. 2021) as well as of the broader surrounding region (Hebblewhite and Merrill 2008). For example, a 3-year study in Alberta used remote cameras to show that use of temporary and gravel roads by wolves increased with low rates of human traffic (<5 vehicles/day) but declined at higher traffic rates (Keim et al. 2019). A study in the vicinity of Kenai National Wildlife Refuge similarly found wolves used secondary roads more than expected by chance but avoided oilfield access roads that received regular traffic and were open year-round (Thurber et al. 1994). Other studies have found wolves temporally adjust their use of roads to avoid peak periods of human activity (Anton et al. 2020, Bojarska et al. 2020, Dennehy et al. 2021).

The behavioral response to roads differs depending on the surrounding road density, with the nature of this functional response also varying by study. Analysis of GPS-locations in Quebec found wolves strongly selected for forest roads in territories where roads occurred in low density, but the strength of positive selection declined as road density increased. (Houle et al. 2010). In contrast, breeding wolves in Scandinavia showed the opposite pattern, in which wolves used gravel roads more often as road density within their home range increased (Zimmerman et al. 2014). In a large study of 172 GPS-collared wolves across multiple Canadian provinces, wolves selected for areas within their home range that had high road density in provinces where the average regional road density was high (for example, >0.075 km/km<sup>2</sup> ), but preferentially chose sites with low road density in provinces where the average regional road density is low (Muhly et al. 2019). Another analysis of 20-years of GPS data from wolves collared in and around Banff National Park found that wolves negatively selected for roads in all contexts, but the avoidance was greatest when road densities were high (Whittington et al. 2022).

Finally, some studies have found no uniform response at the population level, but rather a wide range of individual- or pack-specific responses (Gregovich et al. 2025, Ferreiro-Arias et al. 2024, Anton et al. 2020, Zimmermann et al. 2014). Such lack of uniformity may reflect a wide degree of behavioral plasticity or, alternatively, could be a manifestation of roads exerting opposing effects in different contexts. Regardless, the range of variation observed within and across studies suggests behavioral effects of road construction is likely to be mixed and/or location specific.

Timber/ Vegetation Management

The effects of timber harvest on wolves are predominantly mediated through its influence on ungulate prey and, to a lesser extent, on the human risk landscape. Logging creates early seral forests that provide high-quality forage that attracts deer, elk, and moose and concentrates their distribution (McKay and Finnegan 2023). Simultaneously, the removal of overcanopy can increase sight lines, which along with logging roads, may facilitate prey searching efficiency for wolves (Boucher et al. 2022). Accordingly, many studies in boreal coniferous forests found that wolves select for early regenerating cutblocks, especially those logged within <5 years (Houle et al. 2010, Muhly et al. 2019, Boucher et al. 2022, Johnson-Bice et al. 2023). Other studies have found either no significant habitat selection for regenerating timber harvested areas (Gregovich et al. 2025, Kuzyk et al. 2004) or mixed responses that were mediated by proximity to other types of human disturbance and activity (Lesmerises et al. 2012, Boczulak et al. 2023, Person and Russell 2008). We note that most studies were conducted in the context of large clearcuts in Alaskan or Canadian boreal forest, with considerably less information available on the effects on wolves of other timber harvest practices.

#### Existing Protections

Gray wolves in the United States are protected through a combination of federal, state, Tribal, and land management measures. State regulations for wolf management is varied across the range. For example, in Minnesota, wolves are managed under a state plan that prohibits recreational hunting and trapping, while allowing limited depredation control to protect livestock. In the Northern Rocky Mountains distinct population segment (Idaho, Montana, Wyoming), wolves are managed under state authority following delisting and harvest is permitted subject to established state quotas, but conservation safeguards remain in place such as conflict mitigation strategies such as range riders and carcass removal to reduce livestock conflicts. Conversely, outside of the delisted Northern Rockies DPS in coastal states state regulations emphasize wolf conservation. For example, in Washington state wolves are listed as endangered under state law, and the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife prohibits hunting while implementing a Wolf Conservation and Management Plan that emphasizes recovery zones and nonlethal conflict deterrence. Tribal governments exercise sovereign authority on Tribal lands, such as the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes in Montana, which prohibit wolf hunting on Tribal lands and contribute to regional monitoring. On federal lands, project level decisions must consider wolf impacts under ESA consultation, while state and private lands employ conflict response programs, compensation for verified depredations, and nonlethal deterrents. On Forest Service land, numerous individual forest Land Management Plans also provide additional guidance and protections for gray wolves and their habitat. Collectively, these overlapping protections — ranging from ESA take prohibitions to state population floors and Tribal hunting bans — aim to maintain sustainable wolf populations, reduce human–wildlife conflict, and prevent the need for future federal relisting.

#### Critical Habitat

One percent (1%) of critical habitat is in inventoried roadless areas and of that 89% is in areas that are operable or operable but complex. There are no PBFs for gray wolves; however, given the generalist nature of gray wolves and the primary threat on NFS lands being human conflicts, we determined the proposed activity is not likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species.

#### Effects Determination

A high proportion of gray wolf occurrence records in the NRM and GBIF databases occur in inventoried roadless areas that are operable or operable but complex. However, the exposure of the wolf range to the proposed action differs between the threatened and endangered entities. Due to this difference, the FS has determined that the exposure of the threatened entity to the proposed action is low, whereas the exposure of the endangered entity to the proposed action is high. Despite this difference, there are risks posed to the species by human conflict with increased human access, so the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect both the threatened and endangered entities for this species.

#### _Mexican Wolf_

The Mexican wolf is the southernmost subspecies of gray wolf in North America. It was originally listed in 1976 (41 FR 17736), with reestablishment in the wild in the U.S. in 1998. In 2015 FWS issued a rule to list the Mexican wolf as endangered separately from the gray wolf listing (80 FR 2488). Mexican wolves exist in the wild in the United States in a single introduced population in Arizona and New Mexico south of Interstate 40, designated as the Mexican Wolf Experimental Population Area (MWEPA). Mexican wolves in the MWEPA are accordingly managed as a nonessential experimental population (80 FR 2512, 87 FR 39348) whereas outside the MWEPA they are considered endangered. Mexican wolf conservation strategy is guided by the 2022 Mexican Wolf Recovery Plan, Second Revision (USFWS 2022c).

The experimental population of Mexican wolves is small but steadily growing (USFWS 2017b, USFWS 2024k). In 2023, there were 257 individuals inside the MWEPA (USFWS 2024k). All Mexican wolves today descend from only seven captive founders, resulting in high mean kinship and low genetic diversity, particularly in the wild population where managers have less control over breeding.

The most important biological threats to recovery are 1) excessive human-caused mortality, 2) demographic stochasticity associated with small population size, and 3) loss of genetic diversity and risk of inbreeding depression (USFWS 2017b).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and the Proposed Actions

Highly suitable habitat for Mexican wolves is forested, montane terrain with adequate densities of ungulate prey (elk, white-tailed deer, mule deer) and low density of livestock and human (USFWS 2017b, Martinez-Meyer et al. 2021). National forests make up only 15.5% of the total MWEPA but comprise a disproportionate share of suitable forested habitat: approximately 70% of forest vegetation types in the MWEPA fall on national forest lands (USFWS 2017b, MartinezMeyer et al. 2021). The Service identifies National Forest lands as the most suitable lands for reintroduction and recovery of the Mexican wolf, predominantly due to lower levels of human development and disturbance.

As an experimental population, Mexican wolves do not have designated critical habitat. There are only two records of the species on USFS lands in the NRM and GBIF databases, neither of which are in potentially affected IRAs. Given this low sample size, no meaningful conclusions about the exposure of this species to the action can be drawn based on these data.  We conducted a supplemental analysis overlaying the USFWS ranges of the endangered and experimental populations with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action. The overlap for the endangered population was approximately 1.8% and the overlap for the experimental population was approximately 5.1%.

#### Effects of Roads

The individual effects of roads are expected to be similar to other gray wolves (see above) but carry greater consequences at the level of the population. Low road density is considered a key component of suitable Mexican wolf habitat (USFWS 2017b, Martinez-Meyer et al. 2021). Roads are associated with increased human-caused mortality, either directly from vehicle strikes or indirectly because they act as access points for humans (see gray wolf section). Monitoring data and population viability modeling indicate that adult mortality is a major factor driving population dynamics in the MWEPA, with the potential to slow population growth or cause declines in years when adult mortality is high (USFWS 2017b, Miller 2017, USFWS 2024k). Like other gray wolves, the biggest source of mortality for the Mexican wolf mortality is human caused, predominantly by illegal killings and vehicle collisions. Of 133 mortalities documented between 1998 to 2016, 77 (58%) were attributed to illegal killings and 16 were caused by vehicle strikes (12%) (USFWS 2017b). Human-caused mortalities in the 5 years following 2017 were stable or slightly declining (USFWS 2024k), suggesting management actions to minimize human mortalities outlined in the recovery plan have been effective (USFWS 2024k).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Individual effects of logging are expected to be mixed and highly similar to other gray wolves (see above). Effects that increase ungulate abundance and concentrate their distribution are likely to be positive, whereas effects that increase exposure to human encounters are likely to be negative.

#### Existing Protections

There are some protections for the Mexican wolf in some existing forest plans.
