The ApacheSitgreaves National Forest plan references its commitment to the ESA and a memorandum of understanding for conservation, recovery and persistence of the species (Apache-Sitgreaves, 2015).  The Cibola National Forest, where the wolf is known to forage but not den, states that it will work with the USFWS to aid recovery for listed species like the Mexican wolf in both the experimental and non-experimental range (2022 Cibola NF land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). There are no mentions of the Mexican wolf in the Coconino National Forest Plan (2018) or Kaibab National Forest Plan (2014) or Gila National Forest Plan (1986; available at USFS 2025a.

#### Effects Determination

Given the overlap of both population’s ranges with inventoried roadless areas, we have assigned an exposure level of high to both experimental and endangered populations. Given the potential for roads to bring humans and Mexican wolves into greater conflict, the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect Mexican wolves. This determination is made for both experimental and threatened populations.

#### _North American wolverine_

The North American wolverine ( _Gulo gulo luscus_ ) was listed as threatened in 2023 (Federal Register 83726) and a recovery plan outline was published that same year. The true population size of wolverines in the contiguous United States is not known, but estimates based on habitat modeling place it at approximately 300 individuals (Inman et al. 2013). Trends in this population are also unknown, although work in a wolverine population in southwestern Canada suggests a decline of 41% between 2011 and 2020 (Barrueto et al. 2022). The impacts of this decline on wolverines in the contiguous United States are not known (USFWS 2023d), although the 2023 wolverine listing decision notes that “connectivity with Canada is essential to the long-term viability of North American wolverines in the contiguous United States” citing Cegelski et al. 2006.

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Action

Wolverines in the contiguous United States inhabit small, isolated high-altitude habitats separated from each other by low valleys of less hospitable terrain. Wolverines are known to reproduce in the Northern Rockies of Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming and the Cascade Mountains of Washington (88 FR 83726). Dispersing individuals have been detected in California, Oregon, Utah and Colorado (88 FR 83726) and North Dakota (Rogers 2016). Federal land management decisions are important for wolverine populations in the contiguous United States. Analyses estimate that 96% of wolverine primary habitat identified in Inman et al., 2013 is owned or managed by federal agencies (USFWS 2018c). Critical habitat has not been proposed for this species. Approximately 41% of primary wolverine habitat in the contiguous U.S. is managed as wilderness (USFWS 2018c) and is unaffected by the proposed action.

Of the 137 wolverine detections in inventoried roadless areas, 69 of them were in operable areas or in areas that were classified as operable, but complex in the NRM and GBIF databases.  This analysis places the wolverine in the highest vulnerability category to the proposed action.  This is surprising given that the 2023 listing decision notes that most wolverine reproductive habitat in the contiguous U.S. is rugged and not appropriate for timber harvest. To evaluate whether this analysis was biased due to opportunistic sampling or sampling close to existing infrastructure, we evaluated the proportion of wolverine habitat in the current USFWS range map for the species (USFWS 2026a) that intersected with roadless areas. We found that approximately 10.2% of the range intersects with an inventoried roadless area affected by the proposed action. Given that the spatial extent of the range includes areas that are not wolverine habitat, we would expect that the impact to actual habitat to be higher.

Effects of Roads

The 2023 listing decision for wolverines determined that, in isolation, roads could have negative impacts on individuals, but in combination with other stressors, roads and high road densities could negatively impact population “resilience, distribution and gene flow” (Federal Register 83726). Previous research has found that roads are a mortality risk for wolverines (summarized in USFWS 2018c; Scrafford et al. 2024). Between 2018 and 2023, the USFWS became aware of 4 wolverine mortalities near roads in the contiguous United States (USFWS 2023d)

encompassing both interstates and smaller state roads. Mortalities may be biased towards young dispersing males (USFWS 2023d).

Even though roads are not an absolute barrier to wolverine movement, roads can lead to behavioral avoidance and changes in habitat usage by wolverines. Work by Scrafford et al. 2018 in Alberta, suggests that in summer wolverines “avoid roads, increase speed near roads, and increase speed more near roads with greater traffic volumes.” Several studies have suggested that there is a negative relationship between roads and wolverine distribution or occupancy, although the mechanism behind this relationship is unknown (Rowland et al. 2003, Bowman et al. 2010; Kortello et al. 2019; Mowat et al. 2020; Chow-Fraser et al. 2022; Schepens et al. 2023). Degradation of wolverine habitat quality can occur with the presence of roads even when they have low traffic volume (Scrafford et al. 2018). Wolverine den sites may be located away from roads, but it is unclear whether this is due to available denning habitat or avoidance of roads (USFWS 2023d). Hausleitner et al. 2024 reviewed the literature and found that the distance between recorded wolverine dens and roads varied across studies with some reporting distances as low as 1km from smaller industrial roads or as high as 17 km from major highways.

Overall wolverines are characterized as having “low” tolerance of human disturbance (88 FR 83726) and the construction of new roads may affect wolverines indirectly by increasing access by human recreationists. Wolverines appear to be sensitive to both motorized and non-motorized human recreation (Heinemeyer et al. 2019, Barrueto et al. 2022; Kortello et al. 2019). In some instances, these interactions may be mediated by roads, as one study found that wolverine distribution is negatively correlated with forest roads used by winter snowmachines (Kortello et al. 2019). Females may be especially sensitive to recreational disturbance (Heinemeyer et al. 2019). While lethal trapping of wolverine is prohibited in the contiguous United States, increased road access may affect incidental bycatch of wolverine from trappers legally trapping wolves in Montana (USFWS 2023d), although the likelihood of this is unknown. From 2012-2023, 10 wolverines have been trapped in Montana incidentally and reported, with 3 events resulting in mortality (88 FR 83726).

Increased access by humans may also lead to increased risk of human-caused wildfires. While wildfires are considered a low threat to wolverines (USFWS 2018c; 88 FR 83726), they are projected to increase in the western United States including in wolverine habitat (USFWS 2018c). In addition to the risk of injury or mortality from fire, wolverines may be displaced by wildfire and the habitat modifications that result (88 FR 83726). A study in Idaho found at least occasional use of recently burned areas, and in one instance, even an area still smoldering from fire, by wolverine (Copeland 1996). Overall, however, the literature on this relationship is sparse. In the 2018 SSA, authors indicated that they were not aware of any studies investigating the direct effects of fire on wolverines and the recent listing decision noted that indirect effects of wildfire on wolverines are not well-characterized (USFWS 2018c; 88 FR 83726).

Changes in the density of linear features like roads could also affect wolverines by increasing interactions with predators and competitors. Linear features like roads may affect predation of wolverines by wolves (Scrafford et al. 2024). Additionally, increases in human infrastructure like roads may facilitate use of previously occupied wolverine habitat by coyotes (Chow-Fraser et al. 2022), which authors postulate could displace wolverines and cause range contraction.

As a result of these impacts, the 2023 listing decision notes that wolverine may benefit from “limitations on development and road construction” and” limitations on road densities in certain areas” (88 FR 83726). Multiple federal listing documents have determined that “the fragmented nature and distribution of wolverine habitat in the contiguous United States results in a population that is highly vulnerable to extirpation because of lack of connectivity between subpopulations, and this also makes them more vulnerable to external threats” (75 FR 78030; December 14, 2010 cited in 2023 listing decision). Fragmentation of wolverine habitat by major highways has already been shown to influence genetic connectivity, with gene flow being especially restricted in females (Sawaya et al. 2019). A broad scale analysis of wolverine connectivity also found that human disturbance negatively influenced genetic connectivity (Day et al. 2024).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Several studies in North America suggest that wolverines avoid timber harvested areas. Given the “low” tolerance of wolverines to human disturbance (88 FR 83726) avoidance could occur during the act of timber harvesting, although one study did find usage of timber areas during active logging (Scrafford et al. 2017). The long-term relationship between wolverines and landscapes altered by timber harvest may be nuanced and sensitive to seasonality and time since harvest. Bowman et al. 2010 found that wolverines in Ontario were associated with mature, but not logged, forest. Female wolverines in British Columbia avoided recently logged areas at some sites and during some seasons (Krebs et al. 2007). A study in Alberta found that both males and females avoided the interior of cutblocks aged 11-25 years but used cutblock edges in a sex and season-dependent manner (Scrafford et al. 2017). Franklin et al. 2019 suggest that harvest regimes could affect wolverine habitat usage. They found that logged areas (15-18 yr postharvest) with higher levels of stand retention were used by wolverines more than areas with lower levels of stand retention. Even when wolverines use timber harvested areas, their behavior may be modified by reduced cover. A study in Montana found that wolverines crossed cutblocks, but made directed linear movements at a quick pace when traveling within them (Hornocker and Hash 1981), unlike the slower movements associated with areas without harvest. Recently work by Day et al. 2024 suggested that forest cover is associated with wolverine connectivity. Incidental take of wolverine during vegetation management activities to reduce the risk or severity of wildfire was expressly exempted from the section 9 prohibitions in the wolverine listing determination (88 FR 83726) because these activities were determined to not result in jeopardizing the continued existence of the species.

#### Existing Protections

Some Forest Plans contain management direction for wolverine and/ or roadless areas. For example, the Flathead National Forest land management plan (2018) identifies specific areas within the forest where the desired condition is that it provides connectivity for wide ranging species like wolverine (available at USFS 2025a). Some inventoried roadless areas (e.g. BearMarshall-Scapegoat-Swan Inventoried Roadless Area #1485) in the Flathead National Forest are identified as “Recommended Wilderness” and maternal denning habitat for wolverine and connectivity are listed as one component for why these lands should be considered for Wilderness designation. A forest-wide objective for the Beaverhead-Deerlodge is to “maintain...

winter habitat integrity for wolverine.” A number of additional management areas within the Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest have the stated management objective to “maintain or enhance roadless characteristics and naturalness” (2009 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). The 2015 Kootenai-National land management plan commits to maintaining 16% of IRAs as having “wilderness potential” and that these areas of recommended wilderness contribute “habitats for species with large home ranges such as wide-ranging carnivores... and species found primarily in these habitats” as well as conditions that “contribute to wildlife movement within and across the Forest” (available at USFS 2025a). While this is a small sample of applicable forest plans, this illustrates that at least some plans provide protection beyond the federal designation of IRAs. However, these examples also illustrate that there is tremendous variety in what that protection can look like.

#### Effects Determination

Based on the overlap of the wolverine range with the proposed action area, we have determined that the exposure is high. Given that wolverines have high potential to be exposed to the proposed action and, that if exposed, individuals may exhibit a number of significant responses, the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect this species.

#### _Ocelot_

The ocelot was listed as endangered in 1972 under the authority of the Endangered Species Conservation Act of 1969 (37 FR 6476). Following passage of the ESA in 1973, the ocelot was included on the January 4, 1974, list of “Endangered Foreign Wildlife” that “grandfathered” species from the lists under the 1969 Endangered Species Conservation Act. Endangered status was extended to the U.S. portion of the ocelot’s range for the first time with a final rule published July 21, 1982 (47 FR 31670).

Currently, the ocelot ranges from extreme southern Texas southern Arizona through the coastal lowlands of Mexico to Central America, Ecuador and northern Argentina. Currently there are two known breeding populations in southern Texas, located 30km (19 mi) from one another near the Gulf coast. Together, both populations may potentially total less than 100 individuals (Lombardi et al. 2022). These populations are isolated from populations in Mexico (Janecka et al. 2014). The quality and quantity of optimal habitat in Texas is on a downward trend, with the Lower Rio Grande Valley’s agricultural lands rapidly developing (Wilkens et al. 2000) and much of the area that could be restored to suitable habitat occurs on private lands. Ocelot populations in Arizona are extremely rare, consisting of only a few individuals occasionally dispersing from Mexico, with perhaps two currently known in the state (as of late 2024), but no established breeding population.

Due to its small population, size ocelots are vulnerable to demographic and genetic risks that elevate extinction risk. Demographically, isolated populations are more sensitive to environmental variability and random events, making them less resilient to disturbance. Barriers to connectivity further exacerbate these risks by preventing dispersal, which would otherwise supplement declining populations and allow recolonization of vacant habitat. Consequently, preservation and restoration of habitat connectivity is of critical importance for ocelot recovery.

The vast majority of the U.S. ocelot range is not within National Forest System lands. The remaining U.S. population is almost exclusively confined to small, fragmented populations in southern Texas and some areas of Arizona, primarily on private lands and National Wildlife Refuges, with minimal overlap with National Forests (USFWS 2016a, USFWS 2025g).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

Critical habitat has not been designated for ocelot to date. In the United States, ocelots require dense thorn scrub and brushland habitats with high canopy cover, abundant understory vegetation, and structural complexity that provides concealment, denning sites, and connectivity between patches. These habitats are concentrated in South Texas and southeastern Arizona, where fragmentation from roads, agriculture, and development poses major threats. Most ocelot habitat in the United States occurs on private lands, but federal lands do contain important habitat areas. The Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge in Texas contains the largest block of federally protected thorn scrub, while Forest Service lands in the Coronado National Forest in Arizona offer smaller but strategically important habitat corridors that connect U.S. populations to Mexico. There are no designated roadless areas that overlap occupied ocelot habitat in Texas. In southern Arizona, roadless areas occur throughout potential ocelot habitat on the Coronado National Forest that may be important areas for movement and dispersal (USFWS 2016a). There are no observations of ocelot in inventoried roadless areas in the NRM and GBIF databases, making these data sources insufficient for assessing the relative exposure of the species to the proposed action.

#### Effects of Roads

Roads have been identified as one of the most significant ongoing threats to ocelot populations in the United States. Vehicle collisions are the leading cause of mortality for the small Texas populations, accounting for 45% of mortalities, in a study of 80 radio-tagged ocelots. Vehicle collisions have also been documented in Arizona and Mexico. In addition to direct mortality, roads fragment dense thornscrub and brushland, reducing habitat connectivity and limiting dispersal between patches. This isolation restricts gene flow, prevents recolonization of vacant habitat, and increases extinction risk for small populations. Additionally, some otherwise suitable habitats may not be occupied by ocelots or may serve as a population sink due to the risks posed by vehicles or avoidance of habitat adjacent to roads as has been reported in other species (USFWS 2016a, USFWS 2025g).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Timber harvest poses a secondary but relevant threat to ocelot habitat in the United States. While large-scale commercial forestry does not occur within the thornscrub landscapes of South Texas, where ocelots are most abundant, timber-related activities in southeastern Arizona can reduce habitat quality and connectivity. Removal of canopy and understory vegetation diminishes the dense cover and structural complexity that ocelots require for concealment, denning, and hunting. Timber harvest and its associated infrastructure can further fragment habitat, creating openings that ocelots are reluctant to cross and increasing isolation of small populations. Both the 2016 Recovery Plan and the 2025 Status Review emphasize that maintaining dense woody cover—particularly thornscrub with canopy closure exceeding 75 percent—is critical for ocelot persistence, and that timber operations which reduce this cover or increase fragmentation may undermine recovery objectives (USFWS 2016a, USFWS 2025g).

#### Existing Protections

Existing protections for ocelots in the United States are provided in the 2010 Conservation Plan for the Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge (USFWS 2010) in South Texas which provides the largest block of federally protected thornscrub. In Arizona, lands managed by the Coronado National Forest and other federal units contribute to connectivity with Mexican populations, with management guidance provided in the 2018 Coranado National Forest Land Management Plan (available at USFS 2025a).

In addition to federal protections, ocelots are safeguarded by state-level conservation frameworks. In Arizona and Texas, the species is recognized as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need, included in Arizona’s _Comprehensive Wildlife Conservation Strategy: 2005–2015_ (AGFD 2006) and the _Texas Conservation Action Plan_ (TPWD 2012). These strategies provide policy guidance to agencies and the public but do not confer direct regulatory protection. In Texas, ocelots are legally protected under state law and formally listed as endangered (TPWD 2012).

#### Effects Determination

Given that Arizona is the only location where the ocelot could occur on inventoried roadless, we are assigning the exposure of the species to the proposed action as low. However, given that roads and timber harvest may degrade habitat that is important for ocelot movement the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect this species.

#### _Canada Lynx_

Canada lynx ( _Lynx canadensis_ ) were listed as threatened in the contiguous United States in 2000 (65 FR 16053). The status of this species is currently evaluated for 6 geographic units. In the 2023 Species Status Assessment (USFWS 2023e), population sizes for each unit were estimated based on expert opinion and published estimates of carrying capacity as follows: Northeast (750 – 1,000), Midwest (100 – 200), Northern Rockies (200 – 300), Northern Cascades (30-35), Greater Yellowstone (0-10), and Southern Rockies (75-150). Based on the best available information at the time of the assessment, it was determined that there is no reliable evidence that the distribution or abundance of lynx is reduced from historical levels at the level of the DPS. The status of each of these 6 units is thought to be largely independent from the other units (USFWS 2023e). Connectivity of these units to Canada is important and immigration of lynx from Canada into the contiguous United States is thought to contribute to population persistence (McKelvey et al. 1999a; Schwartz et al. 2002), although the degree to which this is important is unknown (USFWS 2023e).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action

Lynx in the contiguous United States inhabit the patchy southern edge of the boreal forest in areas with high densities of snowshoe hares (USFWS 2017a). This includes subalpine coniferous forest (Douglas-fir, Spruce-fir, and hemlock-fir) in western mountains, boreal forest in the Great Lakes, and mixed coniferous and deciduous forest and high tundra vegetation types in the east (Aubry et al. 1999). There is evidence that, currently, lynx both occur and regularly reproduce within Colorado, Maine, Minnesota, Montana, and Washington (USFWS 2023e). While lynx have been detected in North Idaho, there is only one documented reproductive event in the state in recent decades (USFWS 2017a). There is also evidence suggesting recent lynx reproduction in New Hampshire (2023 SSA) and Vermont (USFWS 2017a).

While lynx have been detected recently in other states, there is no evidence to suggest contemporary resident breeding populations. While a number of lynx reintroduced into Colorado dispersed into northern New Mexico, they did not establish a resident breeding population (USFWS 2023e). Lynx dispersing from the Colorado reintroduction were also briefly detected in Nevada, Utah, Arizona, South Dakota, Nebraska and Kansas (Devineau et al. 2010). Validated records show lynx present in Wyoming as far back as the 1850s (Reeve et al. 1986) and lynx reproduction was verified in Northwest Wyoming in the early 2000s, however more recent detections have been sporadic (USFWS 2023e). Some recent federal survey efforts in the state have failed to detect lynx (USFWS 2023e), although a lynx was photographed in the Wyoming Range in 2024 by a member of the public (Koshmrl 2024). Verified lynx detections have occurred in Michigan, and Wisconsin (USFWS 2023e). There was a reintroduction effort for lynx in the Adirondacks of New York between 1989-1991, however these animals have not been detected since 1993 and there was no evidence that they bred successfully (McKelvey et al. 1999a).

Federal land management decisions have the strong potential to influence lynx populations and lynx habitat. Overall, 64% of lynx habitat in the 6 geographic units are federally managed (USFWS 2017a) and 87% of this land is managed by the US Forest Service (USFWS 2017a), although this percentage varies by geographic unit. In 2000, the inadequacy of Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management land management plans for lynx was central to their listing (65 FR 16053), however the contemporary regulatory landscape has changed considerably from that time (USFWS 2017a; see discussion below). Critical habitat for lynx was designated in 2006 and revised in 2009 and 2014 (79 FR 54782). A proposed rule on revised critical habitat was published in 2024 (89 FR 94656), but this is pending as of 12/1/2025.

The 2017 Species Status Assessment considered the role of roadless areas in its evaluation of factors potentially influencing future conditions for the species. Specifically for the Northern Rockies geographic unit, the 2017 SSA noted that “we anticipate that future Federal management direction will include continued management of national parks, designated wilderness and roadless areas, and other areas with non-developmental land-use allocations to maintain natural ecological processes, which should maintain natural disturbance regimes and landscape-level habitat mosaics to which lynx are adapted” (USFWS 2017a). Of the 160 lynx detections in inventoried roadless areas, 121 of them (~76%) occurred in operable or operable but complex environments. To evaluate whether sampling bias near roads affected this assessment, we conducted a secondary analysis evaluating the overlap of roadless areas with lynx habitat in the Northern and Southern Rockies. Our analysis overlapping with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action with lynx habitat in the Greater Yellowstone Area of Wyoming, Montana, and Washington as modeled by Olson et al. 2021 estimated that approximately 26.6% of lynx habitat in this region occurs in IRAs. While most of the southern Rockies lynx habitat is excluded from the proposed action, a similar proportion of lynx habitat in this part of their range is administered by the U. S. Forest Service as roadless areas (Squires et al. 2025). We also evaluated the overlap between the current USFWS range for the species and inventoried roadless areas and found that approximately 6.8% of the lynx range occurs in these areas. This is likely because the proportion of roadless areas in the midwest and east is lower in lynx habitat than it is in the west. Altogether this shows that, the management of current roadless areas in ways that enhance the conservation of lynx is important at the southern-most range periphery in the continental United States. Approximately 12% of lynx designated critical habitat occurs within the area affected by the proposed action and 46% of that critical habitat within IRAs is on lands designated as operable or operable but complex.

#### Effects of Roads

Roads have direct and indirect impacts on Canada lynx. While overall the negative impacts of roads in lynx habitat are expected to outweigh any benefits (USFWS 2017a), as of the 2017 SSA, negative impacts of roads to the lynx DPS population as a population-level stressor had not been documented.

Direct mortality from vehicle strikes is a threat to individual lynx. The 2017 SSA reported that between 2010 and 2015 lynx were struck and killed 54 times in Maine, 9 times in Minnesota, 5 times in Montana and 1 time in Idaho. Importantly, mortalities occurred on both paved and unpaved roads. For example, 22 out of 54 lynx road mortalities in Maine occurred on low traffic, low speed, dirt forestry roads and 2 out of 9 mortalities in Minnesota occurred on unpaved forest roads (USFWS 2017a). Translocated individuals in re-introduction efforts may be especially vulnerable to vehicle strikes (Devineau et al. 2010).

While lynx have been documented crossing roads successfully, including highways (Squires and Oakleaf 2005; Squires et al. 2013), several studies suggest that lynx avoid crossing highways or that their behavior is modified while crossing these roads. Baigas et al. 2017 showed that lynx regularly crossed two-lane highways present in their home-ranges in Colorado, although they typically crossed in proximity to vegetative cover and at times of day when traffic volume was low. Thirty-nine percent of lynx in this study crossed roads at lower rates than expected. Work by Apps (2007) suggest that the likelihood of lynx crossing a highway decreased with increasing traffic volume.

Road construction may fragment lynx habitat although studies on avoidance behavior near small and low traffic roads are mixed. Fuller et al. 2007 found that while lynx in Maine would travel along unplowed forest roads in winter, they selected against road and road-edge habitat within their winter home range. This may be mediated by prey availability, as lynx killed fewer hares near roads and road edges than in preferred habitat types (Fuller and Harrison 2010). Another study in Maine found that lynx selected against logging roads at the homerange scale, but that logging roads had no effect on third order selection or selection “within core areas” (Vashon et al. 2008). In contrast, one study in central Ontario found no impact of road density on lynx detection in the study area (Walpole et al. 2012), and authors speculate it may have been due to the low traffic volume of area roads during winter. A small study in Washington found no evidence of road avoidance for lynx crossing small forestry roads or evidence of selection against roads (McKelvey et al. 1999b). In the Superior National Forest, lynx were detected within 200m or roads and trails while making long distance movements (Moen et al. 2010). In the same forest, selection for roads did not differ from random expectation for lynx movement within home ranges, but authors note that the density of roads within the study area was homogenous (Terwilliger and Moen 2012). Similarly, a study in the Northern Rockies showed no effect of low traffic forest roads on lynx habitat use (Squires et al. 2010). In Colorado, a study found that lynx and a neutral to slightly positive selection for snow-covered forest roads (Squires et al. 2019). The effects of roads on lynx may be mediated by presence of competitors as well as prey. One study in an area of logging and energy development in Alberta found that higher densities of roads negatively predicted lynx occupancy in places where coyotes were present (Bayne et al. 2008). However, a winter study in Montana did not find evidence that coyotes were eating lots of hares, which would be indicative exploitative competition with lynx (Kolbe et al. 2007). Almost all studies on the impact of roads focused on occupancy and movement behavior, however one study evaluated the impact of roads on denning. Squires et al. 2008 found that lynx den further from forest roads than random expectation, but that this wasn’t driven by avoidance of forest roads open to traffic, specifically.

Road construction also has the potential to fragment lynx habitat, however, attributing the impacts of road construction to habitat fragmentation, as opposed to habitat loss, can be difficult. One study in southern Ontario, also at the southern margin of lynx habitat, evaluated metrics of habitat availability and fragmentation and their ability to predict lynx occupancy (Hornseth et al. 2014). They found that in landscapes with large amounts of suitable habitat, lynx occurred in areas with high proportions of suitable habitat and that occupancy was not related to fragmentation metrics.  In landscapes with less suitable habitat, occupancy was unrelated to habitat suitability and fragmentation metrics (Hornseth et al., 2014), suggesting flexibility in habitat use in marginal areas. The authors suggest that habitat loss, rather than habitat fragmentation, may be more important for lynx. However, in the Northern Rockies of Montana, the proclivity of female lynx to produce kittens did relate to connected patches of mature forests in home ranges (Kosterman et al 2018, Holbrook et al 2019)

A few recent studies shed light on the net effects of habitat loss and habitat fragmentation on lynx connectivity. Several studies suggest that Canada lynx can travel through a wide range of habitat types between core areas (reviewed in Vanbianchi et al. 2017 and Squires et al., 2013). Furthermore, a recent study on dispersing lynx during a crash in snowshoe hare abundance found that dispersing lynx were more tolerant of roads than resident lynx, but that both residents and dispersers were less likely to cross roads as compared to random steps (Arnold et al. 2025). Other work suggests that movement corridors for Canada lynx, particularly between the US and Canada in places like the Rocky Mountains, may be facilitated by a limited number of putative corridors (Squires et al. 2013). To the extent that new forest roads could affect the propensity of Canada lynx to use these corridors, it is theoretically possible that habitat fragmentation from roads could affect lynx connectivity. Nonetheless it is difficult to evaluate how likely this is given that lynx do cross roads (see above), albeit in a context dependent way, and genetic evidence to date does not suggest genetic isolation from core populations in northern North America (Schwartz et al. 2002). However, given the importance of gene flow between southern peripheral populations and Canada (Schwartz et al. 2002), maintenance of connectivity is important for lynx management.

Indirectly, road construction may facilitate access of humans to lynx habitat resulting in mortality from incidental trapping. In Minnesota between 2010 and 2016 11 of 26 lynx trapped incidentally by trappers targeting other species were killed (USFWS 2017a). Increased road networks may also increase access of other recreationists to lynx habitat. Work in Southern Colorado suggests that in areas with high intensity dispersed recreation (backcountry skiing, snowboarding, snowmobiling, and packed trail skiing) lynx became more active at night and less active during the day (Olson et al. 2018). The same study found some evidence that lynx avoided areas with motorized recreation (Olson et al. 2018). Another analysis from the same study system found that lynx avoided areas used by snowmachines and selected areas used by backcountry skiers (Squires et al. 2019).

Increased road networks may lead to increased incidence of human-caused wildfires. Wildfires have the potential to alter lynx habitat, at least temporarily. Large wildfires have reduced the carrying capacity of lynx habitat in the Cascades (Lyons et al. 2023) and the population in this unit has likely declined since listing (USFWS 2023e). Early studies suggested that lynx avoid recently burned habitat (Koehler et al. 2008). In a more recent study, lynx briefly entered fire perimeters only one-year post-fire in Washington, but they primarily used unburned areas with mature trees suitable for snowshoe hares (Vanbianchi et al. 2017). Another recent study in the Northern Rockies focusing on recent burns (<3 years old) found that lynx avoided burned areas within their home-ranges and that they increasingly avoided burned areas as they became more available within the home-range (Squires et al. 2026). Lynx in this study also preferred unburned and low fire severity areas relative to high fire severity areas (Squires et al. 2026). Patterns of habitat use change as time since fire increases. For example, lynx tended to use all areas of older (20+ year) burns in a study in the North Cascades (Vanbianchi et al. 2017). One study in the Yukon has documented lynx use of downed woody debris for denning habitat approximately 30 years postfire (Slough 1999). A study in the Northern Rockies showed lynx using burned areas within 25 years, but use differed depending upon forest management approach (see below) (Olson et al. 2023). The length of time for forest conditions to become favorable to lynx and snowshoe hare again after a burn may also vary across the lynx range (USFWS 2017a).

Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

The initial listing for Canada lynx identified that timber harvest and vegetation management can be “benign, beneficial, or detrimental to lynx depending on harvest methods, spatial and temporal specifications, and the inherent vegetation potential of the site” (65 FR 16053). Recent peer reviewed literature on lynx reflect this heterogeneity.

“Intensive” forest harvesting such as “large scale clearcuts” can be detrimental to lynx by eliminating habitat associated with prey and lynx denning (65 FR 16053). Although lynx generally avoid crossing clearcuts during winter (Squires et al 2010), they either select or avoid harvested landscapes depending on mosaics of forest structure across time (Holbrook et al. 2018). Lynx selected mature forests at the landscape scale, but preferentially used 20-30 yr old advanced generating forests from forest management within home ranges. (Holbrook et al.

2017). In addition, lynx in the Northern Rockies increasingly avoided forests 5 years or less postdisturbance as it became more available in home ranges (Holbrook et al. 2017). Work in Maine shows similar results with lynx avoiding recent clearcuts in winter (Fuller et al. 2007). Regardless of silvicultural treatment, lynx may avoid recently harvested landscapes. Work in the Northern Rockies showed that lynx use of areas subjected to group selection cuts, liberation cuts, improvement cuts, pre-commercial thinning, regeneration cuts with natural regeneration, and regeneration cuts with planting was low for the first 10 years post-action regardless of treatment (Holbrook et al. 2018). After that, it took from approximately 20 yrs (thinning) and 34-40 yrs (selection, regeneration cuts) following tree harvest for vegetation to sufficiently recover as to support 50% of lynx-use (Holbrook et al. 2018)

The time-dependent nature of lynx habitat use post-disturbance is seen in the literature on the value of regeneration cuts to lynx. A study in Western Canada suggested that large patches (>1000 hectares) of regenerating forest (15-40 years post-harvest) had sufficient hare densities to support lynx reproduction (Reid et al. 2024). Similarly, a study in the Northern Rockies showed that advanced regenerating forests (20-80 years old) had hare densities at least 2.8 times that of other structural classes (Holbrook et al. 2019). Related studies found that small-diameter regenerating forest contributed to models that predicted successful reproduction, but within a matrix of connected mature forest (Kosterman et al. 2018, Holbrook et al 2019). An early study in Maine found evidence of lynx selecting regenerating forest (Hoving et al. 2004). Several additional studies in the region have further explored this relationship. Lynx in Maine selected for tall regenerating clearcuts (10+ years post-harvest) and established partially harvested stands (11-21 years post-harvest) (Fuller et al. 2007). Another study in Maine found that both male and female lynx preferred conifer dominated sapling stands (mid-regeneration) at multiple spatial scales (Vashon et al. 2008). A subsequent study suggested that lynx may capitalize on edge habitat, as at the landscape scale, lynx used areas straddling both regenerating forests with high numbers of hares and mature coniferous forest efficient for travel (Simons-Legaard et al. 2013). In contrast, young forests (<5 years post-harvest) are not selected for by Canada lynx. For example, lynx intensity of use of forests in the Rocky Mountains is low for approximately 10 years post silvicultural treatment (Holbrook et al. 2018) and resource selection analyses suggest that lynx use forests in stand initiation phases (<5 years post-disturbance), less than older forests and sparsely forested areas (Holbrook et al. 2017).

There is less literature on the effects of retention harvest on lynx. Retention harvest of different levels did not affect lynx use of habitat in a study by Franklin et al. 2019 in Alberta. During winter, lynx in a study area in Maine selected against recent partially harvested stands (Fuller et al. 2007).

The significance of mature forest may vary across the lynx range. In the Northern Rockies lynx select for mature forest and experience fitness benefits from this habitat type. One study showed that across seasons Canada lynx in the Northern Rockies used mature (50-200 year old) sprucefir forest most (Holbrook et al. 2017). During winter, lynx foraged primarily in areas with mature large diameter trees and high horizontal cover (Squires et al. 2010). Females in this study region were more likely to produce kittens in areas of mature well-connected forest, primarily comprised of spruce-fir (Kosterman et al. 2018; Holbrook et al. 2019).

The significance of mature forest is less clear for lynx in Maine. During winter, lynx in a study in Maine selected against mature forest (40+ years post disturbance) (Fuller et al. 2007). However, another study suggested that lynx may select for mature forest when it borders high quality hare habitat (Simons-Legaard et al. 2013) and a third study found no selection for or against mature forest (Hoving et al. 2004).  We are unaware of a study evaluating the impact of mature forest on lynx productivity in the East.

A few studies have focused on the effects of logging associated with fire mitigation and post-fire salvage on lynx. A study in the Northern Rockies showed that lynx habitat use varied with time post-fire and silvicultural treatment, with lynx using forest with regeneration cuts ~25 years postdisturbance the most (Olson et al. 2023). While pre-fire thinning and salvage reduced high intensity fire within forest stands, lynx only used these stands at a low-level post-fire, albeit consistently and at qualitatively higher levels than stands that did not receive pre-fire management (Olson et al. 2023). The temporal change in use of post-fire habitat by snowshoe hares may be especially important for Canada lynx. Kelly and Hodges (2020) showed that snowshoe hare density decreased immediately following wildfire, but that densities started to rebound by 8-9 years post-fire in areas that were not-salvage logged. In contrast, snowshoe hares were largely absent in salvaged logged areas in Washington even 8-9 years post-fire (Kelly and Hodges 2020). A subsequent study showed that lynx avoided salvage logged areas at the 50 and 150m scales at sites approximately 5-15 years post-fire (Volkman and Hodges 2024).

In sum, the effect of forest management and timber harvest on Canada lynx is nuanced and timedependent. Several studies recommend that managers maintain a mosaic of forest types and/or a minimum percentage of high-quality hare habitat (Simons-Legaard et al. 2013; Holbrook et al. 2018; Holbrook et al. 2019). Overall, management activities that reduce horizontal cover, such as thinning, are thought to degrade lynx habitat (Squires et al. 2010).

#### Existing Protections

The impact of timber and vegetation management on lynx is now informed by additional landmanagement guidance specific to lynx. The Northern Rockies Lynx Management Direction (USFS 2007) and Southern Rockies Lynx Amendment (USFS 2008) direct vegetation management in occupied lynx habitat for most of the intermountain west through incorporation into land management plans. These documents follow the Lynx Conservation Assessment Strategy (LCAS), which identifies risks to lynx and recommends conservation measures for actions that could increase lynx risk through habitat alteration. The LCAS recommends that ≤30% of a lynx analysis unit (LAU) should be currently unsuitable (in stand initiation structural stage) for lynx, that non-salvage timber harvest should not change more than 15% of lynx habitat in an LAU to currently unsuitable over the course of a decade, that no precommercial thinning that reduces hare habitat takes place in stand initiation structure classes until stands no longer provide winter snowshoe hare habitat, and that no vegetation management takes place in multistory forests that reduces winter snowshoe hare habitat. The SRLA provides for some minimal allowances for precommercial treatments in regenerating stands with winter snowshoe hare habitat. The SRLA also provides for limited uneven-aged vegetation management activities in mature multi-story stands with snowshoe hare habitat. These limits apply to all projects, except for fuels management activities within the WUI. These management directions also offer guidelines to forests on minimizing the impact of roads on lynx. Outside of the Rockies, all forest plans have been formally amended to incorporate guidance from the LCAS except for the Okanogan-Wenatchee. The forest manages landscapes according to the LCAS (USFWS 2023e) and the Canada Lynx Conservation Agreement between the USFS and USFWS, which commits the USFS to implement the LCAS until all forest plans are amended to incorporate it (USFS & USFWS 2000).

#### Critical Habitat

The physical and biological features of Canada lynx critical habitat are:

- “(1) Boreal forest landscapes supporting a mosaic of differing successional forest stages and containing: (a) Presence of snowshoe hares and their preferred habitat conditions, which include dense understories of young trees, shrubs or overhanging boughs that protrude above the snow, and mature multistoried stands with conifer boughs touching the snow surface; (b) Winter conditions that provide and maintain deep fluffy snow for extended periods of time; (c) Sites for denning that have abundant coarse woody debris, such as downed trees and root wads; and (d) Matrix habitat (e.g., hardwood forest, dry forest, non-forest, or other habitat types that do not support snowshoe hares) that occurs between patches of boreal forest in close juxtaposition (at the scale of a lynx home range) such that lynx are likely to travel through such habitat while accessing patches of boreal forest within a home range.” (65 FR 54782)

Approximately 12% of lynx designated critical habitat occurs within the area affected by the proposed action and 46% of that critical habitat within IRAs is on land designated as operable or operable but complex. Given that much of this habitat is operable or operable but complex terrain and given the importance of vegetation features for the habitat of this species the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species.

#### Effects Determination

Given that at least 25% of the habitat for the species in the Northern Rockies is in the proposed action area and given that lynx could be subject to mortality and habitat degradation with the proposed action, the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect Canada lynx **.** Given that much of this habitat is operable or operable but complex terrain and given the importance of vegetation features for the habitat of this species the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species.

#### _Coastal DPS of Pacific Marten_

The coastal DPS of Pacific marten ( _Martes caurina humboldtensis_ ), also referred to as the Humboldt marten, was proposed as Federally Threatened in 2018 (83 FR 50574) and then listed as Federally Threatened in 2020 under a 4(d) rule (85 FR 63806) with critical habitat designated in 2024 (89 FR 46576).

The coastal marten had a historical range throughout coastal Oregon and coastal northern California (85 FR 63806). Recently, the species has not been detected throughout much of its historical range. The coastal marten DPS is currently persisting in approximately 7% of its historical range in four small populations with fewer than 100 individuals each (USFWS 2023f). Given the small population size and fragmentation of the remaining habitat, connectivity between the remaining populations is a major concern for species persistence (USFWS 2026b). Both Oregon populations are functionally isolated without connectivity to any other population, and the two California populations only have connectivity to each other (USFWS 2020d). Consequently, if either of these two Oregon populations were eliminated, natural recolonization from other populations would not be feasible (USFWS 2020d).

Exposure to the Proposed Action and the Proposed Action Area

Critical habitat was designated in 2024 and consists of mature, structurally complex, latesuccessional forests primarily in northwestern California and southwestern Oregon, encompassing roughly 1.2 million acres. The vast majority, 92% (1.1. million acres) of critical habitat, is located on federal lands with 88% located on Forest Service lands and 17.6% of total critical habitat is within the affected environment. The essential physical and biological features necessary for the marten's survival and recovery include a dense understory for cover and foraging habitat, a complex forest canopy, and abundant coarse woody debris like large snags and downed logs for denning sites and prey habitat. Coastal marten are found in older, conifer– dominated forests, serpentine habitats, and shore pine and transitional shore pine/Douglas–fir– hemlock forests at the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area (Eriksson et al. 2019). However, the common denominator with serpentine and older forest habitats is the presence of dense, spatially extensive ericaceous shrub understories and diverse and abundant prey.

Martens are more selective of habitat conditions at den sites than at resting sites and can be a limiting factor for the population. Suitable denning habitat requires both denning structures as well as suitable foraging habitat near den sites that supports energy requirements of female during lactation and minimizes time spent away from kits. Research has found most coastal marten den sites are in cavities of live and dead trees that were larger than average diameter compared to the surrounding stand with structural features such as complex crowns, large limbs, broken tops, hollow bases, or multiple cavities. Coastal marten frequently reuse denning structures with 50 percent of reproductive females monitored in multiple breeding seasons reusing a den from a previous season, and 60 percent reusing a site within the same season.

We conducted multiple analyses to evaluate the exposure of Coastal marten to the proposed action. Analyses were not conducted on occurrence data because these occurrence records did not distinguish the coastal marten DPS from other _Martes caurina._ We overlayed the USFWS Coastal marten range map (USFWS 2026a) with the proposed action area and found that 8.9% of the range overlapped with IRAs affected by the proposed action.  We also conducted an analysis using a data product from the USFWS<sup>23</sup> to evaluate the amount of core habitat and linkage corridors for this species that overlap with the proposed action area. Approximately 14% of core habitat and 7.3% of linkage corridor areas overlapped with IRAs affected by the proposed action.

> 23 Used Primary Model Outputs from the USFWS Coastal Marten Analysis available at: https://www.fws.gov/project/coastal- <u>marten-analysis#PrimaryModelOutputs (accessed 1/9/2026).</u>

#### _Direct Effects_

Roads exert several direct impacts on coastal marten populations. Roads can present a direct mortality risk, with individuals vulnerable to vehicle collisions when attempting to cross. Since 1980, nineteen vehicle-caused mortalities have been documented for coastal marten and all were in Oregon. Of the four marten population areas, the central coastal Oregon population appears substantially more vulnerable to roadkill mortalities than the other three, which has been attributed to the increased traffic volume and closer proximity of habitat to busy highways, along with an increased human presence making the reporting of roadkill animals more likely. Roads also have the potential to increase habitat fragmentation, as road construction and associated clearings break up continuous forest into smaller, isolated patches. While research concerning road impacts on coastal marten movement is lacking, studies of populations of American marten have found that roads can reduce habitat quality, finding reduced activity near logged roads in Ontario and reduced marten detection rates with increasing road density in Idaho. This reduces the ability of martens to move freely across their range and can restrict opportunities for dispersal and genetic exchange. In addition, traffic noise and human activity along roads can displace martens from otherwise suitable habitats, forcing them into suboptimal areas. Even relatively small or low-use roads can act as barriers to movement, effectively restricting access to critical resources and diminishing the functional connectivity of the landscape.

#### _Indirect Effects_

Beyond these immediate impacts, roads also generate a suite of indirect effects that further compromise coastal marten viability. Road corridors often alter predator-prey dynamics by creating edge habitats that favor generalist predators such as coyotes or bobcats, thereby increasing predation risk for martens. Displacement from road-adjacent areas can lead to crowding in remaining habitat, intensifying competition, disease transmission, and stress. Human disturbance from off-road vehicles and recreation in dune or forest habitats that overlaps with critical breeding areas may potentially disrupt maternal care and juvenile survival. Finally, roads contribute to long-term connectivity loss, limiting movement between suitable habitat patches and further isolating already small and vulnerable populations (Schrott and Shinn 2020). High– traffic, multi–lane highways have been shown to be significant barriers to movement of American martens although some types of culverts can be used by martens to pass under such highways.

Exposure to rodenticides has potential lethal and sub-lethal effects on coastal martens. Illegal marijuana cultivation sites on public, Tribal, and private forest lands are implicated as the likely source of these rodenticides. In fishers, a similar carnivore species, 85% of carcasses tested were exposed to rodenticides, with the cause of death attributed to exposure in 13% (83 FR 50574). While there is less data on rodenticide exposure in coastal marten they use similar habitats that also have high potential for illegal marijuana cultivation and 3 of the 9 coastal marten tested in recent work were positive for anticoagulant rodenticide exposure (83 FR 50574). As illegal cultivation has been associated with proximity to roads (Wengert et al. 2021) removing roadless area protections could potentially increase use of these areas for illegal cultivation and expand and increase the exposure of coastal marten to toxicants used at these sites.

Timber harvest has been identified as a primary threat to coastal marten (83 FR 50574). Marten habitat loss due to logging of older forests is considered a likely cause of population declines and low population levels in northwest California since trapping has been banned since 1946 (USFWS 2023f). Historically, older forests dominated coastal California, the Klamath–Siskiyou, and the Oregon Coast Range, but as a result of past timber harvest there are only a~ 5%, 20%, and 38% of those forests remaining, respectively. Timber harvest can negatively impact coastal marten habitat by directly reducing the structural complexity of forests that martens require and can result in the removal of mature conifers and dense understory vegetation diminishing the availability of resting, and denning sites, which are often located in large diameter logs, snags, or complex root systems. Clearcutting and intensive thinning eliminate canopy cover, exposing martens to increased predation risk while also increasing preferred habitat their primary predator the bobcat, which have been shown to prefer regenerating harvested stands <30 years old. Harvest operations also disturb martens through noise, machinery, and human presence, which can displace individuals from otherwise suitable habitat. Detection rates of coastal martens rise with the size of late-successional forest patches, indicating that timber harvest practices that reduce patch size likely negatively impact marten populations. Studies have shown that marten occupancy declines sharply in areas subjected to intensive harvest, reflecting the species’ reliance on late-successional forest conditions.

Coastal martens are highly sensitive to habitat fragmentation, which reduces the availability of mature and old forest stands and creates large expanses of unsuitable habitat with little protective cover. Timber harvest and associated forest management practices have been shown to lower marten population density when late-successional forest cover falls below 70 percent of the landscape. Because martens have a small body size, high metabolic rates, and spatial requirements several times larger than similar-sized carnivores, they are particularly vulnerable to habitat loss. Increased fragmentation forces martens to travel longer distances through regenerating forests, which has been linked to reduced body condition. Clearcutting and heavy thinning have been shown to be especially detrimental for marten creating openings that martens consistently avoid. Poor body condition can impair predator avoidance, foraging efficiency, reproduction, and resistance to disease, further compounding the effects of timber-driven habitat degradation.

#### Existing Protections

Conservation and management by a number of federal guidelines. The FWS published a Recovery Outline in 2020 that serves as an interim strategy to guide recovery efforts until a draft recovery plan has been completed. Then in early 2026, a Draft Recovery Plan (USFWS 2026c), an updated Species Status Assessment (USFWS 2026b), a Recovery Implementation Strategy (USFWS 2026d), and a Five-Year Review (USFWS 2026e) were also published.

Management guidance and protections are also provided in the National Forest Land Management Plans for National Forests within the range of coastal marten. Furthermore, coastal marten are managed under the Northwest Forest Plan which provides critical management guidance by conserving late-successional and old-growth forests, limiting clearcutting, and maintaining structural complexity that are critical elements of coastal marten habitat. These measures reduce fragmentation and preserve habitat quality for marten populations.

#### Critical Habitat Determination

Of the total critical habitat designated, 17.6% is within the affected environment. The essential physical and biological features necessary for the marten's survival and recovery include a dense understory for cover and foraging habitat, a complex forest canopy, and abundant coarse woody debris like large snags and downed logs for denning sites and prey habitat. Given this, we have determined that the exposure of critical habitat to the proposed action is high and that the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat.

#### Effects Determination

The exposure of the coastal marten to the proposed action is high. Given this exposure level, and the potential impacts of roads and timber harvest on the DPS, the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species. We have also determined that the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat.

#### _Black Footed Ferret_

The black footed ferret _(Mustela nigripes)_ was initially listed as endangered 1967 under the Endangered Species Preservation Act of 1966 (32 FR 4001) and subsequently incorporated into listing under the ESA (39 FR 1175). Currently the species is listed as endangered and most reintroduced populations are listed as nonessential experimental. Black footed ferrets on Buffalo Gap National Grassland are designated experimental.

The 2019 species status assessment indicates that the ferret population size declined dramatically after 2010.  The sylvatic plague is thought to be a main contributing factor to these losses (USFWS 2019d).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and the Proposed Actions

Black-footed ferrets have a close association with prairie dogs occurring in grasslands and other prairie dog habitat in the Great Plains (USFWS 2013b). They rely on prairie dogs for food and use their burrows for shelter (USFWS 2013b). There are two national grasslands where the ferret is thought to occur in South Dakota.

There is no critical habitat for black-footed ferret.  There is one observation of a ferret in inventoried roadless areas out of more than two hundred for the management units and it is in an area that is not operable, however this low sample size makes it difficult to draw conclusions from these data. We conducted a supplementary analysis overlaying range maps for the endangered population of ferrets and experimental populations of ferrets (USFWS 2026a) with IRAs. There is less than 1 square kilometer of overlap of the endangered ferret range with inventoried roadless on the Custer Gallatin National Forest in Montana. Less than 0.001% of the experimental population range overlaps with inventoried roadless areas, but it all occurs in ~94 square kilometers of the range in Buffalo Gap National Grassland.

Effects of Roads

Roads and road construction could lead to direct mortality of black footed ferrets from vehicle strikes and from predation by raptors using associated infrastructure (USFWS 2019d). Roads may also affect ferrets indirectly through habitat fragmentation and soil compaction (USFWS 2019d).

Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Given that ferrets are largely associated with grasslands, we do not discuss the effects of timber.

#### Existing Protections

The Nebraska Grasslands Management Plan includes standards and guidelines to benefit the black-footed ferret (available at USFS 2025a). They are:

- “18. In prairie dog colonies known or thought to be occupied by black-footed ferrets, limit oil and gas development to one location per 80 acres to help maintain suitable ferret habitat.

- 19. To help provide suitable habitat for black-footed ferrets and their young during the breeding and whelping seasons, prohibit the following activities within 1/8 mile of prairie dog colonies, or those portions of larger colonies, occupied or thought to be occupied by ferrets from March 1 through August 31:

- Construction (e.g., roads, water impoundments, oil and gas facilities),

- Reclamation,

- Gravel mining operations,

- Drilling of water wells,

- Oil and gas drilling.

- 20. To help provide suitable habitat for black-footed ferrets and their young during the breeding and whelping seasons, do not authorize the following activities within 1/8 mile of prairie dog colonies, or those portions of larger colonies, occupied or thought to be occupied by ferrets from March 1 through August 31:

- Construction (e.g., pipelines, utilities, fencing),

- Seismic exploration,

- Permitted recreation events involving large groups of people. Guideline...

- [#21 was stricken by an amendment]

- 22. For routine maintenance, access to oil and gas facilities in prairie dog colonies occupied or thought to be occupied by black-footed ferrets shall be limited to daylight hours. This does not apply to emergency repairs.”

In addition to these forest and grassland-wide directions, there is detailed guidance on the management of black-footed ferret in reintroduction habitat.

#### Effects Determination

Given the extremely small amount of overlap between the endangered population range and the proposed action, the exposure of the ferret to the proposed activity is low.

Given that there is overlap between inventoried roadless areas and the experimental population range, but it is a small portion of the range, the exposure of the ferret to the proposed activity is low.

For both populations, given the low likelihood of exposure to road and timber activities, existing protections, and the limited direct impact roads would have on black-footed ferrets even if exposed, the FS has determined the proposed activity is not likely to adversely affect this species because effects are discountable.

#### _Jaguar_

Jaguar ( _Panthera onca_ ) in the United States was listed as federally endangered in 1997 (62 FR 39147). Jaguars once occupied a range stretching from the southern United States to central Argentina. Today, their distribution extends from the southwestern U.S. down to northern Argentina, with populations present in every country except El Salvador and Uruguay. Current estimates suggest they inhabit roughly 51% of their former range. The IUCN Red List assessment indicates a declining global trend, with a suspected 20–25% reduction over the past three generations (21 years) in occupied area, geographic extent, and habitat quality, leading to a comparable 20–25% decrease in mature individuals during that period (Quigley et al. 2017).

In the United States historically, jaguars were found in California, Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and possibly Louisiana, but were largely extirpated from these states, with only occasional sightings since the early 20th century. Between 1996 and July 2017, only 7-8 male jaguar sightings have been confirmed in the U.S. Because females have been absent for decades, evidence indicates that jaguars in the U.S. represent extensions of populations based primarily in Mexico, which is supported by genetic studies that confirm connectivity between individuals in Arizona and Sonora. Consequently, maintaining connectivity with jaguar populations in Mexico is critical to recovering U.S. populations.

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action and the Proposed Action Area

Jaguar habitat in the U.S. portion of the range is a mix of arid and semi-arid mountain ranges (often called "sky islands") and grasslands that function primarily as a secondary area and corridor for male jaguars dispersing from core populations in Mexico. Critical habitat was designed for jaguar in the United States in 2014 on 764,207 acres in Arizona and New Mexico in six critical habitat units (79 FR 12571). After court ordered revisions to critical habitat there are currently 640,124 acres designated (89 FR 46822) in expansive open spaces in the southwestern US that are at least 100 km<sup>2</sup> in size. There are seven primary constituent elements of jaguar critical habitat, that provide for the needs of the species. These seven elements are: 1) Provide connectivity to Mexico, 2) Contain adequate levels of native prey species, 3) Surface water sources available within 20 km of each other, 4) Contain from greater than 1 to 50 percent canopy cover within Madrean evergreen woodland, 5) characterized by intermediately, moderately, or highly rugged terrain, 6) below 2,000 m (6,562 feet) in elevation, and 7) are characterized by minimal to no human population density, no major roads, or no stable nighttime lighting over any 1-km<sup>2</sup> (0.4-mi<sup>2</sup> ) area (USFWS 2018d).

For the critical habitat in the U.S. approximately 68% is federally owned and 65% is managed by the U.S. Forest Service, mainly within the Coronado National Forest. Of jaguar critical habitat on Forest Service lands there are 63,578 acres (9.9%) in the affected environment and 16% of it is operable or operable but complex.

We also conducted an analysis overlapping the entire USFWS range with the proposed action area. Approximately 2.7% of the USFWS range for jaguar is in the proposed action area.

#### Effects of Roads

No direct mortality of jaguars from vehicle collisions has been documented within the United States. In Mexico and other parts of Latin America, vehicle strikes have been confirmed as a source of jaguar mortality, particularly where major transportation corridors intersect occupied habitat. Studies from Brazil, Mexico, and Central America have reported multiple jaguar fatalities due to vehicle collisions, underscoring the vulnerability of wide-ranging carnivores to road infrastructure. Accordingly, roads within and adjacent to designated critical habitat should be considered a potential stressor, with mitigation measures focused on maintaining connectivity and reducing collision risk.

Roads have been identified as a significant factor contributing to habitat fragmentation and a potential barrier to jaguar ( _Panthera onca_ ) movement and recovery. Habitat loss and fragmentation are listed as primary threats to the species' continued existence, and this fragmentation leads to small, isolated populations that are more susceptible to local extinction. Major roads act as impediments to natural jaguar dispersal, particularly between populations in the United States and Mexico. Furthermore, specific critical habitat criteria exclude areas with major roads, as well as areas with stable nighttime lighting or high human population density, which indicates that roads inherently degrade the quality of suitable habitat. This avoidance behavior is supported by data showing that jaguar activity is negatively correlated with human activity and development, which often accompanies road infrastructure. Consequently, recovery efforts for the species include strategies to mitigate the impediments caused by roads to ensure landscape permeability and connectivity between habitat units.

Roads can also indirectly affect jaguars through illegal hunting and trapping by increasing human entry into otherwise remote habitats; the 2018 Recovery Plan notes that illegal poachers and trappers often use road networks to reach rugged mountain ranges such as the Peloncillo and Santa Rita Mountains in the southwestern U.S., elevating the potential for direct persecution of jaguars and depletion of their prey base (USFWS 2018d). Roads also generate edge effects that alter predator–prey dynamics, with fragmented landscapes with increased edge habitat favoring smaller carnivores like coyotes and bobcats, while reducing prey species such as white-tailed deer and javelina, thereby diminishing habitat quality for jaguars. In addition, human disturbance from noise, light, and recreational activity along road corridors is documented in areas such as the Coronado National Forest, where increased offroad vehicle use and border related infrastructure reduce the suitability of occupied areas and may displace jaguars from critical movement routes (79 FR 12571).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Timber harvest and logging activities can indirectly affect jaguar conservation by altering habitat structure, prey dynamics, and levels of human disturbance. Removal of mature forest cover reduces canopy density and vegetative complexity, diminishing the concealment and stalking opportunities jaguars rely on. Logging operations may also disrupt prey populations such as deer and peccaries by modifying forage availability, thereby reducing prey abundance in occupied areas. Large-scale timber harvest is not currently a primary threat within designated U.S. critical habitat for jaguars but the Recovery Plan emphasizes that these indirect effects can degrade habitat quality and compromise long-term recovery objectives.

#### Existing Protections

In addition to protections under the ESA, the Coronado National Forest Land and Resource Management Plan (2018) identifies jaguar as a federally listed species requiring special management (available at USFS 2025a). The plan emphasizes maintaining habitat connectivity, limiting disturbance in Sky Island Mountain ranges. Arizona Game and Fish Department recognizes jaguar as endangered under state law with state wildlife action plans that emphasize habitat conservation and coordination with federal agencies.

#### Critical Habitat Determination

Given that nearly 10% of critical habitat for jaguar in the United States is in inventoried roadless areas, that 16% of that is in operable or operable but complex landscapes, and that the proposed actions could have the potential to affect canopy cover and road density the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for jaguar.

#### Effects Determination

Our exposure data is insufficient at this time and is classified as “unknown” until further analyses can be done at the project level. Based on the small numbers of jaguars in the U.S. and significant potential negative effects of roads on fragmentation of habitat and connectivity, as well other possible indirect effects on human interactions and predator and prey populations, the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect jaguars. Given that nearly 10% of critical habitat for jaguar in the United States is in inventoried roadless areas, that 16% of that is in operable or operable but complex landscapes, and that the proposed actions could have the potential to affect canopy cover and road density the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for jaguar.

#### _Fisher, Southern Sierra Nevada DPS_

The southern Sierra Nevada (SSN) fisher DPS ( _Pekania pennanti_ ) was listed as Federally Endangered in 2020 with Critical Habitat designated in 2022. At the time of listing both longterm isolation (Knaus et al. 2011, Tucker et al. 2014) and small population size were identified as primary threats to the DPS, with an estimated population size of less than 300 adult fisher before 2015 (Spencer et al. 2011, Spencer et al. 2015). Since 2015 this DPS has experienced substantial habitat loss and fragmentation due to a historic drought and subsequent large scale tree mortality event (Fettig et al. 2019) followed by a series of megafires in 2020-2021 each exceeding 80,000 acres (Ayars et al. 2023). Cumulatively these disturbances have resulted in large losses of fisher habitat. Hart et al. (2025) found a 48% reduction of female fisher habitat between 2012-2022. Population trend assessed through monitoring of population occupancy was generally stable across the DPS through 2022 (Zielinski et al. 2013a, Tucker et al. in Review, Martin et al. in Review). Mean occupancy dropped from 0.32 (2011-2022) to 0.20 in 2023, which is the lowest occupancy rate recorded since monitoring began with even larger magnitude declines regionally within the DPS (Martin et al. in Review).

Recent habitat losses have also resulted in extreme fragmentation of the remaining habitat. Effects of drought and tree mortality through 2019 (excluding subsequent megafires) resulted in an increase in the number of habitat patches from 74 to 558 and decrease in average patch size from 31,500 acres down to 2,600 acres (Thompson et al. 2020). Additional recent megafires have burned through a number or previously identified linkage areas. This fragmentation has resulted in major concerns for connectivity on multiple scales, both between the remaining patches of reproductive habitat critical for juvenile dispersal as well as in the loss of four major linkage areas that may prevent larger scale movement needed to maintain a viable population (Thompson et al. 2020).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Actions

In western North America, fisher habitat is primarily associated with late-successional conifer or mixed-conifer hardwood forests. Within these forests fisher habitat is characterized by an abundance of dead and downed wood, dense, multistory canopies, moderate to high canopy cover, and large trees (Lofroth et al. 2010). In the SSN, fishers occur primarily in dense, mature mixed-conifer and ponderosa pine forests at middle elevations that generally do not accumulate persistent deep snow which has been found to limit the movement and distribution of fisher (Zielinski et al. 2017, Pauli et al. 2022). Fisher are habitat specialists with needs that vary depending on age and sex. In the SSN fisher suitable habitat generally categorized as either foraging, resting, or denning habitat (also alternatively modeled as reproductive or female habitat). Reproductive/denning/female habitat categorization represents the specialized habitat needed to support fisher reproductive females that is considered a limiting factor for population viability (Spencer et al. 2015, Thompson et al. 2020).

#### _Foraging Habitat_

Fisher’s diet in the SSN DPS has been found to include a wide variety of food items suggesting that fishers likely forage diverse vegetation types, though they likely concentrate on foraging in mature forests that are habitat for larger, preferred prey items (e.g., >200 g tree squirrels) (Spencer et al. 2015). However, the widespread tree mortality from 2015-2019 has resulted in dietary shifts finding a reduction in tree squirrels and increase in plant based dietary composition. The post-tree mortality shifts away from medium-sized prey mammalian species that are thought to be the most energetically efficient choice has potential implications for longterm survival SSN fisher and management implications for management of foraging habitat (Pilgrim et al. 2023, Smith et al. 2024).

#### _Resting Habitat_

Fishers need a variety of suitable resting habitats and structures (e.g., cavities or platforms in trees or snags) within their home ranges to provide shelter from weather, conserve energy, avoid predators, and safely survey for and consume prey. They use multiple resting sites within their home range to minimize travel time when foraging and rarely reuse the same rest sites. Canopy cover appears to be the most important variable in resting site habitat selection and resting typically occurs in live trees, snags, and logs that are in the largest available diameter classes, and these structures are typically deformed or in a state of decay (Spencer et al. 2015).

#### _Denning Habitat_

Denning sites and reproductive habitat that provide sufficient resources for females to bear and raise kits, is considered the most limiting habitat element for the fisher population. Females typically use multiple dens during a single denning season. They give birth care for newborns in natal dens, and later often move kits to a succession of several maternal dens until they are weaned.  Therefore, conservation of female reproductive areas requires ensuring clusters of multiple suitable den structures in relatively close proximity persist with their home range. Like resting structures, reproductive dens are usually cavities in large, live or dead trees, in forest stands with dense canopy cover and complex structure. Fishers select den sites in clusters of large, mature trees in stands with variable tree heights and dense canopies, on fairly steep slopes. Suitable denning sites are probably a subset of suitable resting sites, because the requirements are more stringent (Spencer et al. 2015).

#### _Habitat Configuration_

Landscape habitat models show that fisher habitat in the southern Sierra Nevada is arranged in a roughly north-south trending collection of narrow habitat patches in a restricted elevation zone that supports forested habitat but is not subject to consistent deep snow throughout the winter. Habitat patches are bisected by a number of major river canyons (e.g., San Joaquin, Kings, and Kern rivers) that have been shown to limit gene flow within the SSN (Tucker et al. 2014, Tucker et al. 2017). This narrow, undulating distribution of habitat makes it susceptible to fragmentation into even smaller patches (Spencer et al. 2015). The tree mortality epidemic and subsequent large scale megafires in the last decade have burned a number of primary connectivity linkages in the SSN DPS (Thompson et al. 2020).
