We conducted two analyses to assess the exposure of fisher to the proposed action quantitatively. First, we overlapped the USFWS range map for the Southern Sierra Nevada Fisher, DPS (USFWS 2026a) with the proposed action area and found that approximately 7.6% of the DPS’ range was included in IRAs affected by the proposed action. Additionally, we evaluated the overlap of fisher habitat with the action area.  Due to the large-scale vegetation changes due to drought and tree mortality in recent year that significantly impacted fisher habitat, we analyzed both pre- and post-drought fisher habitat maps created as part of the SSN fisher Conservation Strategy Interim Guidelines (Thompson et al. 2020, Conservation Biology Institute 2020). We found that approximately 11.1% of pre-drought suitable habitat for fisher overlapped with the proposed action area and 9.2% of post-drought suitable habitat overlapped.  Our analysis of postdrought denning habitat showed that approximately 5.9% overlapped with the proposed action area. We did use occurrence data for this species, because the databases data were drawn from did not distinguish this DPS from other fisher records.

#### _Critical Habitat_

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service published a revised proposal on November 7, 2022, to designate approximately 595,495 acres of critical habitat across six units (one unit of which is further subdivided into two subunits; 87 FR 66987). This proposed critical habitat has not received a final rule as of the time of publication. Critical habitat was defined as suitable, highquality denning habitat that includes intermixed foraging and dispersal areas. Such habitat provides structural features for parturition, raising kits, protection from adverse weather conditions, facilitation of safe movement, sites to rest and thermoregulate, foraging opportunities, and cover to reduce predation risk for adults and young. More than 90% of designated critical habitat for SSN fisher is on federal lands (U.S. Forest Service, National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management) with the majority of on Forest Service lands. There are 392,167 acres (65.9%) of critical habitat on Forest Service lands of which 63,835 acres (10.7%) are in the action area.

Due to the recent large scale habitat loss, retaining what habitat remains is highly important to ensure long term species persistence given the small and isolated nature of the SSN fisher DPS. Roadless areas overlap with both critical habitat and broader denning, resting, and foraging habitat and these areas are potentially important to preserving the permeability of remaining foraging habitat that is critical for juvenile fisher dispersal and provide connectivity between blocks of high-quality denning habitat. Additionally, roadless areas have considerable overlap with a number of identified key linkage areas that have already experienced significant cumulative disturbances from tree mortality and wildfire in recent years that may result in the creation of barriers to fisher movement and a loss of connectivity between habitat cores (Spencer et al. 2015, Thompson et al. 2020). In 2017 fisher were north of the Merced River for the first time in 100 years and since then fisher have been increasingly found using and reproducing in this area, representing a potentially important northward expansion. Home ranges in this expansion area overlap extensively with a designated roadless area.

#### Effects of Roads

#### _Direct Effects_

Vehicle collisions are a significant mortality factor for fishers both the SSN DPS and throughout their range. Between December 2007 and January 2013, a research study in the northern portion of the SSN DPS recorded 9 vehicle collision mortalities. Another study reported ten road-killed fishers have been found in Yosemite National Park over the past 2 decades and of the 10 roadkilled fishers, 8 were killed during the denning season and of these, 4 were females, 2 were males, and 2 were of unknown sex. Of the 4 females killed during denning season, 2 were lactating (Spencer et al 2015) Another study reported that six percent of necropsied fishers in the SSN between 2007 and 2014 died from vehicular strikes (Gabriel et al. 2015).

A broader review of mortality causes assessed information on 239 radio-collared fishers that died among 7 study sites within the West Coast population segment between 1992 and 2014. Predation was the most common cause of death for radio collared fishers at 5 of the 7 sites, which was linked to 67% of all known-cause deaths. Vehicle strikes occurred at 4 of 7 study sites and contributed to 8% of all known- cause deaths. Overall, they documented 24 roadkill deaths in the West Coast population segment during the study period, and fishers elsewhere in North America commonly die on highways (Sweitzer et al. 2016).

_Indirect Effects_

In addition to the risk of vehicular collisions, forest roads and trails may elevate fisher predation by mountain lions, bobcats, and coyote, the most common predators of fisher in the SSN DPS (Wengert et al. 2014), as all these species use trails and forest roads as travel and hunting corridors. Predation sites are closer to roads, on average, than sites where live fishers were detected. Bobcat and fisher interactions are more likely to occur near roads, hard edges (i.e., abrupt changes between closed and open habitat), open areas, and bushy areas (Spencer et al. 2015, Sweitzer et al. 2016).

SSN fisher have high levels of exposure to anticoagulant rodenticides and other toxicants which result in both direct mortality and harmful sub-lethal effects that impact health and behavior and have been linked to increased risk of predation and vehicle caused mortality. This toxicant exposure has been identified as a major threat to the SSS fisher DPS with numerous research studies documenting exposure rates of >80% to one or multiple toxicants based on the results of fisher necropsies (Thompson et al. 2014, Gabriel et al. 2015). The primary source of rodenticide exposure to fishers is from illegal marijuana grow sites on public, private, and Tribal lands in California and these grow sites are frequently found in fisher habitat. Grow sites also tend to be concentrated 1–2 km from roads, which probably facilitates grower access while avoiding places too close to roads (<1km) to minimize risks of detection (Wengert et al. 2021). Consequently, removing roadless protections may lead to increased use previously roadless areas for illegal cultivation potentially further increasing the risk of toxicant exposure for fisher.

In numerous studies fishers have been found to have a negative association with roads. Linden et al. (2017) found a both fisher occupancy and density had a strong negative relationship with roads, while Gompper et al. (2016) found that fisher distribution was negatively associated with paved roads. Ellington et al. (2017) reported a negative correlative trend between increasing road density and fisher patch use, although this relationship was only weakly supported. Ganoe et al. (2025) found that in areas with high human use fisher avoided roads during the day, and that r in areas of lower human use fisher selected areas far away from roads at all times, regardless of the time of day.

Roads have also been documented to negatively impact genetic connectivity for fisher. Garroway et al. (2011) found that road density, river density, and snow depth impeded gene flow during the fisher population expansion in Ontario, Canada. In the SSN DPS it has also been documented that major roads and rivers impeded gene flow of females, and that the influence of landscape features on gene flow is much greater for females than for males (Tucker et al. 2017).

#### _Direct Effects_

Direct mortality from timber activities for fisher is difficult to detect or quantify due to the species’ elusive behavior, large home ranges, low population density and habitat use that makes detection difficult (e.g. use of tree cavities, platforms or broken tops). Mortalities are unlikely to be detected if they occur in cavities or other inaccessible locations or carcasses may be consumed by scavengers, preventing detection. However, as fisher den inside tree cavities there is the potential for direct mortality from timber activities if a den tree is impacted during denning season when fisher kits spend most of the time in tree cavities.

Fisher can also be subjected to noise disturbance from timber activities which have the potential to disrupt denning fisher and potentially impact reproductive success. However, some fisher tolerance of timber activities has been documented even during denning periods. Smith et al (2025) reported a female denning in an active timber area with high levels of noise disturbance that continued to use that den tree for multiple weeks despite high levels of human activities in the vicinity. Yet, they also reported that fishers responded to anthropogenic stressors on an individual basis, where each animal displayed varying tolerance levels with some showing avoidance of treatment areas. Overall fishers retained the same home ranges after treatments occurred focusing activity in other non-disturbed areas of their home ranges. From a management standpoint, treatment size and configuration, management intensity, and management duration may influence observed differences in fisher behavioral responses to treatments (Smith et al. 2025).

#### _Habitat Alteration_

Extensive clearcut logging, along with fur trapping, during the late 1800’s and early 1900’s caused widespread declines in fisher populations across the country and by the early 1900's were extirpated from large portions of their historic range (Powell 1993, Ruggerio et al. 1994). Local extirpations partially attributed to habitat loss from logging and trapping have been documented across the country (e.g. Aubry and Lewis 2003, Williams et al. 2007, Kontos and Bologna 2008).

The Sierra Nevada DPS area experienced extensive habitat changes due to a combination of logging, trapping, and mining associated with the gold rush in the late 1800s. However, settlement at the southern end of the DPS was minimal in comparison due to the absence of gold deposits and steeper topography that restricted human access to forest lands (Beesley 1996). Historical sample locations and genetic analyses indicate that the SSN fisher DPS underwent a significant population decline and bottleneck associated with human development and habitat loss largely attributed to clear cut logging during and immediately after the goldrush and that the area at southern tip of the Sierra Nevada may have acted as a refuge for fisher maintaining a stable population size while fisher in the rest of SSN was in decline (Tucker et al. 2012).

It has been well documented that fishers avoid large open areas and select home ranges area with larger, more contiguous patches of mature forest and avoid high densities of open areas. Studies from both the northern Rockies and California have found that the median amount of open area in a fisher home range was ~5% (Sauder and Rachlow 2014, Raley et al. 2012). Increasing the amount of open area by an additional 5% was estimated to reduce the relative fisher probability of occurrence by 39% and 50% in different studies (Sauder and Rachlow 2014, Weir and Corbould 2010). Fishers have been reported to avoid clear cut stands but also to continue to use home ranges with a low proportion of clearcuts (<15% of home range area) within them (Zielinski et al. 2013b). Fisher may tolerate some portion of the area treated within their home range, up to a threshold, to gain access to the untreated forest surrounding those areas (Garner 2013).

A number of studies have documented some tolerance of fisher to timber activities, including both non-commercial and commercial logging using forest management strategies that may mitigate timber impacts to fisher habitat. For example, fisher and red squirrel (a potential fisher prey species) habitat use increased with the use of retention harvesting which is the approach of leaving live mature trees behind during forest harvest. Researchers found that higher levels of retention harvest were characterized by greater canopy cover, basal area, and abundance of deadwood were associated with use of forest habitats by late-seral species such as fisher. Many late-seral species showed notable increases in activity between 20% and 50% harvest retention, and use of stands harvested with at least 50% retention was comparable to use of unharvested stands (Franklin et al. 2019).

Sauder and Rachlow (2014) studied fisher used of three comparative management landscapes: roadless and wilderness areas, industrial timberlands managed primarily for timber output, and managed forests with reduced focus on timber and more emphasis on wildlife habitat, recreation and other uses. They found landscapes managed primarily for timber production were not preferred by fisher with capture rates of fishers in industrial landscapes were less than half of those in multiple use forest. While they documented some fisher maintaining entire or significant portions of their annual home ranges in industrial forest, industrial forests as a whole were not in a configuration or pattern preferred by fisher. They also found lands managed as roadless/wilderness were at higher elevation and had significantly more open areas, less mature forest, and reduced proximity of mature forest patches than occupied fisher home ranges.

Zielinski et al. (2013b) investigated the amount of forest management (e.g., timber harvest, vegetation management, prescribed burning) that occurred in areas regularly used by fishers. Most treatment areas were multi-factor with only one area having timber extraction as the dominant activity. Fisher use was lowest in sample areas with above average area treated each year (49.3 treated ha/year) compared to areas with moderate or high fisher use (37.8 and 36.7 treated ha/year, respectively). This suggests that as the area treated increases, fishers may respond by using these areas less frequently. In addition, 3 of the 7 low use areas were dominated by an extractive activity which typically has more intensive effects on habitat elements of importance to fishers. They calculated that fishers consistently occupy at the highest rate of use – places where an average of 2.6% of a home range has been disturbed per year.

From 2009 to 2011 fishers were reintroduced to private timberlands on the Stirling Management Area owned by Sierra Pacific Industries in northern California. The Stirling Management area had a continuous history of selective logging and even aged management dating early 1900s such that by 2008 In 2008, a majority of Stirling (59%) was in a small-tree or moderately dense forest condition with only 23% large tree or moderately dense forest. This reintroduced population was monitored until 2017 and was found to be a well-established and growing population the end of study providing evidence that fisher can persist in forests managed for timber production. The persistence of fishers on Stirling likely benefited from the retention and recruitment of forest conditions left as a legacy of historical selective management practices under contemporary forest management practices and conservation measures (USFWS 2008b).

#### _Indirect effects_

Similar to the potential indirect effects of roads listed previously, timber harvest can impact predator populations as the primary predators of fisher (e.g. bobcat, mountain lion, coyote) are more likely to occur near hard edges (i.e., abrupt changes between closed and open habitat), open areas, and bushy areas that may be created by some types of timber activities (Wengert et al. 2014). Prey populations can also be impacted due to changes in habitat due to logging, but the nature of these changes is variable depending on the type of logging practices uses (Fuller et al. 2004, Escobar and Estades 2021). Timber activities that create reduce forest cover also have the potential to negatively impact genetic connectivity as dense forest has been found to positively influence on genetic connectivity of female fishers (Tucker et al. 2017).

#### Existing Protections

The impacts of vegetation management, timber, and road or other infrastructure development are also regulated by land management directives. Management direction is guided by an interagency SSN Fisher Conservation Strategy that was first published in 2016. The Strategy was intended to meet the needs for fisher conservation and management for multiple agencies in the Sierra Nevada, including the USDA Forest Service, National Park Service, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW), Sierra Nevada Conservancy (SNC), and other local, state, federal, Tribal, and private entities whose actions may affect fishers or their habitat. The SSN fisher distribution is mapped into seven core areas that represent contiguous polygons of modeled suitable fisher habitat that is large enough to support >5 adult females and considers the results of spatially explicit habitat models and landscape genetic and occupancy patterns. The mapped core areas were designed to provide biologically relevant subdivision for planning and management purposes.

Due to the rapid pace and large scale of habitat changes in the SSN due to drought, tree mortality and wildfire that occurred after initial publication, the Conservation Strategy has undergone several updates with the most recent interim version released in 2020. This 2020 Conservation Strategy publication provides interim recommendations for forest management and restoration projects until a new, comprehensive fisher conservation strategy can be completed with updated habitat information.

Further land management directives are found in the individual land management plans for the Sierra, Sequoia (2023), Stanislaus (1991), and Inyo (2019) National Forests (available at USFS 2025a). Additional management direction for the Stanislaus National Forest, which has does not have a revised land management plan under 2012 Planning Rule, is provided in the 2001 Sierra Nevada Forest Plan Amendment (i.e. Sierra Nevada Framework. Land management plans for the Sequoia, Sierra, and Inyo are tiered the habitat definitions and core areas detailed in the Conservation Strategy, with some plan components applying to each core and or habitat category, including fisher linkage or connectivity areas, known fisher den clusters, and other categories of fisher habitat.

#### Critical Habitat Determination

There are 392,167 acres (65.9%) of critical habitat on Forest Service lands of which 63,835 acres (10.7%) are in the action area. Of this 61% of the habitat is defined as operable or operable but complex. Critical habitat was defined as suitable, high-quality denning habitat that includes intermixed foraging and dispersal areas (87 FR 66987). Such habitat provides structural features for parturition, raising kits, protection from adverse weather conditions, facilitation of safe movement, sites to rest and thermoregulate, foraging opportunities, and cover to reduce predation risk for adults and young. Given this, the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for this species.

#### Effects Determination

Roadless areas overlap with both critical habitat and broader denning, resting, and foraging habitat. These areas are potentially important to preserving the permeability of remaining foraging habitat that is critical for juvenile fisher dispersal and provide connectivity between blocks of high-quality denning habitat. Given this overlap, the FS has determined the exposure to the proposed action is high and that the proposed action is likely to adversely affect the Southern Sierra Nevada DPS of fisher.

#### _Grizzly Bear_

Grizzly bear _(Ursus arctos horribilis)_ in the contiguous United States were listed as threatened in 1975 (40 FR 31734). While bears are listed in the contiguous United States, there are several different delineations within that that are important to their recovery. There are 6 different Grizzly Bear Recovery Zones, and these recovery zones are embedded within 6 larger ecosystems: Bitterroot (BE), Cabinet-Yaak (CYE), Greater Yellowstone (GYE), Northern Continental Divide (NCDE), Selkirk (SE), and North Cascades. While the boundaries of these ecosystems have not been officially defined, for the purposes of analyses conducted by the USFWS, they are the area surrounding bear recovery zones in which observed bears are “anticipated to occur as a part of the same population” (USFWS 2024l). Additionally, the bears were listed prior to the 1978 revisions to the Endangered Species Act, which created the concept of distinct population segments (DPS). Most recently, a proposed rule providing a geographically explicit definition of the Grizzly Bear DPS in the contiguous United States was published in the Federal Register in January 2025 (90 FR 4234).

Since listing, populations of bears in the GYE and NCDE ecosystems have tripled (USFWS 2024l). Populations in the SE and CYE are also thought to be increasing (USFWS 2024l). There are no known bear populations in the North Cascades and Bitterroot ecosystems (USFWS 2024l). According to the 2024 SSA, “the primary factors affecting grizzly bears at both the individual and ecosystem levels are excessive human-caused mortality and human activity that reduces the quality and quantity of habitats” (USFWS 2024l).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and the Proposed Actions

Grizzly bears use a diverse range of habitats with habitat size, degree of human access, and food availability being primary factors that determine whether an area can support a bear (USFWS 2024l). Today, grizzly bears occur in portions of Idaho, Montana, Washington, and Wyoming (USFWS 2024l). This is a large retraction from their historic distribution, prior to the arrival of European settlers, which included most of the western half of the contiguous U.S. (USFWS 2024l). Critical habitat was proposed for the species in the 1970s (41 FR 48757), but it was never finalized.

IRAs were mentioned in the 2024 SSA as being a conservation mechanism for grizzly bear populations (USFWS 2024l). Specifically, the SSA stated that “lasting” land designations such as Wilderness and IRAs “ensure that large proportions of recovery zones and additional areas outside the recovery zones remain secure for grizzly bears into the future without the development of new roads, extractive industries, or other human structures” (USFWS 2024l).

Currently, large portions of five out of six grizzly bear recovery zones are IRAs.  The proposed action does not encompass IRAs in the portions of the Cabinet-Yaak, Bitterroot, and Selkirk recovery zones that are in Idaho (approximately 192 mi<sup>2</sup> in the Cabinet-Yaak and 248 mi<sup>2</sup> in the Selkirk recovery zones). In the Cabinet Yaak-Recovery Zone (total area: 2,589 mi<sup>2</sup> ), 785 mi<sup>2</sup> is 2001 Roadless Rule IRA. In the portion of the Selkirk Recovery Zone in the continental US (1,116 mi<sup>2</sup> ), 102 mi<sup>2</sup> is managed as an IRA under the National Roadless Rule (USFWS 2024). A large portion (1,978 mi<sup>2</sup> ) of the North Cascades Recovery Zone (9,777 mi<sup>2</sup> ) is also inventoried roadless (USFWS 2024l). Restricted motorized use areas, which include IRAs as well as Tribal Roadless Areas, Tribal Primitive Areas, and National Recreational Areas, protect approximately 19% of the Northern Continental Divide Recovery Zone (USFWS 2024).  Additional

management delineations for bears in the broader NCDE, just outside of the recovery zone, also include IRAs and additional plan components restricting motorized access in Zone 1 and the Demographic Connectivity Areas (DCAs). While 22% of the 9-mile Demographic Connectivity Area (DCA) is inventoried roadless (USFWS 2024l), plan components restrict motorized access through the entirety of the DCA. Estimates for the contributions of IRAs and other plan components to the GYE focus on “secure” habitat which meet standards for size, distance to motorized access, and other forms of human disturbance (USFWS 2024l). The 2024 SSA estimated that IRAs provide 864 mi<sup>2</sup> of secure habitat within the 9,210 mi<sup>2</sup> Greater Yellowstone Recovery Zone. For the GYE, there is also substantial suitable habitat outside of the recovery zone managed as an inventoried roadless area (2,386 mi<sup>2</sup> / 8,931 mi<sup>2</sup> ) (USFWS 2024l). We provide a brief overview of existing protections for bears in these areas in the “Existing Protections” section below.

In addition to these values from the literature, we also overlayed the entire UWFWS range of the species with inventoried roadless areas affected by the proposed action and found that approximately 11.8% of the range occurs in such areas. An analysis of grizzly bear occurrence records found that of 243 observations in inventoried roadless areas 153 of them (~63%) occurred within areas that were operable or operable, but complex.

Given that occurrence records are likely to be biased towards observations near existing infrastructure, the overlap of recovery zones and the species’ range with inventoried roadless is likely the most informative assessment of exposure.

#### Effects of Roads

A recent review identified four mechanisms by which roads affect grizzly bears: human caused mortality, habitat displacement, habitat fragmentation, and direct habitat loss (Proctor et al. 2020). In addition to the impacts of roads, we also consider the potential indirect impacts of recreation and anthropogenically caused wildfire on bears, two activities which could increase from expansion of the road network.

#### _Mortality_

The 1993 revision to the Grizzly Bear Recovery Plan recommended that road management be given the highest priority in recovery zones as roads “probably” were the biggest threat to bears (USFWS 1993a). Grizzly bear mortality associated with roads can come through multiple mechanisms including direct collisions with vehicles and the negative human interactions that come with increased human use of grizzly bear habitat. Between 2002 and 2023, 57 bears in the demographic monitoring area (DMA) for the GYE and 90 bears in the NCDE DMA died from collisions with vehicles (USFWS 2024l).

“Accidental shooting, poaching, and habituation through direct human contact and/ or food reward all increase with the use of even secondary, unpaved roads by humans” according to the 1993 Recovery Plan (USFWS 1993a). Between 2002 and 2023, 194 bear deaths in the GYE DMA, 69 in the NCDE DMA, 6 in the CYE and 2 in the SE were classified as defense of life (USFWS 2024l). In that same timeframe, 27 bear deaths in the GYE DMA, 18 in the NCDE DMA, 4 in the CYE, and 5 in the SE were classified as cases of “mistaken identity” (USFWS 2024l). Other bears were removed by management after site conflicts with humans or due to concerns for human safety (128 in the GYE DMA and 89 in the NCDE DMA) (USFWS 2024l). One underlying factor influencing human-bear conflict can be food attractants, and many jurisdictions with grizzly bears have implemented food storage requirements to mitigate this risk (USFWS 2024l).

Several studies have shown that grizzly bear survival decreases with increasing road densities (Boulanger et al. 2013; Boulanger and Stenhouse 2014; Ciarniello et al. 2009; Proctor et al. 2017; Schwartz et al. 2010). Boulanger and Stenhouse (2014), showed that both sub-adult and adult female bears had lower survival rates as road densities increased and that adult males suffered similar mortality rates at all road densities. Importantly, of the 19 bear mortalities associated with roads (<500m), 18 occurred in places where the closest road was gravel (Boulanger and Stenhouse 2014). Similarly, bears inhabiting a mountain ecosystem in British Columbia were more likely to die if they were close to secondary or decommissioned roads (Ciarniello et al. 2009). Several other studies show that a large portion of bear mortalities occur within 500m or even 150m of roads (Benn and Herrero 2002; McLellan 2015) or that mortality risk increases as proximity to roads increase (Nielsen et al. 2004a). The impact of roads can have demographic effects- Boulanger and Stenhouse (2014) showed that local population growth decreased when road density exceeded 0.75 km/ km<sup>2</sup> .

#### _Displacement_

Other studies have shown that bear densities are lower in areas with higher road densities (Mace et al. 1996; Graves et al. 2011; Lamb et al. 2018; Proctor et al. 2023) and higher in areas away from paved roads (Whittington et al. 2025). Densities were higher in areas with restricted vehicle use and highest in areas with high habitat quality and few roads (Lamb et al. 2018). Females in Alberta may select areas of high use within the home range that had lower road densities than the home range overall and select home ranges with larger proportions of land 500km from a road (Proctor et al. 2017). Several other studies suggest that bears select against areas with high road density, against areas of all tested road (Mace et al. 1999), and for roadless areas more than expected (Wakkinen and Kasworm 1997). Others show avoidance of habitat near roads (<500km) in spring and summer (Mattson et al. 1987). Females may remain further distances from roads than males (Chruszcz et al. 2003; Gibeau et al. 2002).

Contextual details about the level of vehicular activity may also affect grizzly bear’s use of roads. Some studies suggest bears select against areas near open, as opposed to closed, roads (Kasworm and Manley 1990; Wakkinen and Kasworm 1997; Wielgus et al. 2002). Selection for or against closed roads may be sex-specific, with females showing avoidance even after accounting for habitat (Wielgus et al. 2002). That same study found that neither sex avoided roads used only for forestry after accounting for habitat (Wielgus et al. 2002). Another study found that selection for or against roads may be dependent on road type and road density in the study area, as well as the association of roads and other landscape features of interest (e.g. foraging opportunities) near roads (Ciarniello et al. 2007). Bear use of areas adjacent to roads may be dependent on traffic volume (Chruszcz et al. 2003, Mace et al. 1996; Northrup et al. 2012), with bears avoiding roads with higher volumes. However, in another study in the GYE bears avoided areas near roads regardless of traffic/ road class (McLellan and Shackleton 1988). Habituation also increases how close bears will come to roads (Chruszcz et al. 2003).

A study in Alberta showed that grizzly bears were more likely to cross “narrow unpaved roads” near creeks and open green spaces (Graham et al. 2010). Traffic volume and habitat quality influenced the likelihood of bears to cross roads in another study (Chruszcz et al. 2003). Bears may be more likely to cross roads at night (Waller and Servheen 2005; Northrup et al. 2012), and more likely to cross roads with low (<20 cars per day), traffic volumes (Northrup et al. 2012). While crossing roads, bears may move more quickly (Roever et al. 2010; Waller and Servheen 2005). Sub-adult bears may be more likely to cross roads than adult bears (Waller and Servheen 2005). Another study showed that while all bears avoided crossing highways, female avoidance was stronger than males (Palm et al. 2025).

While traffic is thought to be a deterrent to bears, some of the changes in vegetation that occur near roadsides may be an attractant to bears. For example, one study found that the herbaceous species that are preferred forage by bears in spring were more common near roadsides than in the forest (Roever et al. 2008). One study suggests that the strong association between roads and habitat features (i.e. cutblocks) that provide attractive food resources (Nielsen et al. 2004b) in an industrially developed site may lead bears to be near roads more than otherwise expected (Roever et al. 2010). Another study found that male bears would use areas near high trafficked roads when they were near high quality habitat, but that females would not (Gibeau et al. 2002).

Another study found that bears exhibited a functional response to roads, whereby their use of areas near roads was higher in low productivity areas (Palm et al. 2025). One study suggested that berry food resources may be higher in an area with human infrastructure (roads, towns etc.), but that mortality rates for bears in that same region are higher creating an evolutionary trap (Lamb et al. 2017). Another study found that the positive impacts of huckleberries on bear density and other parameters occurred primarily when food resources were in secure habitat away from roads (Proctor et al. 2023).

#### _Habitat Fragmentation_

There is research indicating that roads can fragment grizzly bear habitat, and that this in turn has an effect on genetic and demographic connectivity. Studies in the Southern Canadian Rockies and Northern American Rockies found that highways and areas of higher human development impeded migration of male and female bears, but that female bears were affected more strongly (Proctor et al. 2005; Proctor et al. 2012). There is some evidence that US Highway 2 and an associated railroad cause some fragmentation within the NCDE (Kendall et al. 2009), although bears have been documented crossing this corridor, dependent on traffic volume (Waller and Servheen 2005). Highway 2 also causes fragmentation between the Yaak and Cabinet mountains (Proctor et al. 2018).

#### _Habitat Loss_

The 4 ecosystems currently inhabited by grizzly bears have defined standards for core habitat that have a minimum standard for distance from road (USFWS 2024l; see below). By definition core habitat for grizzly bears is lost when a road is constructed, unless it is mitigated by the creation of new secure habitat elsewhere through road decommissioning or other actions.

#### _Indirect Effects of Roads_

If road networks are expanded, outdoor recreation in those areas is expected to increase. The primary concern for grizzly bears with recreation is that it will increase the likelihood of bears encountering humans, including encounters that lead to human-caused mortality (USFWS 2024l, see discussion above). Recreation could also displace bears from preferred habitat (USFWS 2024l and below), which could have energetic consequences (White et al. 1999). Typically bears avoid trails with motorized recreation (Graves 2002; Lamb et al. 2018). There is at least one study, however, that suggests bear responses to motorized recreation may be dependent on reproductive state. This study found that male bears and solitary female bears avoided trails with high levels of motorized recreation, but this was not seen in female bears with cubs who responded by moving more quickly (Ladle et al. 2019). The literature on non-motorized recreation and bears suggest that there are many contextual details that influence the way an individual bear may respond to humans recreating nearby. A few studies suggest that bears avoid non-motorized recreationists (Coleman et al. 2013a and Coleman et al. 2013b). Another study suggested that avoidance may be sensitive to the sex of the bear, time of day, and whether bears are near trails or backcountry campsites (Loggers et al. 2025). Additional work suggests avoidance behavior is more likely to be expressed when trails are near low quality habitat (Gibeau et al. 2002). Habituation may also influence the response of bears to non-motorized recreationists (Jope 1985; McLellan and Shackleton 1989; Mace and Waller 1996; Ladle et al. 2019). There is the potential for snowmobiling and other winter sports to disturb bears in dens, affecting cubs or overwinter energetics (USFWS 2024l). Despite this potential, literature on this is scant (USFWS 2024l), although anecdotal evidence suggests that human activity including recreation could cause den abandonment (Swenson et al. 1997). According to the 2024 SSA, “grizzly bear mortality related to non-motorized recreation is rare and population-level impacts have not been documented.”

Increased numbers of anthropogenically-caused fires associated with an expanded road network could affect bears. Despite the species’ mobility, there is evidence that wildfires can cause bear mortalities (Blanchard and Knight 1990). However, bears have also been described moving through areas that were still smoldering and feeding on carcasses of prey that succumbed to the fires (Blanchard and Knight 1990). The years immediately post fire may also improve foraging opportunities for bears (USFWS 2024l).

Effects of Timber Harvest/ Vegetation Management

Timber harvest frequently occurs in grizzly bear habitat in the contiguous United States. Timber harvest has been shown to have both positive and negative effects on grizzly bears due to increases in road density and changes to habitat, specifically changes in food availability on the landscape (Colton et al. 2021). Changes in the selection or avoidance of timber harvest depend on the context of the larger landscape as well as human activity. This variability in the effects of timber harvest was recognized in the 2024 SSA which stated, “depending on the type of project, vegetation management can be beneficial, neutral, or harmful to grizzly bears.” Research has shown consistently that timber harvest alone has minimal or positive effects on grizzly bears, but only if motorized access is controlled after harvest. The increase of roads from timber harvest and other resource extraction activities can have significant negative effects on grizzly bear mortality and population growth (Proctor et al. 2020).

#### _Mortality Risk from Increases in Road Density from Timber Harvest_

Timber harvest requires new roads or the repair and expansion of existing road networks. This increase in road density can lead to increased mortality of grizzly bears through the mechanisms described in the effects of road section above and specific research has shown that road increases from timber harvest can result in higher mortality risk for grizzly bears. Research in British Columbia, Canada compared a population of bears with access to higher quality food but higher road densities because of forestry activities to a population of bears in an area of mountains inaccessible to humans (Ciarniello et al. 2007). The density of bears in the area with better food was less than one quarter than the bears in the mountain area, likely due to a higher mortality risk from humans associated with higher road densities (Ciarniello et al. 2007). Other research in Canada found that bears were illegally killed from roads that were constructed for timber harvest and energy extraction (McLellan 1989) while reviews of grizzly bear mortality across Canada and the contiguous United States have found that human proximity and road access are linked with higher mortality rates across ecosystems (McLellan et al. 1999; Nielsen et al. 2004a).

#### _Grizzly Bear Selection and Avoidance of Timber Harvest and Associated Activities_

Bears can change habitat selection both in the short term, in response to logging activities, and in the longer term, in response to the changes in habitat created by timber harvest. The literature on short-term responses to logging activities is small but suggests the potential for negative impacts to individuals. There is some evidence that bears avoid roads used by trucks hauling logs, and that displacement comes not just from the roads, but from the logging-associated vehicle activity on those roads. A small study of two bears in British Columbia showed that bears avoided the portions of their home range in which log trucks could be heard both during years when trucks were hauling logs and during times of day when trucks were hauling logs (Archibald et al. 1987). A radiotracking study of brown bears in the Greens Creek Drainage in Alaska (n=11) found that while bears remained in the vicinity of an active road construction site (for the mining industry) where blasting was occurring, their proximity to roads decreased during the day while work was ongoing and the number of day beds near the road construction site decreased compared to prior years at the site with no construction activity (Schoen and Beier 1988). In contrast, two observations reported in McLellan and Shackleton (1988) show bears remaining within 1km of heavy machinery use associated with logging. Displacement of bears by machinery is briefly discussed in McLellan and Shackleton 1989, and findings suggest bear responses to heavy machinery may be dependent on surrounding cover.

Grizzly bears show a variety of behavioral responses to areas subject to timber harvest, and these responses depend on the time of year, the amount of other disturbance on the landscape, the amount of bear food in timber harvest areas, and the amount of human activity (Colton et al. 2021). In the Rocky Mountains grizzly bears showed a wide variation in selection, neutral use (use of timber harvest as it was available on the landscape), or avoidance of timber harvest areas depending on the time of year. Two studies found avoidance of timber harvest areas in the spring (McLellan and Hovey 2001; Zager et al. 1983), while five studies found variable selection by individual bears (some mix of selection, avoidance, or neutral use) or neutral use of timber harvest areas (Kearney et al. 2019; Mace et al. 1996; Nielsen et al. 2004b; Stewart et al. 2012, Stewart et al. 2013). Only two studies found selection for timber harvest areas in the spring (Berland et al. 2008; Ciarniello et al. 2015). However, these same studies demonstrated changing habitat use of timber harvest in the summer and fall. Similar to spring, two studies showed avoidance of timber harvest in the summer (McLellan and Hovey 2001; Zager et al. 1983) while five studies showed selection for timber harvest (Ciarniello et al. 2015; Kearney et al. 2019; Mace et al. 1996; Nielsen et al. 2004b; Stewart et al. 2013) and two studies showed neutral or variable selection (Berland et al. 2008; Stewart et al. 2012). In the fall, results were different again with three studies showing avoidance (Ciarniello et al. 2015; McLellan and Hovey 2001; Zager et al. 1983), three studies showing selection (Kearney et al. 2019; Mace et al. 1996; Stewart et al. 2013), and three studies showing variable or neutral selection (Berland et al. 2008; Nielsen et al. 2004b; Stewart et al. 2012).

There are several factors that seem to contribute to this variation in selection, including sex specific selection, varying amounts of bear food in timber harvest units, and the amount of natural disturbance on the landscape (Colton et al. 2021). Several studies found evidence that male and female bears were using timber harvest differently. Stewart et al. (2012) found that male bears used clearcuts more in the spring and summer while females used clearcuts more in the summer and fall. In Alberta, females were also found to use edge habitat created by timber harvest and other human activities more than males, who were more likely to use edges created by natural disturbance (Stewart et al. 2013), while in Montana there was individual variation in selection or avoidance of edge habitat, with some males and females avoiding edges while most females and some males selected for edge (Sells et al. 2022). Female grizzly bears also showed no shift in their home range due to timber harvest (Sorensen et al. 2015).

Grizzly bear selection of timber harvest is also affected by the amount of grizzly bear food that remains or regrows in logged areas. Bears in British Columbia were more likely to use clearcuts that had higher greenness values (Ciarniello et al. 2015), while researchers in in Alberta found that clearcuts had abundant bear food, although the types of plants that bears foraged were different than forested areas (Nielsen et al. 2004c). However, grizzly bear foods responded to timber harvest differently in different areas, and research southwest British Columbia and northwest Montana found that bears often did not select for timber harvest because of a lack of foraging opportunities and more often used natural disturbances (e.g., avalanche chutes) or moist meadows and riparian areas where preferred plant species were more abundant (McLellan and Hovey 2001; Servheen 1983; Waller and Mace 1997). Several studies have also found that attraction to the food contained in timber harvest areas attracts bears even with the roads associated with timber harvest (Proctor et al. 2020; Roever et al. 2010, Roever et al. 2008), raising concerns that timber harvest with unmanaged motorized access could create sink habitats, particularly for females that were more likely to cross roads than males in at least one study area (Graham et al. 2010). Other studies showed that grizzlies preferred timber harvest areas that had low use roads, fewer roads, or were more remote with less human access (Ciarniello et al. 2015; Mace et al. 1996; McLellan and Shackleton 1988), highlighting the variability in grizzly bear use of timber harvest areas between study areas.

Some of the variation in grizzly bear use of timber harvest between study areas seemed to be a result of landscape context, specifically the amount of natural disturbance on the landscape. In some areas with abundant avalanche chutes or recent wildfires bears preferred to use naturally disturbed areas for foraging (Mace et al. 1996; McLellan and Hovey 2001; Servheen 1983; Waller and Mace 1997), although some of these differences were seasonal. For example, in western Montana grizzly bears used avalanche chutes more than timber harvest in the spring but used timber harvest more in the summer and fall than in the spring (Mace et al. 1996). There is also evidence that bear use of timber harvest was higher in areas with less natural disturbance or in areas with less overall availability of green areas (Ciarniello et al. 2007; Nielsen et al. 2004b).

_Effects of Timber Harvest on Grizzly Bear Food_

Timber harvest had variable effects on plant species that were foraged by grizzly bears depending on the study area and post-harvest treatments. Some study areas found that plant species fed on by bears were abundant in timber harvest areas, although they typically differed in species composition and identity from forested areas (Apps et al. 2004; Nielsen et al. 2004c; Souliere et al. 2020), while others found that bear food was lower in logged areas (McLellan and Hovey 2001; Servheen 1983; Waller and Mace 1997). In areas where various berry species were important food items reducing forest canopy tended to increase berry production and abundance (Martin 1983; McLellan 2015). However, treatment after timber harvest had a large effect on the persistence of huckleberries and other berry crops, as well as several other plants eaten by grizzly bears. Scarification was found to reduce berries and other preferred plants in multiple other study areas (Larsen et al. 2019; Martin 1983; Nielsen et al. 2004b; Nielsen et al. 2004c). Planting after timber harvest was also found to speed up tree regeneration but led to a rapid decline in grizzly bear foods because of rapid tree growth (Kearney et al. 2019; Proctor et al. 2018). Overall research supports landscape planning of timber harvest, controlling motorized access after harvest, and consideration of treatments post-harvest to maximize benefits to grizzly bears (Colton et al. 2021).

#### Existing Protections

There are numerous management directives that guide road use and road construction in grizzly bear habitat. As a result of the 1993 recovery plan (USFWS 1993a), and subsequent litigation, each recovery zone has secure habitat standards that define levels of motorized-access and these are codified as supplements to the 1993 recovery plan and recovery strategies. These standards are briefly summarized for each ecosystem below and they have (or will) be codified in forest plans (USFWS 2024l). These standards remain if the 2001 Roadless Rule is modified or rescinded although the 1993 Recovery Plan states that “the Recovery Plan recognized that grizzly bears would move and reside permanently in areas outside the recovery zones; however, only the area within the recovery zone is managed primarily for grizzly bear habitat” (USFWS 1993a, p. 18). Below we summarize secure habitat standards for each recovery zone. While some of these recovery zones are outside of the affected environment for the proposed action, because bears are wide-ranging species we have provided guidelines for all of them here.

GYE: Secure habitat is “any contiguous area ≥10 acres in size and more than 500 m from an open or gated motorized access route (road or trail), prescribed footprint of a developed site, or recurring low level helicopter line during the non-denning period (March 1 – November 30).” (YES 2024). Gated roads, closed year-round to the public but open to personnel are counted as motorized routes, however decommissioned roads are not (YES 2024). The amount of secure habitat must remain at or above levels in 1998 and can only be changed temporarily (or permanently) under certain conditions (USFWS 2007b; YES 2024). Thirty-seven out of 40 bear management units met these standards as of 2007 (USFWS 2024l). Since then, these standards have continued to be met in those 37 units and conditions are improving in the remaining three units (USFWS 2024l).

NCDE: Secure core habitat in the NCDE is at least 10.12 km<sup>2</sup> in size and more than 500m from a road open to motorized use during the non-denning season or a gated route (USFWS 2018e). Other types of roads, including those “restricted with physical barriers (not gates), decommissioned roads, impassable roads, temporary roads, over-the-snow motorized routes/areas, and non-motorized trails” are permitted in secure core habitat. In the NCDE, the amount of secure habitat, open road densities, and total road densities for bear management subunits and the recovery zone must meet or exceed 2011 baseline levels, and there are conditions that govern any temporary or permanent changes to roads and core habitat (USFWS 2018e). These standards are currently met within the NCDE (USFWS 2024l). Some additional areas outside of the recovery zone have restrictions on motorized use/ secure habitat incorporated in forest plans (USFWS 2024l).

CYE/ SE: Secure habitat is any habitat that is more than 500m from an open motorized road or a high use non-motorized trail (USFWS 2024l). The CYE and SE manage for secure core habitat, open road densities, and total road densities using thresholds that are set for each bear management unit (USFS 2011). These standards affect a portion of land outside of the recovery zone, as well as within the recovery zone. According to the 2024 SSA, “although motorized access standards have contributed to a positive population trend in the CYE and SE, these standards have not yet been fully implemented.”

BE: The overwhelming majority of the BE recovery zone is wilderness and motorized standards have not been established for adjacent areas that might facilitate natural recolonization (USFWS 2024l

North Cascades: In the North Cascades, core habitat is defined by the same 500m standard used in the CYE and SE. Management entities have committed to a “no net loss” of core habitat until further work is done to define seasonal habitat (USFWS 2024l).

In addition to these standards, the 2024 SSA summarizes regulatory mechanisms pertaining to grizzly bears (current as of December 31, 2023) that were considered for the most recent species status assessment (USFWS 2024l). This list, which encompasses everything from Forest Plans, to Conservation Strategies and State Management Plans is an additional resource for evaluating existing protections, although we note that some items (e.g. the 2001 Roadless Rule) would no longer apply under the proposed action. Given that these additional protections are diverse and site-specific they will aid project-level evaluation.

#### Species Effects Determination

In the 2024 SSA, two of the scenarios evaluated by the Services included loss of protected areas, including loss or partial loss of inventoried roadless protections (Scenario 1 and Scenario 2). The Services’ analysis included loss or partial loss of wilderness protections under these scenarios as well. Under both scenarios, resiliency (and subsequently redundancy and representation) of some or all bear populations declined (USFWS 2024l), although the relative contribution of loss of IRAs was not analyzed. Given that there is a high degree of overlap between recovery zones, the full species range, and inventoried roadless areas and the abundant information regarding the impacts of road construction on grizzly bears, the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect this species.

#### _San Joaquin Kit Fox_

The San Joaquin kit fox is a subspecies of kit fox that is endemic to the San Joaquin Valley and adjacent valleys and foothills of California. Listed as endangered in 1967 (32 FR 4001), the San Joaquin kit fox is managed according to recovery plans issued in 1983 and revised in 1998 (USFWS 1983a, USFWS 1998a). Critical habitat has not been designated for the San Joaquin kit fox. No range-wide abundance estimates are available; population status is instead monitored using distribution and local monitoring studies (USFWS 2025h, Cypher et al. 2013).

Major threats to the species are land development, predation from other canid species, and disease (USFWS 2025h). Native habitat of San Joaquin kit fox has been reduced dramatically since the 1900s, mainly due to agricultural land conversion but also energy development and urbanization. Today San Joaquin kit foxes occur in fragmented habitat patches of varying quality. They exhibit classic metapopulation dynamics, in which productive patches create a surplus of animals that disperse and sustain populations in lower quality patches. Habitat connectivity is accordingly deemed essential to long-term viability (USFWS 2020e).

#### Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and the Proposed Action

The San Joaquin kit fox is associated with arid scrub and grassland vegetation communities of its namesake and nearby valleys, although they can also be found in human altered habitats such as grazed grasslands, petroleum fields, and urban areas (USFWS 2020e). They tend to avoid steep terrain (>15%) and natal dens are limited to gentle slopes (<10%) with sandy-loam soils that facilitate den excavation (USFWS 2020e). Much of the remaining high-quality habitat occur in a narrow band rimming the San Joaquin Valley, with the highest concentration at the southwest edge of the Valley (Cypher et al. 2013).  While we could not evaluate the relationship between the Cypher et al. 2013 habitat suitability model and IRAs due to accessibility of spatially explicit model results, we did evaluate the overlay of the UWFWS range map for the species and inventoried roadless. Just over 960 sq km of inventoried roadless areas occur within the range of the kit fox, most of it occurring around the southern rim of the San Joaquin Valley. This represents approximately 1.5% of the species’ total range but given that much of the range is comprised of unsuitable habitat (Cypher et al. 2013) the proportion of suitable habitat that is inventoried roadless areas may be much higher. There are no records of the fox in the NRM or GBIF databases, making it impossible to use these records to assess the exposure of the species to the proposed action.

#### Effects of Roads

Potential direct effects of roads include vehicle strikes, habitat loss and degradation, loss of connectivity, and reduced fitness from disturbance. Potential indirect effects include reduced prey availability and increased competition or predation. Most research in the San Juaquin Valley has focused on the two-lane paved roads (Cypher et al. 2009) or multi-lane highways with medians (Bremner-Harrison et al. 2007) in urban environments. Considerably less data are available for single-lane forest and secondary roads, with past reviews presuming their population level effects to be negligible or highly localized (Bjurlin and Cypher 2003).

New road construction can remove or degrade suitable habitat as well as impede movement between habitat patches. These factors may have significant population-level effects in the case of multi-lane paved roads (Bjurlin and Cypher 2003). Secondary, forest roads are thought to be highly permeable to kit foxes (USFWS 2020e, Bjurlin and Cypher 2003).

A study of 67 radio collared kit foxes in Lokern County found no evidence for detrimental effects of kit fox exposure to 2-lane paved roads on survival, reproductive success, space use or dietary patterns (Cypher et al. 2009). Numerous studies have found that vehicle strikes account for a minor proportion of total kit fox mortality on natural lands, rarely exceeding 10% (Cypher et al. 2000, Bjurlin and Cypher 2003). Kit foxes commonly use disturbed and urban areas and have sustainable populations in Bakersfield and Taft, suggesting they acclimate quickly to human disturbance and can tolerate a high degree of human activity. However, a study of 22 GPS-collared kit foxes from the desert subspecies in Arizona found that individuals avoided areas with higher density off-highway vehicle roads during the winter breeding system, and that off-highway vehicle road networks were the most important predictor of space use (Jones et al.

2017). This suggests that at a certain threshold of off-highway vehicle road density, road effects extend beyond the immediate footprint and can constitute habitat degradation for kit foxes.

Little information is available on the effects of roads on the abundance and distribution of kit fox prey, predators, or competitors. According to one review (Bjurlin and Cypher 2003), disturbed habitats adjacent to roads could possibly favor California ground squirrels over kangaroo rats that are commonly consumed by kit foxes. However, kit foxes in the Lokern Natural Area with different degrees of road exposure exhibited no differences in prey composition detected in scats (Cypher et al. 2009). On the Naval Petroleum Reserves in California, shrub density increased along roads at which could provide cover for coyotes and bobcats that predate kit foxes (Bjurlin and Cypher 2003). Coyotes are a significant cause of mortality for kit foxes (Cypher et al. 2009) but the effect of roads on coyote distribution and abundance in the San Joaquin Valley is not well understood. Finally, roads could serve as travel corridors for the larger-bodied red fox, but a study quantifying niche overlap evaluated the threat from competition with red foxes to be relatively low (Cypher et al. 2022).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

As kit foxes predominantly use open vegetation communities with short stature, timber activities are unlikely to have detrimental population-level effects.

#### Existing Protections

There is no mention of the kit fox in the 2023 Sequoia National Forest Plan or the 2005 Los Padres National Forest Plan.

#### Species Effects Determination

Given that there is overlap of inventoried roadless and the kit fox range in southern portions of the San Joaquin Valley where kit fox habitat suitability is high, we have assigned the exposure level to the proposed action as high, especially considering that remaining habitat for the species is already fragmented. Given this and the potential impacts of roads on the species, the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect this species.

#### _Sierra Nevada red fox_

The Sierra Nevada red fox is a montane subspecies of red fox that historically occurred throughout the mountainous regions of California and Oregon. It resides today in three geographically distinct regions: the Sierra Nevada, the vicinity of Lassen Peak, and the Oregon Cascades. The population residing in the Sierra Nevada was listed as an endangered DPS under the ESA in 2021 (86 FR 41743). At the time of listing, USFWS estimated the Sierra Nevada DPS to number fewer than 40 individuals (86 FR 41743) and modeled density of foxes inside the DPS region indicated a similarly low abundance (median 42 individuals; 95% CI 32–62; Green et al. 2023). More recent monitoring since 2018 suggests a growing population and expanding range extent, but still an absolute low abundance (Sacks and Quinn 2025; Quinn and Sacks 2022). The DPS is considered a single connected population with little to no internal genetic structuring and long-distance movements documented up to 120 km (Quinn and Sacks 2022; Hatfield et al. 2021).

The greatest identified risk factor to species viability are deleterious effects associated with small population size, including inbreeding depression and hybridization with other subspecies (86 FR 41743). Environmental and ecological threats to the species are not well understood, with few population-specific studies. Habitat was not considered limiting by USFWS and critical habitat has not been designated (86 FR 41743).

Exposure to the Proposed Action Area and Proposed Action

Sierra Nevada red foxes have historically been associated with upper montane, subalpine, and alpine life zones (Grinnell et al. 1937), which in the Sierra Nevada are almost exclusively federally managed.  Of the 56 observations of this species in the NRM and GBIF databases, 70% of them have been in portions of IRAs classified as operable or operable but complex. Given the potential for bias in these datasets, we also did a custom analysis based on the probable occupied area, defined as the area encompassed by survey grid cells (4-mi<sup>2</sup> ) grid cells that contained verified red fox detections from 2010 to 2024. Of the 97 cells with a known red fox detection in the Sierra Nevada (Hatfield et al. 2025), 45 (46%) overlapped with potentially affected IRAs. Approximately 52 mi<sup>2</sup> of IRA environment occurred within these cells, representing 13.4% of the total area of occupied cells.  The Dardanelles, Tragedy-Elephants Back, Carson-Iceberg, Iceberg-Mill Creek, and Long Meadow IRAs overlapped detection areas that have supported breeding pairs in the monitored portion of the population (Sacks and Quinn 2025; Quinn and Sacks 2022, Quinn et al. 2019). Additionally, we conducted an analysis overlapping the entire UWFWS range of the Sierra Nevada red fox with the proposed action area and found that approximately 12.2% of these lands were affected.

Red fox habitat in the Sierra Nevada is typified by open whitebark pine and mountain hemlock forest, scrub, patchy meadows, and barren rock and talus fields (Sierra Nevada Red Fox Conservation Advisory Team 2022; USFWS 2018f). Most contemporary detections in the Sierra Nevada are concentrated near or above tree line (mean elevation 3,173 m, range = 2,607–3,651 m; Sierra Nevada Red Fox Conservation Advisory Team 2022), with average tree canopy coverage only 10% of occupied 4-mi cells (Sierra Nevada Red Fox Conservation Advisory Team 2022). The single confirmed denning site in the Sierra Nevada was in an isolated whitebark pine stand at 3,100 meters (Sacks 2025); two verified denning sites in the Lassen population were also located in scattered subalpine stands at approximately 2,800 m in elevation (Sierra Nevada Red Fox Conservation Advisory Team 2022). Critical habitat has not been designated for the species.

#### Effects of Roads

Seven of 11 verified mortalities of the Sierra Nevada red fox subspecies collected between 2010 and 2020 were caused by vehicle strikes; six in the Oregon Cascade population and one in the Sierra Nevada DPS (Sierra Nevada Red Fox Conservation Advisory Team 2022). However, all seven mortalities occurred on paved roads with two or more lanes. The Sierra Nevada Red Fox Conservation Advisory Team (2022) stated vehicle strikes as “the most prevalent cause of mortality for [Sierra Nevada red fox] identified to date” and recommended minimizing development of new roads that would result in “substantially increased human or motor vehicle presence in areas used by [Sierra Nevada red fox]. Unpaved forest roads are unlikely to pose a barrier to genetic connectivity within the DPS. In Oregon, cameras placed on trails and forest roads had the highest probability of detection (Mahmoud 2025). A landscape genetic study of the closely related high-elevation Cascade red fox subspecies found no support for roads (paved or unpaved) impeding gene flow (Akins 2017).

Possible indirect effects associated with increased recreation activities could include elevated risk of mortality from pet aggression, disease transmission, vehicle strikes, and other humanwildlife conflicts (Sierra Nevada Red Fox Conservation Advisory Team 2022, Perrine et al. 2010). Red foxes are prone to habituation to humans through food conditioning and have been shown to alter their spatial behavior in areas of concentrated human recreation, presumably to take advantage of anthropogenic food subsidies (Burkholder et al. 2024, Burkholder et al. 2025). Sierra Nevada red foxes have been observed displaying begging behavior toward campers, including within the Sierra Nevada DPS, and human food wrappers have previously been detected inside their scat (Sierra Nevada Red Fox Conservation Advisory Team 2022).

New road construction could facilitate incursion of coyotes, a dominant competitor of Sierra Nevada red fox (USFWS 2018f), into high-elevation Sierra Nevada red fox habitat (Gese et al. 2013). A study in Montana found that coyotes travel on forest roads in snowy winter conditions more than expected based on their availability, even when overlying snow was no more supportive than the surrounding environment (Kolbe et al. 2007). The authors suggested that in addition to compaction, coyotes select for roadbeds as a cleared travel corridor. Similarly, road development has been proposed as a factor that could possibly facilitate incursion of non-native red foxes that are more tolerant of human-disturbed environments into high-elevation Sierra Nevada red fox habitat (Perrine et al. 2010). The USFWS considers genomic integrity vital to the long-term viability of the DPS (USFWS 2018f).

#### Effects of Timber/ Vegetation Management

Present day habitat associations of Sierra Nevada red fox have minimal overlap with timber zones traditionally targeted for commercial harvest and fuels management (Perrine et al. 2010). However, historical observations in the Sierra Nevada extended lower than they are detected presently (down to 1,370 m; Grinnell et al. 1937), and Sierra Nevada red foxes in the Lassen and Oregon Cascade populations are more frequently detected in mid- and upper-montane forests of red fir, lodgepole, and Jeffrey Pine (Sierra Nevada Red Fox Conservation Advisory Team 2022). This differential use of forest across time and space could mean that current habitat associations in the Sierra Nevada may not represent the full suite of habitats they could potentially use.

Indirect effects of timber harvest and fuels management are unknown but are most likely to be mediated through altered species interactions. Timber practices that shift prey abundance or composition could be beneficial or detrimental, depending if changes have a greater effect on the prey base of red foxes or of generalist competitors like coyotes and gray foxes (Perrine et al. 2010). A recent diet study in the Sierra Nevada DPS suggests that snow-adapted subalpine prey, such as white-tailed jackrabbits, snowshoe hares, and pika may play an outsized role in niche differentiation and long-term coexistence with coyotes (Rosburg-Francot et al. 2025).

#### Existing Protections

No specific management conditions for the Sierra Nevada red fox have been specified in any existing forest plans.

#### Species Effects Determination

Given the overlap of verified detections of the Sierra Nevada red fox with inventoried roadless areas and lands within 2 km of inventoried roadless areas, the exposure the species to the proposed action is high. Given this exposure, and the documented impact of roads on the species, the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect this species **.**

## Reptiles

The reptile group includes 16 species that occur within the action area, including 3 Endangered, 9 Threatened, and 4 Proposed Threatened reptile species. The reptile group includes turtles and tortoises (9 species) that are distantly related to snakes and lizards (5 squamate species). The two tortoise species are fully terrestrial species while the 2 alligator snapping turtle species and the flattened musk turtle are fully aquatic, except for females leaving the water to lay eggs terrestrially. The remaining 6 turtle species in this group are considered semi-aquatic to mostly aquatic, spending most of their time in or near water but always nest in terrestrial habitat. This dependency on nesting in terrestrial habitat makes these species vulnerable during their respective nesting seasons. The narrow-headed gartersnake and Northern Mexican gartersnake are highly aquatic while the remaining snake and lizard species are fully terrestrial. Two similarity of appearance (SAT) species, the American alligator and bog turtle are afforded protections but were excluded from the analyses because they are not Threatened, Endangered, or Proposed T&E species. Similarity of appearance listed species are primarily to protect a species that looks similar to the SAT species and meets the definition of threatened or endangered. Our effects analyses do not rely on proper identification of individuals; if relevant and necessary, effects to SAT species will be considered during project-level consultation. The green sea turtle Kemp’s ridley sea turtle were also excluded due to lack of overlap with the proposed action.
