### Forest birds

_California spotted owl (Strix occidentalis occidentalis)_

The California spotted owl (CSO), one of three subspecies of spotted owl, occurs throughout the Sierra Nevada mountain range in California and Nevada, as well as southern and coastal California, with subpopulations distributed among discrete mountain ranges; and in Baja California Norte, Mexico. California spotted owls were proposed for listing in 2023 as two Distinct Population Segments (DPS): threatened in the Sierra Nevada DPS and endangered in the coastal-southern California DPS (88 FR 11600). Spotted owls are long-lived with high adult survival and low reproductive output (USFWS 2022d). They are well-known to prefer mature, structurally complex forests with high canopy cover and large trees. More recently, the importance of habitat heterogeneity has been demonstrated as well as particularly important for foraging and overall fitness (Zulla et al. 2023, Jones et al. 2024a). In the Sierra Nevada, at higher elevations CSO use conifers, with increasing use of hardwoods as elevations decrease. They forage on a variety of small mammals, primarily flying squirrels at higher elevations and woodrats at lower elevations. In southern California, CSO use platforms and old raptor nests more often, and use smaller trees than in the Sierra Nevada, but will still select for larger trees and high amounts of canopy cover when available (USFWS 2022d). They can be found in riparian and hardwood forests and woodlands, riparian/hardwood forests and woodlands, live oak/big cone fir forests, and redwood/California laurel forests. Coarse woody debris is an important component for food, shelter, and protection for prey species in both DPSs.

The Sierra Nevada DPS is particularly threatened by uncharacteristically large and severe wildfires, tree mortality, drought, and invading barred owls (USFWS 2022d). California spotted owls are widely distributed throughout the Sierra Nevada, with ~2200-2300 estimated owls in 2021 (Kelly et al. 2023). Four years of regional surveys indicated that occupancy has declined slightly between 2021 and 2024 (USFS 2025b). The coastal-southern DPS is impacted by fire and habitat fragmentation. Occupancy analyses on San Bernadino National Forest (historically the largest owl population in southern California and the only with demographic information) indicated a decline by more than 50% from 1991 to 2019 (Tempel et al. 2022). Breeding season surveys in 2022 in the San Gabriel Mountains (San Bernadino and Angeles National Forests), Sierra Pelona Mountains (Angeles National Forest), and the Los Padres National Forest only found 8 currently occupied territories (Barry et al. 2025). In 2024, Forest Service surveys across the four southern California national forests detected owls in 15% of the grids, with none on Cleveland National Forests (USFS 2025b). Forest management remains a controversial topic related to species requiring older forest habitat, but increased frequency and extent of high severity fire in California has caused fuels management to become a key issue. The response of California spotted owls to fuel treatments depends on the type and scale of treatment. In general, with careful application, the long-term benefits of fuels treatments to reduce the risk of severe large-scale wildfire likely outweigh short-term negative impacts (88 FR 11600). A recent study using a dynamic habitat model for the southern-coastal DPS indicated that habitat has declined by more than 50% since 1986, with most of the decline attributed to wildfire and a minimal amount attributed to fuels reduction activities (Barry et al. 2026). See the proposed rule for additional information (88 FR 11600).

#### Effects

Seventy-five percent of suitable CSO habitat in the Sierra Nevada is on Forest Service-allocated lands (USFWS 2022d). Given protections outlined in local National Forest Plans, roads themselves are unlikely to impact California spotted owls in the Sierra Nevada DPS. Timber harvest, on the other hand, could have negative or positive impacts on owl habitat, depending on specific methods used (USFWS 2022d). The coastal-southern DPS is already highly fragmented, both naturally and resulting from development (USFWS 2022d). New roads there could exacerbate it further. While fuels treatments may be necessary, currently commercial timber harvest does not occur on public lands within the coastal-southern DPS of the California spotted owl (USFWS 2022d).

Dynamic models of suitable nesting/roosting habitat have been developed for CSO, separately for the Sierra population (developed by Ronan Hart) and the coastal-southern population (Barry et al. 2026). From these models, there are about 1,103,997 acres of suitable habitat in the Sierra, 6.2% of which is inside the action area. There are about 82,109 acres of suitable habitat in the coastal-southern population, 12.8% of which is inside the action area. From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 49,662 occurrences on NFS lands, only 5% of which are in the action area, though 78% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a high chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations.

Given the direct tie to mature forests, any removal of trees may have short-term adverse impacts on California spotted owls, even when done with long-term benefits as a goal. Adverse effects to CSO could be a consequence of removing suitable habitat (nesting/roosting/foraging) or direct encounters resulting in disturbance (of nesting owls/juveniles in particular). Thus, the proposed action _may affect, and is likely to adversely affect_ both the Sierra Nevada DPS and coastalsouthern DPS of California spotted owls.

_Elfin-woods warbler (Setophaga angelae)_

The elfin-woods warbler is a small black and white warbler endemic to Puerto Rico and known in two populations, El Yunque National Forest and Maricao Commonwealth Forest (and adjacent private lands), which are likely isolated from each other (USFWS 2022e). The warbler was listed as threatened in 2016 (81 FR 40534) with critical habitat designated in 2020 (85 FR 39077). It is found on mountain summits in dense stands of short, small, twisted trees and shrubs, such as the dwarf forest type. The essential physical and biological features (PBFs) for its critical habitat include: 1) wet and rain montane forest types ( _Podocarpus_ forest, dwarf forest, Palo Colorado forest); 2) forested habitat areas that contain active or abandoned shade-grown coffee plantation for forest agricultural lands; and 3) forest habitats not contained within the others described but that have exposed ridge woodlands, timber plantations, or secondary forests within elevations 300-850 m (85 FR 39077). Its threats are primarily habitat modification on private lands and stochastic effects related to small, isolated populations (such as from hurricanes). In 2014, USFWS, USFS, and the Puerto Rico Department of Natural and Environmental Resources signed a Candidate Conservation Agreement (CCA) to work together to conserve the warbler and restore habitat on the two forests (USFWS 2016b). Additional conservation actions have been implemented and agreements developed with private landowners to conserve tropical upland forest and riverbank buffers. In 2010, there were estimated to be about 1,800 mature individuals, but no formal assessment has been made since then, and indications are that occupancy has declined (USFWS 2022e). On El Yunque, the population appears to be declining, and there is not additional continuous montane forested vegetation beyond the forest boundaries (USFWS 2016). Maricao Commonwealth Forest appears stable even after Hurricane Maria in 2017, though it is not uniformly distributed (USFWS 2022e). See the 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2022e).

#### Effects

Of the two populations, El Yunque appears to be less stable than that on Maricao (USFWS 2022e). From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 27 occurrences on NFS lands, 15% of which are in the action area, though none of those is in a potentially operable area. This suggests a moderate chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations.

There are approximately 2,902 acres of critical habitat within the action area, which is 10.6% of the total critical habitat. None of the critical habitat is within potentially operable areas. Given the small population size and strictly limited habitat, any additional loss whether to roads or timber would be negative to the species. However, the El Yunque National Forest Land Management Plan Appendix A discusses specific guidelines and management for the Elfinwoods warbler as agreed to as part of the CCA, with a goal of contributing to the recovery of the species. Thus, any future action would need to adhere to those guidelines, which involve ESA consultation (2019 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a).

Given the protections afforded by the forest plan and CCA, and the lack of occurrences or critical habitat within potentially operable areas, road construction and timber harvest are so unlikely to occur where the warbler lives that effects are discountable. Thus, the proposed action _may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect_ the Elfin-woods warbler or its critical habitat.

#### _Marbled murrelet (Brachyramphus marmoratus)_

Marbled murrelets are small, robin-sized diving seabirds that forage in marine waters, but nest in mature forests. Murrelets live along the west coast, from Alaska to California. The Washington, Oregon, and California DPS were listed as threatened in 1992 (57 FR 45328), with critical habitat designated in 1996 (61 FR 26256) and revised in 2016 (81 FR 51348). Murrelets spend most of their time on the ocean. During the breeding season they rest and feed in near-shore marine environments (1-3 miles offshore) and come inland to nest. Murrelets are dependent upon adequate nesting habitat in mature forest, adequate foraging habitat offshore, and connectivity between the two. They nest in large coniferous trees with large branches or deformities for platform nests, laying a single egg on a mat of moss, lichen, or debris accumulation. Nest stands are old-growth forests with multiple canopy layers and moderate to high canopy closure; though they vary in size from several acres to thousands of acres; larger unfragmented stands tend to be of higher quality (USFWS 2024m). Most murrelets nest within 37 miles of the coast, though they have been found to nest up to 52 miles inland. The physical and biological features essential to critical habitat focus on individual trees with potential platform nests and forested areas within 0.5 mile of such trees, and with a canopy height of at least one-half the site-potential tree height (81 FR 51348). Murrelets are threatened by habitat loss due to wildfire, timber harvest, predation, offshore development, and long-term alterations of weather. The most recent population estimate was 19,000 murrelets in 2022, with indications of a relatively stable population size. Low productivity has likely contributed to the species not recovering within the range. See the Species Report for additional information (USFWS 2024m).

#### Effects

Timber harvest was historically the main loss of habitat, although it has slowed considerably, losses continue, particularly on nonfederal lands (96% of nesting habitat lost to timber harvest from 1993-2017 was on nonfederal lands, USFWS 2024m). Historically, fire occurred throughout the range of the murrelet but at varying intensities and frequencies. The increase in large-scale, high-severity fire also poses a threat to murrelet habitat (USFWS 2024).

The Northwest Forest Plan Interagency Monitoring Program tracks MAMU habitat and classifies it by quality (Lorenz et al. 2021). As of the 2023 model (developed by Adam Duarte), there was estimated to be 4,378,091 acres of high-suitability nesting habitat, and about 8.2% of that is in the action area. From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 3,849 occurrences on NFS lands, 17% of which are in the action area, and 34% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a moderate chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. There are approximately 493,889 acres of critical habitat within the action area, which is 13.6% of the total critical habitat. About half of that is within potentially operable areas. New roads and opportunities for timber in previously roadless areas could negatively impact the remaining habitat. However, any work would be guided by the Northwest Forest Plan (NWFP, implemented in 1994<sup>24</sup> ), which is a multiagency effort to maintain and restore biodiversity, especially within late-successional and old-growth forest systems, while maintaining forest productivity, renewable resources, and rural economies. The NWFP applies to all old-growth forest-associated species within the range of the northern spotted owl, including marbled murrelets.

Given the direct tie to mature forests and large trees, any removal of trees may have short-term adverse impacts on marbled murrelets, even when done with long-term benefits as a goal. Adverse effects to murrelets could be a consequence of removing suitable habitat (nesting/roosting) or direct encounters resulting in disturbance (of nesting murrelets/juveniles in particular). Removal of potential nesting trees and surrounding habitat could have adverse impacts to critical habitat PBFs. Thus, the proposed action _may affect, is likely to adversely affect_ the marbled murrelet and its critical habitat.

_Mexican spotted owl (Strix occidentalis lucida)_

The Mexican spotted owl (MSO), one of three spotted owl subspecies, ranges from Utah, Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico, the western portions of Texas, and south into several states of Mexico. MSO lives in disjunct areas that correspond with isolated mountain ranges and canyon systems. The Mexican spotted owl was listed as threatened in 1993 (58 FR 14248) with critical habitat designated in 2004 (69 FR 53182). Like other spotted owls, this species shows high site fidelity to territories and primarily eats small to medium-sized rodents, though it will eat a variety of prey items that vary with location. In forested habitats, the Mexican spotted owl primarily uses ponderosa pine-Gamble oak, mixed-conifer, and riparian forests. It requires complex canopy cover with habitat heterogeneity for its prey base. Individual MSOs will preferentially forage in forests characterized by a mix of stand ages and stages produced by various types of disturbance but avoid severely burned forest (Jones et al. 2025). In rockycanyon habitats it inhabits areas with a variety of desert scrub and riparian vegetation communities, and nests in protected caves, as well as rocky ledges or trees (USFWS 2012a). The physical and biological features essential to critical habitat are divided into forest structure, prey base, and canyon habitat. Forest structure requires a range of tree species of varying size and age, but particularly older trees, with shade canopy as well as large dead trees; the prey base requires woody debris and logs, and a range of vegetation conditions including hardwoods and residual plant cover. Canyon habitats need at least one of the following: presence of water, clumps or stringers of vegetation, canyon wall with crevices/ledges/caves, or a high percentage of ground litter/debris (69 FR 53182). The widespread, but fragmented distribution of MSO makes it vulnerable to high-intensity landscape-scale wildfires, though timber harvest was a historical

> 24 The 1994 Northwest Forest Plan is available at the Regional Ecosystem Office Northwest Forest Plan website: https://www.fs.usda.gov/r6/reo/overview.php

threat. MSO respond to wildfire consistent with their evolutionary history, occupying areas that experience frequent-fire regimes that are not stand-replacing (Jones et al. 2024b). At the time of listing, there were estimated to be 2,160 MSOs (58 FR 14248). Monitoring from the past 10 years indicates a relatively stable population, though there may be a slight non-significant decline in pair occupancy. Suitable nest-roost habitat has declined across the range to varying degrees since the 1980s (USFWS 2023g). See the 2023 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2023g).

#### Effects

Most known MSOs occur on federal lands, the majority of which is managed by the Forest Service in Arizona and New Mexico. To consider potential exposure of the species and habitat, we examined several owl datasets. As part of the conservation strategy, the Recovery Plan recommends that Protected Activity Centers (PACs) around known nest/roost sites of approximately 600 acres be identified (USFWS 2012a). The southwestern forests in AZ and NM currently have about 1,300 PACs totaling 829,906 acres. Of those, 301 PACs intersect the action areas (partially or wholly), totaling 108,819 acres (13%). In the southwestern region, a dynamic model of suitable nest-roost habitat has been developed (Jones et al. 2023, Shirk et al. 2023). As of 2024, there are about 1,070,837 acres of suitable habitat in Region 3, 7% of which is inside the action area. From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 13,691 occurrences on NFS lands, 8% of which are in the action area, and 28% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a moderate chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. There are approximately 796,224 acres of critical habitat within the action area, which is 8% of the total critical habitat. Only 1% of total critical habitat is within potentially operable areas. New roads and opportunities for timber could remove MSO habitat, however all Forest Plans in the southwest contain language that requires following listed species Recovery Plans. The Mexican spotted owl Recovery Plan emphasizes that most fuels reduction work can be completed outside of primary nest-roost habitat and PACs (USFWS 2012a).

Given the direct tie to mature forests, any removal of trees may have short-term adverse impacts on Mexican spotted owls, even when done with long-term benefits as a goal. Adverse effects to MSO could be a consequence of removing suitable habitat (nesting/roosting/foraging) or direct encounters resulting in disturbance (of nesting owls/juveniles in particular). Removal of potential nesting trees and surrounding habitat could have adverse impacts to critical habitat PBFs. Thus, the proposed action _may affect, is likely to adversely affect_ both the Mexican spotted owl and its critical habitat.

#### _Northern spotted owl (Strix occidentalis caurina)_

The Northern spotted owl (NSO), one of three spotted owl subspecies, ranges from southwestern British Columbia, through Washington and Oregon, into northern California. NSO was listed as threatened in 1990 (55 FR 26114). Critical habitat was designated in 1992 (57 FR 1796) and most recently revised in 2021 (86 FR 62606). Like the other subspecies, it is long-lived, territorial, and pair-bonded. Northern spotted owls inhabit structurally complex forests, and primarily eat small mammals, though the focus varies by habitat. They rely on older forest habitats, and the associated structures and characteristics, for nesting, roosting and foraging, including moderate to high canopy over, multi-layer/species canopy with large overstory trees, with various deformities, fallen trees and woody debris (USFWS 2022f). Foraging habitat is the most variable habitat and is closely tied to prey base. Critical habitat physical and biological features include: 1) forest types that may be in early-, mid-, or late-seral stages and that support the owl across its geographic range; 2) nesting and roosting habitat; 3) foraging habitat; and 4) dispersal habitat; and all of the designated units support at least two of the four PBFs (57 FR 1796).

The Northwest Forest Plan in 1994 was designed in part to arrest the downward trends by providing for late successional/old growth forest over the long term. Reserved lands include late successional reserves, managed reserves, as well as adaptive management areas (USFWS 2022f). The NWFP has reduced habitat loss and allowed for development of new habitat. On non-federal lands, however, habitat has continued to decrease. From 1993 to 2022, habitat decreased by 8.6% across all lands, much of that from wildfires since 2017 (Davis et al. 2022, USFWS 2022f). Recent studies have indicated that interior NSO nest/roost forest tends to burn at lower severity than non-nesting forest and may serve as fire refugia (Lesmeister et al. 2021). Trying to maintain suitable amounts of nest/roost habitat alone, however, is not expected to reverse the trend in occupancy (Franklin et al. 2021). The most recent range-wide northern spotted owl demographic study found a 5.3 percent rate of population decline for all study areas combined, with the rate having increased since the 2011 review. Non-native barred owls are currently the stressor with the largest negative impact on northern spotted owls. Barred owl removal efforts positively impact local spotted owls (USFWS 2022f), and USFWS has developed a Barred Owl Management Strategy to try to help address barred owls at a larger scale in the range of both NSO and CSO (USFWS 2024n). USFWS recently found that NSO meets the definition of endangered, however, it was warranted but precluded from uplisting (USFWS 2022f). See the 2022 Species Form for additional information (USFWS 2022f).

#### Effects

The Northwest Forest Plan Interagency Monitoring Program tracks NSO habitat; currently, about 55% of suitable NSO habitat is found on Forest Service lands. This dynamic habitat model includes both nest/roost habitat and dispersal habitat (Davis February 18, 2026). Currently, there are about 10,203,105 acres of suitable habitat, 7.8% of which is in the action area. When considering a cover type model that classifies the suitability of nest/roost habitat specifically, there are about 6,004,365 acres of highly suitable nest/roost habitat, 8.8% of which is within the action area. From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 29,783 occurrences on NFS lands, 11% of which are in the action area, and 86% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a high chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. There are approximately 1,438,583 acres of critical habitat within the action area, which is 15.3% of the total critical habitat. About two-thirds of that is in potentially operable areas. We can assume that habitat will continue to be managed according to the NWFP; however, new roads forest harvest in previously roadless areas could still impact individuals or habitat.

Given the direct tie to mature forests, any removal of trees may have short-term adverse impacts on northern spotted owls, even when done with long-term benefits as a goal. Adverse effects to NSO could be a consequence of removing suitable habitat (nesting/roosting/foraging) or direct encounters resulting in disturbance (of nesting owls/juveniles in particular). Removal of potential nesting trees and surrounding habitat could have adverse impacts to critical habitat PBFs. Thus, the proposed action _may affect, is likely to adversely affect_ both the northern spotted owl and its critical habitat.

#### _Puerto Rican broad-winged hawk (Buteo platypterus brunnescens)_

The Puerto Rican broad-winged hawk is an uncommon raptor, endemic to Puerto Rico, and restricted to closed-canopy, montane forests. The species was listed as endangered in 1994 (59 FR 46710). Current sightings of the species have been reported in Río Abajo, Arecibo, Toro Negro, Guilarte and Guajataca Commonwealth forests, as well as El Yunque National Forest and private lands surrounding these forests. The major threats are habitat loss, fragmentation and degradation. In 2017 before Hurricanes Irma and Maria, there were 123 individuals (USFWS 2024o), but surveys in 2022 only detected 43 individuals. The karst region continues to support the largest number of hawks. Since Hurricane Maria, predation and competition from red-talked hawks also appear to be limiting breeding success. While on public lands the species’ habitat is mainly protected, most suitable habitat is on private lands with limited regulation (USFWS 2019f). See the 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2024o).

#### Effects

The GBIF/NRM dataset does not contain any occurrences for the Puerto Rican broad-winged hawk, so potential exposure as estimated with that dataset is unknown. However, new roads and timber harvest are unlikely where the hawk lives, and the El Yunque National Forest Plan standards include protections for broad-winged hawk nest and roost sites (as well as sharpshinned hawks and parrots), including no adverse management activities to be conducted within 150 meters of a nest and avoiding potential disturbing activities during the breeding season (November to August) (2019 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Given the protections in El Yunque National Forest Plan and that roads and timber operations are unlikely where the hawk lives, the proposed action _may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect_ the Puerto Rican broad-winged hawk because effects are discountable.

#### _Puerto Rican parrot (Amazona vittata)_

The Puerto Rican parrot is the only native _Amazona_ species in the U.S. Though thought to once be abundant and widespread on the Puerto Rican Archipelago’s major islands, it was listed as endangered in 1967 with only 24 individuals on El Yunque National Forest (32 FR 4001). By 1912, the island had been more than 80% deforested, likely causing the dramatic decline of the parrot and other forest-associated species (USFWS 2009). A captive breeding program was established in the 1970s to supplement the population. The parrot is a frugivorous cavity nester that prefers mature forests with large cavity forming trees. Secondary forests in the northwestern karst region were identified as suitable for reintroduction because they contain other types of cavities such as cliff pot-holes. In 2023, there were an estimated 32 parrots in El Yunque, more than 210 in Rio Abajo Forest, and 18 in Maricao State Forest, all of which have captive-reared birds as well as recruitment from wild breeding pairs. There are also more than 500 parrots in two captive populations. Populations are recovering after Hurricanes Maria and Irma, however, only the Rio Abajo population appears to be stable. Limited cavities, potential human disturbance, predation (by red-tailed hawks and pearly-eyed thrasher), small population sizes, and hurricanes continue to be threats to the species. See the 2023 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2023h).

#### Effects

Most parrots live in captivity and on non-federal lands. The growth rate for El Yunque from 2018 to 2022 was estimated to be 8.4% (USFWS 2023h). From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are 12 occurrences on NFS lands, none of which are in the action area. This suggests a low chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. New roads and timber are unlikely in El Yunque, and the El Yunque National Forest Plan standards include protections for parrot nest and roost sites (as well as sharp-shinned hawks and broad-winged hawks), including no adverse management activities to be conducted within 150 meters of a nest and avoiding potential disturbing activities during the breeding season (November to August) (2019 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Given the protections in El Yunque National Forest Plan and the lack of occurrences within the action area, roads and timber are unlikely to occur where the parrot lives. Thus, the proposed action _may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect_ the Puerto Rican parrot because effects are discountable.

_Puerto Rican sharp-shinned hawk (Accipiter striatus venator)_

The Puerto Rican sharp-shinned hawk is a subspecies that nests in the subtropical moist forest and the subtropical/lower montane wet forest of Puerto Rico. Deforestation from human expansion and hurricanes have decreased available lands for the hawk, similar to the other Puerto Rican species. The species was listed as endangered in 1967 (32 FR 4001). The overall population is fragmented with isolated populations, primarily restricted to montane forest reserves. Although Puerto Rico has much mature secondary forest, sharp-shinned hawks have not shown an expansion to occupy those (USFWS 2018g). Populations have declined substantially, and there are no recent observations on El Yunque (USFWS 2019f). Surveys in early 2018 after Hurricane Maria only detected 19 individuals. More recent assessments have documented an increase to 22-41 adults (USFWS 2023). See the 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2023i).

#### Effects

The GBIF/NRM dataset does not contain any occurrences for the Puerto Rican sharp-shinned hawk, so potential exposure as estimated with that dataset is unknown. However, new roads and timber are unlikely where the hawk lives, and the El Yunque National Forest Plan standards include protections for parrot nest and roost sites (as well as parrots and broad-winged hawks), including no adverse management activities to be conducted within 150 meters of a nest and avoiding potential disturbing activities during the breeding season (November to August) (2019 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Given the protections in El Yunque National Forest Plan and that roads and timber operations are unlikely where the hawk lives, the proposed action _may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect_ the Puerto Rican sharp-shinned hawk because effects are discountable.

#### _Red-cockaded woodpecker (Dryobates borealis)_

The red-cockaded woodpecker is a relatively small woodpecker, known for its unique characteristic of excavating cavities exclusively in living pine trees. Red-cockaded woodpeckers were once common throughout the longleaf pine ecosystem with historical estimates of over 1 million family groups (USFWS 2022g). Much of the longleaf pine ecosystem was eliminated from its original range upon early European settlement followed by widespread timber harvesting. The remaining longleaf pine ecosystem differs greatly from its historical counterpart, with second growth currently just reaching the age (90-100 years) to meet the needs of the woodpecker. Red-cockaded woodpeckers are highly sedentary cooperative breeders with a current patchy distribution in AL, AR, FL, GA, LA, MS, NC, OK, SC, TX, VA. The woodpecker was listed as endangered in 1970 (35 FR 16033) and recently downlisted to threatened in 2024 (89 FR 85294). The woodpeckers require open pine woodlands and savannas with individual large, old pines. A tree must be old and large enough to have sufficient heartwood to completely contain a cavity to prevent pine resin in the sapwood from entering the chamber (89 FR 85294). Suitable foraging habitat consists of mature pines with open canopies, low densities of small pines, minimal hardwood or pine midstory, few or no overstory hardwoods, and abundant native bunchgrass and forb groundcover (USFWS 2003). Frequent fire is necessary to maintain these open pine woodlands. Threats to the red-cockaded woodpecker include historical habitat loss, continued habitat conversion, fragmentation, and stochastic events that can threaten a small population. The woodpecker is conservation-reliant and responds well to active management (89 FR 85294). See the 2022 Species Status Assessment for additional information (USFWS 2022g).

#### Effects

The Recovery Plan recommends identifying and managing clusters of active and inactive cavity trees within an area that a family group defends (USFWS 2003). The southern region of the USFS maintains a dataset identifying clusters as active, inactive, recruitment, abandoned, and unsuitable. There are currently 4,530 active/inactive/recruitment clusters in that dataset, totaling 68,448 acres. Only 68 of those clusters intersect (partially or wholly) with the action area, totaling 659 acres. From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 30,726 occurrences on NFS lands, only 1% of which are in the action area, but 94% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a high chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. However, at a population level, very few would be potentially exposed. Active management is often positive for the species, and all forest plans require implementing protective measures and guidelines in the recovery plan. Given the protections afforded by the forest plans and the positive influence of active management on the species, the proposed action _may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect_ the red-cockaded woodpecker.

### Riparian birds

_Least Bell’s vireo (Vireo bellii pusillus)_

The least Bell’s vireo is a small migratory bird, the westernmost of four subspecies that breeds in southern California and winters in southern Baja California, Mexico. For breeding it is an obligate riparian species, though in winter it uses a greater variety of habitats (USFWS 1998b). The vireo was listed as endangered in 1998 (51 FR 16474) due to habitat loss from agriculture and urbanization, flood control and grazing, as well as brood parasitism by brown-headed cowbirds. Critical habitat was designated in 1994 (59 FR 4845). The physical and biological features essential to the conservation of the vireo include riparian woodland vegetation with canopy and shrub layers, and some associated upland habitats. At the time of listing there were only 291 territories known in the U.S., but the number of territories has since increased 10-fold (USFWS 2006). Localized improved condition of riparian habitats and cowbird control has likely contributed to this success. However, riparian habitats continue to be increasingly bordered by urbanization and large areas of the historical range remain unoccupied. See the 5- year review (USFWS 2006) and draft Recovery Plan (USFWS 1998b) for additional information.

#### Effects

From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 67 occurrences on NFS lands, only 9% of which are in the action area, but 100% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a high chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. There are approximately 2,210 acres of critical habitat within the action area, which is 6% of the total critical habitat. Most of that critical habitat is also within potentially operable areas. Vegetation removal for the purpose of roads and/or timber harvest could decrease and further fragment habitat. Timing is the most important component of protecting the vireo; specifically avoiding work during the breeding season is important and would be a consideration in any future consultation. Most forest plans contain protections regarding riparian areas; however, the vireo requires specifics associated with upland habitats as well. Adverse effects to the vireo could be a consequence of removing suitable habitat and could impact PBFs in critical habitat (particularly upland). Habitat is a major limiting factor, and the proposed action _may affect, is likely to adversely affect_ the least bell’s vireo and its critical habitat.

#### _Southwestern willow flycatcher (Empidonax traillii extimus)_

The southwestern willow flycatcher is a migratory subspecies that breeds in the southwest U.S. and migrates to Central America for the winter. It breeds in dense riparian tree and shrub communities, typically classified as forested or scrub-shrub wetlands (USFWS 2002a). It was listed as endangered in 1995 (60 FR 10694) due to extensive loss and modification of breeding habitat from water diversion and damming, changes in flood and fire regimes, disruption of natural hydrologic cycles, increased grazing, and the spread of non-native plants. In addition, brood parasitism by brown-headed cowbirds has further inhibited reproductive success. The southwestern willow flycatcher’s breeding habitats tend to be cottonwood/willow and tamarisk vegetation, although the latter is a non-native species. The spread of the tamarisk leaf beetle is thus a more recent threat to available riparian nesting habitat (USFWS 2025i). Flycatcher critical habitat was designated in 2013 (78 FR 344), with the essential physical and biological features including: riparian habitat along a dynamic river or lakeside that includes dense vegetation with thickets of trees and shrubs, dense ground foliage, nesting sites with dense canopy, and dense patches of riparian forests interspaced with small openings of open water or marsh so it is not uniformly dense. In addition, it requires a variety of insect prey populations within or adjacent to riparian floodplains. See the 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2025i).

From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 661 occurrences on NFS lands, only 1% of which are in the action area, though 22% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a moderate chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. There are approximately 1,626 acres of critical habitat within the action area, which is 0.8% of the total critical habitat. Only one-third of that critical habitat is within potentially operable areas. Most forest plans contain protections regarding riparian areas. New roads are unlikely in flycatcher habitat, though adjacent roads may degrade habitat and allow more non-native species to invade. Timing is the most important component of protecting southwestern willow flycatchers; specifically, avoiding work during the breeding season is important and would be a consideration in any future consultation. Adverse effects to flycatchers could be a consequence of removing suitable habitat and could impact PBFs in critical habitat. Thus, the proposed action _may affect, is likely to adversely affect_ the southwestern willow flycatcher or its critical habitat.

#### _Yellow-billed cuckoo (Coccyzus americanus)_

The Distinct Population Segment of the western yellow-billed cuckoo was listed as threatened in 2014 (79 FR 59992). The cuckoo is a migratory species that travels between wintering grounds in Central and South America and breeding grounds in North America, which includes 12 states in the U.S. and 6 in Mexico. The cuckoo breeds in large tracts of dense riparian woodlands along low-gradient streams that particularly include cottonwood and willow. In parts of Arizona and southwest New Mexico, the cuckoo will also breed in more arid woodlands in perennial, intermittent, and ephemeral drainages (USFWS 2019g). The habitat is especially water-limited, and primary threats include habitat loss and degradation from altered watercourse hydrology, land use encroachment, and more recently mining (85 FR 57816). Critical habitat was designated in 2021 (86 FR 20798), with the physical and biological features focused on range-wide breeding habitat, adequate prey base, and hydrologic processes that maintain the habitats. Range-wide breeding habitat is riparian woodlands within floodplains or in upland areas in large blocks; however, the southwest is more variable, and habitat can include a variety of perennial, intermittent, and ephemeral drainages. See the 2020 findings on a delisting petition for additional information (85 FR 57816).

#### Effects

From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 30,323 occurrences on NFS lands, only 2% of which are in the action area, but 86% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a high chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. There are approximately 1,993 acres of critical habitat within the action area, which is 0.7% of the total critical habitat. Only one-fifth of that critical habitat is within potentially operable areas. New roads are unlikely in cuckoo habitat, though adjacent roads may degrade habitat and allow more non-native species to invade, as well as access for other activities such as mining. Timing is the most important component of protecting yellow-billed cuckoos; specifically, avoiding work during the breeding season is important and would be a consideration in any future consultation. Adverse effects to cuckoos could be a consequence of removing suitable habitat and could impact PBFs in critical habitat. Thus, the proposed action _may affect, is likely to adversely affect_ the yellow-billed cuckoo or its critical habitat.

### Scrub birds

#### _Cactus ferruginous pygmy-owl (Glaucidium brasilianum)_

The cactus ferruginous pygmy-owl is a small, cryptic subspecies that lives in desert scrub in southern Arizona south through Michoacán, Mexico and in southern Texas south through Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas, Mexico. The species was listed as threatened in 2023 (88 FR 46910). It is a diurnal non-migratory owl and requires vegetation in fairly dense thickets with saguaros, organ pipe cactus, trees, or other columnar cacti large enough to support cavities for nesting. The pygmy-owl is threatened by habitat fragmentation and loss due to residential and commercial development, as well as long-term changes to weather and conditions (USFWS 2024p). See the Recovery Plan Outline (USFWS 2024p) for additional information.

#### Effects

Roads could increase habitat fragmentation and remove potential nesting cacti. The GBIF/NRM dataset does not contain any occurrences for the pygmy-owl, so potential exposure as estimated with that dataset is unknown. Furthermore, there are no known occurrences on U.S. Forests (USFWS 2024p). Given the lack of occurrences on National Forest System lands and that new roads would be unlikely to be built in the owl’s desert scrub habitat, the proposed action will have _no effect_ on the cactus ferruginous pygmy-owl.

#### _Coastal California gnatcatcher (Polioptila californica californica)_

The Coastal California gnatcatcher is a small non-migratory songbird that lives in coastal sage scrub in southern California and Baja California, Mexico. They are tightly tied to coastal sage scrub habitat patches within a matrix that supports an insect prey base. The primary threats to the gnatcatcher include urban development, wildland fire, vegetation type conversion, and long-term changes to weather (USFWS 2025j). The species was listed as threatened in 1993 (58 FR 16742) with critical habitat designated in 2007 (72 FR 72010). The physical and biological features considered essential for conservation of the critical habitat include dynamic and successional sage scrub habitats that provide space for all life stages, as well as non-sage scrub habitats such as chaparral grassland and riparian areas in proximity to sage scrub habitats. See the draft Recovery Plan for additional information (USFWS 2025j).

#### Effects

Roads could increase habitat fragmentation and alter vegetation type, bringing in invasive species. The GBIF/NRM dataset does not contain any occurrences for the gnatcatcher, so potential exposure as estimated with that dataset is unknown. There are approximately 2,024 acres of designated critical habitat within the action area, which is only 1% of the total critical habitat. Less than half of that critical habitat is in potentially operable areas. Because the proposed action is unlikely to occur where the gnatcatcher lives, the proposed action _may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect_ the Coastal California gnatcatcher or its critical habitat.

#### _Florida scrub-jay (Aphelocoma coerulescens)_

The Florida scrub-jay is endemic to Florida, non-migratory, sedentary, and restricted to scrub and scrubby flatwoods. The scrub-jay historically occupied 39 counties in peninsular Floria but now only occupies conservation lands in 26 of those counties (private land status is unknown)

(USFWS 2025k). The scrub-jay was listed as threatened in 1987 (52 FR 20715). The primary historical cause of declines was loss and fragmentation of habitat from residential and commercial development (USFWS 2019h). The scrub-jay needs large open landscapes with short oak vegetation and open sandy areas with low densities of pine trees. These landscapes were historically maintained with frequent fire, but reductions in fire frequency have led to overgrown habitat conditions. These conditions also increase predator pressure and competition with the blue jay. See the 2025 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2025k).

#### Effects

From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 2,922 occurrences on NFS lands, only 1% of which are in the action area, but 81% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a high chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. Roads could increase habitat fragmentation and alter vegetation type. However, timber harvest can be used to enhance habitat for the scrub-jay. The species occurs on Ocala National Forest, which has the largest contiguous scrub habitat remaining in peninsular Florida (USFWS 2025k). The Land Management Plan for National Forests in Florida follows guidelines in the scrub-jay recovery plan (1999 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a), to maintain appropriate scrub habitat. Given the protections afforded by the forest plan and the positive influence of active management on the species, the proposed action _may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect_ the Florida scrub-jay.

### Wetland birds

#### _Eastern black rail (Laterallus jamaicensis_ ssp. _jamaicensis)_

The eastern black rail is a sparrow-sized secretive marsh bird that was once distributed widely across interior and coastal areas of the eastern U.S., Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean, but now occupies a small proportion of its former range. Documented or probable breeding locations are found in New Jersey, Delaware, North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, and Colorado. It can live in a variety of salt and brackish marsh, as well as freshwater wetlands. The plant structure seems to be most important, with the rail requiring dense overhead perennial herbaceous cover. The rail is primarily threatened by loss and degradation of wetlands due to habitat conversion (USFWS 2025l). The eastern black rail was listed as threatened in 2020 (85 FR 63764). See the draft Recovery Plan for additional information (USFWS 2025l).

#### Effects

Colorado is not part of the action area in this project, and Colorado has the only known breeding population of interior eastern black rails. The GBIF/NRM dataset does not contain any occurrences for the rail, so potential exposure as estimated with that dataset is unknown. Roads are unlikely to be built through the coastal wetlands, as there are no timber or fuels reduction priorities, however, new roads constructed nearby could cause associated degradation. The proposed action is unlikely to occur where the rail lives (discountable), therefore, the proposed action _may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect_ the eastern black rail.

#### _Everglade snail kite (Rostrhamus sociabilis plumbeus)_

The Everglade snail kite is a medium-sized hawk that occupies freshwater marshes in Florida and feeds exclusively on apple snails. It was listed as threatened in 1967 (32 FR 4001) and critical habitat was designated in 1977 (42 FR 47840). The snail kite is threatened by habitat fragmentation and loss of apple snails, with documented decreases associated with periods of drought. However, its population has recently expanded northward in Florida, in part due to the invasion of the non-native island apple snail, providing an additional food source. However, year-to-year variability is high, with continued uncertainty regarding water and habitat quality, and food availability (USFWS 2023j). See the 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2023j).

#### Effects

The GBIF/NRM dataset does not contain any occurrences for the snail kite, so potential exposure as estimated with that dataset is unknown. There is no critical habitat in or near the action area. Although nomadic, the snail kites are confined to wetland habitats and are not known to occur on Ocala National Forest (which is the only potential forest within their range). Given the lack of known occurrences on National Forest System lands, the proposed action will have _no effect_ on the Everglade snail kite.

#### _Mississippi sandhill crane (Antigone canadensis pulla)_

The Mississippi sandhill crane is a tall gray crane that occupies wet pine savanna exclusively in Jackson County, Mississippi. The subspecies was listed as endangered in 1973 (38 FR 14678) with critical habitat designated in 1977 (43 FR 39985). Specifically, the Mississippi Sandhill Crane National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1975 to protect habitat for this non-migratory population. The population is not yet self-sustaining and captive-raised juveniles are used to sustain it (USFWS 2024q). Habitat loss and degradation outside of the refuge is an ongoing threat, plus predation being the most common cause of death for the subspecies. See the 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2024q).

#### Effects

The only potential habitat on National Forests is on De Soto National Forest, with no known occurrences. The GBIF/NRM dataset does not contain any occurrences for the snail kite, so potential exposure as estimated with that dataset is unknown. There is no critical habitat in or near the action area, and in fact the action area does not include any of the De Soto National Forest. Because the crane and its habitat do not occur in the action area, the proposed action will have _no effect_ on the Mississippi sandhill crane.

#### _Whooping crane (Grus americana)_

The whooping crane is North America’s tallest bird and was listed as endangered in 1967 (32 FR 4001), with critical habitat designated in 1978 (43 FR 20938) and revised in 1997 (62 FR 38932). The only natural self-sustaining population migrates between Aransas National Wildlife Refuge on the Texas coast and Wood Buffalo National Park in Alberta, Canada. All living whooping cranes are descended from 15 that wintered in Texas in 1941. Whooping cranes were historically threatened due to habitat loss and hunting and continue to be threatened by loss of wetlands to cropland conversion, urbanization, roads/powerlines/wind farms that have all impacted the migratory corridor. Decreased river flows have also degraded migration and wintering habitats (USFWS 2012b). In addition to the endangered population, four areas have been designated as experimental nonessential for the reintroduction of whooping cranes: Florida (58 FR 5647), five Rocky Mountain states (62 FR 38932), nineteen eastern states (66 FR 33903), and Louisiana (76 FR 6066). Reintroduction efforts continue in the eastern migratory population and Louisiana, while the non-migratory Florida population reintroduction program has been discontinued. During winter 2023-2024 there were 162 cranes in reintroduced populations and 144 cranes managed under human care. The Aransas-Wood Buffalo population is considered a conservation success story, with over a 4% long term growth rate, with most recent counts about 536 (McAbee and Conkin 2025). See the Whooping Crane Status Report for additional information (McAbee and Conkin 2025).

#### Effects

From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 21 occurrences on NFS lands, none of which are in the action area. This suggests a low chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. Roads are unlikely to be developed in wetland areas that the crane uses as stopover sites. Given the lack of critical habitat or occurrences within the action area, and that the proposed activities are unlikely to occur in habitat, the proposed action will have _no effect_ on the whooping crane.

### Shorebirds

#### _Piping plover (Charadrius melodus)_

The piping plover is a small migratory shorebird that nests and feeds along coastal sand and gravel beaches in North America. It mostly uses sparsely vegetated sandbars or shorelines on river systems and alkaline lakes. The Atlantic and Northern Great Plains populations were listed as threatened in 1986, and the Great Lakes population was listed as endangered (50 FR 50726). Main threats to these populations include habitat loss (in breeding and wintering areas), damming and water withdrawals, predation, and human disturbance (USFWS 2024r). Critical habitat was designated for the Northern Great Plains breeding population in 2002 (67 FR 57638), the Great Lakes breeding population in 2001 (66 FR 22938), and for all wintering piping plovers in 2001 (66 FR 36038, revised 2009 in 74 FR 23476). See the 2024 5-year Review (USFWS 2024r) and the 2016 Draft Revised Recovery Plan for the Northern Great Plains (USFWS 2016c) for current species information.

#### Effects

Like most shorebirds, the piping plover stays close to shorelines and beaches without forest. From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 144 occurrences on NFS lands, none of which are in the action area. This suggests a low chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. As shoreline habitats do not have timber or fuels reduction needed, new roads are not likely to be proposed in piping plover habitat. In the unlikely event that a new road would be proposed in the future, the project would need to comply with ESA at the time. Critical habitat does not occur in the action area. Because activities related to the proposed action are highly unlikely to occur in their habitat, there will be _no effect_ on the piping plover.

#### _Rufa red knot (Calidris canutus rufa)_

The rufa red knot is a robin-sized shorebird known for being an extreme long-distance migrant, requiring spots of habitat from the extreme south of Tierra del Fuego to the far north of the central Canadian Arctic. It nests in dry, slightly elevated tundra locations with sparse vegetation. During migration and winter it uses coastal marine and estuarine habitats with large areas of exposed intertidal sediments. It may also use inland saline lakes in the Northern Great Plains as stopover sites. The rufa red knot is primarily threatened by habitat loss due to coastal development and sea level rise. It was listed as threatened in 2015 (79 FR 73706) and critical habitat was designated in 2023 (88 FR 22530). See the 2021 5-year review for current species information (USFWS 2021c).

#### Effects

Like most shorebirds, the rufa red knot stays close to shorelines and beaches without forest. The GBIF/NRM dataset does not contain any occurrences for the rufa red knot, so potential exposure as estimated with that dataset is unknown. As shoreline habitats do not have timber or fuels reduction needed, new roads are not likely to be proposed in rufa red knot habitat. In the unlikely event that a new road would be proposed in the future, the project would need to comply with ESA at the time. Critical habitat does not occur in the action area. Because activities related to the proposed action are highly unlikely to occur in their habitat, there will be _no effect_ on the rufa red knot.

#### _Western snowy plover (Charadrius nivosus nivosus)_

The Pacific Coast Distinct Population Segment of the western snowy plover was listed as threatened in 1993 (58 FR 12864). The western snowy plover subspecies is a small ground nesting shorebird that ranges from Washington, south along the Pacific Coast to southern Baja California, Mexico, with wintering populations as far north as British Columbia, Canada. The western snowy plover needs sparsely vegetated sandy areas for nesting along the coast. Threats include habitat loss and modification from a variety of factors (development, sea level rise), human disturbance (recreation, drone use, etc.), introduced beachgrass, and increased predator populations (USFWS 2024s). Revised critical habitat was designated in 2012 (77 FR 36727) in Washington, Oregon, and California. The primary physical and biological features essential to conservation are sandy beaches, dune systems, salt/mud flats, etc. that include: 1) areas that are below heavily vegetated/developed areas and above high tides, 2) shoreline habitats with little to no vegetation that support invertebrates as prey, 3) organic debris like seaweed that both supports prey and provides cover, and 4) minimal human disturbance. See the 2024 5-year review (USFWS 2024s) and the 2007 Recovery Plan (USFWS 2007c) for current species information.

#### Effects

Like most shorebirds, western snowy plovers stick closely to shorelines and beaches without forest. The GBIF/NRM dataset does not contain any occurrences for the western snowy plover, so potential exposure as estimated with that dataset is unknown. There are approximately 621 acres of critical habitat in the action area, which is 2.5% of the total critical habitat, almost none of which is in potentially operable areas. As shoreline habitats do not have timber or fuels reduction needed, new roads are not likely to be proposed in snowy plover habitat. In the unlikely event that a new road would be proposed in the future, the project would need to comply with ESA at the time. Because activities related to the proposed action are highly unlikely to occur in their habitat or designated critical habitat, there will be _no effect_ on the western snowy plover or its critical habitat.

### Grassland birds

#### _Greater sage-grouse (Centrocercus urophasianus)_

The greater sage-grouse is the largest North American grouse species, known for elaborate spring mating displays on traditional lekking grounds. The Bi-State greater sage-grouse is a proposed threatened Distinct Population Segment that lives in the California-Nevada border near Mono Lake. The DPS was proposed in 2013 (78 FR 64357) with critical habitat proposed in 2014 (78 FR 64328). The greater sage-grouse is a sagebrush obligate that requires large, interconnected expanses of sagebrush with healthy, native understories. Sage-grouse exhibit strong site fidelity, limiting the degree to which they can adapt when habitat changes. Sagebrush ecosystems are threatened by a range of disturbances including drought, altered wildlife regimes, expansion of invasive species, and human development (Coates et al. 2024). There are multiple impacts to habitat interacting in the Bi-State area including pinyon-juniper encroachment, urbanization and infrastructure development, fire-invasive species cycles, and local increases in predation (USFWS 2020f). However, a 2012 Bi-State Action Plan resulted in planning and implementing conservation actions that have reduced the average annual rate of population decline (Coates et al. 2024). See the 2020 Species Report for additional information (USFWS 2020f).

#### Effects

From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 4,342 occurrences on NFS lands, 25% of which are in the action area, and 11% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a moderate chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. Approximately 439,330 acres of proposed critical habitat occurs within the action area, which is 23.5% of the total proposed critical habitat. Most of that critical habitat, however, is not within potentially operable areas. Physical and biological features essential to the conservation include sagebrush plant communities and interspersed mesic areas of sufficient size and configuration to provide for foraging, nesting, and rearing habitats (78 FR 64328).

Roads are a known factor contributing to habitat fragmentation in sagebrush ecosystems. In addition, roads can increase human access, spread nonnative plants, provide predator access, and cause direct mortality to sage-grouse (USFWS 2020f). Noise associated with roads and energy development have been shown to decrease lek attendance (Blickley et al. 2012). An extensive road network already occurs throughout the Bi-state area, but all federal lands have made efforts for Bi-state conservation including closing unauthorized routes and restricting new road development (USFWS 2020f). Restrictions on new roads exist in both the Inyo and HumboldtToiyabe Forest Plans (USFWS 2020f). As there is already an extensive road network in the area, new roads are not particularly likely to be developed. However, adverse effects could result from removal of suitable habitat and introducing increased nonnative plants and predators. Removal of sagebrush could have adverse impacts on the critical habitat PBFs. Therefore, the proposed action _may affect, is likely to adversely affect_ the proposed Bi-state sage grouse and its proposed critical habitat.

#### _Gunnison sage-grouse (Centrocercus minimus)_

The Gunnison sage-grouse lives exclusively in the sagebrush steppe ecosystems of southwestern Colorado and southeastern Utah. The second largest grouse in North America and a sagebrush obligate, Gunnison sage-grouse are found in eight small populations: seven in Colorado and one in Utah. The species was listed in 2014 (79 FR 69191) with critical habitat designated as well (79 FR 69311). The species requires relatively continuous and healthy sagebrush stands with a welldeveloped understory and uses a mosaic of sagebrush habitats throughout the range (USFWS 2020g). As a sagebrush obligate, it is threatened by loss of sagebrush, particularly due to habitat conversion for agriculture and development, invasive plants, increased pinyon-juniper, recreation, and some grazing practices (USFWS 2024t). See the 2024 5-year review for additional information (USFWS 2024t).

#### Effects

Because the action area does not include Colorado, only one Gunnison sage-grouse population is within the action area – Monticello in Utah. Monticello is a small satellite population that has steadily decreased since 2009 and may have as few as three individuals remaining, in spite of ongoing efforts to develop and maintain habitat. The population struggles with solar development, cropland and grazing pressures, as well as the effects of increases in ravens (USFWS 2024t). This population does not have designated critical habitat. From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 22 occurrences on NFS lands, none of which are in the action area. This suggests a low chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. Given the lack of occurrence overlap with the action area, the proposed action will have _no effect_ on the Gunnison sage-grouse.

### Other birds

#### _California condor (Gymnogyps californianus)_

California condors are the largest landbird in North America and can fly up to 250 miles a day searching for food. They require expansive open spaces such as grasslands for foraging with abundant carrion and well as mountainous cliffs or large broken top trees for nesting. Condors were listed in 1967 (32 FR 4001) and critical habitat was designated in 1974 (41 FR 21914). At the time of listing, condors were restricted to the southern end of the San Joaquin Valley in California. The range continued to contract until a captive breeding program was established in 1982, with the last wild condor captured at Bitter Creek National Wildlife Refuge in 1987. Since 1992, when captive-bred condors were first reintroduced back into the wild, the species has slowly recolonized its former range. Nonessential Experimental Populations were designated in specified portions of Arizona, Nevada, and Utah in 1996 (61 FR 54043) and more recently in specified portions of northern California, northwest Nevada, and Oregon in 2001 (86 FR 15602). The primary threat to species recovery is lead poisoning from spent ammunition. In addition, powerlines, diseases (specifically highly pathogenic avian influenza, HPAI), intentional shooting, and wind energy contribute to mortalities. The wild populations continue to be supplemented by captive populations, and provided food, as the populations are not yet selfsustaining. See the 2023 5-year review for current species information (USFWS 2023k).

#### Effects

Condors are primarily threatened by lead poisoning and are not particularly sensitive to habitat loss or fragmentation, as they use such expansive areas. From the GBIF/NRM dataset, there are a total of 1,642 occurrences on NFS lands, 18% of which are in the action area, and 15% of those are in potentially operable areas. This suggests a moderate chance of exposure for individuals to potential future roads and/or timber operations. There are approximately 13,345 acres of critical habitat in the action area, which is 2.2% of total critical habitat. Less than half of that critical habitat is within potentially operable areas. Critical habitat when designated did not provide essential physical and biological features beyond land, water, and airspace up to 3,000 ft in elevation. The proposed action is unlikely to impact the critical habitat PBFs to the degree that they are no longer functional. New road development into previously roadless areas could remove potential nesting trees, however, nesting locations is not a limiting factor for condors.

As mentioned with other species, before any new roads were constructed, or any associated activities occurred in the action area that were previously not allowed, site-specific analyses and ESA compliance would be required. Thus, the proposed action _may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect_ the California condor or its critical habitat.

## Insects and Arachnids

To assist analyzing effects to a large number of species, ESA-listed species were grouped taxonomically. The insect and arachnid group includes 21 total species including 11 endangered, 7 threatened, 1 proposed endangered, and 2 proposed threatened insects and arachnids (Table 18). Insects and arachnids are widely varied in life history and habitat requirements. Most of the listed insects and arachnids are primarily terrestrial except for larval stages of dragonfly and stonefly species. Most of the insect species are capable of flight and can move around in search of food and nesting sources.  Two insect species, the monarch butterfly and Suckley’s cuckoo bumble bee, occur on many forests while many of the other species occur on just one or two forests.
