Road construction, road use, and timber harvest can affect insect and arachnid species by removing habitat and host plants, fragmenting habitat leading to a loss of gene flow between populations, creating edge effects that destabilize environmental conditions that support the species, causing direct mortality through vehicle strikes and right-of-way maintenance equipment, and increasing toxins associated with herbicide and road salt, if used. The primary effects of the proposed action on insect and arachnid species are discussed below and presented in Table 12. A discussion on species protection afforded by land management plans and other documents beyond the protections of the 2001 Roadless Rule is also included.

### Major Stressors

#### _Direct Mortality_

Mobile adult insects are expected to avoid activities that might cause direct mortality, except for the use of roads by vehicles. Momeni-Dehaghi et al. (2024), estimate migratory monarchs migrate 3,283 km and cross 3,089 roads during fall migration. Migrating monarch butterflies have an estimated 40% probability of surviving migration that probability drops precipitously with increasing time spent flying at vehicle height. Further, monarch butterflies are not known to avoid roads and vehicles (Momeni-Dehaghi et al. 2024). However, vehicular traffic on NFS roads typically occurs at slow speeds and low volume, minimizing the likelihood of striking flying insects (Munoz et al. 2014). Baxter-Gilbert et al. (2015) found insect mortality rates from vehicle collision to differ among insect families with lepidopterans dying at a rate of 10.1 individuals/km/day and hymenopterans at 26.8 individuals/km/day. Adjacent habitat type appears to affect the impact of roads on pollinating insects. Keilsohn et al. (2018) found that road mortality of insects was greatest when adjacent habitat was meadows or curated lawns and lower when the area was wooded. Road structure also has an impact on insect mortality from strikes as Keilsohn et al. (2018) found lepidopteran mortality was highest when a median was present. NFS roads in remote areas are generally unpaved and single lane, which also minimizes the likelihood of vehicle collision with flying aquatic insects, that often mistake paved roads for water in which to lay their eggs (Munoz et al. 2014). In contrast, insect larvae and pupae are less mobile and can be directly killed by vegetation removal, vehicular strikes, and trampling. Much of the anticipated impacts of roads on insect communities are related to the use of salt to alleviate icy conditions during winter. However, NFS roads do not use salt to remove icy conditions.

Bees and butterflies are important pollinators that may be impacted by road construction and timber harvest. Listed bees can use forested habitat for nesting, overwintering, and foraging.  For instance, timber harvests and road construction during overwintering could lead to direct mortality of rusty patched and Suckley’s cuckoo bumble bee queens that inhabit leaf litter and shallow soils (89 FR 102074, USFWS 2024u). Similarly, American burying beetles reproduce on buried carcasses just below the soil surface. Soil disturbing activities such as road surfacing and the movement of heavy equipment can crush nesting beetles. However, those same activities can kill small animals that burying beetles can then use for breeding and feeding. In contrast to risks of direct mortality from vehicle strikes for most flying and some ground insects, the spruce-fir moss spider inhabits high elevation moss-covered rocks and is unlikely to be affected by moving vehicles.

Because future timber and road projects may or may not include seasonal restriction for removing trees, prescribed fire, or road construction activities during active flight periods, it is possible an active colony (nest) or hibernating female of insect species could be disturbed, crushed, or burned during project implementation. These effects would result from the crushing or caving-in of burrows used by colonies, or other similar underground cavities or decaying logs that offer resting and sheltering.

#### _Habitat Fragmentation and Edge Effects_

Road construction and subsequent habitat fragmentation pose threats to threatened and endangered insects. The primary effects include outright habitat loss, the creation of barriers to movement, and the degradation of remaining habitat quality through "edge effects" (Munoz et al. 2014). These factors collectively increase the risk of local extinctions and undermine the longterm viability of vulnerable insect populations.

Habitat fragmentation is the physical destruction and division of continuous landscapes into smaller, isolated patches. For threatened and endangered insects, these remaining fragments often become too small to support viable populations, lacking sufficient resources like host plants, breeding grounds, or diverse microhabitats. The reduction in total habitat area is often a key driver of species decline.

Roads act as physical and behavioral barriers to insect movement and are particularly detrimental to species with limited dispersal capabilities. Flightless insects, such as some ground beetles, are highly susceptible, with major roads like highways acting as near-absolute barriers to gene flow (Munoz et al. 2014). Even highly mobile flying insects, like butterflies and bees, often exhibit reluctance to cross roads, even when suitable habitat is nearby. This behavioral avoidance, combined with physical limitations for smaller species, results in the isolation of populations, reduced gene flow, and genetic bottlenecks, which severely compromise a population's ability to adapt to environmental changes.

Habitat degradation around roads further exacerbates the challenges faced by endangered insects. The "edge effect" is a major consequence, where conditions along the road's edge differ drastically from the interior of the habitat patch. These altered conditions, including changes in light, temperature, and humidity, may be unsuitable for species adapted to more stable environments. The disrupted conditions also favor the establishment of non-native and invasive species that outcompete the native flora and fauna the insects rely on.

Finally, roads disrupt essential species interactions, such as predator-prey dynamics and vital pollination processes. Roadsides can attract pollinators with abundant flowering plants but simultaneously expose them to higher risks of mortality. The balance between potential breeding benefits in road rights-of-way and the costs of mortality and exposure to pollutants remains an area of active research.

#### _Loss of Host Plants_

The loss and decline of host plants can adversely affect threatened and endangered insects, primarily because many herbivorous insects are specialists that rely exclusively on specific plant species for their survival and reproduction. This specialization means that the disappearance or reduction of a particular host plant directly translates to a loss of food, habitat, and a site for laying eggs, which can lead to a cascade of negative effects that significantly heighten extinction risk for these vulnerable insects (Boggs and Ehrlich 2007).

Most herbivorous insects have evolved to overcome the specific physical and chemical defenses of one or a few closely related plant species. These specialized insects cannot simply switch to another plant when their primary host declines as other plants may be unpalatable, lack the necessary nutrients, or even be toxic (Haan et al. 2018). A classic example is the Monarch butterfly ( _Danaus plexippus_ ), whose caterpillars can only survive by feeding on plants in the milkweed genus ( _Asclepias_ ). The loss of milkweed due to changing land management practices and habitat destruction is directly linked to significant Monarch population declines. Without milkweed, Monarchs cannot complete their life cycle, highlighting how the fate of an insect species is tied directly to the availability of its specific host plant (USFWS 2020h).

There may be a direct loss of floral resources (crushing, uprooting) from heavy equipment use, though this loss is considered temporary and limited to one to two seasons after implementation. Short-term loss of these plants is not expected to cause a wide-spread reduction in host plants or their pollinators. Removing timber will result in varied reductions of canopy cover. The creation of small and large canopy gaps and removal of the smaller understory vegetation is expected to promote improved growing conditions for host plants. Canopy reduction is also expected to increase solar radiation to the ground and support plant and shrub growth, considered favorable to pollinators. On the periphery, tree removal is likely to reduce some of the shade and cover considered important for maintaining overwintering and nesting sites of some insect species (Ulyshen et al. 2024). Roadsides can often act as pollinator breeding habitat if increased light availability results in host plant proliferation (Meinzen et al. 2024). However, insect populations are also negatively affected by roads and traffic. Where roadside habitat is managed for pollinators and traffic is low and slow moving, roadsides could provide a net benefit to pollinator species.

The effects of host plant loss manifest through several mechanisms, the first being reproductive failure (Haan et al. 2018). Adult female insects typically lay their eggs exclusively on their specific host plants. The absence or scarcity of these plants results in fewer places to lay eggs, leading to reduced reproductive success and a smaller next generation. This is particularly true when native plants are displaced by non-native species, which insects often do not recognize as suitable for feeding or oviposition (Tallamy et al. 2020). Furthermore, a decline in host plant abundance means increased competition for food, lower nutritional intake for larvae, slower development, and potentially higher mortality rates. Changes to abiotic factors such as temperature and precipitation can exacerbate this issue by disrupting the synchronized timing of insect life cycles and the availability of their host plants. If a host plant emerges earlier or later than the insect larvae are ready to feed, mass starvation can occur, creating a critical mismatch between the insect's needs and resource availability (Abarca and Spahn 2021).

As host plants become scarce and fragmented, insect populations that rely on them also become isolated in small patches of remaining habitat. This fragmentation prevents insects from moving between populations, leading to reduced gene flow, decreased genetic diversity, and a higher vulnerability to local extinctions.

Insects are a foundational part of the food web, serving as a critical food source for other animals, especially birds and small mammals. The loss of host plants reduces the insect biomass, which in turn impacts the reproductive success and survival of animals at higher trophic levels, demonstrating a broader ecological impact beyond the initial plant-insect relationship.

#### _Sedimentation and Pollution_

Only two ESA-listed insect species have an aquatic lifecycle, the Hine’s emerald dragonfly and western glacier stonefly. Aquatic insect larvae are susceptible to being buried by sedimentation, which could lead to direct mortality by clogging their gills.  However, Hine’s emerald dragonfly larvae primarily inhabit shallow, slow-moving waters of marshes and fens, where sedimentation is not considered a major threat to the species (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2021). In contrast, western glacier stoneflies inhabit cool glacier-fed streams in northern Montana, where sedimentation could be an issue. However, sedimentation is not identified as a stressor to this species as it inhabits remote, undeveloped areas. The major threat to this species is the loss of glacier melt that supports their aquatic life stage. Given the low likelihood these species will be exposed to sedimentation given their habitat and range, and that the other ESA-listed insect species do not have aquatic life stages, the effects of sedimentation on listed insects are not expected to occur.

### Existing Protections

The Cleveland, Los Padres, and San Bernardino National Forests are required to avoid activities that result in removal, crushing, burying, burning, or mowing of host plants within critical and occupied habitat for threatened, endangered, and proposed butterfly species, unless guided differently by a species-specific consultation (land management plans available at USFS 2025a). Regardless of the existence of the roadless rule, this design criteria ensures effects to Hermes copper butterfly, Laguna Mountains skipper, Kern primrose sphinx moth, and Quino checkerspot butterfly are minimized or avoided. Similarly, the Huron-Manistee forest plan requires implementation of the Karner Blue Butterfly Recovery Plan and minimization of effects to that species, suggesting in the absence of the Roadless Rule, protections will continue into the foreseeable future.

The USDA Forest Service published Conservation and Management of Monarch Butterflies: A Strategic Framework (USFS 2015) to provide a meaningful approach to monarch conservation on NFS lands. The USDA Forest Service also supports implementation of the North American Monarch Conservation Plan (Commission for Environmental Cooperation 2008).

The Shoshone Forest management plan does not contain species-specific protective measures for the western glacier stonefly.

### Critical Habitat

Effects to designated critical habitat are analyzed by reviewing the physical and biological features associated with that habitat and determining the effects the action may have on those features. Most insect critical habitat includes host plants in addition to abiotic characteristics suitable for species growth and reproduction. Only five listed insect species have designated critical habitat within the action area and of those only one, the laguna mountain skipper (3.5%) exceeds more than 2% overlap.  In the event activities occur in designated critical habitat the effects to physical and biological features will be minimized or avoided as dictated by local conditions. Some features of critical habitat, such as open canopy, may be positively affected by future timber and road activities. Most insect species utilize plants that are shrubs and flowering plants that are quicker to establish after disturbance compared to fully mature trees and larger vegetation. Given the small amount of overlap with designated critical habitat, that most vegetation impacts will be temporary, and that some effects may be positive, the proposed action is not likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for insect species.

## Amphibians

The amphibian group includes 19 total species that occur within the affected roadless areas, including 7 Endangered, 8 Threatened, 2 Proposed Endangered and 2 Proposed Threatened amphibian species. The Amphibian group consists of 11 frog and toad species and 10 salamander species. Amphibians are known for their biphasic life histories where most species have an aquatic larval stage and a terrestrial adult stage. For additional discussion of how the aquatic environment may be affected by the proposed action see the effects section for fish, bivalves, and crustaceans.  However, there are some exceptions that vary in their life-histories. In this group, the 4 species of salamanders in the family Plethodontidae, the Cheat Mountain salamander, Jemez Mountains salamander, Kern Canyon slender salamander, and relictual slender salamander, do not have an aquatic larval stage, therefore all of the threats to these species will be from impacts to the terrestrial habitat. The Plethodontid species are lungless and are sensitive to changes in microclimate. The 2 hellbender (salamander) species, in this group, are completely aquatic and do not have a terrestrial life-stage. Most of the species are known to occur in several forest districts except 5 species, the Cheat Mountain salamander, Jemez Mountains salamander, Kern Canyon slender salamander, Ozark Hellbender, and relictual slender salamander, have small geographic ranges and only occur in one forest district.

### Exposure to the proposed action

Exposure of amphibian species to the proposed action was calculated using the NRM and GBIF data and categorized as high, moderate, low, or unknown.  When unknown, the FS assumes some level of exposure is likely.

### Frogs and Toads

All the frog species in this group exhibit a biphasic life history with a terrestrial adult life stage and an aquatic tadpole stage with the exception of the guajon that is fully terrestrial. This is relevant because each species will be exposed to aquatic and terrestrial threats. In the terrestrial stage common threats include habitat loss and direct mortality. Amphibians seem exceptionally vulnerable to death on roads (Beebee 2013). Amphibians rely heavily on vibration detection. Salamanders can sense substrate vibrations (Ross and Smith 1980), and several frog species use ground-borne vibrations as part of their breeding communication (Narins 1990). All amphibian species studied so far demonstrate strong sensitivity to such vibrations (Caorsi et al. 2019). While research on how anthropogenic vibrations influence animal behavior remains limited (Cross et al. 2021), evidence shows that simulated human-made sounds and vibrations can reduce the calling rate of male toads, which may ultimately decrease reproductive success (Caorsi et al. 2019). Anthropogenic disturbances can also have negative physiological effects. For instance, the non-native African clawed frog showed increased stress and mortality when exposed to construction-related noise and vibrations (Felt et al. 2012). In addition, traffic noise can alter calling behavior in frogs that can ultimately affect fitness (Hoskin and Goosem 2010).

In the aquatic stage, amphibians may be exposed to sedimentation caused by runoff after road construction or timber harvest (Jones et al. 2011; Wagner et al. 2013), leading to mortality of these life stages.

#### _Arroyo toad (Anaxyrus californicus)(E)_

The arroyo toad occurs in 4 National Forests in the Pacific Southwest Region of the Forest Service. Threats on national forest lands include introduced aquatic predators, road and trail traffic, and tamarisk invasion (Arroyo Toad Recovery Plan, USFWS 1999). Arroyo toad populations are driven by surface water availability (Fisher et al. 2018). Declines of the arroyo toad are attributed to habitat degradation, invasive predators, and altered hydrological regimes (Treglia et al. 2015).

#### Existing Protections

The Angeles NF Forest Plan has designated Critical Biological Land Use Zones for the protection of species-at-risk and conservation strategies for riparian and aquatic habitats for species of concern, including the arroyo toad. Project planning includes habitat acquisition, vegetation management, invasive species control and fire management to benefit species of concern including the toad. The plan recommends withdrawal from mineral entry to T&E species key habitats in areas of mineral potential where habitat is not protected by any other means and would benefit by withdrawal. Protective measures will be maintained for the period of time needed to provide the necessary protection for sensitive species and key habitats.

The Los Padres, Cleveland and San Bernardino NF Plans have conservation strategies for the arroyo toad including; education on the importance of riparian and aquatic habitat and importance of keeping vehicles on roads; inventory of aquatic species including the arroyo toad; and restricted human access during critical life stages of the toad

#### _California red-legged frog (Rana draytonii)(T)_

The California red-legged frog occurs in 3 National Forests in the Forest Service Pacific Southwest Region. Doubledee et al. (2003) suggest that invasive species (bullfrog) are the primary drivers of decline.

#### Existing Protections

The Angeles NF Forest Plan has a conservation strategy for the California red-legged frog including; education on the importance of riparian and aquatic habitat and importance of keeping vehicles on roads; inventory of aquatic species including the red-legged frog; habitat restoration and control of invasive species. The plan recommends withdrawal from mineral entry to T&E species key habitats in areas of mineral potential where habitat is not protected by any other means and would benefit by withdrawal. Protective measures will be maintained for the period of time needed to provide the necessary protection for sensitive species and key habitats.

The Los Padres NF Plan mentions protecting the California red-legged frog and other sensitive species but does not list specific protections. The California red-legged frog is not mentioned in other Forest Plans where it occurs.

#### _Chiricahua leopard frog (Rana chiricahuensis)(T)_

The Chiricahua leopard frog occurs in 4 National Forests in the Southwestern Region of the Forest Service. Increased sediment flows into occupied stock tanks will likely increase the need and frequency of maintenance to remove those sediments, resulting in increased likelihood of mortality of the frogs (USFWS 2007d). Post-fire sediment movement can be especially dramatic, filling in pools and covering stream beds in rocks and cobble. Harris et al. (2022) suggest that the main threats to the Chiricahua leopard frogs are _Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis_ (Bd) and invasive bullfrogs.

#### Existing Protections

The Coronado NF Forest Plan states that efforts are underway to restore a number of species including the Chiricahua leopard frog and new issuance, renewal, modification, and management of grazing permits shall comply with the Coronado National Forest’s “Stockpond and Aquatic Habitat Management and Maintenance Guidelines for the Chiricahua Leopard Frog.”

The Apache, Cibola, Coconino and Gila NF Plans mention that the leopard frog occurs on the district, but no specific protections are listed. The leopard frog is not mentioned in the Prescott or Tonto NF Forest Plans.

#### _Guajon (Eleutherodactylus cooki)(T)_

The guajon occurs on the El Yunque National Forest in Puerto Rico in Region 8. The Listing Rule (62 FR 31757) states that the guajon may require special management considerations or protection due to threats to the primary constituent elements from road construction, agriculture, development, and fishing with chemicals. This species has direct development from egg to froglet, no aquatic larval stage (Townsend and Stewart 1985).

#### Existing Protections

The Guajon is not mentioned in the El Yunque NF Forest Plan.

#### _Foothill yellow-legged frog (Rana boylii)(E)_

The Foothill yellow-legged frog occurs in 7 National Forests in the Pacific Southwest Region of the Forest Service. Lind et al. (2016) suggest that the primary threats to the yellow-legged frog are large human-caused disturbances such as dams and diversions. Ashton et al. (1998) stated that logging and road related mass wasting events have resulted in periodically high levels of siltation. High levels of silt may inhibit the attachment of the egg mass to the substrate. Excessive accumulation of silt on the egg masses may have adverse effects on embryo development, but this needs further study.

#### Existing Protections

The Foothill yellow-legged frog is not mentioned in any Forest Plans where it occurs.

#### _Mountain yellow-legged frog (Rana muscosa)(E)_

The mountain yellow-legged frog occurs on 5 National Forest in the Pacific Southwest Region. Knapp et al. (2007) suggest that disease and invasive fish are major causes of decline. The Mountain yellow-legged frog Recovery Plan (USFWS 2018h) states that each population is small and highly susceptible to stochastic events. Measures have been taken to reduce the impact of certain threats, including recreation, nonnative trout, and stochastic extinction. However, these threats and other threats to the habitat remain, including illegal activities (cannabis cultivation and suction dredge mining), and legal activities (recreational activities, fire suppression activities, and roadwork construction). Wildfire and long-term alteration of weather patterns both have a high likelihood of affecting southern mountain yellow-legged frog and its habitat; however, the timing and options available to reduce these threats are either limited or unclear.

#### Existing Protections

The mountain yellow-legged frog is listed as a primary protected species in Angeles NF Forest Plan. There is conservation strategy emphasis on habitat, invasive species control and monitoring. Additional emphasis will be placed on the use by recreationists and urban and national forest infrastructure that is sustainable such that it has minimal effects to species (mountain yellow-legged frog) and their habitat. The San Bernadino NF Plan states the importance of riparian and aquatic species and habitat, value of vegetation management to species at risk, species monitoring, and keeping vehicles on roads for species including the mountain yellow-legged frog.

Inyo, Sequoia and the Sierra NF Plans mentions mountain yellow-legged frog but do not list specific protections.

#### _Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog (Rana sierrae)(E)_

The Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog occurs in 10 National Forests across the Intermountain and Pacific Southwest Regions of the Forest Service. The declines in populations of Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frogs have been largely attributed to the introduction of trout to historically fishless lakes in high elevations and to the spread of the chytrid fungus (Brown et al. 2019). Threats to all the yellow-legged frog species are similar.

#### Existing Protections

The Lake Tahoe BMU Land Management Plan has a section for Special Status Species Habitat areas that are defined as areas of quality habitat for Federal Threatened, Endangered, Candidate, and Proposed species, including the Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog. It calls for work collaboratively with partners to identify and implement additional habitat restoration efforts that expand the range of Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog within historic habitat throughout the Basin. Specific objectives include; complete restoration of seven high alpine lakes (composed of habitat areas that would support four sub-populations) adjacent to current yellow-legged frog populations in the Desolation wilderness by removing introduced trout species by 2029

The Inyo NF Plan specifies that where pesticide applications are proposed within 500 feet of known occupied sites for Yosemite toad, Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog, and Mountain yellow-legged frog, applications will be designed to avoid adverse effects to individuals and their habitats. The Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog is not mentioned in the other Forest Plans where it occurs.

#### _Oregon spotted frog (Rana pretiosa)(T)_

The Oregon spotted frog occurs in 2 National Forests in the Pacific Northwest Region of the Forest Service. The Oregon spotted frog Recovery Plan (USFWS 2024v) states that population declines are the results of habitat degradation and fragmentation caused by altered hydrology, invasive vegetation, and non-native predators. Blouin et al. (2010) suggests that there is something about the biology of the Oregon spotted frog that predisposes it to substantial fragmentation, even in relatively undisturbed habitat.

#### Existing Protections

The Gifford Pichot NF Forest Plan lists the Oregon spotted frog as a sensitive species but does not list protections. The Oregon spotted frog is not mentioned in the Deschutes NF Forest Plan.

#### _Western spadefoot (Spea hammondii)(PT)_

The western spadefoot occurs in 7 National Forests in the Pacific Southwest Region of the Forest Service. Shedd (2016) stated where roadways intersect areas inhabited by spadefoot populations, adults and younger terrestrial stage individuals may be observed on road surfaces. Roads increase danger for spadefoots as well, as road-killed western spadefoots have been documented.

#### Existing Protections

The San Bernardino NF Forest Plan mentions conservation strategies for inventory of riparian and aquatic species, habitat improvement and acquisition, and vegetation treatments for several species of concern, including the western spadefoot. The western spadefoot is not mentioned in any of the other Forest Plans where it occurs.

#### _Yosemite toad (Anaxyrus canorus)(T)_

The Yosemite toad occurs in 4 National Forests across the Intermountain and Pacific Southwest Regions of the Forest Service. Sherman and Morton (1993) suggest that chytrid fungus and changing weather (dry winters) are major factors in this species decline.

#### Existing Protections

The Sierra NF Forest Plan has a species-specific direction intended to minimize adverse impacts of activities on the Yosemite toad including suitable breeding and rearing habitat. This plan direction will help achieve conditions at the meadow scale that enable attainment and maintenance of desired conditions for Yosemite toad and its habitat. Guidelines include; 1) Grazing management practices, such as deferred seasonal grazing, meadow fencing, and modifying grazing period, will be used to avoid negative impacts to Yosemite toad and their habitat to the maximum extent feasible; 2) Yosemite toad breeding dates should be determined locally to avoid co-occurrence of cattle grazing and egg masses, tadpoles, juveniles, and breeding adults to the maximum extent feasible; and 3) monitor if there is sufficient breeding and rearing habitat to support the survival and recovery of local Yosemite toad populations. Specific protections include; 1) Check around equipment for Yosemite toad individuals prior to moving equipment and follow approved handing guidelines if moving individuals is necessary; 2) Check for Yosemite toad use in open dry lupine covered areas where numerous rodent burrows occur. Reduce impacts to high-quality upland habitat by considering avoiding or minimizing working or walking in or crossing these areas and avoiding vehicle use or storage and equipment storage in these areas; 3) Consider impacts of activities on Yosemite toad dispersal, especially the use of erosion control materials, 4) Reduce impacts on Yosemite toads by implementing a process for monitoring and relocating individual toads from travel ways during motorized special use events or using temporary elevated road or trail structures to avoid direct mortality to toads; and 5) Use burning techniques that allow Yosemite toads to escape burn piles and that leave patches of hiding cover in broadcast burns.

The Inyo NF Plan specifies that where pesticide applications are proposed within 500 feet of known occupied sites for Yosemite toad, Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog, and Mountain yellow-legged frog, application will be designed to avoid adverse effects to individuals and their habitats. The Yosemite toad is not mentioned in the other Forest Plans where it occurs.

### Salamanders

Roads have negative effects on salamanders through direct mortality, damaging habitat, and fragmenting populations. Traffic and wetland proximity increased negative impacts in some studies; abandoned logging roads showed negative effects. Positive effects were limited to habitat creation along roads (Ochs et al. 2024). Semlitsch et al. (2007) found that salamander abundance was significantly lower on old, abandoned logging roads compared with the adjacent upslope sites. These results indicate that forest roads and abandoned logging roads have negative effects on forest-dependent species such as plethodontid salamanders. Further, amphibians rely heavily on vibration detection and salamanders can sense substrate vibrations (Ross and Smith 1980). While all amphibian species studied so far demonstrate strong sensitivity to such vibrations (Caorsi et al. 2019), research on how anthropogenic vibrations influence animal behavior remains limited (Cross et al. 2021). Water siltation and sedimentation are serious threats that can follow logging and road activity.

#### _Fully Aquatic salamanders_

Threats are primarily to the aquatic environment.

#### Neuse River waterdog ( _Necturus lewisi_ )(T)

The Neuse River waterdog is a fully aquatic salamander species that occurs in the Croatan National Forest in the Southern Region of the Forest Service. There is a strong negative effect of fine sediments on occupancy of _Neuse River waterdog_ . Analyses support the hypothesis that observed declines in the occurrence of Neuse River waterdog are a delayed result of sedimentation-induced recruitment limitation (Teitsworth et al. 2024).

#### _Existing Protections_

The Neuse River waterdog is not mentioned in the Croatan NF Forest Plan.

Eastern hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis lleganiensis)(PE)

The eastern hellbender is a fully aquatic salamander species that occurs in 9 National Forests across the Southern and Eastern Regions of the Forest Service. Habitat alterations, including siltation, water impoundment, and water quality degradation are likely the greatest threats to eastern hellbenders. Other threats include incidental take by anglers, collection for the pet trade, and predation by non-native fish (Mayasich et al. 2003).

#### _Existing Protections_

The Nantahala and Pisgah FN Forest Plans state that management actions will focus on key species, including eastern hellbenders. The plan calls for maintaining water quality for hellbenders in waters that support them, enhance hellbender and native brook trout populations where habitat is suitable, and restore and/or maintain healthy populations of hellbenders in East Fork and West Fork Pigeon River. Specific protections state that installation of new stream crossings, or their replacement, should avoid fragmenting existing populations of native aquatic species. Replacement of existing crossings should reconnect fragmented populations of native species (including hellbenders) or avoid fragmenting existing populations wherever relevant. Crossings that are barriers should be retained where they protect populations of native species. The eastern hellbender is mentioned in the Daniel Boone NF Plan but no specific protections are listed. The hellbender is not mentioned in any of the other Forest Plans where it occurs.

Ozark hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis bishopi)(E)

The Ozark hellbender is a fully aquatic salamander species that occurs in the Mark Twain National Forest in the Eastern Region of the Forest Service. The use of interstitial spaces by larval the Ozark hellbender may make them particularly vulnerable to siltation and sedimentation (Pitt et al. 2016). Siltation and sedimentation have been suggested as factors contributing to the decline of the hellbender and its prey due to the degradation and reduction of habitat (Briggler et al. 2007).

#### _Existing Protections_

The Ozark hellbender is not mentioned in the Mark Twain NF Forest Plan.

_Salamanders with terrestrial adults and aquatic larvae_

California tiger salamander ( _Ambystoma californiense_ )(T)

The California tiger salamander occurs in 3 National Forests in the Pacific Southwest Region of the Forest Service The apparent causes of this decline are habitat loss due to urbanization, adult salamander mortality from automobiles, loss of larvae through habitat drainage, and possibly predation by transient fish populations (Barry and Shaffer 1994). The California tiger salamander recovery plan (USFWS 2017c) states that multiple factors have contributed to population declines of this species, including habitat loss and fragmentation; predation from, and competition with, invasive species; hybridization with nonnative barred tiger salamanders ( _Ambystoma tigrinum_ ); mortality from road crossings; contaminants; and small mammal burrow control efforts (69 FR 47212; USFWS 2014b). Other potential threats include introduction of diseases such as ranaviruses and chytrid fungi, and long-term alteration of weather patterns (69 FR 47212; USFWS 2014b).

#### _Existing Protections_

The California tiger salamander is not mentioned in any of the Forest Plans where it occurs.

#### Frosted flatwoods salamander ( _Ambystoma cingulatum_ )(T)

The frosted flatwoods salamander occurs in 4 National Forests in the Southern Region of the Forest Service. The frosted flatwoods salamander recovery plan (USFWS 2021d) states that the improper or overuse of pesticides and herbicides, presence of predatory fish in breeding ponds, lack of regular lightning season fire to maintain suitable habitats, disruptions to hydrology including ditching and addition of impervious surfaces, road construction or increased traffic near breeding ponds, invasive plants, and disease are all threats. Westervelt et al. (2013) Suggest that even modest reductions in annual rainfall (5–10%) would affect the persistence of breeding habitat and result in further population declines and more moderate reductions (20–25%) would result in population extirpation.

#### _Existing Protections_

The Florida (Apalachicola and Osceola) NF Forest Plans outline specific protections for the flatwoods salamander. Within the primary buffer zone (600 ft. radius) of breeding ponds: prohibit mechanical site preparation, use only selective timber harvest methods, timber harvest will only occur during dry periods, and no application of pesticides, herbicides, or fertilizers, except directed foliar application of herbicide can be used to control noxious weeds. Injection, frill, girdle, thin-line basal spray or cut stump herbicides may be used to treat undesirable trees if prescribed fire cannot be employed. Within the secondary buffer zone (600-1,500 ft. radius) of breeding ponds: prohibit mechanical site preparation, if clearcutting is used, remove no more than 25 percent of the buffer in a single entry, harvest will only occur during dry periods, and no application of pesticides, herbicides, or fertilizers, except directed foliar application of herbicide can be used to control noxious weeds. Injection, frill, girdle, thin-line basal spray or cut stump herbicides may be used to treat undesirable trees if prescribed fire cannot be employed. The Conecuh NF Forest Plan mentions, in general terms, providing habitat for the salamander and other sensitive species but does not list specific protections.

#### _Lungless terrestrial salamanders_

This group is fully terrestrial, sensitive to changes in microclimate, and dependent on woody debris as habitat. Several studies have demonstrated reduced abundances of Plethodontid salamanders following timber harvests (Petranka et al. 1993, 1994).

#### Cheat Mountain salamander ( _Plethodon nettingi_ )(T)

The Cheat Mountain salamander occurs in the Monongahela National Forest in the Eastern Region of the Forest Service. Kroschel et al. (2014) suggest that a primary driver of decline is competition with another native salamander species. Dillard et al. (2008) suggest that extensive logging may have contributed to decline by altering the microclimate. Mielke et al _._ (1986) estimate that when the first European settlers entered what is now West Virginia, there were nearly 1.5 million acres of red spruce _(Picea nibens),_ and that spruce was reduced to approximately 750,000 acres by 1865 due to natural and human-caused factors.

#### _Existing Protections_

The Monongahela NF Forest Plan outlines management directions for the Cheat Mountain salamander. The goal is to identify opportunities to reduce fragmentation of populations and habitat. To Achieve this goal, surveys must be conducted and occupied habitat must be delineated prior to proposed vegetation or ground disturbance in known or potential habitat. Ground and vegetation-disturbing activities shall be avoided within occupied habitat and a 300foot buffer zone around occupied habitat, unless analysis can show that the activities would not have an adverse effect on populations or habitat. Personal use mineral permits shall not authorize removal of material within stream channels or their banks, or within suitable Cheat Mountain salamander habitat.

#### Jemez Mountains salamander ( _Plethodon neomexicanus_ )(E)

The Jemez Mountains salamander occurs in the Santa Fe National Forest in the Southwestern Region of the Forest Service. Margolis and Malevich (2016) suggest that fire exclusion has diminished habitat and increases the risk of high severity fire that can cause direct mortality. Bartlow et al. (2022) stated that the lungless Cheat Mountains salamander requires moist surface conditions for activities such as mating and foraging.

#### _Existing Protections_

The Santa Fe NF Forest Plan mentions the Jemez Mountains salamander as occurring on the district and makes general comments regarding aquatic habitat management. No specific protection are listed for the salamander.

Kern Canyon slender salamander ( _Batrachoseps simatus_ )(PT)

The Kern Canyon slender salamander occurs in Sequoia National Forest in the Pacific Southwest Region of the Forest Service. The proposed rule (87 FR 63150) states wildfire and long-term alteration of weather patterns are the primary ongoing threats to the habitat.

#### _Existing Protections_

The Sequoia NF Forest Plan lists three watersheds where the Kern Canyon slender salamander in known to occur. The Forest Plan makes general statements regarding sustaining healthy watersheds but does not list specific protections for the salamander.

#### Relictual slender salamander ( _Batrachoseps relictus_ )(PE)

The relictual slender salamander occurs in Sequoia National Forest in the Pacific Southwest Region of the Forest Service. The proposed rule (87 FR 63150) states that wildfire and long-term alterations of weather patterns are the primary ongoing threats to the habitat. The maintenance and improvement of Highway 178 through the Kern River Canyon has been implicated in the decline and eventual extirpation of low-elevation populations of _relictual slender salamander_ (Hansen 1988; Hansen and Wake 2005). Expansion of the highway involved the destruction of several small spring and seep habitats on the south side of the river that had previously supported populations of this species. Although suitable microhabitat was not entirely destroyed in the stretch of canyon occupied by _relictual slender salamander_ , it is probable that the hydrologic function of roadside waterways was modified significantly. Moss et al. (2025) suggest that removal of downed woody debris may contribute to decline.

#### _Existing Protections_

The Sequoia NF Forest Plan mentions the relictual slender salamander as a proposed species for ESA listing but does not list protections.

### Response

Although direct mortality from vehicle strikes associated with roads and heavy equipment can occur, most impacts to amphibian species are expected to result from degradation of the aquatic environment and fragmentation of terrestrial habitat as described above.  Responses to degradation of aquatic and terrestrial habitats can be as extreme as mortality or lesser effects such as suppression of breeding, feeding, and sheltering.

### Effects Determination

Given the potential exposure of most amphibian species and the potential of the proposed activity to result in death or loss of reproduction, feeding, and sheltering the FS has determined the proposed activity is likely to adversely affect all of the ESA-listed amphibians in the action area. Similarly, designated critical in the action area is likely to be adversely affected, primarily through degradation of aquatic habitat by sediment except for critical habitat for the Oregon spotted frog. Critical habitat for this species has less than 1% overlap with the action area and is not likely to be adversely affected.

### Effects of Roads and Timber

The impact/benefit crosswalk with pathway for fish effects in Table 17 was utilized in the effects analysis for fish when USFWS documents did not align with the described impact/benefits descriptions in Table 16. The impacts/benefits potential effects to fish species and critical habitat from the deconstruction table are summarized in the effects section. When species and/or critical habitat effects are described, duration of short-term effects subside immediately or up to one year, and long-term effects persist over a year. Direct and indirect effects were not distinguished in the analysis because they are hard to differentiate between them in some cases and the effects of each could be close together in timing.

A generalized effects (impact/benefit) analysis has been completed separately and should be referred to when fish species analysis identifies the impact/benefit as one that will affect the species or critical habitat. When fish species were analyzed and the impact/benefit analysis was general to effects pathways for the species, the crosswalk from Table 17 was used to relate back to the impact/benefit for activities in Table 16. For example, if the USFWS document for a species said water quality degradation was a threat without specifics, Table 17 under column pathway for fish effects has two entries for water quality, one is next to change in riparian vegetation (temperature) and sediment/turbidity; therefore, both change in riparian vegetation (temperature) and sediment/turbidity were analyzed for the species. In some cases, assumptions were made for species and the effects of the activity. If assumptions were made for the effects to individual species or critical habitat, assumptions were spelled out and included in the write-up under the species. Typically, assumptions were made based on identified threats within the referenced USFWS documents.

#### _Change in Riparian Vegetation (Temperature)_

Change in riparian vegetation is associated with stream temperature. Tree canopies disrupt the solar radiation from reaching the stream and increasing stream temperatures. Timber felling, landing creation and yarding corridors typically involve the loss of the tree canopy resulting in shade loss. Fish species would be affected differently from any change in riparian vegetation (temperature) based on their specific life history needs and habitat locations.

While stream shade correlates with the width of stream protection buffers, the relationship is quite variable, depending on site-specific factors such as stream size, substrate type, stream discharge, topography (Caissie 2006), channel aspect, and forest structure and species composition. Inputs of cold water from the streambed, seepage areas on the stream bank, and tributaries can help cool the stream on hot summer days if they are sufficiently large relative to the stream discharge (Wondzell 2012). The density of vegetation in riparian areas affects shade and thermal loading to a stream due to the penetration of solar radiation through gaps in the canopy and among the branches and stems (Brazier and Brown 1973; DeWalle 2010). In some instances (such as narrow streams with dense, overhanging streamside vegetation, or stands on the north sides of streams with an east-west orientation), no-harvest buffers as narrow as 30 feet adjacent to clearcuts can maintain stream shade (Brazier and Brown 1973). Wider buffers, in general, will provide increased protection of stream temperature (Anderson et al. 2007, Leinenbach et al. 2013, Groom et al. 2011a, Groom et al. 2011b).

Timber harvest adjacent to riparian buffers can influence the riparian microclimate adjacent to streams, which can, in turn, influence stream temperatures (Moore et al. 2005a). Gomi et al. (2006) reported that inclusion of a 30m (98’) buffer in clear-cut harvesting units increased maximum daily temperatures by <2C in British Columbia. Wilkerson et al. (2006) reported maximum increases of 1.0-1.4 degrees C with 11 m buffers and negligible increases with 23m (75') or partially cut buffers in Maine. DeWalle (2010) theorized that at least 80% shade could be attained with 12m (39') wide buffers on small (<6m [20'] wide) streams. In western Oregon, Zwieniecki and Newton (1999) reported that the presence of near continuous shade from an uncut buffer positioned on the south side of water led to protection from the effect of solar radiation. On the Oregon Coast Range, Groom et al. (2011a) found that on post-harvest lands with a protection buffer (no-cut zone) of 6m (20’) and limited harvest in the remainder of the riparian management area increased stream temperature by an average of 0.7 ˚C, but no change to maximum stream temperatures on lands managed to the more stringent state standard of 8m (26’) protection buffer and limited harvest in the remainder of the riparian management zone. The high variability in buffer width and shade condition is a function of the many variables that influence the amount of shade produced by riparian vegetation. Low-density stands with limited vertical distribution of branches and foliage will require wider buffer widths to produce the same amount of shade as high-density stands.

Riparian treatments on perennial streams greater than 1,000’ from Listed Fish Habitat (LFH) are not expected to increase stream temperatures in LFH when there is hyporheic flow and flow accumulation. Several papers have been published recently indicating that hyporheic flow and stream substrate composition has a significant influence on stream temperature. Janishch et al. (2012) found that that the canopy cover of “buffers” was not a strong predictor for temperature in small (<7 feet wide) headwater streams. Streams with coarse-textured streambeds tended to be thermally unresponsive as compared with fine-textured streambeds or those with small, nearstream wetland areas. Moore et al. (2005b) found that heat exchange associated with hyporheic flow paths was a cooling effect during daytime, with a magnitude up to approximately 25% that of net radiation during the period of maximum daytime warming in clear cut harvest units on streams in British Columbia. Davis et al. (2015) found that in Western Oregon streams, preharvest to post-harvest temperature approximately 300m downstream of the harvest will be 56% of the temperature change that occurred within the harvest reach. Rapid cooling has been observed after an extensive exposure to the sun after water re-entered forest cover in Australia (Rutherford et al. 2004), and, in Idaho, warming of headwater streams with no buffers did not lead to warming of fish-bearing streams downstream (Gravelle and Link 2007). Zwieniecki and Newton (1999) indicated that stream temperature increases from harvesting activity were frequently lost within 150–300 m (492-984') beneath downstream cover. This re-emphasizes the important role gravel and large wood play in channels. Therefore, thinning on perennial channels 1,000’ or greater from LFH is expected to have only minor negative effects to temperature in LFH.

Accurately predicting the magnitude of stream temperature increases on a highly variable landscape is extremely difficult. However, the research cited above supports the conclusion that while there may be a decrease in effective shade, localized increases in stream temperature are likely to be too small to differentiate from background variability. If localized increases in stream temperature occur, they will likely be less than 1˚C and are unlikely to be measurable in LFH. The tributary streams that flow through the harvest units are small in size (<1-5 cfs in most cases) and research has shown that the magnitude of temperature effect is a function of the amount of water entering (or exchanged with) the stream relative to the stream discharge (Johnson and Jones 2000, Story et al. 2003, Wondzell 2006, Wondzell 2012) and the difference in temperature between the stream and the inflowing water. Therefore, any localized increase in stream temperature from commercial thinning activities would typically have minor negative effect on LFH streams.

Typically, timber harvest activities are associated with an aquatic conservation strategy that provides for a stream protection buffer to limit the solar radiation reaching the stream. It is probable future projects will include some type of minimization measure for stream buffers for LFH areas, but since buffers are unknown for now, there could be projects that will have limited stream protection buffers and therefore have effects on stream temperature. As described above, most of the time timber harvest activities result in insignificant localized stream temperature increases because rapid cooling should occur as the stream flows into the uncut aquatic management zone buffer; therefore, effects should last less than an hour.

Road maintenance typically includes tree removal or brushing near streams and has the potential to create small minor changes to stream temperature. If there are drainage needs for road maintenance, such as culvert replacements, there may be a need to dewater the area and move it to a different location using pumps and screens. Depending on how this is accomplished, it could cause water temperatures to increase. If there are increases in the water temperature, the changes should be minor but could be measurable as future projects are unknown at this time. Past consultations have provided minimization measures that limit effects to temperature fluctuations.

There are a lot of unknowns for future projects in the action area. Even with the unknowns, we know there will be some shade loss from timber harvest, road maintenance and reconstruction, permanent and temporary road construction if implemented with one site potential tree height. Effects are expected to mostly be insignificant, unmeasurable effects, but could result in small localized measurable stream temperatures. Temporary road removal would not create measurable effects to increases in stream water temperature and can regrow shrubs quickly in the area, which would be beneficial.

Fish species react differently to these changes and will be discussed in the species sections below.

#### _Chemical Contamination/Nutrients_

Chemical contamination and nutrients for projects in this consultation are associated with equipment utilizing petroleum products and dust abatement chemicals. Timber vegetation management, road maintenance, road construction, and road removal activities all utilize heavy machinery, some utilize hand tools (e.g., chainsaws), water pumps, and dust abatement chemicals have the potential to create chemical contamination reaching the streams.

Coarse woody debris is an important component of forest ecosystems because it can provide cover for many wildlife species, provide important structures for small mammals, reptiles, and amphibians, and the decomposition of logs on the forest floor that provides nutrients to plants, habitat for wildlife, and food for insects and microorganisms. This process of nutrient input is important for the food web processes for salmonids as they feed on insects and microorganisms during certain life stages. Where timber harvest has been implemented, replanting is important for this process to continue. Harvest areas are typically localized to units and timber harvest must meet certain criteria if it is to be implemented within the aquatic management zones. For many of the forests in the action area, future projects will maintain a no-cut buffer for the aquatic management zone. This will insulate some food-web negative effects.

Any work utilizing chemicals and petroleum products typically requires an approved Spill Prevention Control and Containment Plan (Spill Plan) as required by contract provisions G.3.4.1/BT6.341. The Spill Plan would include a description of the hazardous materials that would be used; and a spill containment kit would be located on-site. All heavy equipment used for refueling would carry a hazardous material recovery kit. All vehicles and machinery would be free of petroleum leaks. Any leaks that occur would be immediately repaired. Power equipment would be refueled at least 150 feet from water bodies or as far away as possible to prevent direct delivery of contaminants into a water body. If local site conditions do not allow for a 150-foot setback, then refueling would be as far away as possible from the water body (USFS 2012a). For all immobile equipment, absorbent pads would be used. All petroleum products being transported or stored would be in approved containers meeting Occupational Safety and Health Administration and appropriate state standards. The Forest Service Contracting Officer would be notified of any spills. Any contaminated soil, vegetation or debris must be removed from National Forest System lands and disposed of in accordance with state laws.

Fuel spills of petroleum products from heavy equipment for all management activities have the potential to result in chemical contamination of streams. Hand tool fuel capacity is small (<1/4 gallon), and thus any potential spills during refueling would be unlikely to reach the stream channel resulting in a neutral effect for hand tools. Water pump fuel capacity is also small, and refueling is completed outside of the stream. It is extremely unlikely that heavy equipment in these activities will spill contaminants due to the contract clause requiring the Spill Plan. It is a standard contract clause that vehicles are checked regularly for leaks by purchasers and timber sale administrators and any leaks are promptly repaired before the vehicle is allowed to continue operating. Based on over 2 decades of experience that encompasses tens of thousands of log truck loads, as well as contractor supplied equipment for instream and road work, there is very low probability of chemical spills, and there have been no known spills from these activities that have impacted LFH. Forest Service best management practices require spill kits to be available if there is a spill and require fueling stations to be located 150 feet from streams when possible, and as far as practical when not possible.

The Forest Service expects limited applications for dust abatement. Dust abatement is typically only implemented during the dry season. Dust abatement can utilize water and chemicals (e.g., lignosulfonate, Magnesium Chloride), depending on the conditions in the work area. The Forest Service has a guide on applications for dust suppression (USFS 1999). The application of dust abatement chemicals would reduce fine sediment delivery to streams typically from dry season haul. Several different chemicals are discussed in the Forest Service guide, with pros and cons of each including an environmental impact section. Most chemicals do have negative environmental impacts, and these will be taken into consideration when utilized.

Lignosulfonate is an organic, nonpetroleum product that has limited ability to migrate since it is a bonding agent that adheres to material in dry conditions. Lignosulfonate is the chemical expected to be utilized near LFH, but there may be other chemicals utilized as well. There is potential for the dust abatement product to directly enter waterways. However, the single application of lignosulfonate during the dry season would reduce the likelihood of it entering a stream channel. There would not be an effect to LFH fish from applying lignosulfonate on road surfaces. Lignosulfonate has been tested to determine its potential impact on water quality and fish species when introduced directly into surface waters and it is rather benign. A 48-hour LC50 of 7,300 parts per million (ppm) was observed by Roald (1977) in rainbow trout ( _Oncorhynchus mykiss_ ). Compounds with values greater than a value of >1,000 are considered to have a low order of toxicity. Due to the limited use and application of lignosulfonate, the timing of application, the use of best management practices for application, and the known non-toxicity to fish at dust abatement concentrations, the probability of affecting listed fish is discountable.

Magnesium chloride can negatively impact aquatic systems by reducing macroinvertebrates (Kotalik et al. 2017) and directly affecting fish (Lewis 1998). If Magnesium chloride is utilized, there will be direct and indirect effects to fish through death (at high enough concentrations) and food web processes. The magnitude of effect is difficult to determine without having project specific information. Future project consultation will determine which chemical is utilized for dust abatement if it is needed but if utilized, we hypothesize the effects will be short-term but not discountable.

Timber harvest, road maintenance and reconstruction, and temporary road removal could cause short-term negative direct effects to the transport of nutrients downstream when implementing the projects, however, when projects utilize a water bypass system, effects would be limited to project implementation. These activities could provide for long-term beneficial effects when maintaining or repairing the current drainage system, installing appropriate sized drainage systems for the stream, and utilizing water bypass systems during the maintenance process.

Road construction could cause short-term negative direct effects to the transport of nutrients downstream when implementing the projects and fuel spills of petroleum products from machinery and equipment used in road work have the potential to result in chemical contamination of streams. Fuel powered equipment (hand tools and heavy machinery) will be used within the Riparian Reserves for road construction, including over stream crossings, where they are needed.

#### _Drainage Network_

The natural drainage networks of streams and rivers can be increased through road building and impervious road ditching and channeling that redirects surface flow and increase the active channel network. The primary management effect is associated with the road network, especially road compaction and road drainage systems. An increased drainage network can increase peak volume discharge and cause peak flows to occur earlier than unroaded drainages.

Wemple et al. (1996) studied the effect of channel network extension on two basins in the western Cascades of Oregon and found that 57% of the road network was connected to the stream network (road segments draining to streams, or road segments draining to culvert outlets with gullies incised below them), resulting in an increased drainage density of 21-50%. They concluded that this increase in road drainage density, and enhanced water routing efficiency was a possible explanatory mechanism for the changes in hydrograph shape (i.e., earlier peak, higher volume discharge) as presented in Jones and Grant (1996). Many other watershed factors (e.g., soil percolation rates, soil stability, road construction type) may influence the magnitude or probability that road extension will affect flows.

System road reconstruction, road (system and non-system) maintenance, and permanent (system roads) and temporary (non-system roads) roads will be built, and decommissioning may occur in areas adjacent to streams with LFH as well as in areas that may be several miles upstream from LFH.

Road reconstruction and maintenance have the potential for reducing the distance water travels along roadways, with the implementation of larger cross drain culverts, reduced spacing between culverts, and/or better placement of near-stream cross drains and their outflows. Road Decommissioning may occur near LFH streams, or on tributary streams that feed into LFH streams.

There are no causal effects of timber harvest on the drainage network, and the effects of timber harvest would be neutral to this element.

The only causal mechanism for effects for road maintenance and road re-construction would be through snow plowing. These would create short-term negative effects during the spring when snow melts. These would be localized effects to the area where snow plowing occurs. Snow plowing is not an action that is routinely implemented on Forest Service roads, so the probability of occurrence is low, but now zero. If effects do occur to drainage networks, these effects would be minor and localized.

Permanent and temporary road construction will have negative effects for drainage network lasting as long as the road is in place.

Temporary road removal will have long-term beneficial effects on drainage network. The process would be the opposite of road building.

#### _Large Woody Debris_

Large woody debris (LWD) enters streams through chronic and episodic processes (Bisson et al. 1987). Chronic sources include streamside tree mortality and bank undercutting (Murphy and Koski 1989). Episodic sources include windthrow (for example, Harmon et al. 1986; Lienkaemper and Swanson 1986; May and Gresswell 2003), wildfire (Agee 1993), infrequent flooding, landslides/debris flows (Benda et al. 2002, 2003), and insect infestations or disease. The quality, complexity, and function of fish habitat is often affected by the level of instream large woody debris. Large woody debris influences the size and distribution of stream habitat units, provides cover from predators, shades the water surface, and increases the sorting of substrate, providing suitable spawning areas (Megahan 1982; Bilby and Ward 1991; Crispin et al. 1993; Montgomery et al. 1995; May and Gresswell 2003). Large woody debris is instrumental in nutrient retention and provides a substrate for macroinvertebrates (Cederholm and Peterson 1985; Bilby and Ward 1989; Bilby and Bisson 1998; Gregory et al. 1991; Wallace et al. 1995). Large woody debris influences channel morphology (Swanson and Lienkaemper 1978; Heede 1985; Bisson et al. 1987; Swanston 1991). Fish densities are higher in streams with abundant large woody debris (Fausch and Northcote 1992; Roni and Quinn 2001).

The quality, complexity, and function of fish habitat is often affected by the level of instream LWD. LWD influences the size and distribution of stream habitat units, provides cover from predators, shades the water surface, and increases the sorting of substrate, providing suitable spawning areas (Megahan 1982; Bilby and Ward 1991; Crispin et al. 1993; Montgomery et al. 1995; May and Gresswell 2003). LWD is instrumental in nutrient retention and provides a substrate for macroinvertebrates (Cederholm and Peterson 1985; Bilby and Ward 1989; Bilby and Bisson 1998; Gregory et al. 1991; Wallace et al. 1995). LWD influences channel morphology (Swanson and Lienkaemper 1978; Heede 1985; Bisson et al. 1987; Swanston 1991). Fish densities are higher in streams with abundant LWD (Fausch and Northcote 1992; Roni and Quinn 2001).

Timber felling, landings creation, and yarding create pathways for effects to salmonids and critical habitat if they are done within the aquatic management zone. Projects where these activities are completed in aquatic management zones are typically implemented to move the aquatic management zone to a better desired condition, which are better for species and critical habitat. Where large woody debris is lacking, ESA consultations typically contain criteria for large woody debris to be left onsite where it can contribute to future in-stream wood. It is expected that future proposed projects will contain the same requirements. There are direct shortterm negative effects from removing large woody debris from aquatic management zone even with minimization measures.

Road maintenance could cause some minor short-term direct negative effects to large woody debris when vegetation management occurs next to the road and is within the aquatic management zone. Large woody debris is important to some fish species and their critical habitat needs. Negative effects would be localized to road sections near LFH. Effects would still be localized and minor even where roads parallel LFH.

Road construction could cause some minor longer-term direct negative effects to large woody debris when roads are built in the aquatic management zone. Large woody debris is important to some fish species and their critical habitat needs. These negative effects would be localized to roads built near LFH. Longer-term effects would still be localized if new roads are built parallel to LFH. Proposed future projects would need to complete ESA consultation prior to any new road building in the affected environment. Past ESA consultations that contain road building as an activity require minimization measures to reduce effects to salmonids and critical habitat. Any future projects would most likely also contain minimization measures as well. The magnitude of effects is difficult to predict. However, road building would be associated with timber harvest and roads for timber harvest are built once to use throughout the harvesting timeframe. This does mean that the effects of large woody debris may be years to re-establish in the area if it is cut. The effects would be localized to the stream segment where the road is built.

Temporary road removal includes removal of culverts, re-establishment of natural drainage patterns, and blocking vehicle access. The most likely point of entry for sediment will be during activities that occur next to streams, typically culvert removal or reducing the fill over culverts that are left in place. It is likely that temp road removal will result in short-term localized sediment delivery to streams. It is also expected that in the long-term, temporary road removal will have a positive effect on sediment delivery by removing roads, and stream crossings, where pulsed sediment delivery can potentially occur.

#### _Peak/Baseflows_

Peak/baseflows can be defined as quantity of water and the timing of input of water to an area. Loss of trees and vegetation may change the rate of evapotranspiration, increasing soil moisture and overall water yield. A short term (5-10 years) increase in discharge during the wet and the dry periods could occur from two mechanisms for the thinned stands: increased snow accumulation (wet period) will create small increases in peak flows (Jones and Grant 1996), and reduced canopy (dry periods) will reduce transpiration rates which will account for small increases in summer flows.

Peak (and pulsed) stream flows occur regularly in the some of the action area and carry most of the sediment load with high stream energies that may erode and change channel form (Cooper 2005).

Tree harvest and new permanent and temporary road construction do have potential to change the peak and base flows by decreasing the current canopy cover within the treated stands. Loss of trees and vegetation may change the rate of evapotranspiration, increasing soil moisture and overall water yield. A short term (5-10 years) increase in discharge during the wet and the dry periods could occur from two mechanisms for the thinned stands: increased snow accumulation (wet period) will create small increases in peak flows (Jones and Grant 1996), and reduced canopy (dry periods) will reduce transpiration rates which will account for small increases in summer flows.

Timber harvest has two causal mechanisms for peak/baseflows, these are timber yarding and timber landing construction. The pathway for effects for these two activities is based on compaction of soil. Soil compaction may cause water runoff to increase when there is heavy rainfall. These effects would be localized and small in magnitude.

The causal effect of road maintenance or reconstruction for peak/baseflows are due to water withdrawals, dewatering of a work site, or water pumping to a different location. These activities create localized short-term direct negative effects that last the duration of the implementation time for these activities but could have long-term beneficial effects if appropriately sized culverts are installed. These activities can last less than an hour for dust abatement to a few days for culvert replacement.

The causal effect of road building for peak/baseflows creates the largest effects to peak/baseflows of any other activity in this consultation. Depending on where roads are built and the associated water diversion systems used for the road, longer-term direct effects are expected since the roadbed can create a dam-like effect on water flow. These effects will last as long as the road is in place.

Temporary road removal will re-establish the natural drainage patterns to the streams resulting in a beneficial effect. Temporary road removal will re-vegetate over time resulting in an intact canopy and a reduction in openings. Temporary roads will be decommissioned at the end of the project. Although this increase in canopy cover on decommissioned roads is positive, at the watershed scale, the road area is small and the creation of temporary roads will offset the canopy closures, thus it is discountable in terms of the potential to affect peak and base flows.

Predicted changes in peak or base stream flows due to the implementation of this action should be minimal.

Water withdrawals have direct effects to peak/base flow. Drafting from streams may occur during spring, summer and fall, which encompasses the base flow period when the impact locally will be greatest, but will be isolated in space and time in that multiple drafting operations is unlikely to occur simultaneously in the action area. Stream flows may be temporarily reduced downstream from the withdrawal point. The amount of flow decrease from water withdrawals would depend on the amount of stream flow, how much water is withdrawn, and the duration of water drafting. Water trucks commonly hold 500 gallons of water, with a withdrawal rate of up to approximately 7.5 gal/sec. This means the maximum withdrawal would last at least 67 sec, and the maximum withdrawal period commonly is less than 5 minutes at lower rates of withdrawal. The magnitude of flow reductions will be insignificant due to the high stream flow volume available and the short period of withdrawal.

Water withdrawal for road work typically occurs during the dry season (generally June to October) in the Pacific Northwest or areas in higher elevation. Timing may change depending on where the work will occur. While water quantity to LFH may be temporarily reduced for short periods of time, the magnitude of flow reductions will be insignificant to affect the species or quality of their critical habitat because the periods of withdrawal will be short and will not affect inflow from adjacent tributary streams and hyporheic flow downstream from the point of withdrawal.

The implementation of projects covered by this programmatic consultation will result mostly in insignificant overall effects to peak and base flows, mainly through drafting of surface water for fuels treatment (during peak flow from fall through spring), and road maintenance (during base flow in summer and early fall). However, future projects may create small significant effects to peak and base flows, it would depend on the specifics of the project.

Vegetation changes will result in short term reduced evapotranspiration, increasing soil water, and therefore increasing yield. Road work will reduce soil water infiltration affecting storage, delivery and timing of flow to stream channels.

#### _Riparian Resilience_

Riparian resilience is related to the effects and processes of aquatic management zone to move toward more desirable conditions. Typically, treatments within the aquatic management zone area designed to maintain or improve riparian conditions even though some short-term local impacts are possible. These short-term impacts include a potential slight loss of large wood recruitment from treated riparian stands, potential short-term sediment, and potential minor increase in stream temperature, resulting in a short-term negative effect to this indicator at the local scale. In the long-term the effect will be positive as riparian stand diversity and diameters increase. Utilizing a stream protection buffer determined by the Aquatic Conservation Strategy or the Land Management Plan minimizes short term effects. In the long term, riparian resilience may improve due to benefits expected with future project development.

Timber felling and site restoration can have direct short-term negative effects and long-term beneficial effects, depending on the prescribed treatment within the aquatic management zones. Timber thinning prescriptions within the aquatic management zones can provide long-term beneficial effects by reducing competition between trees allowing trees left to grow and provide future large woody debris. Effects from timber treatments in the aquatic management zone come with short-term negative effects as well just because it takes time for causal mechanisms to improve. Forest thinning remains one of many forest management tools employed to meet ecological, social, and economic objectives on Forests. Thinning within the aquatic management zones is expected to result in a closed canopy within 3-5 years. The temporal boundary for cumulative effects on aquatic species is 5 years. Timber harvest projects within aquatic management zones are expected to be low and the objectives would be to improve the condition of the riparian areas, which would provide for long-term beneficial effects.

Timber yarding and landings have short-term negative effects through compaction of soil, which would take time to rebound. There are measures that are typically used during timber yarding to minimize soil compaction depending on what types of yarding will be utilized. This can range from utilizing slash for heavy equipment to drive over, to skyline yarding. There is no way to predict what type of yarding practices will be utilized for future projects, but we do know any future project will need ESA consultation, and all previous consultations contain project designs that minimize effects to species and critical habitats. The expectation for effects would still be measurable low-level effects to species and critical habitat for this action.

There are no causal effects of road maintenance or reconstruction and permanent and temporary road construction for riparian resilience, and the effects of road maintenance or reconstruction would be neutral to this element.

There are no causal effects of permanent and temporary road construction for riparian resilience, and the effects of permanent and temporary road construction would be neutral to this element.

Temporary road removal will have long-term beneficial effects for riparian resilience by removing the road prism, soil decompaction, and recontouring the landscape within the aquatic management zone.

#### _Road Density/Location_

Road density/location is based on where new permanent roads and temporary roads will be built. Almost all forest watersheds in the action area have existing primary and secondary road systems in place. Current road systems need maintenance and repairs over time to maintain safety standards. Any effects to fish and their critical habitats would occur on roads that are hydrologically connected to LFH or where effects can reach LFH. The probability of new roads being built somewhere in the action area is high. The probability of the new road being a permanent road is relatively low, as new permanent roads need funding to build and maintain. Temporary roads are associated with timber harvest needs. If timber is harvested in an area, temporary roads will be built.
