There are no causal effects of timber harvest for road density/location, and the effects of timber harvest would be neutral to this element.

There are no causal effects of road maintenance or reconstruction for road density/location, and the effects of road maintenance or reconstruction would be neutral to this element.

New road building would be the largest contributor to increased road density of all actions for the affected environment. Permanent roads are considered system roads, while temporary roads are considered non-system roads. Temporary roads will increase road density for a short time during logging operations, but the increase will be minor over the existing condition as all temporary roads will be fully decommissioned (temporary road removal) after sale contract harvest and yarding operations are complete. Increased road density may affect fish and their critical habitat typically through habitat fragmentation and sedimentation. Legacy roads on Forest Service lands are the largest contributor to habitat fragmentation. New roads would need to meet certain Forest Service standards, which are designed to minimize effects on aquatic systems. Even so, all new roads could have negative effects on fish for as long as they are in place.

#### _Sediment/Turbidity_

Sediment and turbidity tend to be the most frequent effects associated with timber harvest tasks, road maintenance and reconstruction and road construction. The potential for surface erosion is directly related to the amount of bare compacted soil exposed to rainfall and runoff and timber road haul; hence timber harvest activities may contribute large quantities of fine sediment to streams (Chamberlin et al. 1991, Swanston and Swanson 1976). Not all hillside erosion reaches stream channels (Chamberlin et al. 1991, Rice et al. 1972), but the potential exists for negative effects to the sedimentation/turbidity pathway. Heavy equipment can cause compaction and rutting of the ground which aids the movement of sediment- laden runoff. Excessive erosion may occur on poorly designed and placed skid trails, skid trails used during wet conditions, and trails that have connection to stream channels. Soil compaction from ground-based systems can be reduced when this equipment is restricted to dry soil conditions (Sidle and Drlica 1981). Fine sediment deposited in spawning gravels can reduce egg survival and developing alevins (Everest et al. 1987; Hicks et al. 1991) by reducing the availability of dissolved oxygen in the gravel.

The capacity of headwater streams to retain sediment is supported by many studies. The channels contain vegetation and woody debris of varying amounts, much of it small in diameter but in these small streams this material acts as an important obstruction to store sediment (Sullivan et al. 1987). Some studies indicate that annual sediment yields from small watershed make up less than ten percent of the sediment stored in channels (Swanson and Lienkaemper 1978), in other words, headwater stream channels with have a tremendous capability to store large amounts of fine sediment (Benda et al. 2005).

Chase et al. (2019) completed a soil and streamside effects study on 30 harvest units across Western Oregon and Washington on Weyerhaueser ownership on slopes up to 160%; with most 0-60%. Timing of clear-cut harvest was during the wet season (November – March). They observed that streams with riparian buffers >15m (49’) wide had little to no stream-adjacent disturbance.

Broderson (1973, cited in Castelle et al. 1992) found that 50-foot buffers were sufficient for controlling most sedimentation on less than 50% slopes, while steeper slopes required wider buffers. Broderson noted that buffers have little or no effect on sediment removal if sedimentladen water flows across the buffers as channelized flow; buffers can be effective only if they resist channelization and maintain overland flow as sheetflow. A maximum buffer width of 200 feet was found to be effective even on extremely steep slopes.

The timing of turbidity delivery to non-LFH stream channels will coincide with the rainstorms (and snowmelt) from fall through spring that will also naturally increase flow volume and turbidity in LFH. Aquatic conservation plans tend to limit the usage of heavy equipment within 150 feet of a stream. Even when following the aquatic conservation strategy and utilizing BMPs, there is the possibility of sediment entering streams and creating direct and indirect effects to species. These effects are typically short-term effects lasting less than one year. The nature and timing of future projects, and inclusion of minimization measures are unknown which means the effects of sediment and turbidity magnitude is uncertain. It is typical to include minimization measures when there is LFH within the action area. Even with minimization measures, sedimentation and turbidity could reach measurable effects for any given project based on the incremental effects of almost every timber harvest activity creating sedimentation/turbidity. Even if measurable effects occur, these effects should be low level effects but would still reach a level of significance to LFH.

Road maintenance and reconstruction may create source areas for sediment input to streams, particularly during heavy rainfall events. Failures of road fill at stream crossings are common source areas for landslide and debris torrents. Vegetated buffer areas ranging in width from 40 to100 feet were successful in keeping sediment out of streams (Corbett and Lynch 1985, Lynch et al. 1985, Moring 1982, Newbold et al. 1980, and Gomi et al. 2005). Broderson (1973, cited in Castelle et al. 1992) found that 50-foot buffers were sufficient for controlling most sedimentation on less than 50% slopes, while steeper slopes required wider buffers. A maximum buffer width of 200 feet was found to be effective even on extremely steep slopes. Previous consultations have design measures that minimize sediment effects to streams.

Surfacing roads with rock aggregate or pavement can significantly reduce the amount of erosion from the road surface (Burroughs and King 1989), particularly if used in the wet season. The type of rock used for surfacing can also influence sediment production. Hard, durable rock is more resistant to breakdown while softer rock is more easily crushed into particles small enough to be washed from the road surface (Bilby et al. 1989). Timber hauling may occur year-round, or seasonally depending on the road surface, design, and condition. The Forest Service Roads Standards are described in several different Forest Service publications, including but not limited to the list in Appendix B.

The turbidity generated by restoring flow at a culvert site is likely to affect the channel at the installation and removal sites and for approximately 1,000 feet. Foltz and Yanosek (2005) found that turbidity decreased by an order of magnitude within 328 feet of the disturbance and that turbidity was not expected to be detectable more than 2,400 feet (800 meters) downstream from the project site.

Overall, road maintenance and reconstruction activities are ground disturbing actions and localized increase in sedimentation to streams is expected. However, future projects will most likely include minimization measures in their consultations which will help alleviate effects to species and critical habitats.

In general, modern road construction practices produce less sediment delivered to streams from forest roads than older road construction practices (Copstead et al. 1998). Road construction and maintenance may create source areas for sediment input to streams, particularly during heavy rainfall events. Failures of road fill at stream crossings are common source areas for landslide and debris torrents. Vegetated buffer areas ranging in width from 40 to 100 feet were successful in keeping sediment out of streams (Corbett and Lynch 1985, Lynch et al. 1985, Moring 1982, Newbold et al. 1980, and Gomi et al. 2005). Broderson (1973, cited in Castelle et al. 1992) found that 50-foot buffers were sufficient for controlling most sedimentation on less than 50% slopes, while steeper slopes required wider buffers. A maximum buffer width of 200 feet was found to be effective even on extremely steep slopes.

Some increases in sedimentation (and resulting increases in turbidity) can be expected during culvert and bridge replacement, as equipment is operating in the stream channel and some trees would need to be removed from the stream bank. However, such increases are likely to be of local extent and of short duration. From experience, typically only 1-2 yards, or less, of sediment enters a stream during culvert projects.

Forest roads are compacted surfaces and can potentially allow for accelerated erosion and potential sediment delivery to stream channels from a variety of sources, including small slumps and slides into the roadway from the cut bank, water channeling from the road or ditches if not properly directed and controlled, and blocked culverts and road fill washouts during floods. Road construction is a ground disturbing action, and the potential exists for some increased sedimentation to streams.

Past consultations include minimization measures to decrease the effects of new road construction to streams. There is reason to believe these minimization measures will be included in any potential future consultation in the action area. Even if minimization measures were included in future consultation, there is reason to believe the effects of sedimentation for new road building would be the largest contributor of sedimentation to stream systems.

#### _Spawning Substrate_

Timber harvest activity effects have similar mechanisms between spawning substrate and sediment/turbidity. Spawning substrate can be defined by water quality, water quantity, and substrate. Spawning substrates are necessary for successful reproduction of many fish species. For fish that build redds in gravels, fine sediment deposited in can reduce egg survival and developing alevins (Everest et al. 1987; Hicks et al. 1991) by reducing the availability of dissolved oxygen in the gravel. Sedimentation/turbidity is discussed above as well as temperature. Water quality factors such as dissolved oxygen and water quantity are also important for spawning substrate.

Road reconstruction and new roads construction has the potential to have the largest negative effects to spawning substrate within the affected environment if they are built near the aquatic management zone. Habitat fragmentation would have negative effects on bedload movement and potential become an impediment to habitat connectivity if inappropriate sized culverts were installed. Effects would occur throughout the duration of the road.

### Acipenseridae Family - Sturgeon

#### _Gulf sturgeon_

Gulf sturgeon are found in the Gulf of America and streams flowing into the Gulf of America. The Gulf sturgeon is an anadromous fish which migrates from salt water into large coastal rivers to spawn and spend the warm months. Most of its life is spent in fresh water. Major population limiting factors are thought to include barriers (dams) to historical spawning habitats, loss of habitat, poor water quality, and overfishing (USFWS 1995b). Historically, the Gulf sturgeon occurred from the Mississippi River east to Tampa Bay. Its present range extends from Lake Pontchartrain and the Pearl River system in Louisiana and Mississippi east to the Suwannee River in Florida. When listed, Gulf sturgeon threats were identified as threats and potential threats identified in the listing rule included modifications to habitat associated with dredged material disposal, desnagging (removal of trees and their roots), and other navigation maintenance activities; incidental take by commercial fishermen; poor water quality associated with contamination by pesticides, heavy metals, and industrial contaminants; aquaculture and incidental or accidental introductions; and the Gulf sturgeon’s slow growth and late maturation (68 FR 13370). Young-of-the-year Gulf sturgeon remain in freshwater feeding on aquatic invertebrates and detritus approximately 10 to 12 months after spawning occurs (68 FR 13370). Additional Gulf sturgeon feeding habits for juvenile and adult life stages can be found in 68 FR 13370.

Gulf sturgeon critical habitat is not located in the action area.

#### _Pallid sturgeon_

Pallid sturgeon are found in the Mississippi River system. The Pallid Sturgeon is native to the Missouri and Mississippi rivers and adapted to the pre-development habitat conditions that historically existed in these rivers. These conditions generally can be described as large, free flowing, warm-water, and turbid rivers with a diverse assemblage of dynamic physical habitats. Limiting factors include: 1) activities which affect in-river connectivity and the natural form, function, and hydrologic processes of rivers; 2) illegal harvest; 3) impaired water quality and quantity; 4) entrainment; and 5) life history attributes of the species (i.e., delayed sexual maturity, females not spawning every year, and larval drift requirements). The degree to which these factors affect the species varies among river reaches (USFWS 2014c). Pallid Sturgeon are a bottom-oriented, large river obligate fish inhabiting the Missouri and Mississippi rivers and some tributaries from Montana to Louisiana (USFWS 2014c). Habitat requirements of larval and young-of-year Pallid Sturgeon remain largely undescribed across the species’ range, primarily because of low populations of spawning adults and poor recruitment. Scientists think the habitat requirements of larval and young-of-year for pallid sturgeon are similar among all geneses. Pallid Sturgeon have been collected from a variety of turbidity conditions including areas with consistently low turbidities (i.e., 5-100 nephelometric turbidity units (NTU)) to comparatively natural systems with seasonally high turbidity levels (> 1,000 NTU) (USFWS 2014c). Given their physical attributes, the species appears to be highly adapted to low visibility environments (USFWS 2014c).

Pallid sturgeon critical habitat has not been designated.

#### _White sturgeon_

White sturgeon are found in the Columbia River system with the Kootenai River Distinct population segment being a landlocked population living their entire life in freshwater. Kootenai River white sturgeon are restricted to approximately 168 miles of the Kootenai River, in Idaho, Montana, and British Columbia, Canada, primarily upstream from Cora Linn Dam at the outflow from Kootenay Lake, British Columbia. Kootenai River white sturgeon critical habitat is contained entirely in Idaho, more than 2 miles downstream of the state border with Montana and will not be considered in this consultation. At the time of ESA listing, threats to the species were decline in the adult population and the almost complete lack of natural recruitment; loss of suitable spawning and rearing habitat because of Libby Dam operations; reduced biological productivity in the basin; and contaminants leading to poor water quality (USFWS 2019i). New information in the revised recovery plan (USFWS 2019i) identified the primary threats stem from the presence and operations of Libby Dam, and fall into three main categories: (1) reductions in peak spring flows; (2) alterations to the annual thermal regime in the Kootenai River; and (3) reductions to/losses of nutrients and fundamental ecosystem processes ( _e.g_ ., food web, floodplain interaction, riparian function).

White sturgeon, Kootenai River DPS, critical habitat does not occur in the action area.

#### _Acipenseridae Effects_

Generally, sturgeon are long lived species, utilize large river systems for most of their life history needs, and take years to reach sexual maturity, move upstream in large rivers to spawn in freshwater when water flow and temperature conditions they need for spawning are met. All three of the sturgeon species considered in this consultation have been affected by river impoundments affecting spawning, survival of hatchlings, and gene flow (USFWS 2014c; USFWS 1995b; USFWS 2019i). Poor water quality conditions from pollutants, such as heavy metals and agricultural run-off, is believed to negatively affect their survival.

Since all these sturgeon live in large rivers, the pathway for effects would be limited to water quality effects such as increased temperature and sedimentation/turbidity. Activity effects in this consultation would be minor and indistinguishable from background levels since they live in large river systems.

The effects determination is **may affect, not likely to adversely affect** Gulf sturgeon, Pallid sturgeon, and white sturgeon, Kootenai River DPS because effects will be insignificant.

### Catostomidae Family - Suckers

_Lost River sucker and shortnose sucker_

Lost River sucker and shortnose sucker will be discussed together because shortnose suckers significantly with Lost River sucker in the Upper Klamath Lake, its tributaries, or within any of the reservoirs along the Klamath River and in nearby Lost River Basin. Both species have similar life histories, life cycles, and threats to their continued existence. At the time of listing, Lost River sucker and shortnose sucker were known from Upper Klamath Lake and its tributaries and outlet, including a “substantial population” of shortnose sucker in Copco Reservoir, as well as collections of both species from Iron Gate Reservoir and J.C. Boyle Reservoir. Remnants and/or highly hybridized populations were also documented to occur in the Lost River system including both species in Clear Lake Reservoir, but it was apparently presumed that Lost River sucker populations in Sheepy Lake, Lower Klamath Lake, and Tule Lake had been “lost”. Although not stated explicitly, shortnose sucker within Gerber Reservoir were likely part of the “highly hybridized populations” in the Lost River Basin referenced in the listing (77 FR 73740). Currently, Clear Lake Reservoir and Upper Klamath Lake and their tributaries support the largest populations of both species. Populations in Klamath River below Keno Dam and in the Lost River drainage below Clear Lake Dam are comprised mostly of adults. These populations are probably functioning as sink populations, as they are not likely self-sustaining because of low recruitment due to the lack of access to spawning habitats. All life stages of these listed suckers have been found in Link River, the outlet of Upper Klamath Lake (USFWS 2013c).

A main factor cited at the time of listing as contributing to population declines was loss or degradation of spawning, rearing, and adult habitats. Current factors limiting species recovery also include high mortality of larvae and juveniles due to reduced rearing habitat, entrainment in water management structures, poor water quality and negative interactions with introduced species (USFWS 2013c).

Lost River and shortnose suckers have complex life histories that include stream/river, lake, marsh, and shoreline habitats. Both spawn during the spring over gravel substrates in habitats less than 1.3 meters (4 feet) deep in tributary streams and rivers. A smaller but significant number of Lost River sucker also spawn over gravel substrates at shoreline springs along the margins of Upper Klamath Lake. Larvae spend relatively little time in rivers or streams before drifting downstream to the lakes by mid-summer. Larval habitat is generally along the relatively shallow shoreline where emergent vegetation provides cover from predators, protection from currents and turbulence, and abundant food (including zooplankton, macroinvertebrates, and periphyton). Juvenile suckers utilize a wide variety of near and off-shore habitat including emergent wetlands and non-vegetated areas. They increasingly move off-shore into the lake as they grow. Adults occupy open water lake habitats (USFWS  2013c).

Lost River sucker are relatively large fish, up to 0.8 meter long and 4.5 kilograms in weight, distinguished by an elongate body and sub-terminal mouth with a deeply notched lower lip that are relatively more papillose. They have dark backs and sides that fade to yellow or white on the belly. Lost River sucker resiliency for this species is still low and is declining with time as the adult spawning populations reach the end of their expected lifespan. Redundancy is also critically low. There are only three distinct spawning populations: Upper Klamath Lake-springs, Upper Klamath Lake-river, and Clear Lake Reservoir. Two of these spawning populations (Clear Lake Reservoir and Upper Klamath Lake-springs) have very low numbers and are extremely vulnerable to localized catastrophic events (USFWS 2013c, 2024x).

Shortnose sucker is generally distinguished by a smaller head than Lost River sucker also with an oblique, terminal mouth, and thin, but fleshy, lips. The lower lip is deeply notched, giving the appearance of two separate lobes. Coloration is very similar to Lost River sucker, with dark back and sides and a silvery or white belly. Shortnose sucker are generally smaller than Lost River sucker but can still grow to about 0.65 meters. Shortnose sucker are one of three extant species in the genus _Chasmistes_ , with the other two being the cui-ui sucker ( _Chasmistes cujus_ ) in Pyramid Lake, Nevada and the June sucker ( _Chasmistes liorus_ ) in Utah Lake, Utah (USFWS 2013). Shortnose sucker suffer from low resiliency as a species. The low resiliency is due to the extremely low numbers in most populations, inadequate access to suitable spawning habitat for most populations, and genetic impurity in most populations (such as impaired representation). Shortnose sucker have more populations across a broader area compared to Lost River sucker, but overall, the species’ redundancy remains quite low. There are currently only three known spawning populations (Upper Klamath Lake, Clear Lake Reservoir, and Gerber Reservoir) (USFWS 2013, 2024w).

Water quality conditions in Upper Klamath Lake, one of two lakes supporting the largest populations of the two suckers, are driven by extensive nutrient loading. The lake was highly productive or eutrophic prior to settlement by Europeans in the mid-19th century, but it has become hypereutrophic from increased external loading (pumping of diked wetlands, farm/ranch run-off, and roads) that has enriched the naturally high internal (lake sediments) loads. Much of the nutrient load entering Upper Klamath Lake comes from non-point sources. Nevertheless, on average, approximately 60 percent of the biologically available phosphorus is derived from internal loads, such as lake sediment, although it has been suggested that these internal loads have been enriched by modern land management practices (USFWS 2013c). Poor water quality in Upper Klamath Lake is particularly associated with high abundance of the blue-green algae _Aphanizomenon flos-aquae_ . Core samples of bottom sediments indicate that _Aphanizomenon flos-aquae_ was not present in Upper Klamath Lake prior to the 1900s. Its appearance is believed to be associated with increases in productivity of the lake. This alga now dominates the algal community from June to November, and, because of the high phosphorus concentrations and its ability to fix nitrogen, is able to reach seasonally high biomass levels that eventually produce highly degraded water quality. Once the algal bloom subsides, decomposition of the massive amounts of _Aphanizomenon flos-aquae_ biomass can lower dissolved oxygen to levels harmful or fatal to fish. The processes that produce these conditions are complex and vary on many time scales: daily, seasonally, and annually. In some years the massive bloom of blue-green algae experiences near catastrophic die-offs (crashes), which provides an abundant source of organic material for bacterial decomposition. During these periods of high levels of decomposition, the bacteria can deplete dissolved oxygen from the water column as they respire, and as a by-product of decomposition nitrogen is also released, which can then convert to toxic forms (un-ionized ammonia) when the pH is basic (greater than 7). There are many other factors, such as winddriven mixing of the water column, that determine the severity and extent (whether it is localized or lake-wide) of these crashes. Additionally, other cyanobacteria ( _Microcystis sp_ .) may produce toxins harmful to sucker liver tissue (USFWS 2013c).

Lost River sucker and shortnose sucker critical habitat physical and biological features from (77 FR 73740):

1. Water. Areas with sufficient water quantity and depth within lakes, reservoirs, streams, marshes, springs, groundwater sources, and refugia habitats with minimal physical, biological, or chemical impediments to connectivity. Water must have varied depths to accommodate each life stage: Shallow water (up to 3.28 ft (1.0 m)) for larval life stage, and deeper water (up to 14.8 ft (4.5 m)) for older life stages. The water quality characteristics should include water temperatures of less than 28.0 °C (82.4 °F); pH less than 9.75; dissolved oxygen levels greater than 4.0 mg per L; low levels of microcystin; and un-ionized ammonia (less than 0.5 mg per L). Elements also include natural flow regimes that provide flows during the appropriate time of year or, if flows are controlled, minimal flow departure from a natural hydrograph.

2. Spawning and rearing habitat. Streams and shoreline springs with gravel and cobble substrate at depths typically less than 4.3 ft (1.3 m) with adequate stream velocity to allow spawning to occur. Areas containing emergent vegetation adjacent to open water, provide habitat for rearing and facilitates growth and survival of suckers, as well as protection from predation and protection from currents and turbulence.

3. Food. Areas that contain an abundant forage base, including a broad array of chironomidae, crustacea, and other aquatic macroinvertebrates. With this designation of critical habitat, the USFWS have identified the physical or biological features essential to the conservation of the species, through the identification of the features’ primary constituent elements that support the life-history processes of the species.

#### _Warner sucker_

Warner suckers are in the Warner Basin located in southcentral Oregon. Warner suckers mature at 3 to 4 years of age at approximately 5 to 6 inches in length. The species is a moderate-sized member of the family Catostomidae and reaches a maximum length of about 20 inches (50 FR 39117). Habitats of Warner sucker include large natural lakes and associated marshes. Although primarily lacustrine, this species spawns in headwaters of streams, tributary to lakes. Instream barriers and diversion structures have often prohibited the movement of suckers into spawning streams during recent years. During years with high precipitation, enough water flows by the diversion structures so that the suckers can utilize limited reaches of the streams for spawning. However, during periods of low flows, all water is often diverted, thereby eliminating any change for the fish to spawn. If suckers are successful in ascending the barriers, spawned-out fish and progeny are likely to be restricted to small areas of streams because of instream barriers, or sometimes diverted into agricultural fields where they die (50 FR 39117). Connectivity of water is one of the important needs for the species as passage between waterbodies is dependent on connectivity for species success (USFWS 2025n). No threats exist that would likely threaten the survival of the species over a significant portion of its range, although rising temperature is considered to be an upcoming concern since the thermal tolerance of Warner sucker is 23°C and access to cooler water such as springs and deep pools will be important for the continued survival of the species (USFWS 2025n). The three main concerns for the species are human induced stream channel and watershed degradation, irrigation diversion practices, and predation and competition from introduced fishes (USFWS 1998c).

Warner sucker critical habitat is not located in the action area.

#### _Razorback sucker_

Razorback sucker is a long lived (40+), large catostomid fish endemic to the Colorado River Basin of the southwestern United States. Historically, razorback suckers were widely distributed in warm-water reaches of larger rivers of the Colorado River Basin from Mexico to Wyoming. Habitats required by adults in rivers include deep runs, eddies, backwaters, and flooded offchannel environments in spring; runs and pools often in shallow water associated with submerged sandbars in summer; and low-velocity runs, pools, and eddies in winter. Spring migrations of adult razorback sucker were associated with spawning in historic accounts, and a variety of local and long-distance movements and habitat-use patterns have been documented. Spawning in rivers occurs over bars of cobble, gravel, and sand substrates during spring runoff at widely ranging flows and water temperatures (typically greater than 14<sup>o</sup> C). Spawning also occurs in reservoirs over rocky shoals and shorelines. Young razorback suckers require nursery environments with quiet, warm, shallow water such as tributary mouths, backwaters, or inundated floodplain habitats in rivers, and coves or shorelines in reservoirs. Threats to the species include streamflow regulation, habitat modification, competition with and predation by nonnative fish species, and pesticides and pollutants (USFWS 2002b). The razorback sucker is jeopardized by large mainstem dams, water diversions, habitat modification, nonnative fish species, and degraded water quality.

Persistent recruitment failure has depleted and extirpated numerous razorback sucker populations. In the case of lower basin reservoirs (such as, Mead, Mohave, Havasu), the characteristic chronology of extirpation is 40–50 years following dam construction; i.e., the fish that were produced prior to habitat inundation and fragmentation reach maximum longevity with little or no recruitment to replace adult mortality. This occurred because of inundated riverine habitat and poor survival of reproduced young because of predation by nonnative fishes (USFWS 2002b). Razorback suckers are currently found in the Green River, upper Colorado River, and San Juan River subbasins; lower Colorado River between Lake Havasu and Davis Dam; reservoirs of Lakes Mead and Mohave; and in small tributaries of the Gila River subbasin. The razorback suckers in most populations are aged and senile adults with little or no recruitment, except for the middle Green River and Lake Mead, where small numbers of juveniles and young adults indicate low recruitment levels. Currently, the largest concentration of razorback sucker remaining in the entire Colorado River Basin is in Lake Mohave.

Razorback sucker critical habitat physical and biological features include (59 FR 13374):

1. Water - This includes a quantity of water of sufficient quality (such as, temperature, dissolved oxygen, lack of contaminants, nutrients, turbidity, etc.) that is delivered to a specific location in accordance with a hydrologic regime that is required for the particular life stage for each species.

2. Physical Habitat- This includes areas of the Colorado River system that are inhabited or potentially habitable by fish for use in spawning, nursery, feeding, and rearing, or corridors between these areas. In addition to river channels, these areas also include bottom lands, side channels, secondary channels, oxbows, backwaters, and other areas in the 100-year flood plain, which when inundated provide spawning, nursery, feeding and rearing habitats, or access to these habitats.

3. Biological Environment- Food supply, predation, and competition are important elements of the biological environment and are considered components of this constituent element. Food supply is a function of nutrient supply, productivity, and availability to each life stage of the species. Predation and competition, although considered normal components of this environment, are out of balance due to introduced nonnative fish species in many areas.

Special consideration was given to habitats required for reproduction and recruitment. The following selection considerations were used by the Service to help determine areas necessary for survival and recovery of the razorback sucker.

1. Presence of known or suspected wild spawning populations, although recruitment may be limited or nonexistent.

2. Areas where juvenile razorback suckers have been collected or which could provide suitable nursery habitat (backwaters, flooded bottom lands, or coves).

3. Areas presently occupied or that were historically occupied that are considered necessary for recovery and that have the potential for reestablishment of razorback suckers.

4. Areas and water that are required to maintain rangewide fish distribution and diversity under a variety of physical, chemical, and biological conditions.

5. Areas that need special management or protection to ensure razorback survival and recovery.

These areas once met the habitat needs of the razorback sucker and may be recoverable with additional protection and management.

#### _Santa Ana sucker_

The Santa Ana sucker is a small, generally less than 6.3 inches, short-lived fish. Santa Ana suckers feed mostly on algae, diatoms, and detritus scraped from rocks and other hard substrates, with aquatic insects making up a very small component of their diet. Larger fish generally feed more on insects than do smaller fish. Santa Ana suckers generally reach sexual maturity in just over 1 year and typically do not live more than 3 years (65 FR 19686). Its range include the Los Angeles River, San Gabriel River, and Santa Ana River basins. The Santa Ana sucker is one of only a few native freshwater species of fish currently extant in southern California. The listed species’ range has been reduced in the three watersheds where it occurs and there is no opportunity for natural movement between watersheds. Santa Ana suckers are also patchily distributed within each watershed, with dispersal to other reaches limited by barriers that prevent or severely limit two-way (upstream and downstream) fish passage within the respective watersheds. The primary threat to the Santa Ana sucker includes past and ongoing habitat loss through hydrological modifications throughout the range of the species. The loss and degradation of available habitat (caused by dams, changes in water allocations, and other hydrological modifications) combined with other increasing threats (such as degraded water quality, recreational pressures, and potential effects of nonnative vegetation and predation) have a cumulative effect on Santa Ana sucker and its habitat. Additionally, impassable barriers or areas of unsuitable habitat limit gene flow, thus increasing the vulnerability of small populations to a range of environmental stochastic factors and inbreeding depression (USFWS 2017d).

In streams or rivers that are not restricted by artificial barriers, such as the San Gabriel River (North and East Forks), the upper limit of where fish are likely to occur is determined by the instream gradient and the fish’s inability to physically swim upstream when a certain gradient (and thus flow rate) is exceeded. Santa Ana suckers occur in the watersheds draining the San Bernardino and San Gabriel Mountains of southern California. Their historical distribution extended from upper watershed areas to the Pacific Ocean; hence, they can occupy habitats as diverse as mountain streams and rivers in alluvial floodplains (relatively flat landform created by the deposition of sediment over a long period of time from one or many rivers) (USFWS 2017d). The streams that the Santa Ana sucker inhabits are generally perennial streams with water ranging in depth from a few inches to several feet and with currents ranging from slight to swift. Perennial flows with suitable water quality and substrate are needed to support breeding, feeding, and sheltering. These streams are also naturally subject to periodic, severe flooding and may experience extended periods of low flow as a result of drought conditions that are typical of southern California climate cycles (USFWS 2017d).

Santa Ana sucker critical habitat physical and biological features include a functioning hydrological system that provides sources of water and course sediment necessary to maintain all life stages, including adults, juveniles, larvae, and eggs. Physical and biological features essential to the conservation of Santa Ana sucker are (75 FR 77962):

1. A functioning hydrological system within the historical geographic range of Santa Ana sucker that experiences peaks and ebbs in the water volume (either naturally or regulated) that encompasses areas that provide or contain sources of water and coarse sediment necessary to maintain all life stages of the species, including adults, juveniles, larvae, and eggs, in the riverine environment;

2. Stream channel substrate consisting of a mosaic of loose sand, gravel, cobble, and boulder substrates in a series of riffles, runs, pools, and shallow sandy stream margins necessary to maintain various life stages of the species, including adults, juveniles, larvae, and eggs, in the riverine environment;

3. Water depths greater than 1.2 in (3 cm) and bottom water velocities greater than 0.01 ft per second (0.03 m per second);

4. Clear or only occasionally turbid water;

5. Water temperatures less than 86 °F (30 °C);

6. Instream habitat that includes food sources (such as zooplankton, phytoplankton, and aquatic invertebrates), and associated vegetation such as aquatic emergent vegetation and adjacent riparian vegetation to provide:

- i. Shading to reduce water temperature when ambient temperatures are high,

- ii. shelter during periods of high water velocity, and

- iii. protective cover from predators; and

7. Areas within perennial stream courses that may be periodically dewatered, but that serve as connective corridors between occupied or seasonally occupied habitat and through which the species may move when the habitat is wetted.

All occupied units designated as critical habitat contain the physical and biological features in the appropriate quantity and spatial arrangement essential to the conservation of this species and support multiple life processes for Santa Ana sucker.

#### _Catostomidae Effects_

Generally, Lost River sucker, shortnose sucker, and razorback sucker are long lived species, take years to mature, move up rivers to spawn, and have been subjected to habitat modifications where it is difficult to complete their life history needs. The main threats to the species are water quantity and quality including timing.

Lost River and shortnose suckers live in a system where dissolved oxygen levels become during the summer under certain conditions. They spawn in the spring March – April, when conditions for timber and road building are not appropriate. Sedimentation for this species is typically not a concern for eggs, juveniles, or adults. Although it may create increased nutrient input that could create conditions for algae growth that is tied to dissolved oxygen sinks, the amount of sediment would be insignificant compared to what would be needed to increase algae growth causing dissolved oxygen sinks. Critical habitat in the action area is very small, less than 1 percent. Forest Service best management practices (USFS 2012a) would minimize the amount of sediment reaching connected waters. Any future consultation would most likely contain measures to minimize effects on species. Therefore, the Roadless Rule Rescission **may affect, not likely to adversely affect** Lost River sucker, Lost River sucker critical habitat, shortnose sucker, and shortnose sucker critical habitat because effects are discountable.

Razorback sucker live in highly modified large river systems where dams have created habitats insufficient for recruitment of young into the population. Due to the nature of the large river systems, any minor changes in temperature or sedimentation to the habitat would be indistinguishable from background levels. The amount of critical habitat in the affected environment is minimal, < 0.01%. Forest Service best management practices (USFS 2012a) would minimize the amount of sediment reaching connected waters. Any future consultation would most likely contain measures to minimize effects on species. Therefore, the Roadless Rule Rescission **may affect, not likely to adversely affect** razorback sucker and razorback sucker critical habitat because effects are discountable.

Although in the same family, Santa Ana sucker have a different life history than the others listed under Catostomidae Family in this analysis. Effects of future projects on Santa Ana sucker would most likely be due to sedimentation, potential increase in water temperatures, and habitat fragmentation when projects are implemented. Implementing Forest Service best management practices (USFS 2012a) will help alleviate negative effects of any future project. Low level effects from sedimentation, increase in water temperatures, and habitat fragmentation could occur during future project implementation, the magnitude of which is unknown, but expected to be low. Any future projects that would affect species would still need to complete project level consultation. Due to the unknowns, we might expect some effects on species that are susceptible to reach **may affect, likely to adversely affect on individual** Santa Ana suckers (Table 15).

The amount of critical habitat in the affected environment is minimal, 0.02%. Forest Service best management practices (USFS 2012a) would minimize the amount of sediment. Any future consultation would most likely contain measures to minimize effects on species but there may be some effects that are measurable. Therefore, the Roadless Rule Rescission **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Santa Ana sucker critical habitat.

### Leuciscidae Family

The Leuciscidae family has the most species in this consultation and includes all the shiners, chubs, dace, spinedace, loach minnow, spikedace, Colorado pikeminnow, and bonytail identified in Table 15.

#### _Blue shiner_

The blue shiner is a medium-sized minnow that grows to about 4 inches in total length. Blue shiner live for 3 years, and most spawning fish are 2 years old. It is represented by approximately six populations occurring in headwater streams of the Coosa River system in Northwest Georgia and Southeast Tennessee, and in smaller tributaries of the  Coosa River in Northeast Alabama. Populations are isolated by impoundments, inappropriate habitat, inadequate water quality, and distance (USFWS 1995c). The blue shiner requires water of relatively high quality and appears sensitive to turbidity and siltation. Major threats are habitat alteration and water quality degradation (USFWS 1995c).

Blue shiner primarily occupies second to fourth order, moderate gradient streams within the Ridge and Valley and Piedmont physiographic provinces of Alabama, Georgia, and Tennessee (USFWS 1995c). Most watersheds where it is found are predominately forested, and agriculture and urban development are minimal. The headwaters of Choccolocco and Shoal creeks are in Talladega National Forest. The Weogufka watershed is also primarily forested. The Little River flows through Little River Canyon National Preserve, which is managed by the National Park Service. In Georgia and Tennessee, the blue shiner is found in the upper reaches of streams flowing through two National Forests. The Conasauga River originates within the Chattahoochee National Forest in Georgia and flows into Tennessee where it enters the Cherokee National Forest. Mmnnewauga Creek is within the Cherokee National Forest. Rock Creek, in Georgia is mostly within the Chattahoochee National Forest. Perry and Holly Creek have headwaters in the Chattahoochee National Forest (USFWS 1995c).

The blue shiner can be abundant in the proper habitat and is rare or absent elsewhere, suggesting that it is habitat dependent. It is a fluvial specialist, being found only in flowing water. It prefers sand or sand and gravel substrate sometimes with cobble, low to moderate velocity current, and a depth of about 0.15 to 1 meters (0.5 to 3 feet). Blue shiners are sometimes associated with submerged tree roots and fallen branches. They also occur near water willow (Justicia americana) beds, especially in eddy currents downstream from the beds. In the Little River and Choccolocco Creek, lateral pools away from the main current, and backwaters with sandy substrates were preferred. In Weogufka Creek, a concentration of blue shiner were observed below a leaky beaver dam where flows were moderated. In the Conasauga River and Weogufica Creek, this shiner is also prevalent in long, low-velocity pools (USFWS 1995c).

The diet of the blue shiners is dominated throughout the year by terrestrial insects, indicating that the blue shiner is a visual, drift feeder. The importance of riparian vegetation and a tree canopy along the stream margin of blue shiner habitat is suggested by the importance of terrestrial insects in the diet. Successful visual foraging may be dependent on water clarity (USFWS 1995c).

Blue shiner threats include water quality degradation, for example, nutrification and probable low dissolved oxygen levels. The blue shiner’s range has been reduced and fragmented by construction of dams, loss of habitat, and/or water pollution. This has created isolated and relatively small populations. Isolated populations are especially vulnerable to habitat degradation and decreased genetic diversity. Any event that adversely affects an isolated population has the potential to eliminate it. This is especially true for stream-dwelling species since recolonization may be prevented by a variety of barriers, e.g., dams, inappropriate habitat, poor water quality, and distance. Thus, a single, even ephemeral incident or event such as a chemical spill or an extreme drought can permanently reduce the range of an aquatic species with fragmented populations and make it very susceptible to extinction (USFWS 1995c).

The range of the blue shiner within Alabama, Georgia and Tennessee has been reduced and fragmented by geomorphic and hydrologic changes such as reservoirs, bridges, pipelines and roads; aggregate extraction; major pollution events; an increase in turbidity caused by sedimentation; and general declining water quality attributed to non-sustainable urbanization and land use practices. These threats to habitat, primarily poor water quality and fragmentation of populations, are still the major driver in limiting the species distribution, abundance, and viability (USFWS 2021e).

#### Blue shiner critical habitat has not been designated.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. The pathway for effect to blue shine is through water quality and habitat access. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing change in riparian vegetation (temperature), sediment/turbidity, and road density/location may have effects on blue shiner. Habitat access could be affected by temporary or permanent road building, these effects would be in place as long as the temporary road is in place. BMPs would help alleviate negative effects but overall the effects of the action would be **may affect, likely to adversely affect** blue shiner.

#### _Spotfin chub_

Spotfin chub is a small cyprinid (maximum standard length 92 mm), with a slightly compressed, elongated body, and live to year 3 (USFWS 1983b; USFWS 2019j). Spotfin chub are more benthic than most other cyprinids and feed primarily on the surfaces of boulders, bedrock, and other substrates that are largely free of vegetation or sediment. Spotfin chub are typically oriented at an angle downward several degrees from horizontal when foraging, move about with quick zigzag motions, remain close to the bottom, and apparently do not opportunistically take drifting insects in the water column like most other shiners. The species is an insectivore, feeding diurnally presumably by both sight and taste in benthic areas of slow to swift current over various substrates with little siltation. The streams may range from 15-60 m width and, where occupied, 0.3-1.0 m depth. Water temperature in their summer habitat usually reaches greater than 20° C, and submerged macrophytes are usually absent, occasionally common. The species has been observed associated with sand, gravel, rubble, boulder, and bedrock substrates (USFWS 1983b; USFWS 2019j).

Spotfin chub is a rare large-stream fish that was widely distributed historically in most of the Tennessee River drainage. A total of 41 streams have records for the species, but at least 16 streams are thought to have lost their population. At present, four population clusters continue to support this species. Spotfin chub is generally sporadic or occasional in distribution and usually occurs at varying levels of abundance from very rare to relatively common in discrete reaches in most streams of occurrence. Spotfin chub typically inhabits moderate runs over bedrock, large boulders, and other substrates in large, clear, upland streams. Spawning and foraging substrates must be swept relatively free of fine sediments (USFWS 2019j).

The construction of major impoundments in much of the range of spotfin chub contributed heavily to habitat alterations for the species and resulted in highly disjunct current populations. Additional losses were likely realized from contaminants, sedimentation, and other habitat alterations (for example, middle North Fork Holston River). Losses from these sources were such that current habitat levels represent but a small percentage of historical habitat available for the species (USFWS 2019j).

Spotfin chub populations continue to be threatened by habitat fragmentation and population isolation, sedimentation and legacy contaminants events, and are susceptible to varying degrees by stochastic events (USFWS 2019j). Anthropogenic stresses such as silt or coal fine sedimentation; pollution; inundation by reservoir; temperature depression of dam tailwater; and channelization are invoked to have exterminated populations. Most of these factors also affect master streams of tributaries, some of whose populations may have been at least partly dependent upon ingress of chubs from the exterminated populations (USFWS 1983b).

The 1983 Recovery Plan listed nine "anthropogenic and natural limiting factors on all known populations" of spotfin chub and divided them into direct and indirect impacts for each extant and extirpated population. These included: 1) impoundment, 2) cold tailwaters, 3) channelization, 4) siltation and/or coal fine sedimentation, 5) pollution (inorganic and/or organic), 6) population renovation, 7) localized collecting, 8) natural cool temperature, and 9) small stream size (USFWS 1983b).

Actions that create sedimentation and contamination to spotfin chub habitat over the long term would be deleterious to the species. BMPs would help alleviate negative effects but overall the effects of the action would be may affect, likely to adversely affect spotfin chub.

Spotfin chub critical habitat is not in the action area.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. The pathway for effect to spotfin chub is through water quality and habitat access. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing change in riparian vegetation (temperature), sediment/turbidity, and road density/location may have effects on spotfin chub. Habitat access could be affected by temporary road building; these effects would be in place as long as the temporary or permanent road is in place. The probability of spotfin chub being in the action area are low since they have not been found in over 20 years, but not zero. Considering the species pathway of effects, best management practices, and probability

of presence in the action area, project activities may affect, not likely to adversely affect spotfin chub because effects are discountable.

#### _Owens tui chub_

Owens tui chub is dusky-olive above and has blue and gold sides, a gold-colored head, and olivebrown to reddish brown fins. Individuals range from 15 mm to 180 mm in length. It is distinguished from other tui chubs by the presence of lateral radii on the scales with a rounded or shield shaped scale base. This species occurs in low-velocity waters with well-developed beds of aquatic vegetation, rocks, and undercut banks. Vegetation is important for predator avoidance, reproduction, food, and water velocity reduction. The Owens tui chub is an opportunistic omnivore, consuming aquatic insects, vegetation, and detritus. Owens tui chubs feed mainly by gleaning and grazing among submerged vegetation. Its diet varies seasonally; the dominant items in its diet are chironomid larvae and algae in spring, chironomid larvae in summer, hydroptilid caddisflies in fall, and chironomid larvae in winter. Owens tui chub are found in constant water temperature springs and reach sexual maturity at 2 years of age for females and 1 year for males. Males and females will both reach sexual maturity at age 2 in varied temperature waters. Spawning in spring systems is likely triggered by day length and occurs from late winter to early spring. Spawning in riverine and lacustrine or lake-like habitats is triggered by warming water temperatures and occurs in spring and early summer. Spawning typically occurs over gravel substrate or aquatic vegetation, with eggs adhering to these features. Life expectancy is likely several years, with the oldest fish captured estimated at 7 years (USFWS 2026a).

Owens tui chub (populations that have not hybridized with Lahontan tui chub ( _Siphateles bicolor pectinifer_ )) are restricted to five small, isolated sites within its historical range in the Owens Basin: Hot Creek headwaters (only CD Spring), Little Hot Creek Pond, Upper Owens Gorge, Mule Spring, and White Mountain Research Center, operated by the University of California. The Hot Creek headwaters population site consists of two currently separate springs, AB Spring and CD Spring; however, only the population in CD Spring is not hybridized with Lahontan tui chub (USFWS 2022h).

Threats to Owens tui chub are disease; catastrophic events; demographic, genetic and environmental stochasticity; and long-term alteration of weather patterns (USFWS 2022h).

Although only a few studies have examined Owens tui chub behavior, life history, and habitat use, several aspects of its ecology can be generally surmised from studies of other tui chub subspecies. Tui chubs congregate from late winter to early summer to spawn over aquatic vegetation or gravel substrate. Females may produce many eggs. Tui chubs may reach sexual maturity at 2 years and may live more than 30 years (USFWS 1998d).

Owen’s tui chub critical habitat is not in the action area.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing sediment/turbidity may have effects on Owen tui chub. Activities that include water quality pathways associated with impacts/benefits for change in riparian vegetation (temperature), would not be included as an activity causing effects because the species would not

be affected by downstream water temperature fluctuations within the expected effects range. Project activity effects would be limited to connected actions that might cause downstream effects such as timber haul that might cause some sediment/turbidity. Best management practices will minimize sediment/turbidity near riparian areas. After considering the species pathway of effects, and best management practices that would be implemented, project activities would not have measurable effects to species or their critical habitat; therefore, the project **may affect, not likely to adversely affect** Owen tui chub.

#### _Humpback chub_

The humpback chub is a large fish endemic to the Colorado River Basin. Adults attain a maximum size of about 480 mm total length and 1.2 kg in weight (USFWS 1990; USFWS 2002c). The greatest numbers of humpback chub have been found in relatively inaccessible canyons. The humpback chub has been referred to as “remarkable” and “bizarre.” It is certain that the humpback chub is an unusual and striking fish. It is a medium-sized less than 20 inches total length, freshwater fish, with silvery sides and a brown or o1ivaceous back. It has a narrow, flattened head that may be dorsally concave, a long, fleshy snout with an inferior-subterminal mouth, and small eyes. Adults generally have a pronounced dorsal hump that begins approximately at the dorsal origin of the gill covers, protrudes anteriorly, then ends at the origin of the dorsal fin. The fish’s body tapers abruptly to the narrow caudal peduncle, then flares posteriorly into a deeply forked caudal fin. These morphologic adaptations of the humpback chub aid the fish in negotiating turbulent waters in deep canyons of the Colorado River (USFWS 1990; USFWS 2002c).

Six extant wild populations of humpback chub are known: (1) Black Rocks, Colorado River, Colorado; (2) Westwater Canyon, Colorado River, Utah; (3) Yampa Canyon, Yampa River, Colorado; (4) Desolation/Gray Canyons, Green River, Utah; (5) Cataract Canyon, Colorado River, Utah; and (6) the mainstem Colorado River in Marble and Grand Canyons and the Little Colorado River, Arizona. The first five populations are in the Upper Colorado River Basin (i.e., upstream of Glen Canyon Dam, Arizona), and the sixth population is in the Lower Colorado River Basin. Populations of humpback chub are restricted to deep, swift, canyon-bound regions of the mainstem and large tributaries of the Colorado River Basin (USFWS 2002c).

Adults require eddies and sheltered shoreline habitats maintained by high spring flows. These high spring flows maintain channel and habitat diversity, flush sediments from spawning areas, rejuvenate food production, and form gravel and cobble deposits used for spawning. Spawning occurs on the descending limb of the spring hydrograph at water temperatures typically between 16 and 22°C. Young require low-velocity shoreline habitats, including eddies and backwaters, that are more prevalent under base-flow conditions. Threats to the species include streamflow regulation, habitat modification, predation by nonnative fish species, parasitism, hybridization with other native Gila, and pesticides and pollutants (USFWS 1990).

Humpback chub reside in larger river systems where any effect from forest service actions, if it reached the larger river system, would return to background levels quickly but may still have negative impacts to young since they tend to utilize low-velocity shoreline habitats. BMPs would help alleviate negative effects but overall, the effects of the action would be **may affect, likely to adversely affect** humpback chub.

Humpback chub critical habitat is not in the action area.

#### _Sonora chub_

Sonora chub is a member of the Leuciscidae family and is generally less than 5 inches in total length. It is a moderately chubby, dark colored fish, with two prominent black lateral bands on the sides and a dark oval spot at the base of the tail. In breeding males, a red coloration develops at the bases of the lower fins and some orange coloration is present on the belly. The Sonora chub is primarily a pool dweller but is highly secretive and little is known of its behavior and habitat preferences (51 FR 16042).

The Sonora chub is a desert fish adapted to the fluctuations of a desert environment; after drought conditions it has been known to rapidly expand and recolonize California Gulch and newly re-wetted reaches. If habitat conditions along water ways can be maintained, then this ability to respond to favorable water conditions is encouraging for the population to avoid the danger of extinction. Construction of roads or bridges as described above might have temporary adverse effects, but long-term effects can be beneficial to the chub if it reduces off road use. there are two known wild populations within the U.S. and a captive population (USFWS 2019k).

The species occurs in southern Arizona and in northern Sonora, Mexico. The Coronado National Forest monitors and implements conservation projects for the Sonora chub regularly. The Coronado National Forest noted Sonora chub were present in California Gulch in 2012. All Coronado National Forest reports stated that international border security issues make it difficult to monitor populations of this species. The majority of habitat occupied by Sonora chub within the U.S. exists within the Coronado National Forest. Portions of Sycamore Canyon and its tributaries are critical habitat and include the Pajarito Wilderness and Goodding Research Natural Area, each of which lends a high degree of administrative protection for the species. Roadless Rule Rescission could remove the administrative protection for the species. Land ownership patterns in México are variable, and the species has comparatively little administrative protection there (USFWS 2022i).

The three primary threats to the Sonora chub are: 1) non-native species, 2) degradation of habitat, and 3) continued demand for water for human consumption. Current threats to the United States population include the stocking of exotic fishes and their associated parasites, and possible uranium mining activities (51 FR 16042).

Sonora chub critical habitat is not in the action area.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing water quality associated with sediment/turbidity may have effects on Sonora chub and Sonora chub critical habitat. Sediment/turbidity is associated with most activities proposed in the project. The amount of sediment/turbidity that would accompany proposed project activities would be short-term negative effects and indistinguishable from background conditions after a

wildfire. Process based restoration and temporary road removal activities would have short-term negative effects but long-term beneficial effects. Temporary road building would create adverse conditions as long as the road is in place. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects. Removal of the high degree of administrative protection within the Coronado National Forest Plan; any future project could reach the level of not being discountable and **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Sonora chub.

#### _Bonytail_

The **bonytail** is a large cyprinid fish endemic to the Colorado River Basin. Adults attain a maximum size of about 550 mm total length and 1.1 kg in weight. The bonytail is rare in the wild and an unknown, but small number of wild adults exist in Lake Mohave on the mainstem Colorado River of the Lower Colorado River Basin (i.e., downstream of Glen Canyon Dam, Arizona), and there are small numbers of wild individuals in the Green River and upper Colorado River subbasins of the Upper Colorado River Basin (USFWS 2002d).

The bonytail was historically common to abundant in warm-water reaches of larger rivers from Mexico to Wyoming. Little is known about the specific habitat requirements of bonytail because the species was extirpated from most of its historic range prior to extensive fishery surveys. The bonytail is considered adapted to mainstem rivers where it has been observed in pools and eddies. Similar to other closely related _Gila_ spp., bonytail in rivers probably spawn in spring over rocky substrates; spawning in reservoirs has been observed over rocky shoals and shorelines. It is hypothesized, based on available distribution data, that flooded bottomland habitats are important growth and conditioning areas for bonytail, particularly as nursery habitats for young. Threats to the species include streamflow regulation, habitat modification, competition with and predation by nonnative fish species, hybridization, and pesticides and pollutants (USFWS 2002d).

Currently no self-sustaining populations of bonytail exist in the wild, and very few individuals have been caught throughout the basin. Releases of hatchery-reared adults into riverine reaches in the upper basin have resulted in low survival, but in 2023 there was evidence of reproduction and recruitment of juveniles (USFWS 2002c; USFWS 2024y).

Bonytail critical habitat is not in the action area.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Although difficult to determine based on the available information for young, we assume activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing water quality related to sediment/turbidity may have effects on bonytail young within the pools and eddies as sediment/turbidity could decrease sight feeding. The amount of sediment/turbidity that would accompany timber harvest activities would be short-term negative effects. Temporary and permanent road building would create adverse conditions as long as the road is in place. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects. Therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely** affect bonytail.

#### _Gila chub_

In June 2025, the USFWS proposed to delist Gila chub due to findings that it is not a listable entry (90 FR 25552). There has been considerable uncertainty in the scientific literature regarding the taxonomy of Gila chub in the Lower Colorado River basin, specifically relationship between the roundtail chub, headwater chub, and Gila chub ( _Gila intermedia_ ) (from SSS of roundtail chub [USFWS 2025o]). The Gila chub has been listed as endangered with critical habitat since 2002 (70 FR 66664). In the recent Species Status Assessment (USFWS 2025o), information indicated a lack of differentiation between the three species, although there was also contrary information as well. USFWS concluded that that the available information did not support recognizing the Gila chub or headwater chub as distinct taxonomic entities and instead should be classified as roundtail chub. USFWS noted this in their 12-month finding for the roundtail chub and issued an advanced notice of proposed rulemaking to delist the Gila under the justification that it was not a listable entity (87 FR 19657).

Gila chub critical habitat is in the action area and consists of approximately 0.1% of the total designated critical habitat. Gila chub’s primary constituent elements are:

1. Perennial pools, areas of higher velocity between pools, and areas of shallow water among plants or eddies all found in headwaters, springs, and cienegas, generally of smaller tributaries;

2. Water temperatures for spawning ranging from 17 to 24 °C (62.6 to 75.2 °F), and seasonally appropriate temperatures for all life stages (varying from approximately 10 °C to 30 °C).

3. Water quality with reduced levels of contaminants, including excessive levels of sediments adverse to Gila chub health, and adequate levels of pH (for example, ranging from 6.5 to 9.5), dissolved oxygen (for example, ranging from 3.0 to 10.0) and conductivity (for example, 100 to 1000 mmhos).

4. Food base consisting of invertebrates (for example, aquatic and terrestrial insects) and aquatic plants (for example, diatoms and filamentous green algae);

5. Sufficient cover consisting of downed logs in the water channel, submerged aquatic vegetation, submerged large tree root wads, undercut banks with sufficient overhanging vegetation, large rocks and boulders with overhangs, a high degree of streambank stability, and a healthy, intact riparian vegetation community;

6. Habitat devoid of nonnative aquatic species detrimental to Gila chub or habitat in which detrimental nonnatives are kept at a level that allows Gila chub to continue to survive and reproduce; and

7. Streams that maintain a natural flow pattern including periodic flooding.

**Effects:** Gila chub have been found to not be a listable entity by the USFWS, although they have not been removed from the ESA list at the time of writing this biological assessment. The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit

column in Table 16. Effects to this species may occur; however, the fact that Gila chub is not a listable entity (87 FR 19657), effects analyses for the species and critical habitat is not necessary. Since this is still a listed entity, the assumption for this document is the project **may affect, not likely to adversely affect** Gila chub and Gila chub critical habitat.

#### _Chihuahua chub_

The Chihuahua chub has a fusiform body that resembles some trout. It has a terminal mouth that extends backward to about the margin of the eye. The Chihuahua chub averages 5-6 inches in length at maturity and may reach 12 inches. In individuals over 100 millimeters, the back and sides are brassy green to slate gray, sometimes with two indistinct lateral stripes, and the abdomen is whitish (USFWS 1986b; USFWS 2023l). Chihuahua chub is suggested to be an opportunistic carnivore, feeding on invertebrates and possibly fish. However, no specific studies on food habits have been conducted (USFWS 2023l).

The Chihuahua chub is endemic to the Guzman Basin, where it occurs from the Mimbres River in New Mexico, southward to northwestern Chihuahua, Mexico (USFWS 1986b). The historical range of Chihuahua chub is difficult to determine because of the lack of early collections. Most likely all but the uppermost reaches of permanently watered portions of the Mimbres River, New Mexico, and streams in the Guzman and Laguna Bustillos basins in Mexico were occupied. All streams within the historical range flow into a closed (endorheic) basin; none have a connection with the ocean (USFWS 2023l). Adult Chihuahua chub are considered habitat specialists. They are found in their natural habitats primarily in lateral scour pools, beneath undercut banks, or under other solid objects (e.g., logs, boulders) adjacent to moderate to fast flowing water in small to medium sized streams. Corner and backwater pools containing large woody debris are also used as habitat. Almost all natural habitats occupied by Chihuahua chub have extensive cover composed of organic debris or root wads of large trees. Pools are typically 1-2 m deep with a water velocity of less than 15 cm/second, and substrates are small-grained (sand to pea-size). Juveniles are found in shallower water with or without cover. This habitat type provides both escape cover and a suitable foraging situation. Chubs are rather trout-like in much of their feeding, taking terrestrial insects on the surface as well as aquatic invertebrates and perhaps some fish and vegetation (USFWS 1986b; USFWS 2023l).

The decline of the Chihuahua chub in the Mimbres River appears to be primarily related to loss of habitat. This loss has been due to severe flooding caused by degradation of the watershed and loss of riparian vegetation, and to action taken by local landowners to protect their property from future flooding. The Mimbres River has been channelized and leveed by local landowners in an effort to confine flood waters. As a result, chub habitat has been destroyed. The work has not been effective or enduring, and must be repeated each spring at or near the time the chub spawns, making these activities especially detrimental.

Diversions have reduced the quantity of water in the river, while uneven flows, flooding, and repeated stream modifications by local landowners have combined to eliminate the historical habitat conditions to the point the river terminus is usually dry (USFWS 1986b). Exotic species introductions probably led to predation on and competition with the chub. However, these factors probably played a minor role in the declining status of the chub compared to the influence of loss of habitat (USFWS 1986b).

Propagation and restocking of the Chihuahua chub has been ongoing since the 1970’s. There have been continued stocking efforts. The management direction for the Chihuahua chub is to stock the species as needed to maintain populations and expand their range with the intention of creating a self-sustaining population(s) (USFWS 2023l).

The Chihuahua chubs’ distribution and abundance in the US has declined in recent years due to catastrophic effects of wildfires and subsequent ash flow during monsoons. Currently, the US population consists of a few isolated individuals in the Mimbres River basin, found during surveys in late 2022 and early 2023. The species has not been surveyed in Mexico since the 1990s. Given its declining state at that time, lack of regulatory mechanisms, and likely increase of stressors due to alterations of weather patterns, it is presumed the species condition has continued to decline in Mexico. Numerous conservation actions have benefited the species, including obtaining property ownership along the Mimbres River, habitat improvements in stream and riparian areas, and the construction of an off channel refugia pond. Further, the species is maintained in captivity for propagation and release (USFWS 2023l).

Chihuahua chub critical habitat has not been designated.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing water quality associated with sediment/turbidity may have effects on Chihuahua chub. However, sediment/turbidity within the range of Chihuahua chub may only be an issue when monsoon rain occurs. Activities that create sediment/turbidity would add to sediment movement into the river. It’s difficult to determine whether these sediment inputs from the activities would be measurable or not. Best management practices will help minimize the amount of sediment reaching the river but will not eliminate it. These effects would be short-term effects. Therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Chihuahua chub.

#### _Yaqui chub_

Yaqui chub are considered a medium-sized minnow, where adults rarely exceed 6 inches in length. The head and anterior portion of the body are thick and narrows towards the posterior region. Yaqui chub are generally dark colored, but in sunlight can exhibit combinations of green, blues and purples. The most prominent feature of Yaqui chub is a dark, nearly black, triangular caudal spot, which is located at the base of the tail. They live in springs, spring-fed ditches, creeks, (and have adapted favorably to ponds) over substrates of silt, clay, sand, and gravel. Water may be clear or muddy, with associated vegetation including watercress, cattail, sedges, and willows. Depths of capture vary to >1.5 m; and currents are none to moderate. Spawning occurs mostly during spring – early summer and has been recorded in all but midwinter months. The reproductive potential of this fish is very high, with large populations able to quickly develop from only a few adults when habitat conditions are favorable. The species feeds mostly on algae, invertebrates, and detritus (USFWS 2020i). Growth to maturity is rapid, often within the first summer of life. Spawning is protracted throughout the warmer months, with greater activity in spring. Reproductive potential is high and large populations develop quickly from a few adults (USFWS 1995d). Young fish will spatially separate from larger individuals by occupying areas near shore and in shallow water. Threats to this species include very limited range, making potential loss from catastrophic events more likely; loss, alteration, and degradation of suitable wetland habitat; competition with, and/or depredation by, non-native species; and long-term drought combined with expanding human populations, which are creating increased demand for water for human consumption (USFWS 2020i).

Yaqui chub are restricted to the Rio San Bernardino system in Arizona and Sonora. It was historically and still remains known in Mexico but only from a <3.0 km perennial reach of Rio San Bernardino, immediately south of the international border in Sonora. Most of its range is now restricted within the U.S., and the majority of that is directly protected on San Bernadino National Wildlife Refuge.

Approximately 35 managed populations of Yaqui chub currently occur across the known range with one population occurring in West Turkey Creek on the Coronado National Forest. The 2018 Coronado National Forest Land Management Plan (available at USFS 2025a) contains guidelines and management approaches included in their forest plan that are intended to implement projects that will achieve desired ecosystem conditions for animals and rare plants (Chapter 2 under Animals and Rare plants page 65) where they occur.

Yaqui chub critical habitat is not in the action area.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing water quality associated with sediment/turbidity may have effects on Yaqui chub. Sediment/turbidity is associated with activities proposed in the project. Temporary and permanent road building would create adverse conditions as long as the road is in place. Yaqui chub reside in spring-fed areas where sediment/turbidity would dissipate quickly but may still cause adverse effects. Guidelines within the Coronado National Forest would evaluate projects for effects to the species prior to determining to implement in Yaqui chub habitat. Best management practices will help minimize the adverse effects but may not eliminate them. Therefore, project activities **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Yaqui chub.

#### _Clear Lake hitch_

The Clear Lake hitch is a subspecies of fish in the North American freshwater fish in the Leuciscidae family. It is restricted to the Clear Lake watershed in Lake County, California. Clear Lake is located approximately 100 miles north of San Francisco in the Coast Ranges and experiences hot, dry summers and cool, wet winters, with most precipitation occurring from November to March. The lake is fed by numerous tributaries, most of which are ephemeral and low gradient as they drain into the lake. Historically, the Clear Lake hitch occurred in numerous lakes and ponds found throughout the Clear Lake watershed, including Clear Lake, Thurston Lake, Upper Blue Lake, Lower Blue Lake, and Lampson Pond. There are no population or abundance estimates for the historical population of Clear Lake hitch. Historical data on the hitch were primarily from observations and incidental catch data from past commercial fishing operations, and local Tribal knowledge and observations (USFWS 2024z).

Adult Clear Lake hitch have a deep and elongated body and can grow to over 350 mm standard length (SL). They have a relatively small conical head, a terminal or slightly upturned mouth, and the morphology of their pharyngeal teeth are evidence of their limnetic lifestyle.
