Juvenile Clear Lake hitch have been known to have a black spot at the end of the tail that extends to the head region as a gradually fading black stripe; however, as individuals age, their coloring fades and they become a brownish-yellow. Clear Lake hitch are thought to live 4 to 6 years, but it is possible some individuals can live longer (USFWS 2024z).

For most of the year, Clear Lake hitch are only found within their lacustrine environment. However, between February and May, a portion of the reproductive population begins to migrate into the surrounding tributaries to spawn. Eggs are deposited on fine to medium sized gravel within the tributary stream. Fertilized eggs develop and hatch within 7 to 10 days, fry are freeswimming after another 7 to 10 days, and fry stay in the streams anywhere between 11 to 152 days, migrating to the lake once streams dry up. Juvenile Clear Lake hitch are found within the nearshore habitat of the lake where they depend on submerged aquatic vegetation for cover and prey. Juvenile Clear Lake hitch move from the nearshore portion of the lake into open water in early- to late-fall. There is evidence that Clear Lake hitch do not require tributary streams with gravel to spawn but can also spawn successfully in different portions of the lake (such as, along the shore, the mouths of tributaries, and Rodman Slough) that lack a gravel substrate (USFWS 2024z).

Clear Lake hitch critical habitat has not been designated.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing water quality associated with sediment/turbidity may have effects on Clear Lake hitch eggs and fry within the tributary streams. Adult Clear Lake hitch are found in open water and project activity causing sediment/turbidity may occur in localized areas depending on environmental conditions. Temporary or permanent road building would create adverse conditions as long as the road is in place. Clear Lake hitch eggs and fry if located in tributaries could be covered with sediment/turbidity causing death to this lifestage. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects to all life stages but not eliminate the adverse effects. Therefore, project activities **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Clear Lake hitch.

#### _Little Colorado spinedace_

Little Colorado spinedace is a small fish, generally less than 100 mm in total length, has a moderately oblique mouth, a strong second “spine” of dorsal fin, moderately high and acute dorsal fin (USFWS 1998e). Little Colorado spinedace is a fish with a limited, highly fragmented distribution and relatively low numbers, making it highly vulnerable to stressors, particularly drought, ground-water and surface water withdrawals, high-severity landscape-scale wildfires, and predation and competition with non-native warm water fishes (USFWS 2019l). Currently, the Little Colorado spinedace occurs in disjunct locations in three subbasins of the Little Colorado River Basin: the Middle Little Colorado, Chevelon Canyon, and Little Colorado Headwaters (USFWS 2019l). Populations are small and the true population size for any occupied stream is unknown due to yearly fluctuations in their numbers and the difficulty in locating fish (USFWS 2023m).

Little Colorado spinedace live in springs, streams, and rivers with perennial flow, tend to prefer pools, but occurs sporadically throughout the habitat. Little Colorado spinedace has a tolerance for wide temperature fluctuations and habitat types. Little Colorado spinedace’ s survival is threatened by habitat loss, habitat modification, competition and predation from non-native fish and introduced parasites (USFWS 2019l).

Current or potential future threats to Little Colorado spinedace include habitat alteration and destruction due to high intensity, landscape scale wildfire, increased groundwater pumping, and long-term drought, and competition and predation with nonnative species. The USFS is implementing thinning and prescribed burning within spinedace watersheds to reduce the threat from high intensity landscape-scale wildfires. Thinning and prescribed burning will also improve water infiltration and increase base flows to occupied, potential, and critical habitat within the project area. Improving water retention in these drainages is vital to maintaining Little Colorado spinedace habitat in a warming and drying climate (USFWS 2023m).

Uncertainties and data gaps that may impede recovery progress include the effects of extended drought and increased groundwater pumping for human water consumption to the persistence of spinedace habitat; the lack of knowledge regarding genetic diversity; and the ability to develop techniques to assist with the control of invasive non-native fishes and other aquatic organisms. The number of areas within the East Clear Creek watershed where spinedace are persisting has increased over the last several years. In addition, occupied sites in the Little Colorado River (upstream of Lyman Reservoir), West Chevelon Creek, Nutrioso Creek, and Rudd Creek continue to support spinedace; although there are long-term concerns regarding habitat in Chevelon Creek. Efforts by Arizona Game and Fish Department, the USFWS, USFS, and Bureau of Land Management have resulted in an increased number of small habitats, in which Little Colorado spinedace occupy (USFWS 2023m).

**Little Colorado spinedace critical habitat** is in the action area and consists of approximately 0.17% of the total designated critical habitat. Physical and biological features, for all areas of designated critical habitat, include clean, permanent flowing water, with pools and a fine gravel or silt-mud substrate (52 FR 35034).

**Effects** : The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing water quality associated with sediment/turbidity may have effects on Little Colorado spinedace. Sediment/turbidity is associated with most activities proposed in the project. Temporary and permanent road building would create adverse conditions as long as the road is in place. Little Colorado spinedace reside in streams with clean, flowing water, where sediment/turbidity would dissipate quickly under normal conditions. Best management practices and Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest Plan and Coronado National Forest Plan guidelines would minimize effects. Even so, project activities **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Little Colorado spinedace and Little Colorado spinedace critical habitat.

#### _Spikedace_

The spikedace is a small, stream dwelling fish endemic to the Gila River system of Arizona and New Mexico. The body is slender, almost spindle shaped, and lightly compressed laterally. The species also likely occurred in the past in the San Pedro River in Sonora, Mexico. Once widely distributed among moderate sized, intermediate elevation streams in the Gila River system, at least upstream of Phoenix, Arizona, the spikedace is now restricted to scattered populations in relatively short stream reaches (USFWS 1991a). Generally, the species must have been common and likely locally abundant in preferred habitats. Although habitat suitable for spikedace was probably not continuous, it was widespread throughout the species’ range. Like most western cyprinids, population abundances and distributions of spikedace probably fluctuated in natural response to local and regional environmental conditions (USFWS 1991a).

Spikedace remain limited in distribution in Aravaipa Creek, the mainstem Gila River, and the West and Middle Forks of the Gila River. Spikedace have not been detected in the Verde River since 1999, and in Eagle Creek since 1989. Translocated populations in Spring Creek, Fossil Creek, the Blue River, and the San Francisco River show promise and, given more time to establish and recover from setbacks, may help in expanding the distribution of spikedace across a great portion of its historical range. Translocation efforts at Muleshoe Canyon, Redfield Canyon, and Bonita Creek have proven unsuccessful. Spikedace are believed to be extirpated from Mangas Creek at this time (USFWS 2023n).

Across their range, spikedace continue to face many threats that were identified in the 2012 reclassification rule (77 FR 10810), including nonnative aquatic species which prey on or compete with them, as well as dewatering of existing habitats, drought, and wildfire. Nonnatives are present in all locations except for the Blue River, Spring Creek, and Fossil Creek, all of which are protected by barriers, and all of which have had to have nonnative removals completed after barrier construction. Nonnative species are present in the Verde River, Eagle Creek, Aravaipa Creek, the Gila River, and the West and Middle Forks of the Gila River. Dewatering also continues at these locations, with intermittent stretches of river now occurring on the Gila and Verde Rivers, Aravaipa Creek, and Eagle Creek (USFWS 2023n).

In addition to the effects outlined in the reclassification rule in 2012, drought, and wildfire have increased since 2012, affecting many spikedace locations including the Verde River, Fossil Creek, Blue River, the Gila River, and the West Fork Gila River. The synergistic effects of drought, and wildfire are likely to result in additional threats to the species in the near future (USFWS 2023n).

Spikedace critical habitat physical and biological features are:

1. Habitat to support all egg, larval, juvenile, and adult spikedace, which includes:

- a. Perennial flows with a stream depth generally less than 1 m (3.3 ft), and with slow to swift flow velocities between 5 and 80 cm per second (1.9 and 31.5 in. per second).

- b. Appropriate stream microhabitat types including glides, runs, riffles, the margins of pools and eddies, and backwater components over sand, gravel, and cobble substrates with low or moderate amounts of fine sediment and substrate embeddedness;

- c. Appropriate stream habitat with a low gradient of less than approximately 1.0 percent, at elevations below 2,100 m (6,890 ft); and

- d. Water temperatures in the general range of 8.0 to 28.0 °C (46.4 to 82.4 °F).

2. An abundant aquatic insect food base consisting of mayflies, true flies, black flies, caddisflies, stoneflies, and dragonflies.

3. Streams with no or no more than low levels of pollutants.

4. Perennial flows, or interrupted stream courses that are periodically dewatered but that serve as connective corridors between occupied or seasonally occupied habitat and through which the species may move when the habitat is wetted.

5. No nonnative aquatic species, or levels of nonnative aquatic species that are sufficiently low as to allow persistence of spikedace.

6. Streams with a natural, unregulated flow regime that allows for periodic flooding or, if flows are modified or regulated, a flow regime that allows for adequate river functions, such as flows capable of transporting sediments.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing water quality may have effects on spikedace. Changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) is associated with removal of trees within the riparian area. Any tree removal within the riparian area would create localized non-measurable increase in water temperature, that would return to background levels a short distance downstream. Sediment/turbidity is associated with most activities proposed in the project. Temporary or permanent road building would create adverse conditions as long as the road is in place. Spikedace critical habitat is in the action area and consists of less than 0.01% of the total designated critical habitat. Physical and biological features for their insect food base may be impacted by sedimentation with USFS actions. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects. Project activities **may affect, likely to adversely affect** spikedace and spikedace critical habitat.

#### _Cape Fear shiner_

The Cape Fear shiner is a small minnow native to the upper Cape Fear River Basin in central North Carolina. The Cape Fear shiner is a minnow native to five counties in the upper Cape Fear River Basin in central North Carolina. It is a narrow endemic, with a single population comprised of three subpopulations based on river subbasins – the Haw, Rocky-Deep, and Cape Fear. The species is most often found in rocky pools and runs adjacent to riffles in wide, shallow segments of rivers with gravel, cobble and/or boulder substrates with forested banks and abundant water willow ( _Justicia americana_ ), riverweed ( _Podostemum ceratophyllum_ ), stream mosses, and filamentous green algae. It is distinguished from all other Notropis minnows by having a long doubly twisted alimentary tract, has 8 anal fin rays, and its lip coloration includes a small black line on its lower lip margin (aka, “lip liner”). The Cape Fear Shiner feeds mostly on detritus, algae and plant material, and small invertebrates. Spawning begins in early spring and can run through summer, and the species has an assumed lifespan in the wild of two to three years (USFWS 2022j; USFWS 2022k).

It was listed as an endangered species due to its small population size and threats to its habitat from dams and pollution. Over the past three decades, significant conservation actions, particularly successful captive propagation and two dam removals, have benefited the species and improved and connected habitat within the Rocky-Deep River subbasin. Despite these habitat improvements, Cape Fear Shiner resiliency remains very low in the Haw and Cape Fear subbasins, accounting for 62% of its range.

Cape Fear shiner critical habitat is not in the action area.

**Effects:** The pathway for effects to Cape Fear shiner are through pollution. The assumption made in this document is related activities would be most similar to chemical contamination. The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing chemical contamination may have effects on Cape Fear shiner. Chemical contamination from project activity implementation is included in many activities due to the utilization of petroleum products by the equipment needed for implementing projects. As the analysis under the chemical contamination section states, motorized hand tools have small fuel capacities and if spills occur these are not expected to reach the streams. Best management practices will limit fueling near riparian areas, and experience over the years of implementing projects has shown large spills of petroleum products have not occurred. After considering the species pathway of effects, best management practices, that would be implemented, project activities would not have measurable effects on species; therefore, the project **may affect, not likely to adversely affect** Cape Fear shiner.

#### _Colorado pikeminnow_

Colorado pikeminnow is a large, long-lived fish and the largest member of the taxonomic family Leuciscidae native to North America. It is endemic to warmwater reaches of large rivers in the Colorado River basin. Prior to the introduction of nonnative, predatory fish species, Colorado pikeminnow was the apex predator in these reaches and adults are mostly piscivorous. Colorado pikeminnow can grow to a large size, historically greater than 5 feet in length and can live over 50 years in the wild. Colorado pikeminnow make long distance migrations (409 miles (mi) [658 kilometers (km)] round trip) to spawn and return to their home range, where they inhabit deep runs, pools, and eddies. Colorado pikeminnow eggs hatch in cobble spawning bars as spring high flows decline, and larvae subsequently emerge and are carried long distances by river flows to low velocity nursery habitats downstream. In these reaches, larvae and juveniles seek low to zero velocity backwaters that provide warm temperatures for growth and abundant macroinvertebrates and small fish prey. Individual Colorado pikeminnow reach sexual maturity between 7 and 10 years of age and may spawn each year during their lifetime (USFWS 2023o).

Historically, Colorado pikeminnow occurred throughout the Colorado River basin, including the Green, Colorado, and San Juan rivers subbasins of Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, and New Mexico; downstream through the Colorado River mainstem in Arizona, Nevada, California, and Mexico; and the Gila River subbasin in Arizona and New Mexico. Colorado pikeminnow inhabit river reaches that historically experienced extremes in both flow and temperature on an annual basis, in addition to high turbidity from sediment inputs as a result of spring snow melt or flash floods. Colorado pikeminnow was extirpated from the Lower Colorado River Basin by the 1970s. The range of Colorado pikeminnow in the Upper Colorado River Basin contracted and populations declined in the Green and upper Colorado River subbasins; the species was functionally extirpated from the San Juan River subbasin in the late 1990s (USFWS 2023o).

Changes in the flow regime as a result of water development throughout the Colorado River basin led to initial declines in Colorado pikeminnow populations. In some cases, this development created barriers to movement in the form of dams and diversions, which have fragmented river reaches and limited access to historical habitats. Diversions can also entrain fish into water delivery systems and lead to direct mortality. Large dams can alter water temperatures through hypolimnetic releases, creating conditions too cold for Colorado pikeminnow growth and reproduction. Water storage and flow management often reduce spring peaks necessary to create and maintain spawning and nursery habitats needed by Colorado pikeminnow, and also reduce base flows, which can limit Colorado pikeminnow range and reduce habitat availability. Predation and competition from invasive, nonnative fishes reduce survival and recruitment of Colorado pikeminnow in all life stages. Contaminants that impact water quality can reduce reproduction and survival of individuals or lead to population reductions in the case of large, toxic spills. Lastly, extended drought reduces streamflow in many river reaches, which strains efforts to manage flows to benefit Colorado pikeminnow (USFWS 2023o). The stressors identified are reductions to natural flow regimes, water temperature depression because of hypolimnetic releases from large dams, physical barriers to movement and the resultant loss of habitat and connectivity, entrainment into water diversion facilities, nonnative fish competition and predation, contaminants, channel simplification, and long-term alteration of weather patterns (USFWS 2025p).

Colorado pikeminnow critical habitat is not in the action area.

**Effects:** One pathway for effects to Colorado pikeminnow is through toxic spills. The assumption made in this document is related activities would be most similar to chemical contamination. Colorado pikeminnow are also suspectable to degraded water quality, specifically higher sediment/turbidity and lower water temperatures. The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing chemical contamination and sediment/turbidity may have effects on Colorado pikeminnow. Changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) effects of proposed activities would create insignificant increases in water temperature, therefore, will not be considered in the analysis. Chemical contamination from project activity implementation is included in many activities due to the utilization of petroleum products by the equipment needed for implementing projects. As the analysis under the chemical contamination section states, motorized hand tools have small fuel capacities and if spills occur

these are not expected to reach the streams. Best management practices will limit fueling near riparian areas, and experience over the years of implementing projects has shown large spills of petroleum products have not occurred. Sediment/turbidity is associated with activities proposed in the project. The amount of sediment/turbidity that would accompany proposed project activities would be short-term negative effects for timber harvest. Temporary or permanent road building would create adverse conditions as long as the road is in place. Colorado pikeminnow reside in large rivers with flowing water, where sediment/turbidity would dissipate quickly under normal conditions. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects from project activities and project effects would be short-term adverse effects. Therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Colorado pikeminnow.

#### _Santa Ana speckled dace_

Santa Ana speckled dace has recently been designated as a distinct species (USFWS 2024aa). Santa Ana speckled dace was historically found throughout river systems at the bases of the San Gabriel, San Bernardino, and San Jacinto Mountain ranges in Los Angeles, San Bernardino and Riverside Counties, California. The northern extent of this species’ range was likely the northern San Gabriel Mountains in Los Angeles County and the southernmost extent south of Hemet in Riverside County. The majority of currently occupied habitat is on Federal lands, including Forest Service lands, and the species occurs in four small populations distributed across four isolated river systems. These four populations are composed of 17 extant occurrences found in a highly fragmented environment in the isolated remnants of the headwaters that resulted from historical habitat loss and habitat degradation. Currently Santa Ana speckled dace is found in the headwaters of San Jacinto, Santa Ana, San Gabriel, and Los Angeles rivers. Compared to the historical distribution, the remaining dace populations are relatively small and isolated (USFWS 2024aa).

Adult Santa Ana speckled dace inhabit a variety of stream habitat, commonly inhabiting the same stretches of water as Santa Ana sucker, with a preference for moving water. Although dace have been found in streams with a gradient as high as 10%, gradients above 5% seem to limit their movement due to cascading water from the steep terrain (USFWS 2024aa). Santa Ana speckled dace is a hardy fish where populations can naturally fluctuate through boom-and-bust cycles. To determine the current species needs, it is important to put the current distribution in the context of its historical distribution. Currently the species inhabits only small remnants of its historical range (making up four analysis units), due to habitat loss and habitat degradation. The species now exclusively occupies headwaters in relatively steep mountainous regions that are susceptible to drought, fire, and debris flows during high water years. The species needs adequate flows of low gradient (5% or less) cold, clear water with gravel or cobble substrate for reproduction. The dace also needs adequate numbers of aquatic invertebrates for food and limited or no invasive predators for higher abundances. Dace also require connectivity among remaining occurrences to maintain genetic diversity and allow for recolonization of extirpated occurrences in response to stochastic events like drought, fire, and debris flows (USFWS 2024aa).

Primary threats on Santa Ana speckled dace could include: (1) habitat loss (urban development and agricultural activities); (2) habitat degradation (recreational activities, mining, roadways, hydrological activities and diversions); (3) habitat fragmentation; (4) increased risk of wildfire; (5) changing climate trends (for example, increased temperatures and longer, more frequent drought periods); (6) nonnative species (increased competition and predation); and (7) small population effects (USFWS 2024aa).

**Effects:** Santa Ana speckled dace reside in headwater streams of steep mountainous regions and could be in areas where the forest service could implement actions. Actions such as road building could create negative impacts. BMPs would help alleviate negative effects from sedimentation and potentially localized increase in water temperature, road building effects last as long as the road is in place. At this time, there are no plans to implement projects in Santa Ana speckled dace habitat as this consultation is for rule making. Overall, the effects of this action, if implemented within Santa Ana speckled dace habitat could cause adverse effects; however, the National Forest Management Act provides for some protection of the aquatic management zone and forests need to analyze for effects to species for future project planning. The effects of the action **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Santa Ana speckled dace.

Santa Ana speckled dace critical habitat has not been designated since it is still a proposed species.

_Long Valley speckled dace_

Long Valley speckled dace is a subspecies of the speckled dace ( _Rhinichthys osculus_ ), a small fish that typically measures less than 8 cm but can reach 11 cm standard length (SL). It has a small downfacing mouth, a thick caudal peduncle, small scales, and a pointed snout. Long Valley speckled dace are morphologically adapted to springs and exhibit fewer scales in the lateral line, fewer lateral line pores, deeper bodies, and shorter fins than fluvial speckled dace populations (USFWS 2024ab).

Long Valley speckled dace was historically found throughout seven historical sites, including Hot Creek and various isolated springs and ponds, within the 700,000 year-old Long Valley volcanic caldera in Mono County, CA. This subspecies was likely isolated from other speckled dace populations when Speckled Dace colonized the upper Owens Valley region from the Mono Lake Basin. The formation of steep waterfalls in the Owens River Gorge separated the Owens Valley from Long Valley approximately 100,000 years ago, isolating Long Valley speckled dace from other speckled dace populations. The subspecies generally lives in isolated spring habitats and is genetically distinct from other members of the speckled dace complex (USFWS 2024ab).

Long Valley speckled dace has been extirpated from all historical collection sites except Whitmore Marsh (a 4,000–8,000 m2 (1-2 ac) spring-fed marsh) due primarily to the effects of nonnative species, water diversion, and degraded water quality from recreational activity and cattle grazing. The recent population declines observed at Whitmore Marsh are concerning because multiple threats exist on the landscape, including a recreational swimming pool, grazing, and geothermal development, which can all be characterized as posing a risk to the current viability of the species. Multiple nonnative species and a trout hatchery exist within the historical range and have potentially contributed to the extirpation of populations at historical sites (USFWS 2024ab).

Long Valley speckled dace critical habitat has not been designated since it is still a proposed species.

**Effects:** Long Valley speckled dace do not occur on National Forest System Lands but are downstream of the forest within a 2-mile buffer. Long Valley speckled dace threats do not coincide with project activity effects; however, there may be a few effects pathways for effects not included in the listing document. Although they are not located on Forest System Lands, if effects occurred, it would be through utilizing the road system. Best management practices will minimize effects that could occur on the road system. Best management practices and geographic distance suggest effects are discountable, thus, project activities **may affect, not likely to adversely affect** Long Valley speckled dace.

#### _Kendall Warm Springs dace_

Kendall Warm Springs dace is endemic to one stream (984 feet in length) that originates from a series of thermal springs and seeps. The stream ends in a waterfall and empties into the Green River in Sublette County, Wyoming. The dace’s entire habitat occurs on property administered by the U.S. Forest Service, Bridger-Teton National Forest. The number of fish present in the population has never been accurately estimated; however, catch per unit effort data may indicate a possible decline in relative abundance over the last decade. The Kendall Warm Springs dace adults range in size from 0.9 to 2.1 inches (23 to 54 millimeters) (USFWS 2015a).

The Kendall Warm Springs dace is found in only one small thermal spring-fed stream of fastflowing waters over cobble and gravel substrate associated with emergent aquatic vegetation. The Kendall Warm Springs dace are believed to occupy their entire historic range. The warm springs themselves remain a constant 85°F (29.4°C) year-round. The stream temperature is more variable than the warm springs and has been recorded as low as 78°F (25.6°C) in the winter at the point where it cascades over a waterfall into the Green River (USFWS 2015a; USFWS 2022l).

Primary threats at the time of listing were limited distribution, habitat manipulation, and small population size. Additional threats identified since the time of listing are potential catastrophic habitat loss due to manipulation or pollution of the aquifer that supplies the springs, degradation in habitat quality from potential oil and gas development, and potential non-native species introductions (USFWS 2015a).

Since 1975 the U.S. Forest Service has prohibited bathing, wading, and washing clothes in the Kendall Warm Springs area, but, rarely, illegal activities have been documented over the last several decades. At the time of its listing, its habitat was fragmented into two sections by a road built across the stream prior to 1934. The road culvert bisected the stream at a point approximately two-thirds of the way downstream from the stream’s origin. The road culvert has since been removed and replaced with a bridge that spans the stream allowing reconnection of the habitat (USFWS 2015a; USFWS 2022l).

Kendall warm springs dace critical habitat has not been designated.

The Bridger-Teton National Forest Land and Resource Management Plan includes provisions for Kendall Warm Springs dace conservation, such as establishing the spring as a Special Interest Area and establishing protection of Kendall Warm Springs dace as a management objective (1990 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Due to this, there would be **no effects** to Kendall Warm Springs dace.

#### _Loach minnow_

The loach minnow is a small, secretive fish endemic to the Gila River basin of Arizona and New Mexico, USA, and Sonora, Mexico. The loach minnow is a small, slender fish less than 80 mm (3 in) in length. Loach minnow are found in small to large perennial streams and use shallow, turbulent riffles with primarily cobble substrate and swift currents. The loach minnow uses the spaces between, and in the lee (sheltered) side of, rocks for resting and spawning. It is rare or absent from habitats where fine sediments fill these interstitial spaces (77 FR 10810).

Currently, loach minnow are restricted to: portions of the Gila River and its tributaries, the West, Middle, and East Fork Gila River; the San Francisco and Tularosa rivers and their tributaries, Negrito and Whitewater Creeks (Catron County, New Mexico); the Blue River and its tributaries, Dry Blue, Campbell Blue, Pace, and Frieborn Creeks (Greenlee County, Arizona, and Catron County, New Mexico); Aravaipa Creek and its tributaries, Turkey and Deer Creeks (Graham and Pinal Counties, Arizona); Eagle Creek (Graham and Greenlee Counties, Arizona); the North Fork East Fork Black River (Apache and Greenlee Counties, Arizona); and possibly the White River and its tributaries, the East and North Fork White River (Apache, Gila, and Navajo Counties, Arizona) (77 FR 10810).

The loach minnow is a small, stream dwelling fish with an elongated body, little compressed, and flattened ventrally (USFWS 1991b). Loach minnow are associated only with flowing water in shallow, turbulent riffles where there are swift currents (77 FR 10810).

Two of the primary threats to loach minnow are nonnative fishes and loss of water due to diversions, pumping, drought, or other causes (77 FR 10810).

Loach minnow critical habitat is in the action area and consists of approximately 0.10% of the total designated critical habitat. Loach minnow critical habitat physical and biological features are (77 FR 10810):

1. Habitat to support all egg, larval, juvenile, and adult loach minnow which includes:

- a. Perennial flows with a stream depth of generally less than 1 m (3.3 ft), and with slow to swift flow velocities between 0 and 80 cm per second (0.0 and 31.5 in. per second);

- b. Appropriate microhabitat types including pools, runs, riffles, and rapids over sand, gravel, cobble, and rubble substrates with low or moderate amounts of fine sediment and substrate embeddedness;

- c. Appropriate stream habitats with a low stream gradient of less than 2.5 percent and are at elevations below 2,500 m (8,202 ft); and

- d. Water temperatures in the general range of 8.0 to 25.0 °C (46.4 to 77 °F).

2. An abundant aquatic insect food base consisting of mayflies, true flies, black flies, caddisflies, stoneflies, and dragonflies.

3. Streams with no or no more than low levels of pollutants.

4. Perennial flows, or interrupted stream courses that are periodically dewatered but that serve as connective corridors between occupied or seasonally occupied habitat and through which the species may move when the habitat is wetted.

5. No nonnative aquatic species, or levels of nonnative aquatic species that are sufficiently low to allow persistence of loach minnow.

6. Streams with a natural, unregulated flow regime that allows for periodic flooding or, if flows are modified or regulated, a flow regime that allows for adequate river functions, such as flows capable of transporting sediments.

**Effects:** The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing water quality associated with sediment/turbidity may have effects on loach minnow but any sedimentation would be expected to be a pulse short-term effect returning to background levels quickly as sedimentation may only be an issue when monsoon rains occur. Activities that create sediment/turbidity would add to the amount of sedimentation/turbidity but the amount would be unmeasurable from background conditions during the monsoon rains. Loach minnow critical habitat consists of approximately 0.10% of the total designated critical habitat. Physical and biological features for their insect food base may be impacted by sedimentation with USFS actions but would only occur during the monsoon rains and would be indistinguishable from background conditions. Best management practices will minimize the amount of sediment/turbidity created by activities and is expected to result in discountable effects. Therefore, the project **may affect, not likely to adversely affect** loach minnow and loach minnow critical habitat

### Cyprinodontidae Family

#### _Desert pupfish_

The desert pupfish is in the Cyprinodontidae family and contains several subspecies that all fall under the ESA. Minimal subspecies information is provided.

At the time of listing in 1986 (51 FR 10842), the historical range of desert pupfish included the Lower Colorado River Basin, the Gila River Basin, Laguna Salada, and the Rio Sonoyta Basin. What was desert pupfish in 1986 is now recognized as three separate species<sup>25</sup> , but the ESA listing has not been changed to reflect the taxonomic changes (USFWS 2019m). If a taxonomic name change is made under the ESA, any sub-group split off from the listed entity ( _C._

> 25 The USFWS ECOS website (https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/7003) accessed 12/11/2025 (USFWS 2026a), still refers to the desert pupfish as two subspecies Desert Pupfish ( _C.m. macularis_ ) and Quitobaquito Pupfish ( _C.m. eremus_ ) and not three separate species as the 2019 Recovery Plan states (USFWS 2019).

_macularius_ ) also would be listed ( _C. eremus_ ). This geographic area includes three species, _C. macularius, C. eremus, and C. arcuatus_ . However, the listed entity remains _C. macularius_ (USFWS 2019m). In this section all three species will be referred to as desert pupfish since that is what is listed under the ESA and information in USFWS publications and on their websites are inconsistent in the number of species/sub-species they include under the desert pupfish listing. Only two of the species/sub-species are listed under the ESA, _C. macularius_ and _C. eremus_ .

Desert pupfish is a small, laterally compressed fish with a smoothly rounded body shape that rarely grow larger than 75 millimeters in total length (51 FR 10842). Two subspecies of desert pupfish are recognized: Desert Pupfish ( _C.m. macularis_ ) and Quitobaquito Pupfish ( _C.m. eremus_ ). Desert pupfish was historically widespread, but probably not continuous within its historic range, and abundant in portions of southern Arizona and southeastern California, United States, and northern Baja California and Sonora, Mexico. Historical habitats varied in size, complexity, character and permanence, and included cienegas, springs, streams, and margins of larger lakes and rivers. Although remarkably tolerant of extreme environmental conditions, the species is threatened with extinction throughout its native range primarily because of habitat loss or modification, pollution, and introductions of exotic fishes (USFWS 1993b). Naturally occurring populations of desert pupfish are now restricted in Arizona to Quitobaquito Springs and in California to two streams tributary to, and a few shoreline pools and irrigation drains of the Salton Sea (USFWS 1993b).

Desert pupfish have an extraordinary ability to survive under conditions of high water temperature (to 45˚C), low dissolved oxygen concentration (0.1-0.4 milligrams per liter), and high salinity (salt concentrations twice (68 grams per liter) that of seawater), which exceed tolerances of virtually all other freshwater fishes. They also survive abrupt, absolute changes in both salinity (10-15 grams per liter) and temperature (22-26˚C) that are lethal to most fishes. In less harsh environments where a greater diversity of fishes was found (for example, margins of larger streams and rivers), pupfish typically occupied water shallower than that inhabited by adults of most other species (USFWS 1993b).

Under conditions of abundant food and suitable temperature (mid-to-upper 20s ˚C), desert pupfish may become sexually mature as early as six weeks of age at 1.5 centimeters total length, may breed as early as their first summer but most do not breed until their second summer when they reached a maximum of 7.5 centimeters (USFWS 1993b). Lifespan in the wild is highly variable from less than a year for some populations, two years for others, and up to three years for Quitobaquito pupfish (USFWS 1993b).

Larval desert pupfish in the laboratory begin feeding on tiny invertebrates within a few hours to a day after hatching and presumably do so in the wild as well. As they grow, wild fish become opportunistic omnivores, consuming whatever variety of algae, plants, suitably sized invertebrates, and detritus is available. Adult foods include ostracods, copepods, and other crustaceans and insects, pile worms, mollusks, and bits of aquatic macrophytes torn from available tissues. Detritus or algae are often predominant in their diets. Pupfish at Quitobaquito Spring have been reported to eat their own eggs and young. Foraging is typically a daytime activity, and fish may move in response to daily warming from shallower water during morning to feed in deeper places later in the day (USFWS 1993b).

The two main threats to the desert pupfish are loss and degradation of aquatic habitats, and continual spread and introduction of non-native aquatic species, which prey upon and compete with all pupfish species (USFWS 2019m). More specifically threats include habitat loss (dewatering of springs, some headwaters, and lower portions of major streams and marshlands), habitat modification (stream impoundment, channelization, diversion, and regulation of discharge, plus domestic livestock grazing and other watershed uses such as timber harvest, mining, and road construction), pollution, and interactions with non—native species. These threats of habitat loss, predation, and competition continue to be exacerbated by increasing human development and demand for water, as well as interactions with predicted trends for warmer, drier, and more extreme hydrological conditions associated with long-term alteration of weather patterns (USFWS 1993b, USFWS 2019m).

Desert pupfish critical habitat is not in the action area.

**Effects** : The pathway for effects to desert pupfish include pollution, timber harvest, and road construction. The assumption made in this document is related activities would be most similar to chemical contamination. The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing chemical contamination, timber harvest, and road construction may have effects on desert pupfish. Chemical contamination from project activity implementation is included in many activities due to the utilization of petroleum products by the equipment needed for implementing projects. As the analysis under the chemical contamination section states, motorized hand tools have small fuel capacities and if spills occur these are not expected to reach the streams. Best management practices will limit fueling near riparian areas, and experience over the years of implementing projects has shown large spills of petroleum products have not occurred. Timber harvest and road construction are threats to the species. The pathways in Table 16 for these activities could cause effects on species along the different pathways listed. Temporary and permanent road building would have effects for as long as the road is in place and may reach a measurable level. Project implementation may come with shortterm and long-term negative effects. After considering the species pathway of effects and best management practices, project activities could have measurable effects on species; therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** desert pupfish.

### Poeciliidae Family

#### _Gila topminnow_

The Gila topminnow may be in the action area and is the only species in the Poeciliidae family considered in this consultation Table 15. The Gila topminnow is native to the Gila River Basin of the United States and Mexico, and the Ríos de la Concepción and Sonora of northern Mexico. It was considered one of the most common fishes in the southern part of the Colorado River basin prior to 1940. However, habitat loss and interaction with nonnative fishes, particularly western mosquitofish ( _Gambusia affinis_ ) caused range-wide disappearances and decreases in abundance within the United States. Western mosquitofish is the main reason for decline of the Gila topminnow. The Gila topminnow is the only member of the family Poeciliidae that is native to the Gila River drainage (USFWS 1998f).

Habitat requirements of Gila topminnow are broad. They prefer shallow, warm, fairly quiet waters. However, they can become acclimated to a much wider range of conditions. Both lentic habitats and lotic habitats with moderate current are easily tolerated. Temperatures from near freezing under ice to 37˚C have been reported, with a maximum tolerance of 43˚C for brief periods. Topminnows can live in a wide range of water chemistries, with recorded values of pH from 6.6 to 8.9, dissolved oxygen readings from 2.2 to 11 milligrams/liter, and salinities from very dilute to sea water. The widespread historic distribution of Gila topminnows throughout rivers, streams, marshes, and springs of the Gila River Basin is evidence for their tolerance of these environmental extremes. One reestablished population, Mud Springs, survived for 16 years in a simple cement watering trough before being moved (USFWS 1998f).

Destruction of historically occupied habitats such as the marshes, sloughs, backwaters, and edgewaters of larger rivers and presence of nonnative fishes in such habitats that remain has undoubtedly forced Gila topminnow out of their preferred historic habitats and into the springheads and smaller erosive creeks we see them in today. Their tolerance of conditions in these habitats has allowed them to maintain populations with less impact from nonnative fishes (USFWS 1998f).

Gila topminnows are viviparous fish, meaning embryos grow and mature within the female and are born living. Eggs are fertilized internally through deposition of spermatophores (packets of sperm) into the female's genital pore by the male's gonopodium. Female Gila topminnow can store spermatozoa for several months and may produce up to 10 broods after being isolated from males.  Sexual maturity can be attained as early as two months or as late as 11 months following birth, dependent upon the season of birth. Breeding occurs primarily during January through August, but in thermally constant springs young may be produced throughout the year.  Brood size and the onset of breeding in topminnows can be influenced by several factors including food abundance, photoperiod, temperature, predation upon the population, and female size. Increased food supply and larger female size are believed to contribute to the greater fecundity seen in some topminnow populations (USFWS 1998f).

Gila topminnows are opportunistic omnivorous feeders, having a gut length 1.5 to 2 times SL of the individual. They have weakly spatulate dentition characteristic of an omnivorous diet. Primary food items include detritus, vegetation, amphipods, ostracods, and insect larvae; and rarely, other fishes (USFWS 1998f).

Historic events permanently altered much of the aquatic habitat in the arid southwest, but current and future activities also present a great risk. Land use practices such as livestock grazing, mining, timber cutting, road maintenance, and recreation pose threats through increased erosion, intensified flood events, and decreased groundwater storage to both existing populations and habitats proposed for reestablishment. In addition, continued urban and suburban development and population growth affects potential recovery of the species through increased groundwater pumping and diversions to supply the growing populations, stream and river channelization, and increased water pollution (USFWS 1998f).

Introduction of nonnative pathogens, parasites, plants, invertebrates, amphibians and fish may negatively affect the native fishes of the Southwest. Introduction of the western mosquitofish has caused the most problems for Gila topminnow. Mosquitofish tolerate similar environmental extremes and occupy similar habitats as Gila topminnow. Mosquitofish prey directly on young topminnows and cause the death of adults due to infection following the shredding or removal of fins. Mosquitofish possess open cephalic canals that improve their ability to detect and find invertebrate and vertebrate prey, a trait lacking in topminnows. Competition for space, resulting in harassment of male and female topminnows by larger, dominant, more aggressive female mosquitofish also seemed instrumental in replacement of Gila topminnow by mosquitofish (USFWS 1998f).

Gila topminnow critical habitat has not been designated.

**Effects:** Timber harvest and road maintenance are threats to the species. One pathway for effects to Gila topminnow is through water pollution. This is relatively vague when trying to compare effects to project activities. The assumption made in this document is related activities would be most similar to chemical contamination. The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. The pathways in Table 16 for these activities could cause effects on species along the different pathways listed. Chemical contamination from project activity implementation is included in many activities due to the utilization of petroleum products by the equipment needed for implementing projects. As the analysis under the chemical contamination section states, motorized hand tools have small fuel capacities and if spills occur these are not expected to reach the streams. Best management practices will limit fueling near riparian areas, and experience over the years of implementing projects has shown large spills of petroleum products have not occurred. USFWS documents did not detail the specific pathway for effects of timber harvest on Gila topminnow so the assumption is any timber harvest would have negative effects to the species. After considering the species pathway of effects, best management practices that would be implemented, project activities could have measurable effects on species; therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely** affect Gila topminnow.

### Gasterosteidae Family

#### _Unarmored threespine stickleback_

The unarmored threespine stickleback could be in the action area and is the only species in the Gasterosteidae family considered in this consultation (Table 15). Unarmored threespine stickleback is a small, scaleless, freshwater fish (approximately 5 centimeters in length), inhabiting slow-moving reaches or quiet-water microhabitats in streams and rivers. Fish typically live one year, with most breeding activity occurring between February and September. Historically, unarmored threespine sticklebacks were found throughout a much larger area including the Los Angeles, San Gabriel, and Santa Ana Rivers, but were extirpated from these areas as a result of habitat loss and degradation due to urbanization. Unarmored threespine sticklebacks were also present in the Santa Maria River drainage in San Luis Obispo County, where they were lost to introgression. Unarmored threespine sticklebacks are currently restricted to a few small, local sites in the Santa Clara River watershed in Los Angeles County, the San Antonio Creek drainage in Santa Barbara County, and isolated occurrences in inland San Bernardino and San Diego counties (USFWS 2021f).

Unarmored threespine sticklebacks prefer rivers or streams with a slow, continuous flow of water with moderate algal cover, which is typical of the conditions in headwaters and tributaries that they tend to occupy. They have been observed in rivers with rapid flows (to 1 meter per second) to static pools with virtually no surface flow. In habitats where water velocity is higher, they reside along the channel edge in areas occupied by aquatic vegetation (watercress, Nasturtium spp.), under the edge of algal ( _Cladophora_ spp.) mats, or behind obstructions. Unarmored threespine sticklebacks are not distributed uniformly throughout the rivers and streams in which they occur. Sand or gravel substrates, with the presence of detritus and aquatic vegetation, are required for reproduction (USFWS 2021f).

Currently, unarmored threespine sticklebacks occur in the upper Santa Clara River and its tributaries in Los Angeles County, San Antonio Creek in Santa Barbara County, and a cluster of sites in San Bernardino County. Unarmored threespine stickleback was transplanted outside its native range in upper San Felipe Creek in San Diego County, and are presumed extant based on recent surveys. An additional location has been established in Fish Canyon Creek, another tributary of the Santa Clara River. Also, a potential previously unrecognized unarmored threespine stickleback site may occur in Pine Valley Creek, San Diego County (USFWS 2021f).

The unarmored threespine stickleback recovery plan (USFWS 1985) identified the following threats: stream channelization, urbanization, introduction of predators and competitors, introgression, agricultural impacts, oxygen reduction, groundwater removal, transpiration, offroad vehicles, water releases from Drinkwater Reservoir, toxic spills and discharges, addition of water, and impoundment of water. Additionally, the 5-year reviews identified ongoing effects of urbanization, eutrophication, stream channelization, addition of water (water releases), groundwater removal, and water quality were identified as the most critical threats to the species and included other not as critical threats such as non-native predators, disease, introgression, competition, and stochastic extinction (USFWS 2021f).

Unarmored threespine stickleback critical habitat was found to be not prudent in 2022, therefore, has not been designated.

**Effects:** Unarmored threespine stickleback threats relevant to this consultation are water quality and toxic spills. Toxic spills term is vague, and an assumption was made in this document that it is most similar to chemical contamination. Chemical contamination from project activity implementation is included in many activities due to the utilization of petroleum products by the equipment needed for implementing projects. As the analysis under the chemical contamination section states, motorized hand tools have small fuel capacities and if spills occur these are not expected to reach the streams. Best management practices will limit fueling near riparian areas, and experience over the years of implementing projects has shown large spills of petroleum products have not occurred. The pathway for effect to the species is through the water quality pathway. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing change in riparian vegetation (temperature), sediment/turbidity may have effects on the species but it is unknown if the magnitude of the effect would be measurable. Any future projects that would affect species

would still need to complete project level consultation. Due to the unknowns, the assumption in this document is that some effects on species to reach **may affect, likely to adversely affect** unarmored threespine stickleback.

### Percidae Family

Darters and logperch are in the Percidae family. There are 17 species of Percidae that that were considered in this consultation (Table 15). Many were not found in the affected environment and not analyzed. These species fall into two geneses: _Etheostoma_ and _Percina_ . Generally, these species are small, less than 3 inches, live about 3 years, inhabit specific locations within one or two watersheds, spawn in the spring, and need free flowing, clear, cool water free of contaminants and sedimentation. The main threats to most of these species have been impoundment of their habitat that inhibits their habitat needs and/or fragments their habitat. Other threats tend to be road construction that creates a barrier to fish movement and sediment/turbidity impacts.

#### _Etowah darter_

The Etowah darter is a small-sized percid fish, adults being about 45 to 75 mm total length. The body is elongate, moderately compressed, and has a moderately pointed snout. The background body color is medium brown or gray-olive. The lower opercle (gill covers) has a have a pale bluish-green wash which is intensified in breeding males. The side is usually pigmented with 13 or 14 small dark blotches just below the lateral line. The breast in breeding males is dark greenish-blue. The spinous dorsal fin is suffused dusky black olive with a red margin. The soft dorsal fin has four bands: dusky black olive on the basal two-thirds, followed by red, white (sometimes with hint of yellow), and black bands of nearly equal width. The caudal (tail) fin is similarly pigmented except the ventral (on the abdominal side of the body) leading rays have a pale blue wash. The anal fin is suffused with greenish-blue and never has red marks, like greenbreast darters do. The pelvic fins are clear to dusky black with a pale green blue wash; pectoral fins are dusky black. All these color patterns are more vivid in breeding males. Life history is unknown. However, like most darters, the species spawns in spring, and probably lives two to three years.

The Etowah darter is endemic to the Etowah River system in north Georgia. Historically, it may have occurred further downstream in the Etowah River mainstem. However, pre-impoundment (Allatoona Lake) records are not known. The Etowah darter persists in the uppermost Etowah River mainstem and two headwater tributaries, Amicalola and Long Swamp Creeks. The species is known from a total of 19 sites in these streams. Population size at known sites is generally small. However, total population level is not known. Etowah darters inhabit medium to larger creeks and small rivers of moderate to high gradient in swift current areas in riffles with large gravel, cobble, and small boulder substrates. Threats to the species include deteriorating water and benthic habitat quality resulting from siltation and other pollutants (USFWS 2000b).

Etowah darter critical habitat has not been designated.

**Effects:** The pathway for effects to Etowah darter are through pollution and sediment/turbidity. The assumption made in this document is pollution is most similar to chemical contamination as

an impact. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing chemical contamination may have effects on Etowah darter. Chemical contamination from project activity implementation is included in many activities due to the utilization of petroleum products by the equipment needed for implementing projects. As the analysis under the chemical contamination section states, motorized hand tools have small fuel capacities and if spills occur these are not expected to reach the streams. Best management practices will limit fueling near riparian areas, and experience over the years of implementing projects has shown large spills of petroleum products have not occurred. Sediment/turbidity is associated with most activities proposed in the project. The amount of sediment/turbidity that would accompany proposed project activities would be short-term negative effects for timber activities and long-term negative effects for temporary and permanent road building as effects occur as long as the roads are in place. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects but would still be measurable. After considering the species pathway of effects and best management practices that would be implemented, project activities there could be measurable effects on species; therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Etowah darter.

#### _Candy darter_

The candy darter is a small, freshwater fish endemic to 2nd order and larger streams and rivers within portions of the upper Kanawha River basin, which is synonymous with the Gauley and greater New River watersheds in Virginia (VA) and West Virginia (WV). The species is described as a habitat specialist, being most often associated with faster flowing stream segments with coarse bottom substrate (for example, gravel, cobble, rocks, and boulders), that provides shelter for individual darters. Candy darters are intolerant of excessive sedimentation and stream bottom embeddedness (the degree to which gravel, cobble, rocks, and boulders are surrounded by, or covered with, fine sediment particles). The available candy darter occurrence data, all of which were collected after the aquatic habitat in the region was degraded by widespread forest clearing in the late 1800s, indicate the species prefers cool or cold water temperatures, but that warm water conditions may also be tolerated. The fish are opportunistic feeders, eating mostly benthic macroinvertebrates such as mayflies and caddisflies. In streams maintaining favorable habitat conditions, through natural or managed condition, candy darters can be abundant throughout the stream continuum (USFWS 2018i).

Candy darters are sexually mature at 2 years of age and live to a maximum age of 3 years. They are classified as brood-hiding, benthic spawners. It is uncertain whether individual candy darters complete their life cycle within single riffles or riffle complexes spanning just a few hundred meters or are capable of longer, seasonally mediated movements within suitable habitat. Although data are sparse regarding the minimum habitat size and degree of genetic connectivity required for candy darter population viability, the historical distribution of the species and the fundamentals of conservation biology suggest these factors are important to the species. Primary factors needed to support the candy darter include: 1) an absence of nonnative species; 2) unembedded gravel and cobble substrates with minimal sedimentation, 3) adequate water quality (temperatures, physical and chemical parameters), 4) an abundant, diverse benthic macroinvertebrate community; and 5) sufficient water quantity and velocities. Absence or degradation of these features could limit populations of the candy darter (USFWS 2018i).

One of the primary threats that resulted in the listing of the candy darter under the Endangered Species Act is the spread of the introduced variegate darter ( _Etheostoma variatum_ ). This species hybridizes with the candy darter (USFWS 2018). Other ongoing contributing threats include excessive sedimentation, warming water temperatures, habitat fragmentation, changes in water quality and flow, catastrophic events, and competition or predation associated with other introduced species (USFWS 2018i).

Historically, the candy darter occurred in 35 populations distributed across 7 metapopulations located in the Bluestone, Lower New River, Upper Gauley, Lower Gauley, Greenbrier, Upper New, and Middle New watersheds. However, the candy darter has been extirpated from almost half of its historical range; 17 of 35 known populations and 2 of 7 known metapopulations have been extirpated. The species is no longer known to occur in the Bluestone and Lower New River watersheds (USFWS 2018i).

Candy darter critical habitat is located within the action area. The candy darter is the only species in the Percidae family with critical habitat in the action area. There is less than one percent of critical habitat that could be affected by any future action within the affected environment (Table 15). Candy darter physical and biological features are (86 FR 17956):

1. Ratios or densities of nonnative species that allow for maintaining populations of candy darters.

2. A blend of unembedded gravel and cobble that allows for normal breeding, feeding, and sheltering behavior.

3. Adequate water quality characterized by seasonally moderated temperatures and physical and chemical parameters (e.g., pH, dissolved oxygen levels, turbidity) that support normal behavior, growth, and viability of all life stages of the candy darter.

4. An abundant, diverse benthic macroinvertebrate community (e.g., mayfly nymphs, midge larvae, caddisfly larvae) that allows for normal feeding behavior.

5. Sufficient water quantity and velocities that support normal behavior, growth, and viability of all life stages of the candy darter.

**Effects:** The pathways for effects to candy darter are through degraded water quality, specifically higher sediment/turbidity and higher water temperatures. The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) and sediment/turbidity may have effects on candy darter. Changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) is associated with timber harvest activities. Any individual tree removal within the riparian area would create localized increase in water temperature. Sediment/turbidity is associated with most activities proposed in the project. The amount of sediment/turbidity that would accompany proposed project activities would be short-term negative effects if activities are outside the riparian area. Temporary or permanent road building would create adverse conditions as long as the road is in place. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects from activities, but project effects could be measurable. Critical habitat effects pathways

would probably be through sediment and potential impacts to benthic macroinvertebrates through the sediment/turbidity pathway as it would decrease the candy darters ability to find food and through nutrient pathway where there could be less nutrients reaching the stream for growth of candy darter prey. After considering the species pathway of effects and best management practices that would be implemented, project activities could have measurable effects on species; therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** candy darter and candy darter critical habitat.

#### _Duskytail darter_

Duskytail darter is a small 2 1/2-inch fish that has a straw to olivaceous colored body, the top of the head is medium to dark gray. It has 10 to 15 long dark vertical bars on the sides of its body, 38 to 48 lateral scales. and 17 to 20 dorsal spines and rays. It is difficult to determine the sex of nonbreeding individuals in the field. during the breeding season. the males become very distinctive. In breeding males, their heads became dark and swollen, and the humeral spot and lateral vertical bars intensified, the first dorsal saddle and vertical bar formed a particularly intense dark yoke, and a dark border of melanophore develops along the pectoral and anal fin margins, and the anal fin whitens proximally, and brilliant gold fleshy knobs develop on the tips of the dorsal fin spines and were conspicuous in contrast to the clear medial and dark basal portions of the fin membrane.

The duskytail is primarily an insectivore. The youngest individuals consume microcrustaceans, chironomid larvae, and sometimes large quantities of heptageniid nymphs. Larger individuals are also mainly benthic insectivores, but they generally feed on larger prey items (chironomid larvae, ephemeropteran nymphs, microcrustaceans. and trichopteran larvae) than the young. Heptageniids were the dominant food item in the three largest duskytail size classes, and large duskytail darter sometimes feed on fish eggs (USFWS 1994, 2021g).

The duskytail darter inhabits the Tennessee and Cumberland River systems. Duskytail darter utilize the edges of gently flowing shallow pools, eddy areas, and slow runs in usually clear water of large creeks and moderately large rivers (10 to 80 meters [33 to 264 feet]) (USFWS 2021g).

Duskytail darters have been and continue to be impacted by water quality deterioration. This deterioration results from siltation (contributed by coal mining and poor land use practices), other water pollution, and impoundments (USFWS 1994).

Duskytail darter critical habitat has not been designated.

#### _Rush darter_

The rush darter is endemic to spring fed creeks and spring runs in North Central Alabama. The lifespan is estimated to be 2 to 3 years. The species inhabits tributaries and spring systems of the Clear Creek Drainage, Winston County, Alabama (Wildcat Branch, Doe Branch, Mill Creek); Turkey Creek drainage, Jefferson County, Alabama (Beaver Creek, Tapawingo/Penny Springs, Cunningham Creek, and several unnamed tributaries); and upper Locust Fork drainage, Etowah County, Alabama (Little Cove, Bristow, and Dry Creeks).

When listed, the rush darter was known from localized collection sites within approximately 14.5 km of stream channel. Since listing, rush darters have been collected from 12 sites within approximately 17.9 km of stream or spring runs. All collection sites are separated geographically. Rush darter are found in low densities, and individual rush darters may only be sporadically collected at specific sites within their range. No quantitative population estimates are available for the species; however, where it occurs it is usually uncommon and in low numbers (USFWS 2011c; USFWS 2019n).

All rush darter populations are located above the Fall Line (the inland boundary of the Coastal Plain physiographic region) in the Black Warrior River drainage and in portions of the southern Appalachian Plateau and Valley and Ridge physiographic provinces, Alabama. The species continues to persist in all stream systems it is known to have historically occupied (USFWS 2019). Rush darters prefer springs, spring-fed reaches of relatively low-gradient small streams, and wetland pools which are generally influenced by springs. They have been collected from root masses of vegetation in very shallow, clear, cool, and flowing water, including both small clumps and dense stands of bur reed ( _Sparganium_ sp.), coontail ( _Ceratophyllum_ sp.), watercress ( _Nasturtium officinale_ ), and rush ( _Juncus_ sp.). Substrates have included silt, sand, sand and silt, woody material, muck, and gravel with sand. Water depth at all collection sites ranged from 3.0 cm to 0.5 m, with moderate water velocity in riffles and little to no flow in pools. Rush darters have not been found in higher gradient streams with bedrock substrates and sparse vegetation (USFWS 2019n).

Rush darter populations and habitats remain vulnerable to common land use and water practices despite the protections of regulatory mechanisms afforded by State and Federal laws and regulations. Sedimentation, flow alterations, and non-point source pollution continue to adversely affect the species and its habitats. Information available to us since listing does not indicate that the magnitude or imminence of this threat has changed (USFWS 2019n).

Rush darter populations remain vulnerable to localized extinctions from intentional or accidental toxic chemical spills, rapid urbanization and habitat modification, progressive degradation from runoff (non-point source pollutants), natural catastrophic changes to their habitat (for example, flood scour, drought), other stochastic disturbances, and to decreased fitness from reduced genetic diversity (USFWS 2019n).

Rush darter critical habitat is not located within the action area.
