Therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** rush darter.

#### _Cherokee darter_

The Cherokee darter is a small-sized percid fish, adults being about 40 to 65 millimeters total length. The body is elongate, subcylindrical (slightly compressed), with a relatively blunt snout. The side of adults is usually pigmented with eight small dark olive black blotches which develop into vertically elongate, slightly oblique bars in breeding adults, especially in males. The back usually has eight small dark saddles and intervening pale areas. The spinous dorsal (situated on the back) fin of breeding males has a dark olive black band at the base of the fin and nearly uniform russet orange red on the remaining fin, except for a blue margin (USFWS 2000b).

The Cherokee darter is endemic to the Etowah River system in north Georgia. Historically, it was thought to have occurred in most tributaries of the watershed. The Cherokee darter persists in about two dozen tributary streams of the middle and upper Etowah River. Present populations are isolated by Allatoona Reservoir and stretches of degraded habitat in tributary streams (USFWS 2000b).

Cherokee darter inhabit small to medium size creeks of moderate gradient in low current areas with large gravel, cobble, and small boulder substrates. Life history is unknown. However, like most darters, the species spawns in spring, and probably lives two to three years. Threats include impoundments and deteriorating water and benthic habitat quality resulting from siltation and other pollutants (USFWS 2000b).

Cherokee darter critical habitat has not been designated.

**Effects:** The pathways for effects to Cherokee darter are through pollution, water quality impacts, and siltation. The assumption made in this document for non-point source pollution and accidental toxic chemical spills is most related to the pathway for chemical contamination. The pathways for fish effects are listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing chemical contamination may have effects on Cherokee darter. Chemical contamination from project activity implementation is included in many activities due to the utilization of petroleum products by the equipment needed for implementing projects. As the analysis under the chemical contamination section states, motorized hand tools have small fuel capacities and if spills occur these are not expected to reach the streams. Best management practices will limit fueling near riparian areas, and experience over the years of implementing projects has shown large spills of petroleum products have not occurred. Water quality is associated with Changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) and sediment/turbidity (Table 17). Changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) is associated with almost all activities. Any removal of riparian trees would create localized increases in water temperature. Sediment/turbidity is associated with most activities proposed in the project. Sediment/turbidity created by project activities would have short-term negative effects. Combined, there may be effects on the species and under certain conditions could be measurable. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects from activities but may not be eliminated. Temporary or permanent road building would create adverse effects lasting as long as the road is in place. After considering the species pathway of effects, best management practices that would be implemented, project activities could have

measurable effects on species. Therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Cherokee darter.

#### _Kentucky arrow darter_

The Kentucky arrow darter is a small, compressed fish, with a background color of straw yellow to pale green and a body covered by a variety of stripes and blotches. Breeding males exhibit the most vibrant coloration, including scattered scarlet spots and scarlet to orange vertical bars. Kentucky arrow darters can reach 2 inches in length by the end of the first year and reach a maximum length of 4.7 inches. The species' lifespan is approximately four years. The primary threat to this darter species is habitat modification or destruction from surface coal mining, logging, oil/gas development, land development, agriculture, and inadequate sewage treatment, coupled with ongoing threats associated with inadequate regulatory mechanisms. The species' small, isolated populations also make it vulnerable to natural and catastrophic events related to human activity (for example, drought, resource extraction, pollution spills, etc.) (USFWS 2017e).

Kentucky arrow darters typically inhabit pools or transitional areas between riffles and pools (glides and runs) in moderate- to high-gradient, first- to third-order streams with rocky substrates. The species is most often observed near some type of cover (for example, boulders, bedrock ledges, large cobble, or woody debris) in depths ranging from 10 to 45 centimeters and in streams ranging from 1.5 to 20 meters wide. Kentucky arrow darters typically occupy streams with watersheds of 25.9 square kilometers or less, and many of these habitats, especially in firstorder reaches, can be intermittent in nature. During the driest periods, the species appears to survive by retreating into shaded, isolated pools or by dispersing into larger tributaries (USFWS 2017e; USFWS 2022m).

Spawning occurs in riffle habitats from late March to May, with peak activity occurring when water temperatures reach 13°C. Young Kentucky arrow darters can reach 2 inches in length by the end of the first year, when these individuals are generally sexually mature and participate in spawning with older age classes. Juvenile Kentucky arrow darters can be found throughout the channel but are often observed in shallow water along stream margins near root mats, rock ledges, or some other cover. Kentucky arrow darters feed primarily on mayflies (Order Ephemeroptera) and other aquatic insects, but large individuals 2.8 inches often feed on small crayfishes (USFWS 2017e).

The Kentucky arrow darter occurred historically in at least 74 streams in the upper Kentucky River basin of eastern Kentucky. Its distribution spanned portions of 6 smaller sub-basins or watersheds (North Fork Kentucky River, Middle Fork Kentucky River, South Fork Kentucky River, Silver Creek, Sturgeon Creek, and Red River) in 10 Kentucky counties (Breathitt, Clay, Harlan, Jackson, Knott, Lee, Leslie, Owsley, Perry, and Wolfe) (USFWS 2017e).

The primary threat to the Kentucky arrow darter is habitat modification or destruction from resource extraction (surface coal mining, logging, oil/gas development), land development, agriculture, and inadequate sewage treatment, coupled with ongoing threats associated with inadequate regulatory mechanisms. The species' small, isolated populations also make it vulnerable to natural and human-induced catastrophic events (for example, droughts, resource extraction, pollution spills, etc.). The Kentucky arrow darter's habitat and range have been destroyed, modified, and curtailed due to a variety of anthropogenic activities in the upper Kentucky River drainage. Resource extraction (for example, coal mining, logging, oil/gas well development), land development, agricultural activities, and inadequate sewage treatment have all contributed to the degradation of streams within the range of the species. Another threat to the Kentucky arrow darter is water quality degradation caused by a variety of nonpoint-source pollutants (contaminants from many diffuse and unquantifiable sources), with coal mining being the main contributor to water quality concerns (USFWS 2017e).

The isolated nature of Kentucky arrow darter populations restricts the natural exchange of genetic material between populations and makes natural repopulation following localized extirpations of the species unlikely without human intervention. Populations can be further isolated by anthropogenic barriers, such as dams, perched culverts, and fords, which can limit natural dispersal and restrict or eliminate connectivity among populations. Such dispersal barriers can prevent reestablishment of Kentucky arrow populations in reaches where they suffer localized extinctions due to natural or human-caused events. The isolated nature and small size of many populations also likely make them vulnerable to extirpation from intentional or accidental toxic chemical spills, habitat modification, progressive degradation from runoff (nonpoint-source pollutants), natural catastrophic changes to their habitat (for example, flood scour, drought), and other stochastic disturbances (USFWS 2017e).

Kentucky arrow darter critical habitat is not located within the action area.

**Effects:** The pathways for effects to Kentucky arrow darter are through toxic chemical spills, water quality, and sediment/turbidity. The assumption made in this document for toxic chemical spills is to relate chemical contamination and will be analyzed in this report as chemical contamination. The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing chemical contamination may have effects on Kentucky arrow darter. Chemical contamination from project activity implementation is included in many activities due to the utilization of petroleum products by the equipment needed for implementing projects. As the analysis under the chemical contamination section states, motorized hand tools have small fuel capacities and if spills occur these are not expected to reach the streams. Best management practices will limit fueling near riparian areas, and experience over the years of implementing projects has shown large spills of petroleum products have not occurred. Water quality is associated with changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) and sediment/turbidity (Table 17). Changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) are associated with almost all activities. Any removal of riparian trees would create localized increases in water temperature. Sediment/turbidity is associated with most activities proposed in the project. The amount of sediment/turbidity that would accompany proposed project activities would result in short-term negative effects. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects from activities and project effects. After considering the species pathway of effects, best management practices that would be implemented, project activities could have measurable effects on species; therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Kentucky arrow darter.

#### _Trispot darter_

The trispot darter is a small, freshwater fish that occurs in the Coosa River system in the Ridge and Valley ecoregion of Alabama, Georgia, and Tennessee. It is a migratory species that uses distinct breeding and nonbreeding habitats. From approximately April to October, the species occupies its nonbreeding habitat, which consists of small to medium margins of rivers and lower reaches of tributaries with slower velocities. It is associated with detritus, logs, and stands of water willow, and with a substrate that consists of small cobbles, pebbles, gravel, and often a fine layer of silt. During low flow periods, the darters move away from the peripheral zones and toward the main channel; edges of water willow beds, riffles, and pools; and mouths of tributaries. Migration into spawning areas begins in approximately late November or early December, with fish moving from the main channels into tributaries and eventually reaching adjacent seepage areas where they will congregate and remain for the duration of spawning, until approximately late April. Breeding sites are intermittent seepage areas and ditches with little to no flow; shallow depths (12 inches (30 centimeters) or less); moderate leaf litter covering mixed cobble, gravel, sand, and clay; a deep layer of soft silt over clay; and emergent vegetation. Additionally, breeding sites possess channels that maintain base flow throughout the winter and early spring. Trispot darters predominantly feed on mayfly nymphs and midge larvae and pupae (85 FR 61619).

All known records of the trispot darter occur above the fall line in the Ridge and Valley ecoregion of Alabama, Georgia, and Tennessee. Historically, this species occurred throughout the middle to upper Coosa River Basin with records from the mainstem Coosa, Conasauga, and Coosawattee rivers, their tributaries, and tributaries to the Oostanaula River (USFWS 2023p). The long-term viability of the trispot darter is affected by habitat degradation and hydrologic alteration. Specifically, incompatible land-use practices and the associated impacts to habitat connectivity, water quantity, water quality, and linear distribution of occupied habitat influence the darter's viability. To maintain stable and increasing populations of tripsot darter, connectivity of breeding and non-breeding habitat, channel integrity, adequate water quantity and water quality are required (USFWS 2023p).

Trispot darter critical habitat is not located within the action area.

**Effects:** The pathway for effects on tripsot darter is through water quality. The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Water quality is associated with changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) and sediment/turbidity (Table 17). Changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) is associated with almost all activities. Any removal of riparian trees would create localized increases in water temperature. Sediment/turbidity is associated with most activities proposed in the project. The amount of sediment/turbidity that would accompany proposed project activities would result in short-term adverse effects. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects from activities and project effects could be measurable. After considering the species pathway of effects, best management practices that would be implemented, project activities would have measurable effects on species; therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** tripsot darter.

#### _Amber darter_

Amber darter occurs in a 33.5- mile (53.9 km) reach of the Conasauga River, Georgia and Tennessee, and a 28-mile (45.1 km) reach of the Etowah River, Georgia; these two populations are isolated from each other by Lake Allatoona on the Etowah River (USFWS 2019o). In both systems amber darter have been extirpated or greatly reduced in abundance in downstream reaches within the historic range.  Amber darters generally are found in the rivers' mainstems, preferring shoals with a moveable gravel/small cobble substrate and moderate to swift currents. The presence of clean moveable gravel and high water quality in shoal habitat appears to be highly important in determining distribution. Amber darters forage primarily on snails, limpets, and aquatic insects (USFWS 2019o).

Amber darter current stressors are (1) habitat/water quality degradation associated with agriculture and urbanization that increases levels of sediment, nutrients, estrogens, and herbicides in the river, (2) loss of riparian buffers, (3) decline in Podostemum, an aquatic plant , (4) natural demographic, environmental, and genetic stochastic events that affect small populations with limited geographic range, and (5) climate change (USFWS 2019o).

Long-term alteration of weather patterns is expected to bring more extreme weather events, such as flooding and drought. Hydrologic flows impact the availability and connectivity of shoal habitat, as well as spawning and recruitment behaviors of amber darters. For example, spring floods may be a factor limiting recruitment of amber darters, who benefit from windows of low spring flow for spawning and recruitment success. High flows may damage eggs, wash larvae from nursery areas, prevent juveniles from migrating upstream to suitable shoal habitat, and increase turbidity and sedimentation that degrades habitat. Successive years of high spring flows may limit or eliminate juvenile recruitment at a given site with implications for the population (USFWS 2019o).

#### Amber darter critical habitat is not located within the action area.

**Effects:** The pathways for effects to amber darter are through water quality and nutrients; however, the nutrient pathway is through fertilizer and human/animal waste. The proposed actions do not include activities that will increase the nutrient pathway for amber darter and will not be discussed in this analysis. The pathway for fish and habitat effects listed in Table 17 are crosswalked to the impact/benefit column in Table 16. Activities found in Table 16 under the impact/benefit column containing chemical contamination may have effects on amber darter. Water quality is associated with changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) and

sediment/turbidity (Table 17). Changes in riparian vegetation (temperature) are associated with almost all activities. Any removal of riparian trees would create localized increases in water temperature. Sediment/turbidity is associated with most activities proposed in the project. The amount of sediment/turbidity that would accompany proposed project activities would have short-term negative effects. Best management practices will help minimize adverse effects from activities and project effects could be adverse. After considering the species pathway of effects, best management practices that would be implemented, project activities could have measurable effects on species; therefore, the project **may affect, likely to adversely affect** amber darter.

#### _Goldline darter_

The goldline darter is a slender, medium-sized fish, about 75 mm (3 in) long with brownish-red and amber dorsolateral (on the upper side) stripes. It differs from other members of the subgenus Hadropterus in the color pattern of its back, which is pale to dusky (USFWS 2000b).

Goldline darter is known from 43 km of the Cahaba River, historically 79 km, 11 km of the Little Cahaba River, and from Schultz Creek, Cahaba River drainage, Alabama. The species also continues to be found in the Coosawattee River and its tributary Talking Rock Creek; Ellijay River, Mountaintown and Boardtown Creeks; and the Cartecay River, Georgia. Populations appear to be small and localized (USFWS 2000b).

The goldline darter prefers a moderate to swift current and water depths greater than 0.5 meter. It is found over sand or gravel substrate interspersed among cobble and small boulders. Little is known about goldline darter life history (USFWS 2000b). The primary threat to goldline darter is water quality degradation, particularly sedimentation, which has reduced the goldline darters range within the Cahaba River System (USFWS 2000b).

Goldline darter critical habitat has not been designated.

#### _Pearl darter_

The pearl darter is a small bottom dwelling freshwater fish that reaches a maximum standard length of 2.5 inches. The species is short-lived, with a life span of one to three years. The pearl darter historically inhabited the bottom of stream and river channels of the Pearl River drainage and Pascagoula River drainage. Microhabitat features needed to complete the life cycle of the species consist of substrate mixtures of sand, silt, loose clay, gravel, fine particulate organic matter, and coarse particulate organic matter at the steep ends of sandbars and inside river bends where vegetative detritus (for example, decomposing wood and leaves) is deposited. Likely spawning habitats have been described as shallow, swift moving riffles with firm, gravel substrates. Spawning occurs in March to June on gravel riffles in shallow, swift flowing water (USFWS 2023q).

Reduction of the pearl darter to a single surviving population, as well as its rarity, leaves it vulnerable to persistent threats within the Pascagoula River drainage, including geomorphic instability, excessive sedimentation, and water quality degradation from point and non-point sources. It is also vulnerable to random events such as spills and weather events (for example, drought, floods). Pearl darter are not found in impounded waters and are intolerant of lentic habitats that may be formed by gravel mining or other landscape-altering practices. Increased temperatures and decreased precipitation is expected to adversely affect the species due to alteration of hydrologic cycles of headwater reaches, but the extent or magnitude of this threat has not been quantified (USFWS 2023q). Sedimentation and degraded water quality are thought to be major factors in the decline, and ultimately, the extirpation of the pearl darter from the Pearl River drainage (USFWS 2023q).

Peral darter critical habitat is not located within the action area.

#### _Conasauga logperch_

The Conasauga logperch is a larger darter, sometimes exceeding 6 inches in length, and is characterized by having many “tiger-like” vertical dark stripes over a yellow background (50 FR 31597). It most often is encountered in deep gravel runs or pools with small stones and sandy bottoms. Even within suitable habitat, this species is rare, typically observed at low densities of scattered individuals or pairs. Captive mortality in Conasauga logperch suggests maximum lifespan is at least five years. Logperch feed on aquatic insect larvae using its fleshy pig-like snout to flip stones to expose prey. Spawning behavior and details of spawning season conditions are unknown (USFWS 2019). The species occurs only in a 34-mile reach of the Conasauga River mainstem, from near the confluence of the Conasauga and Jacks Rivers, Polk County, Tennessee, downstream to Mitchell Bridge, Murray County, Georgia. No other population, current or historic, is known (USFWS 2019p).

The recovery team determined it was unlikely the Conasauga logperch would ever be removed from the list of endangered and threatened species due to the single population's vulnerability to extinction. Primary threats, at the time of listing, included siltation, proposed reservoir construction on the river's mainstem, catastrophic events, increased silviculture, road and bridge construction, stream channel modification, and land use changes. Research over the past 30+ years has identified current stressors likely are (1) habitat/water quality degradation associated with agriculture and urbanization that increases levels of sediment, nutrients, estrogens, and herbicides in the river, (2) loss of riparian buffers, (3) decline in _Podostemum_ , (4) natural demographic, environmental, and genetic stochastic events that affect small populations with limited geographic range, and (5) climate change (USFWS 2019p).

Conasauga logperch critical habitat is not located within the action area.

### Salmonidae Family

Five trout and two charr in the Salmonidae family may be within the action area (Table 15). Members of the Salmonidae family typically inhabit cool, clean, well-oxygenated freshwater streams and lakes for spawning and juvenile rearing, with many species migrating to the ocean (anadromous) as adults. They require complex, diverse habitats, including gravel beds for spawning, and quiet, deeper, or shaded areas for refuge. Since all members of the Salmonidae family have similar effects pathways, effects determinations will be combined below in the Salmonidae Effects section.

#### _Gila trout_

Gila trout is in the Pacific trout clade (a common ancestor and all lineal descendants) along with rainbow trout ( _O. mykiss_ ) and cutthroat trout ( _O. clarkii_ ). Gila trout and rainbow trout are the most closely related of the three species (USFWS 2022n). Gila trout are relatively small salmonids that reach sexual maturity at approximately 6 inches long which would be anywhere from age 2 to age 4 for both females and males (USFWS 2022n). Spawning typically occurs in April when water temperatures reach 8˚C. Redds are constructed in three to four centimeters water depth in fine gravel and coarse sand substrate (USFWS 2022n). Most adult Gila trout live to about age 5 (USFWS 2022n). Gila trout are generally insectivorous feeding on adult Diptera (true flies), Trichoptera (caddisfly) larvae, Ephemeroptera (mayfly) nymphs, and aquatic Coleoptera (beetles) but occasionally eat other fishes (USFWS 2022n).

Current distributions of Gila trout occur in the Gila River drainage basin, while, historical distribution likely included montane, cold-water stream habitats in Sierra, Grant, and Catron counties in New Mexico and Greenlee, Apache, Graham, Gila, Maricopa, and Yavapai counties in Arizona (USFWS 2022n). Habitat of Gila trout currently consists of montane streams ranging from approximately 1,660 m to over 2,800 m elevation (USFWS 2022n). Water-quality impairment in cold-water streams within the historical range of Gila trout falls into two main categories: chemical or physical impairment and water temperature impairment.

Gila trout threats were determined to be habitat degradation from livestock grazing, timber harvest, and wildfire; sport fishing; predation from brown trout ( _Salmo trutta_ ) and disease; inadequate regulatory mechanisms to protect and enhance Gila trout populations and their habitat; and hybridization and competition with nonnative trout, drought, wildfire, and floods.

Gila trout critical habitat has not been designated.

#### _Paiute cutthroat trout_

Paiute cutthroat trout is a distinctive member of the cutthroat trout complex, distinguishable from other cutthroat trout by body coloration and the absence, or near absence, of body spots. It is native to Silver King Creek in the East Fork Carson River drainage on the Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest, Alpine County, California that is approximately 14.7 kilometers (9.1 miles) of stream habitat within a single watershed (USFWS 2004). The life history and habitat requirements for Paiute cutthroat trout are similar to those reported for other western streamdwelling salmonids. All life stages require cool, well-oxygenated waters. Adult fish prefer stream pool habitat in low gradient meadows with undercut or overhanging banks and abundant riparian vegetation. To spawn successfully, they must have access to flowing waters with clean gravel substrates.

Paiute cutthroat trout reach sexual maturity at the age of 2 years. Paiute cutthroat trout are opportunistic feeders, utilizing whatever aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates occur in the drift. In stream environments Paiute cutthroat trout seldom reach sizes more than 250 millimeters (10 inches) total length. Disease is apparently a significant cause of adult mortality, particularly in the post-spawning period. Few Paiute cutthroat trout apparently live beyond the age of 3 years in a wild stream environment (USFWS 2004).

The Paiute cutthroat trout faces several threats to its existence because of its limited distribution and its susceptibility to displacement by other salmonids. Several events have occurred in the past to imperil its existence, including:

1. The early introduction of rainbow trout and Lahontan cutthroat trout into the Silver King Creek drainage and subsequent introgression,

2. the introduction of beavers into the Silver King Creek drainage,

3. the occurrence of a flood in Silver King Creek that may have eliminated a natural barrier and allowed nonnative salmonids to enter the drainage, 4. the degradation of habitat caused by livestock grazing and off-highway vehicle use in the North Fork of Cottonwood Creek, and

5. excessive angling (USFWS 2004).

Paiute cutthroat trout critical habitat has not been designated for the Paiute cutthroat trout.

#### _Lahontan cutthroat trout_

**Lahontan cutthroat trout** is an inland subspecies of cutthroat trout endemic to the Lahontan basin of northern Nevada, eastern California, and southern Oregon. Lahontan cutthroat trout typically exhibit spots on the top and sides of the head extending to the tip of the snout. Lahontan cutthroat trout inhabit lakes and streams and require spawning and nursery habitat characterized by cool water, pools near cover and velocity breaks, well vegetated and stable stream banks, and relatively silt free rocky substrate in riffle-run areas. Lahontan cutthroat trout mature between 2 and 4 years. Lahontan cutthroat trout can be opportunistic feeders, with diets consisting of drift organisms, typically terrestrial and aquatic insects, zooplankton and fish, but varies depending on which habitat types they reside (USFWS 1995e).

Principal threats to Lahontan cutthroat trout include:

1. habitat loss associated with livestock grazing practices, urban and mining development;

2. water diversions;

3. poor water quality;

4. hybridization with non-native trout; and

5. competition with introduced species of fish (USFWS 1995e).

Lahontan cutthroat trout critical habitat has not been designated.

#### _Little Kern golden trout_

The **Little Kern golden trout** is a subspecies of rainbow trout ( _Oncorhynchus mykiss_ ) in the family Salmonidae and endemic only to the Little Kern River drainage in Tulare County, California. The Little Kern River drainage occurs primarily within the Golden Trout Wilderness on the Sequoia National Forest. Smaller areas of the drainage occur outside of designated wilderness in either Sequoia National Park or Sequoia National Forest (USFWS 2023r). The Little Kern golden trout is known only from the Little Kern River in Tulare County, Calif. In the Little Kern River watershed, the water quality of the streams inhabited by this fish is generally good. At the time of listing, the following threats to the subspecies were identified: potential for uncontrolled use of off-road vehicles, improper road construction, careless logging activities, pollution from mining operations or overgrazing, and hybridization with non-native rainbow trout (43 FR 15428). Current threats to the subspecies include: grazing and habitat loss, hybridization and low genetic diversity, limited range and small population size, and long-term alteration of weather patterns. There is no information indicating mining and logging currently threaten the subspecies (USFWS 2023r).

Rainbow trout were introduced into the Little Kern River System in the 1930’s. Subsequent hybridization between the Little Kern golden trout and the introduced rainbow trout resulted in a reduction in the number of pure populations of Little Kern golden trout. At present, pure populations of Little Kem golden trout exist only in headwater streams which were not stocked with rainbow trout or have barrier falls which have prevented upstream migration of rainbow trout.

Little Kern golden trout critical habitat include streams in the Little Kem River watershed that are sufficient for individual and population growth and dispersal of the Little Kem golden trout. The pools in stream areas within the designated area are proper habitat for aquatic insects which provide food for the trout. The cobbles and larger rocks provide cover for both juvenile and adult fish. The gravel bottom in pool areas of the Critical Habitat streams provides proper substrate for redds (43 FR 15428).

#### _Dolly Varden_

Dolly Varden, a char species, are ESA proposed due to similarity in appearance to bull trout. Prior to 1978, bull trout and Dolly Varden were considered a single species but it had been demonstrated these are two different species. In the coterminous U.S., Dolly Varden only occurs in western Washington, overlapping somewhat with the current bull trout distribution (USFWS 2024ac). Dolly Varden will not be analyzed in this document since they overlap in geography with bull trout and are ESA proposed because of their similarity in appearance to bull trout, an ESA listed species. This project will have the same effects for Dolly Varden as they would for bull trout (Table 15).

#### _Bull trout_

Bull trout is a char species and has the largest range of any other salmonid considered in this consultation. Bull trout are distributed from coastal Alaska and western Canada, south to the Pacific Northwest, and east to portions of the middle and northern Rocky Mountains. Within the coterminous United States portion of the range, bull trout are currently known to occur in the Columbia and Snake River basins, the Puget Sound and Olympic Peninsula coastal basins, and the Saint Mary and Upper Klamath River basins. Bull trout are grouped into six recovery units that are biologically important to the rangewide conservation of bull trout and provides recovery criteria for each unit. These six recovery units (Coastal Recovery Unit, Klamath Recovery Unit, Mid-Columbia Recovery Unit, Upper Snake Recovery Unit, Columbia Headwaters Recovery Unit, Saint Mary Recovery Unit; Figure 1) encompass 110 core areas that were occupied at the time of listing, 7 historical core areas, and 1 Research Needs Area (RNA), and comprise over 600 local populations (USFWS 2015b, USFWS 2024ac). When future projects occur in the action area and the action area is within a bull trout core area, analysis at the core area scale for bull trout will be completed at that time. Core area information and maps can be found in the 2015 recovery plan for the coterminous United States population of bull trout (USFWS 2015b) and in the species status assessment for the coterminous distinct population segment of bull trout (USFWS 2024ac).

**Figure 1. Locations of the six bull trout recovery units in the coterminous United States.**

Historical habitat loss and fragmentation, interaction with nonnative species, fish passage issues, and changing climate are the most significant threats affecting bull trout. The magnitude of those threats and their potential synergistic effects vary greatly across recovery units, core areas and among local populations. Historical habitat loss and fragmentation, interaction with nonnative species, and fish passage issues are widely regarded as the most significant primary threat factors affecting bull trout (USFWS 2015b, USFWS 2024ac).

Bull trout have both resident and migratory life history strategies. The size and age of bull trout at maturity depends upon habitat capacity and subsequent life history strategy. Resident fish tend to be smaller at maturity than migratory fish and produce fewer eggs. Bull trout normally reach sexual maturity in 4 to 7 years. They frequently live for 10 years, and occasionally for 20 years or more (USFWS 2015b, USFWS 2024ac).

Of native salmonids in the Pacific Northwest of the United States, bull trout have the most specific habitat requirements, often referred to as “the four Cs”: cold, clean, complex, and connected habitat. Habitat components that influence bull trout distribution and abundance include water temperature, in-stream and stream-bank cover, channel form and stability, valley form, spawning and rearing substrate, and unobstructed migratory corridors. Juveniles remain in the substrate after hatching; the time from egg deposition to emergence of fry can exceed 200 days. During the relatively long incubation period in the gravel, bull trout eggs are especially vulnerable to fine sediments, streambed scour, and water quality degradation (USFWS 2015b, USFWS 2024ac).

Bull trout need the following core area habitat factors in sufficient condition to successfully complete all stages of their life cycle (USFWS 2015b, USFWS 2024ac):

1. Water Quality – enough clean and cold water to support breeding and feeding, and provide shelter for each life stage to survive.

2. FMO Habitat Access – connectivity for subadults and adults between spawning and rearing habitats and feeding, migrating and overwintering habitats that provide diverse resources.

3. Fish Community Quality – habitat for all life stages with limited interaction with deleterious nonnative species.

4. Instream Quality – in-water habitat with complex substrates, stream morphology, and structure to meet the needs of each life stage.

5. Riparian Quality – intact habitat for all bull trout life stages within the riparian corridor, which provides shade, channel complexities, insect communities, and allochthonous inputs leading to higher quality instream habitat and water quality.

6. Spawning and Rearing Habitat Quantity –sufficient amount and quality of habitat to allow for individual adults to spawn and juveniles to rear.

Most threats described in the recovery plans fall into the category of destruction, modification, or curtailment of habitat. Many of these impacts, such as dewatering, sedimentation, thermal modification, and water quality degradation, are a consequence of specific land and water management activities. There have been increased efforts to mitigate impacts, especially on federal lands where there is a greater conservation emphasis, such as headwater areas where bull trout spawn and rear. For example, improved land management practices, declining timber harvest, and cessation of road building have reduced impacts in riparian habitats. However, legacy effects of past land use continue to degrade bull trout habitat across the range where habitat restoration has not yet occurred, or ecological benefits have not been realized. Loss of connectivity from dams and water diversions continue to isolate and fragment populations, reducing the species’ viability today. In the absence of substantially increased conservation effort, these threats are predicted to continue reducing bull trout viability across the range into the future (USFWS 2015b, USFWS 2024ac). Within affected environment, timber harvest and permanent road building in bull trout habitat could create localized threats to the species through water quality impacts and habitat access if roads are built over streams.

Nonnative fish were identified as a significant threat in the original listing of bull trout, and the threat has increased since that time. Today, nonnative fishes are a primary threat in many core areas across the six recovery units. Nonnative fish of primary concern include both lake trout ( _Salvelinus namaycush_ ) and brook trout ( _Salvelinus fontinalis_ ). Lake trout, a congeneric species whose niche closely overlaps with adfluvial bull trout, can outcompete and prey upon bull trout in lake environments where they co-occur. Brook trout is also a congeneric species that competes with, and can hybridize with, bull trout. Negative effects of brook trout on bull trout appear to vary substantially between watersheds, being relatively severe in small, low-gradient streams with resident or small migratory populations of bull trout. Bull trout populations containing robust numbers of large individuals with migratory life histories can often successfully coexist with brook trout, although the long-term impacts from hybridization are unknown. The presence of either brook trout or lake trout in bull trout waters results in diminished resiliency and ultimately reduced viability. Other piscivorous species that can prey on bull trout can also be found in many bull trout core areas (USFWS 2015b, USFWS 2024ac).

Bull trout require cold water habitat and are vulnerable to the effects of warming climates, changing patterns of precipitation, and dynamic instream hydrologic regimes. Changing climate can also exacerbate other threats. Drought, increased wildfire intensity and frequency, reduction of snowpack, and general warming of waterways all have negative impacts on bull trout. In general, all climate scenarios project some degree of warming, although severity and the effects on amount and seasonality of precipitation are scenario-dependent and the impacts on bull trout populations are expected to vary geographically. Bull trout may not be able to adapt quickly enough to avoid population declines in the future with continued alteration of weather patterns (USFWS 2015b, USFWS 2024ac).

Bull trout critical habitat physical and biological features are essential for the conservation of bull trout critical habitat and may require special management considerations or protection (75 FR 63898):

1. Springs, seeps, groundwater sources, and subsurface water connectivity (hyporheic flows) to contribute to water quality and quantity and provide thermal refugia.

2. Migration habitats with minimal physical, biological, or water quality impediments between spawning, rearing, overwintering, and freshwater and marine foraging habitats, including but not limited to permanent, partial, intermittent, or seasonal barriers.

3. An abundant food base, including terrestrial organisms of riparian origin, aquatic macroinvertebrates, and forage fish.

4. Complex river, stream, lake, reservoir, and marine shoreline aquatic environments, and processes that establish and maintain these aquatic environments, with features such as large wood, side channels, pools, undercut banks and unembedded substrates, to provide a variety of depths, gradients, velocities, and structure.

5. Water temperatures ranging from 2 to 15 °C (36 to 59 °F), with adequate thermal refugia available for temperatures that exceed the upper end of this range. Specific temperatures within this range will depend on bull trout life-history stage and form; geography;

elevation; diurnal and seasonal variation; shading, such as that provided by riparian habitat; streamflow; and local groundwater influence.

6. In spawning and rearing areas, substrate of sufficient amount, size, and composition to ensure success of egg and embryo overwinter survival, fry emergence, and young-of-theyear and juvenile survival. A minimal amount of fine sediment, generally ranging in size from silt to coarse sand, embedded in larger substrates, is characteristic of these conditions. The size and amounts of fine sediment suitable to bull trout will likely vary from system to system.

7. A natural hydrograph, including peak, high, low, and base flows within historic and seasonal ranges or, if flows are controlled, minimal flow departure from a natural hydrograph.

8. Sufficient water quality and quantity such that normal reproduction, growth, and survival are not inhibited.

9. Sufficiently low levels of occurrence of nonnative predatory (e.g., lake trout, walleye, northern pike, smallmouth bass); interbreeding (e.g., brook trout); or competing (e.g., brown trout) species that, if present, are adequately temporally and spatially isolated from bull trout.

#### _Salmonidae Effects_

Effects of future projects on members of the Salmonidae family could be varied but would most likely be due to sedimentation, potential increase in water temperatures, and habitat fragmentation when projects are implemented. Impacts would not be the same because of limited distribution of the Paiute cutthroat trout, Little Kern golden trout, Lahontan cutthroat trout, and Gila trout, while bull trout is distributed widely across the affected environment. Implementing Forest Service best management practices (2012) will help alleviate negative effects of any future project. Many National Forests are actively involved in protecting species and protections are expected to continue. Low level effects from sedimentation, increase in water temperatures, and habitat fragmentation could occur during future project implementation, the magnitude of which is unknown, but expected to be low. Any future projects that would affect species would still need to complete project level consultation. Due to the unknowns, we might expect some effects on species that are susceptible to reach **may affect, likely to adversely affect** individual Paiute cutthroat trout, Little Kern golden trout, Lahontan cutthroat trout, Gila trout, bull trout, and Dolly Varden. Individual species effects are listed in Table 15.

Little Kern golden trout and bull trout are the only species with designated critical habitat in the affected environment. The amount of Little Kern golden trout critical habitat in the action area is very minimal, less than 0.0001 percent. Effects to Little Kern golden trout critical habitat are through the same pathways as for the species, so effects analyses will not be duplicated here. Best management practices would minimize effects to Little Kern golden trout critical habitat but may not eliminate adverse effects. The amount of bull trout critical habitat in the action area is minimal, less than 0.10 percent. Land Management Plans within the range of bull trout contain aquatic management strategies that have standards and guidelines for activities that can and cannot occur in the aquatic management zones. They are the Northwest Forest Plan (NWFP) (USFS and USDI 1994); the interim strategies for managing anadromous fish-producing watersheds in eastern Oregon and Washington, Idaho, and Portions of California (PacFish) (USFS and USDI 1995); and the inland native fish strategy (InFish) (USFS 1995). Within these aquatic strategies, riparian management objectives within the area covered by each strategy need to be met for actions implemented within the aquatic management zones. Aquatic management zones are generally identified within the three strategies as 1 site-potential-tree height or 150 feet, whichever is greater. Combined with the Forest Service best management practices (USFS 2012a), effects to species and critical habitat should be minimized but may not be eliminated. Effects from previous projects have been short-term negative effects for sedimentation/turbidity and water temperature, with long-term beneficial effects from the aquatic conservation strategy guidance. Because of these reasons, future projects in some areas may rise to the level of measurable effects on bull trout critical habitat. The Roadless Rule Rescission **may affect, likely to adversely affect** Little Kern golden trout critical habitat and bull trout critical habitat (Table 15).

### Ictaluridae Family

Three species in the Ictaluridae family may be in the action area (Table 15). Since all members of the Ictaluridae family, if affected, have similar effects pathways, effects determinations will be combined below in the Ictaluridae Effects section.

#### _Yaqui catfish_

Yaqui catfish<sup>26</sup> are profusely speckled and exhibit a brownish gray coloration on the back, or dorsally, with lighter coloration beneath, ventrally. Their barbels are black, except for the barbels located on the chin, are 15.7 inches average length, cylindrically shaped, lacking scales. weigh 2.2 pounds, making them one of the medium-sized North American catfish species. Yaqui catfish are bottom-dwelling omnivores representing the only known native Ictalurid west of the Continental Divide. Very little is known about the species’ biology but believed that it parallels that of channel catfish ( _Ictalurus punctatus_ ). Yaqui catfish are cavity spawners, where males will create or utilize holes in banks, hollow logs, rocks and other submerged material to build a nest. Females are attracted to the nests where spawning occurs, and eggs are laid on the bottom of the nest. Males will stay and protect the nest until the young fish, known as fry, leave the nest. Outside of breeding season, Yaqui catfish live relatively solitary lives in dark shady areas in deeper pools. Catfish will feed during the day or night and tend to feed near the water bottom. Diets can consist of plant and animal material like insects, snails, crawfish, green algae, aquatic plants and small fish. Catfish detect food with their sense of taste, and the barbels around their mouth, which are specialized sensory organs that are covered in tastebuds. Yaqui catfish inhabit moderate to large streams in areas of medium to slow current with sandy or rocky bottoms, at elevations between 4,000 to 5,000 feet.

Currently, the Yaqui catfish is found only in the Rio Yaqui drainage of Sonora, Mexico. It was extirpated from the United States, and in 1997, the Yaqui catfish was reintroduced to San

> 26 Much of the species’ description and current range was collected from: https://www.fws.gov/species/yaqui-catfish-ictalurus- <u>pricei accessed on 2/13/2026.</u>

Bernardino National Wildlife Refuge and West Turkey Creek in Cochise County, Arizona. However, these introductions did not produce sustained populations and the Yaqui catfish is again considered extirpated from the United States, as is documented in the USFWS 2019 5- Year Review of the species. The USFWS (2019q) 5-year review suggested uplisting the Yaqui catfish.

Many threats to this fish continue or have increased, and these include: loss, alteration, and degradation of suitable habitat through the construction of dams used throughout the Rio Yaqui for agricultural and hydroelectric development; the presence of channel catfish, a common nonnative species that hybridizes with Yaqui catfish; and long-term drought combined with expanding human populations, which are creating increased demand for water for human consumption (USFWS 2019r).

Yaqui catfish critical habitat is not in the action area.

#### _Smoky madtom_

The Smoky madtom is a small madtom species endemic to the Little Tennessee River basin. The species was thought to be extinct when first described from specimens collected in 1957. In 1980 the species was rediscovered in Citico Creek and was listed as federally endangered in 1984 (49 FR 43065). Currently, there are three known populations, all occur within tributaries of the Little Tennessee River. Two of the populations, Abrams Creek and Citico Creek, are within the known historical range. The USFWS designated a nonessential experimental population for the Smoky madtom in Tellico River that has been stocked from captive propagated individuals from the Citico Creek population. The Abrams Creek and Citico Creek populations appear to be stable. The Tellico River population has documented natural reproduction since 2010 and may also be getting close to being fully self-sustaining. Threats to Smoky madtom habitat have been greatly reduced by management actions by the Forest Service and National Park Service, as most of the range occurs within the Cherokee National Forest and Great Smoky Mountains National Park. While the species continues to be isolated by impoundments, a genetic plan is being implemented to manage gene flow between populations. Source and nonpoint source pollution pose a minor threat to populations due to conservation efforts and watershed management practices of federal land management agencies. Because of the successful establishment of two additional populations (Abrams Creek and Tellico River), active management of the Smoky madtom in the Cherokee National Forest and Great Smoky Mountains National Park, and due to all current populations being stable or increasing (USFWS 2024ad).

The Citico Creek population occupies 14.6 km of habitat almost entirely within the Cherokee National Forest, Monroe County, Tennessee. Protected land surrounding Citico Creek is primarily managed by the Forest Service as part of the Citico Creek Wilderness Area to protect and preserve the natural environment from human influences and allow ecological and biological processes to progress naturally (2004 Cherokee National Forest land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). In the Citico Creek watershed, the USFS (2004 Cherokee National Forest land management plan) prioritizes and implements treatments to improve riparian condition and reduce sediment transport to streams and provide high water quality (USFWS 2024ad).

Most of the species’ current habitat lies within lands managed by the Forest Service and the National Park Service, which have restoration, monitoring, and forest management programs with the potential to benefit the species and reduces some impacts from sedimentation and water quality. Sedimentation poses only a minor threat to Smoky madtom populations due to active management by Forest Service and National Park Service. The Cherokee National Forest, for example, is also a vital partner in upgrading and improving road-stream crossings on the Forest to benefit species like the Smoky madtom.

Recreational activities (swimming, wading, horse access to the water) within the Cherokee National Forest can and have resulted in visitors disturbing rocks, impacting nests and dislodging eggs. Smoky madtom populations are also vulnerable to the potential of increased frequency of intense flooding and severity of drought. Alteration of weather patterns is expected to result in increased temperatures, increase in droughts, and increases in extreme weather events, which have the potential to impact species. Reduced water availability may be a significant threat to the Smoky madtom in the long term because an increase in the frequency and duration of dewatering events of suitable habitat may lead to reduced reproduction, nest success, or increase mortality due to the shallow-water habitat occupied by this species (USFWS 2024ad).

Each Smoky madtom population occurs within one watershed. Catastrophic events that could severely impact or extirpate entire Smoky madtom populations include chemical spills, changes in upstream land use that alter stream characteristics and water quality downstream, new impoundments, and potential effects of drought and increases in occurrence of flash flooding events. The likelihood of many of these events are low given the Federal protections afforded to the populations by the National Park Service and Forest Service (USFWS 2024ad).

Smoky madtom critical habitat is not located within the action area.

#### _Yellowfin madtom_

The yellowfin madtom is a moderately elongated madtom (maximum known length 92 millimeters slot length). It has a depressed head, large eyes, and a truncate to slightly rounded caudal fin. The pectoral spines are long with highly developed serrae (USFWS 1983c). Yellowfin madtoms are known to occupy small-to-medium size warmwater streams with moderate current, often occurring in pools or backwaters (USFWS 2020j). The yellowfin madtom is vulnerable to loss of genetic diversity and fitness due to small population sizes. Species that are restricted in range and population size are more likely to suffer loss of genetic diversity due to genetic drift, potentially increasing their susceptibility to inbreeding depression and decreasing their ability to adapt to environmental changes (USFWS 2020j).

They probably occurred in many of the lower gradient streams of the Tennessee River basin and has been extirpated from known locations in Chickamauga Creek, Georgia, and Hines Creek, Tennessee. Since the Service listed yellowfin madtom under the ESA, the range of the species has expanded through rediscoveries and reintroduction efforts in the upper Tennessee River drainage. The species was rediscovered in Citico Creek in the Little Tennessee River system, Tennessee, and Copper Creek in the Clinch River system, Virginia. In addition, reintroduction efforts helped bring back the yellowfin madtom to Abrams Creek and the Tellico River in the Little Tennessee River system, Tennessee, and the North Fork Holston River, Virginia (USFWS 2020j).

Physical habitat destruction resulting from a variety of human-induced impacts such as siltation, disturbance of riparian corridors, and changes in channel morphology continues to plague the Tennessee River watershed. The most significant of these impacts is siltation caused by excessive releases of sediment from activities such as agriculture, resource extraction (for example, coal mining, silviculture), road construction, and urban development. Activities that contribute sediment discharges into a stream system change the erosion or sedimentation pattern, which can lead to the destruction of riparian vegetation, bank collapse, excessive instream sediment deposition, and increased water turbidity and temperatures (USFWS 2020j).

Agriculture continues to threaten the yellowfin madtom in the Clinch and Powell rivers and Copper Creek. Cattle continue to threaten yellowfin madtom habitat in Copper Creek. Agricultural livestock and other unconfined animals often have direct access to waterbodies and can provide a concentrated source of coliform bacteria loads that can directly enter a stream and destroy riparian by trampling vegetation that holds streambanks in place (USFWS 2020j).

Two of seven streams with extant yellowfin madtom populations are located on the Cherokee National Forest and receive management and protection through the National Forest Management Act of 1976 (16 U.S.C. 1600 et seq.) and Cherokee National Forest’s 2004 land management plan (available at USFS 2025a). The land management plan is implemented through a series of project-level decisions based on appropriate site-specific analysis and disclosure. It does not contain a commitment to select any specific project; rather, it sets up a framework of desired future conditions with goals, objectives, and standards to guide project proposals. Projects are proposed to solve resource management problems, move the forest environment toward desired future conditions, and supply goods and services to the public (2004 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). The land management plan contains protective standards that are designed to avoid and minimize potential adverse effects to the Yellowfin Madtom and other sensitive species; however, the Cherokee National Forest continues to consult with the Service when their activities may adversely affect streams supporting the species. The Cherokee National Forest’s management under the land management plan contributes substantially to the conservation of the species, and we expect the Cherokee National Forest to continue to implement management actions that benefit the species (USFWS 2020). The populations in Citico Creek and the Tellico River are in the Cherokee National Forest boundaries.

Yellowfin madtom critical habitat is not located within the action area.

#### _Carolina madtom_

The Carolina madtom is a small (5 inches), bottom-dwelling member of the catfish family. It has potent venom glands at the spines and is the most strongly armed North American catfish, earning the “furiosus” name. Carolina madtoms typically feed from dusk to dawn and eat aquatic insects, including larval midges, mayflies, caddisflies, dragonflies, and beetles. They nest from mid-May to late-July under natural or artificial cover (for example, mussel shells, bark and other woody debris, glass jars, beverage cans, or other containers). Found only in the Neuse and Tar- Pamlico River Basins of North Carolina, it typically inhabits medium to large streams and rivers in the Piedmont and Coastal Plain physiographic regions and it requires clean, flowing water habitat and substrates of coarse sand and gravel with leaf litter and abundant cover. Preferred habitats of this species include riffles, runs, and pools of shallow to moderate depth, with leaf packs and sand and gravel substrates, and adequate cover (for example, boulders or woody debris). They are often found in swift waters and will shift to areas of moderate or slow flow during the breeding season (USFWS 2021h).

The Carolina madtom require free-flowing, highly oxygenated streams, water temperatures of 20 – 25°C (68 – 77°F) for breeding, and physical cover for nesting habitat. They rely on uncompacted sand, gravel, and boulder substrates and clean leaf packs that can support insect larvae, which comprise 95% of their diet. Their small body size leaves Carolina madtoms vulnerable to predation. Slow growth delayed reproductive maturity, and a relatively short life span limits the lifetime recruitment potential and their ability to adapt to rapidly changing habitat conditions or respond to punctuated or long-term impacts to populations (USFWS 2021h).

The Carolina madtom was listed as an endangered species with designated critical habitat on June 9, 2021 (86 FR 30688). The primary threat to Carolina madtom is habitat degradation resulting from stressors that affect water quality, water quantity, instream habitat suitability, and habitat connectivity, including watershed-level effects of development on water quality, instream habitat fragmentation, sedimentation from a variety of land uses, and the effects of long-term weather alteration. The remaining small, isolated populations and contracted range of the Carolina madtom further increase their vulnerability to stochastic and catastrophic events (USFWS 2021h).

The greatest threat to the future viability of the Carolina madtom (such as, the ability to sustain populations in the wild over time) is habitat degradation from stressors that influence water quality, water quantity, instream habitat, and habitat connectivity. Sedimentation is induced by variety of land uses (for example, development, agricultural, or forestry activities without adequate riparian protections or proper erosion/sediment control). Carolina madtom are known to avoid areas dominated by fine silts. Sedimentation can result in degraded or unsuitable cover and foraging habitats by increasing substrate embeddedness or rendering leaf packs hypoxic and unable to support insect prey. Some other significant physical and biological stressors include instream barriers, invasive species, and severely diminished populations (USFWS 2021h).

The Croatan National Forest would be the only forest that may have impacts to Carolina madtom within the Trent River system. There are a few smaller tributary streams, Will, Island, and Reedy creeks, that flow into the Trent River near the action area, but Carolina madtom do not inhabit these streams and are found upstream of these creeks in the Trent River system. There may be current roads that could be utilized as haul route for timber and road aggregate, but those would be unknown at this time. If these roads are utilized the effects would be minimal amounts of sediment, depending on the road surface type.

Carolina madtom critical habitat is not located within the action area.

#### _Frecklebelly madtom_

The frecklebelly madtom is a small, stout catfish reaching about 4 inches in length and distinctively marked with dark saddles. The species inhabits the main channels and larger tributaries of large river systems in Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, and Tennessee. The species has a broad but disjunct distribution across the Pearl River watershed and Mobile River Basin, with populations in the Pearl River and Bogue Chitto River in the Pearl River watershed and the Tombigbee, Alabama, Cahaba, Etowah, and Conasauga river systems in the Mobile River Basin (88 FR 13038).

Primary habitat for frecklebelly madtom is associated with fast moving streams often associated with rivers and their tributaries, with substrate consisting of various sizes of gravel. Cover is an important habitat factor for the species, as it provides for concealment against predators, foraging habitat, and nesting habitat. Areas providing firm gravel substrates, such as small pebbles and rocks, are preferred, thus muddy waterway sand still streams are not desirable habitat for this species (88 FR 13038).

The frecklebelly madtom is primarily active at night and has a lifespan of up to five years. There is a lack of information on the breeding behavior and nesting habitat of the species, although it is believed that reproduction occurs between June and July. Nesting sites for madtoms are typically cavities under natural material, such as rocks, logs, empty mussel shells, or human litter, such as inside cans or bottles or under boards. They are opportunistic insectivores and feed on aquatic insect larvae, with the primary food sources being caddisflies, mayflies, blackflies, and midges (USFWS 2023s).

The frecklebelly madtom prefers fast-moving streams with gravel substrate for cover, foraging, and nesting habitats. They avoid muddy waterways and still streams. The presence of coarse and stable gravel substrate is also important for the occurrence of other madtom species. Aquatic vegetation is also important for some parts of their range, where they are often found in or near river weed ( _Podostemon_ ) and under large, flat rocks. They have been collected in moderate to swift currents over boulders, rubble, cobble, and coarse gravel, and around concentrations of river weed in the upper Etowah and Conasauga rivers. Shoal complexity could limit the recovery of the species because stabilizing shoals and recruiting river weed may be unattainable with the surrounding land use and hydrology (USFWS 2023s).

Frecklebelly madtom are sensitive to pollutants from agricultural land use. Hormones, excess nutrients, and herbicide surfactants are postulated to contribute to the species declines observed in the Conasauga watershed. Nonpoint source sediment and agrochemical discharges in predominantly agricultural areas within the frecklebelly madtom's current range could potentially alter its habitat's physical and chemical characteristics, thereby impeding its feeding, sheltering, and reproductive abilities (USFWS 2023s).

Frecklebelly madtom critical habitat is not located within the action area.

_Ictaluridae Effects_

Yaqui catfish have been extirpated from the U.S.; therefore, there would be **no effect** to Yaqui catfish.

Effects of future projects on all madtoms analyzed in this BA would most likely be from sedimentation and habitat fragmentation. Effects to Smoky and yellowfin madtoms would be low due to protections provided by the Cherokee National Forest Land Management Plan. Implementing Forest Service best management practices (USFS 2012a) will help alleviate negative effects of any future project. National Forests are actively involved in protecting species and protections are expected to continue. Low level effects from sedimentation and habitat fragmentation could occur during future project implementation, the magnitude of which is unknown. Any future projects that would affect species would still need to complete project level consultation. Due to the unknowns, we might expect some effects on individual Smoky madtom, yellowfin madtom, and frecklebelly madtom that are susceptible to reach **may affect, likely to adversely affect** to the species. Carolina madtom could be in adjacent tributaries near the Croatan National Forest. If they are within adjacent tributaries effects would only be from haul which would be dependent on the road surface type. The amount of sedimentation that would reach the stream during haul would not be measurable. We expect Carolina madtom effects, if any, to be discountable; therefore, the determination is **may affect, not likely to adversely affect** Carolina madtom. ## Bivalves

To assist analyzing effects to a large number of species, ESA-listed species were grouped taxonomically. The bivalve group includes 45 total species including 25 endangered, 12 threatened, 6 proposed endangered, and 2 proposed threatened freshwater bivalves (Table 18). All the listed bivalve species occur in the southeastern United States and are located in either regions 8 or 9 of the Forest Service. Freshwater bivalves of the United States inhabit a number of freshwater environments, though a majority of those listed under the ESA prefer flowing riverine habitat.  Freshwater bivalves are filter feeders that live on or in the substrate. Locomotion is limited and performed with the assistance of a muscular hydraulic foot. Freshwater bivalves of the U.S. have a parasitic larval stage that infect the gills or body of the host fish.  Host fish are often species specific to the freshwater bivalve. Threats to native freshwater bivalves of the U.S. are typically associated with decreases in water quality and quantity.

Road construction and timber harvest primarily affects freshwater bivalves through two main pathways: physical and chemical degradation of their habitat and the fragmentation of populations. The most significant impact is often increased sedimentation resulting from soil erosion at construction sites and runoff from new road surfaces. Excess sediment can directly harm bivalves, which are sessile filter feeders, by clogging their gills, interfering with feeding and respiration, and physically burying and smothering individuals, leading to direct mortality or reduced growth rates.

Beyond sedimentation, road construction introduces other stressors. Instream work, like installing culverts, can cause direct mortality and permanent changes to hydrology and streambed composition. This physical alteration may eliminate the stable, clean habitat necessary for bivalve survival. Chemically, runoff from new roads can introduce toxic pollutants such as heavy metals, oils, and de-icing salts, further compromising water quality and the health of the bivalves and their host fish. The FS does not regularly use toxic chemicals to manage the land and does not use salt to clear icy roads.  Any activities that use chemicals with toxic properties will be required to analyze their potential effects to the environment, including ESA-listed resources, prior to implementation.

Finally, road-stream crossings like culverts can act as barriers to the movement of fish that serve as essential hosts for the bivalve larval stage (glochidia). Improperly designed culverts can have high water velocities or insufficient water depth, preventing fish from moving upstream and effectively blocking bivalve dispersal and reproduction. This habitat fragmentation can lead to isolated mussel populations with reduced genetic diversity and a higher risk of local extinction (Vaughan 2002).

#### _Sedimentation_

Sedimentation impacts freshwater bivalves by physically degrading their habitat and impairing essential physiological processes. As filter feeders, bivalves rely on relatively clean water and stable substrate. Increased levels of suspended solids directly interfere with feeding and respiration by clogging gills and siphons, which can lead to reduced food intake, energy depletion, and chronic stress. Deposition of fine sediment on the streambed is also detrimental, as it potentially smothers and buries bivalves, leading to suffocation and mortality. Accumulated sediment also alters the natural, stable substrate that mussels require for secure habitation and successful reproduction.  Furthermore, increased sedimentation can negatively affect the fish hosts necessary for the larval stage of most bivalves, creating a compounding negative effect that ultimately contributes to population declines and increased extinction risk for many vulnerable species.

Zhu et al. (2024), in a published synthesis on this topic, offer the following on sedimentation effects on bivalves. Freshwater mussels have a complex life cycle that includes fertilization by broadcasting sperm, embryos brooded in marsupial gills, parasitic larvae that attach to fish, and a free-living juvenile stage that typically occupies interstitial spaces in river sediment. In some cases, suspended solids may adversely affect fertilization and brooding of some species. Both juvenile and adult mussels are suspension feeders, and feeding can be inhibited by suspended solids. Because of their small size and rapid metabolism and growth, juvenile mussels are often more sensitive than adults to stressors in laboratory experiments. For example, researchers associated turbidity and sedimentation with recruitment failure in 14 of 24 populations of freshwater pearl mussel ( _Margaritifera margaritifera_ ) that they investigated. Absence of juvenile mussels from a lack of recruitment is considered to be a characteristic feature of many declining mussel populations, which may eventually cause population collapse.

In 2013, Landis et al. linked the reproductive failure of pondmussel ( _Ligumia subrostrate_ ) females to elevated suspended solids. They found that (a) 98-99% of eggs were fertilized regardless of total suspended solids (TSS) levels and (b) total fecundity was not related to TSS levels.  Sperm production was not correlated with TSS concentrations.  In another study, Landis et al. (2015) assessed the stage-specific disruption of reproduction due to high TSS levels in two mussel species, including a short-term brooding mussel species (Ebonyshell, _Reginaia ebenus_ ) and a long-term brooding species (Pondmussel, _Ligumia subrostrata_ ). Although reduced reproductive success was observed in both species at high TSS levels, the effects were different. More female ebonyshell (33-93%) were found fertilized across the TSS gradient (11-92 mg/L) tested, but few glochidia developed when TSS was higher than 20 mg/L. In the case of female pondmussel, similar to the 2013 study, much less female (0- 28%) were fertilized at higher TSS levels, but all those gravid successfully produced fully developed glochidia. The observed differences might be explained by the differences in gill structure (the density of cilia on the gills) and gill function related to habitat use and/or brooding strategies.

#### _Fragmentation_

Habitat fragmentation impacts freshwater bivalves by isolating populations and disrupting their complex life cycles, leading to population decline. Improper construction of culverts and other in-stream infrastructure can convert flowing river habitat into non-flowing water features, an unsuitable environment for many river-dwelling mussel species. This not only causes direct habitat loss but also alters environmental conditions such as temperature, flow regimes, and oxygen levels (Lopes-Lima et al. 2018; Pires et al. 2020).

One of the most critical effects of fragmentation is the blockage of native host fish movement, which is essential for the dispersal of bivalve larvae (glochidia). With their host fish unable to pass barriers, mussel populations become physically and genetically isolated. This isolation prevents gene flow between populations, leading to reduced genetic diversity and an increased risk of inbreeding, which can diminish fitness and adaptive potential. Consequently, isolated populations are more vulnerable to environmental stochasticity, disease, pollution events, and local extinction (Osterling and Soderberg 2015).

Further, barriers to natural flow can alter the riverbed dynamics, causing sediment retention upstream and scouring of substrates downstream, which degrades essential microhabitats and negatively affects suspension feeders like bivalves. These impacts, combined with other stressors, have made freshwater bivalves one of the most imperiled animal groups globally (Lopes-Lima et al. 2018; Pires et al. 2020).

Although in-stream work has the potential to fragment riverine habitat, the Forest Service designs and installs culverts in a manner to improve streamflow, not restrict it. Fragmentation can still occur during construction, but those effects are assumed to be temporary and that surface flows will return to normal, or better than normal, when construction has ended. Shortterm fragmentation of aquatic habitat is not expected to have population level effects to listed bivalves.

### Existing Protections

Land Management Plans or similar planning documents for the following forests provide direction specifically to protect and recover listed bivalve species: Nantahala and Pisgah NF, George Washington and Jefferson NFs, Hoosier NF, Cherokee NF, Kisatchie NF, and Mark Twain NF (available at USFS 2025a). Given land management plan direction on these forests, the Forest Service anticipates a majority of effects to listed bivalve species in these areas to be avoided or minimized. The following species are known to occur on only these forests within the action area: Appalachian elktoe, Atlantic pigtoe, fanshell, finerayed pigtoe, fluted kidneyshell, James spinymussel, Louisiana pearlshell, pink mucket, shiny pigtoe, slabside pearlymussel, spectaclecase, Tennessee clubshell. Where exposure is anticipated to be low or is unknown and planning documents contain protections for ESA-listed bivalves, a determination of NLAA is being made.

### Critical Habitat

Effects to designated critical habitat are analyzed by reviewing the physical and biological features associated with that habitat and determining the effects the action may have on those features. Most bivalve critical habitat includes sufficient water quality and quantity to support breeding, feeding, and sheltering. Only nine listed bivalve species have designated critical habitat within the action area and their overlap with the action area are all less than 1%. In the event activities occur in designated critical habitat the effects to physical and biological features will be minimized or avoided as dictated by local conditions. Impacts to critical habitat from instream work are expected to be temporary and conditions will return to normal after work is complete. Some features of bivalve critical habitat may be positively affected by future timber and road activities by increasing sunlight on surface waters, which in turn produce higher abundances of algae and zooplankton upon which freshwater bivalves feed. Given the small amount of overlap with designated critical habitat, that most in-stream work effects will be temporary, and that some effects may be positive, the proposed action is not likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for bivalve species.

### Determinations

A majority of listed bivalves are expected to have a low likelihood of exposure to future projects in the affected environment. However, if exposed the response to sedimentation could include mortality and decreased reproductive capability, which could impact individuals and the population as a whole. Only where exposure to the stressors associated with road and timber activities is so low as to be discountable has the Forest Service made a not likely to adversely affect determination (Table 18).  If the Forest Service was unable to conclude exposure was unlikely due to location or existing protections, the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule is likely to adversely affect these listed bivalves (Table 18). Given the small amount of overlap with designated critical habitat, that most in-stream work effects will be temporary, and that some effects may be positive, the proposed action is not likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for bivalve species (Table 18).

## Crustaceans

To assist analyzing effects to a large number of species, ESA-listed species were grouped taxonomically. The crustacean group includes 9 total species including 4 endangered and 5 threatened crustaceans (Table 20). These species are aquatic at all life stages, although fairy shrimp eggs can persist through dry conditions until water returns. Two species, the riverside fairy shrimp and Shasta crayfish, potentially occur on two National Forest Service units based on IPAC, while the rest of the listed crustaceans may only occur on one NFS unit (see Appendix A).
