Four of the ESA-listed crustaceans are fairy shrimp, including the Conservancy fairy shrimp, vernal pool fairy shrimp, riverside fairy shrimp, and San Diego fairy shrimp. Two of these fairy shrimp have critical habitat in the affected environment, the vernal pool fairy shrimp and Conservancy fairy shrimp (71 FR 7118). All four of these fairy shrimp species have short life cycles tied to the wet and dry conditions of vernal pools and other ephemeral freshwater ponds in grasslands, rural areas, and wetlands. Eggs can remain viable as cysts in dry conditions and hatch in response to the return of water in the pool. These species have limited dispersal ability. Dispersal can be facilitated by aquatic birds and mammals that unintentionally distribute eggs or cysts that get caught on their bodies or that they have ingested. All of four of these species have a small range in the United States limited to California, and southern Oregon in the case of the vernal pool fairy shrimp (USFWS 2025q).

Four of the nine ESA-listed crustaceans in the action area are crayfish, including the Big sandy crayfish, Big Creek crayfish, St. Francis River crayfish, and Shasta crayfish. The St. Francis River crayfish has <1% of its total critical habitat overlapping with the action area (88 FR 25512). These crayfish species inhabit streams or rivers with rocky substrate (cobbles, boulders, gravel, volcanic rock) suitable for burrowing, sheltering, and as protective cover. The Big Creek crayfish and St. Francis River crayfish have small ranges limited to the Upper St. Francis River watershed in southeast Missouri. The majority of public land within the Upper St. Francis River watershed is part of the Mark Twain National Forest (USFWS 2023t). The Big Sandy crayfish has a larger range than the other listed crayfish which includes the Appalachian region of Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia. The Shasta crayfish also has a small range and is restricted to the Pit River drainage system in Shasta County, California (USFWS 2025r).

One of the nine ESA-listed crustaceans in the action area is an isopod, the Madison cave isopod. The Madison cave isopod inhabits deep karst groundwater habitats associated with caves and fissures in West Virginia and Virginia. More specifically, this species occurs in underground lakes or deep karst aquifers (USFWS 1996). The recovery plan for this species describes known populations as extremely small and with low reproductive potential, however it also notes that this species is difficult to study and collect (USFWS 1996). In 1996, the known sites of this species were located on privately-owned property, however the recharge zone of the aquifer at any occupied site is unknown and therefore the zone of potential sources of contamination is also unknown (USFWS 1996).

Road construction, road reconstruction, road use, and timber harvest can affect crustacean species by fragmenting habitat, degrading habitat features and water quality, altering hydrology, and facilitating the spread and introduction of non-native species. Primary threats to the listed fairy shrimp which are relevant to road- and timber-related activities include direct mortality from off-highway vehicles, habitat loss, fragmentation and degradation from ground-disturbing activities, non-native plants, and altered hydrology. Primary threats to the listed crayfish which are relevant to road- and timber-related activities include habitat degradation from grounddisturbing activities that cause erosion and sedimentation, and non-native invasive species.  The primary threat to the one listed isopod species in general is thought to be an increasing probability of pollutants entering groundwater due to urban and agricultural development.

The primary effects of the proposed action on crustacean species are discussed below and presented in Table 21. A discussion on species protection afforded by land management plans and other documents beyond the protections of the 2001 Roadless Rule is also included.

### Major Stressors

#### _Direct Mortality_

**Fairy shrimp:** Road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvest activities could result in direct mortality to individuals of listed fairy shrimp species if they are present within project boundaries or within road rights-of-way. Since all four of the listed fairy shrimp species are dispersal limited, the use of heavy equipment and off-road vehicles near or through occupied vernal pools or ephemeral wetland habitat for road construction or timber harvest could result in direct mortality to any life stage via vehicular strikes or trampling. Cysts during the dormant life

stage may be particularly at risk of direct mortality from ground-disturbing activities, since they cannot move on their own and dispersal of cysts is predominantly limited to incidental contact with birds or mammals (USFWS 2025q). Additionally, ground-disturbing activities can result in changes to hydrology and inundation periods which can result in the loss of cysts if pools are lost entirely (no water returns to hatch cysts or sedimentation buries pool and cysts), inundation does not last long enough for cysts to hatch, or less water returns to the pools seasonally (fewer cysts exposed to water needed to hatch) (USFWS 2024ae).

#### _Habitat Fragmentation and Edge Effects_

**Fairy shrimp:** Habitat fragmentation is a major threat to fairy shrimp because it can isolate populations, alter hydrology, and hinder dispersal. Physical barriers like roads can separate vernal pools and other ephemeral wetlands, making it difficult for fairy shrimp to disperse which can lead to reduced genetic diversity, increase susceptibility to environmental disturbances, and reduced reproduction. Altered hydrology caused by nearby development can sometimes result in vernal pools that are no longer suitable as habitat for fairy shrimp species. The surrounding watershed supplies most of the water in vernal pools, up to 60%, so changes to nearby land can indirectly lead to habitat loss even if the pools themselves remain untouched. While direct destruction from development poses a greater threat, altered hydrology is also a growing concern (USFWS 2024ae). Besides direct loss of vernal pools, after a road is constructed, ongoing maintenance of roads or road reconstruction within vernal pool ecosystems may subject the pools to repeated disturbance from off-road vehicles, management activities like vegetation removal or firebreak creation, and the introduction of invasive plants (USFWS 2024ae).

#### _Invasive Species Proliferation_

**Fairy shrimp:** Road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvest activities can act as disturbances that facilitate the introduction and spread of non-native invasive plants into vernal pool complexes, where they can pose a threat to fairy shrimp species by altering hydrology and water temperature. Invasive grasses at pool margins can block light, retain moisture, and increase thatch (dense layer of dead and living plant material on the soil surface), leading to shorter hydroperiods that may prevent fairy shrimp species from completing their lifecycles (USFWS 2024ae). Additionally, increased vegetative cover due to non-native invasive plant species on the margins of pools can result water temperature changes that are unsuitable thermal conditions for hatching or development. For example, the time to maturity and reproduction for vernal pool fairy shrimp is temperature dependent; they require water temperatures of low enough for cysts to hatch, while immature and adult shrimp may die off if temperatures rise too high (USFWS 2026a, USFWS 2024ae).

**Crayfish:** Three of the four listed crayfish species are threatened by invasive species proliferation. Invasion by the woodland crayfish ( _Faxonius hylas_ ) has been documented as a primary threat to the viability of the Big Creek crayfish and St. Francis River crayfish, with both of these native species experiencing displacement, hybridization, and range contraction in areas where the woodland crayfish has established (88 FR 25512). The introduction and expansion of the signal crayfish ( _Pacifastacus leniusculus_ ), a generalist species suited to a variety of conditions, is a primary threat to the viability of the Shasta crayfish, a specialist species requiring clean volcanic cobbles and boulders on top of gravel or sand (USFWS 1998g). In areas where

the signal crayfish has rapidly expanded, the Shasta crayfish has shown declines (USFWS 1998g). While the invasive virile crayfish ( _Faxonius virilis_ ) occurs in the same areas and competes with the Big Sandy crayfish in Kentucky, the implications of this competition on Big Sandy crayfish populations are not yet clear (USFWS 2025r). Exposure to invasive species may cause reduced carrying capacity and density of subpopulations, increased predation, increased competition, and displacement.

#### _Sedimentation and Pollution_

**Fairy shrimp** : Ground-disturbing activities in vernal pool watersheds can lead to sedimentation during the wet season, which can have negative impacts on both the hydrology and ecological health of vernal pools and wetlands inhabited by fairy shrimp. Increased sedimentation can alter hydroperiods by changing how water is retained, reduce species richness and abundance of plant and invertebrate communities, bury cysts, clog filter feeding apparatuses, and reduce forage by smothering plant matter or blocking light (USFWS 2024ae).

**Crayfish:** All four listed crayfish species are threatened by ground-disturbing activities that increase erosion and sedimentation which can lead to smothering of rocky substrates and suitable cavities required by these species. Streams within the Upper St. Francis River watershed, occupied by the Big Creek crayfish and St. Francis River crayfish, may experience increased sedimentation if land uses change or if riparian corridors are cleared (88 FR 25512). Commercial forestry, unpaved roads, gas and road construction were documented as some of the sources of sedimentation within the range of the Big Sandy crayfish (USFWS 2025r). Loss of cover and refugia from sedimentation can lead to reduced carrying capacity and density of subpopulations, increased predation risk, reduced foraging success, and increased competition with non-native crayfish (USFWS 2025r, 2023t, and 1998g).

**Madison cave isopod:** As a subterranean aquatic obligate species, potential threats to the Madison cave isopod include the loss and modification of habitat (including the surface environment that is their primary source of water and nutrients), groundwater contamination, and groundwater drawdown (USFWS 1996). Groundwater contamination where this species occurs could result in reduced species fitness and reproduction, or depending on the degree and type of contamination it could result in direct mortality to individuals and reduced genetic diversity in subpopulations.

### Existing Protections

Federally listed threatened, endangered, and proposed species on NFS Lands, including inventoried roadless areas, would continue to be planned for and managed according to the requirements of law, regulation, and policy. All current Forest Service land management plans, through the National Forest Management Act (NFMA) and planning regulations (1982 Planning Rule or 2012 Planning Rule), are required to maintain and contribute to the recovery of threatened and endangered species and conserve proposed species in the plan area (39 CFR 219.9, 2012 Planning Rule; Sec. 219.19, 1982 Planning Rule). Specifically, under the 2012 Planning Rule, federally listed species are maintained in the plan area by providing the ecological conditions necessary to support the persistence of those species. These ecological conditions may include standards or guidelines related to habitat features, condition, or connectivity. It is assumed that under all alternatives, future land management plan revisions or amendments would comply with ESA, NFMA, and planning regulations to meet this requirement to the extent feasible within Forest Service authority and consistent with the inherent capability of the plan area (36 CFR 219.9 and FSH 1909.12).

Relevant to the Madison cave isopod, the George Washington National Forest FEIS states there will be no direct or indirect effects to Madison Cave isopod from Forest Service management activities, and only a fraction (less than a tenth of one percent) of potential habitat was determined to be on Forest Service land at the time of the analysis. It was determined that any cumulative effects to the quality or quantity of Madison Cave isopod habitat would be from private land. The strategy of the George Washington National Forest on groundwater issues that cross national forest boundaries and are affected by multiple regionwide impacts, such as increased agricultural use or growing urban development, is to focus on sustaining and improving watershed areas within national forest control while working cooperatively with other agencies and landowners to improve statewide watershed health (USFS 2014).

Relevant to the four listed fairy shrimp, the Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement for the Southern California National Forests and the design criteria for the Southern California National Forests, including the Los Padres and Cleveland National Forests, state that implementation of the land management plans will be consistent with Recovery Plans for all ESA-listed species (USFS 2013a, USFS 2005). Further, the known occupied site of the Conservancy fairy shrimp in the Los Padres National Forest is fenced to exclude impacts according to the 2005 land management plan for the Los Padres National Forest (available at USFS 2025a).

Big Creek crayfish and St. Francis River crayfish were federally listed in 2023 and the big sandy crayfish was listed in 2016. The current land management plans for the Mark Twain National Forest and George Washington and Jefferson National Forests (where these species potentially occur based on IPAC) pre-date the listing of these three crayfish species and therefore do not include plan-level analysis or plan components specific to these species (land management plans available at USFS 2025a).

The Shasta crayfish was federally listed in 1988 and the current Northwest Forest Management Plan (which includes the Shasta-Trinity and Lassen National Forests) contains an aquatic conservation strategy that addresses generally managing riparian reserves, key watersheds, watershed analysis, and watershed restoration (FEMAT 1993).

### Critical Habitat

Effects to designated critical habitat are analyzed by reviewing the physical and biological features associated with that habitat and determining the effects the action may have on those features. Only three listed crustacean species have designated critical habitat within the action area. The Conservancy fairy shrimp has 15.4% of its total critical habitat within the action area, the vernal pool fairy shrimp has 4.8% of its total critical habitat within the action area, and the St. Francis River crayfish has less than 1% (Table 20). In the event activities occur in designated critical habitat the effects to physical and biological features will be minimized or avoided as dictated by local conditions.

Critical habitat for the Conservancy fairy shrimp and vernal pool fairy shrimp includes sufficiently connected pools, adequate seasonal water quantity, and suitable structure of inorganic and organic materials within pools to support incubation, maturation, reproduction, sheltering, and feeding (71 FR 7118).  For the Conservancy fairy shrimp and vernal pool fairy shrimp, future timber and road activities in occupied critical habitat could result in habitat fragmentation that permanently reduces connectivity between pools and alters hydrology. The designated critical habitat unit that overlaps the action area for the Conservancy fairy shrimp is Unit 8 in Ventura County, California (71 FR 7118). There is a 15.4% overlap of the Conservancy fairy shrimp’s critical habitat with the action area and approximately 40% of that overlap area is “likely not operable”. The known occupied site of the Conservancy fairy shrimp in the Los Padres National Forest, where the critical habitat overlaps and the only NFS unit this species potentially occurs based on IPAC, is fenced to exclude impacts (2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a); therefore, the proposed action may affect, is not likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for the Conservancy fairy shrimp.

For the vernal pool fairy shrimp, there is a 4.8% overlap of its critical habitat with the action area and approximately 50% of that is “likely not operable”. While the Los Padres FEIS states that the vernal pools on the Los Padres are not subject to loss by agriculture or urban development (available at USFS 2025a), the proposed action could result in development of new roads in the long-term which could impact vernal pool critical habitat features. In the short-term, the Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement for the Southern California National Forests (USFS 2013a) states that implementation of the land management plans will be consistent with the Vernal Pool Ecosystems of California and southern Oregon Recovery Plan (71 FR 11441). New road construction within occupied critical habitat could potentially result in permanent impacts to the primary constituent elements of this species’ critical habitat in the long-term (connectivity, hydrology); therefore, the proposed action may affect, is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for the vernal pool fairy shrimp.

Critical habitat for the St. Francis River crayfish includes streams with low flow velocity, shallow depths, appropriate water temperature, connectivity between occupied stream reaches, low stream embeddedness, sufficient forage (invertebrates, periphyton, and plant detritus), and low densities of non-native species (88 FR 25512). For the St. Francis River crayfish, impacts to critical habitat from in-stream work are expected to be temporary and conditions should return to normal after work is complete. Some features of crustacean critical habitat may be positively affected by future timber and road activities by increasing sunlight on surface waters, which in turn produces higher abundances of periphyton upon which crayfish feed. Given the small amount of overlap with designated critical habitat, that most in-stream work effects will be temporary, and that some effects may be positive, the proposed action may affect, is not likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for the St. Francis River crayfish.

For the Madison Cave isopod, of the occurrences available in the GBIF and NRM layers one record was documented on NFS lands, but outside of the action area. The recharge zone of the aquifer at any of the occupied sites is unknown, and therefore the zone of potential sources of contamination is also unknown (USFWS 1996). The recovery plan for this species indicates it may be highly sensitive to disturbances due to its low reproductive potential and small population sizes at some sites, but it is also noted that this species is difficult to study and collect (USFWS 1996). Karst and cave resources can be expected to occur on NFS lands underlain by limestone or marble or areas having exposed basaltic flows. Road construction or reconstruction activities and other developments are sources of sediment, debris, and other pollutants that, when entering karst or cave systems can damage them and their associated resources. While, the analysis done for the George Washington National Forest FEIS states only a fraction (less than a tenth of one percent) of potential habitat was determined to be on NFS lands (USFS 2014), the one occurrence record available is on the Jefferson National Forest, which does not mention this species specifically in the land management plan or FEIS. Because the recharge zone of occupied aquifers is unknown and the amount of potential habitat on the Jefferson National Forest is unknown, the proposed action could lead to groundwater contamination that would be **likely to adversely affect the Madison cave isopod** .

For the Conservancy fairy shrimp, although the exposure is high, it should be noted that this is due to a low number of occurrences overall from GBIF and NRM. This species has been known to occur in inventoried roadless areas on the Los Padres National Forest (2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a). Threats to this species include habitat loss, fragmentation, and degradation from development and agriculture. However, the known location of Conservancy fairy shrimp in the Los Padres National Forest is fenced to exclude impacts (2005 land management plan, available at USFS 2025a), therefore the proposed action is **not likely to adversely affect the Conservancy fairy shrimp** .

For the vernal pool fairy shrimp, although the potential exposure to activities within the action area is high, it should be noted that this is due to a low number of occurrences overall from GBIF and NRM. The Los Padres FEIS states that the vernal pools on the Los Padres are not subject to loss by agriculture or urban development (available at USFS 2025a), but the proposed action could result in development of new roads in the long-term which could impact vernal pool habitat. Roads and timber-related activities could impact the vernal pool fairy shrimp resulting in direct mortality, decreased reproduction, decreased gene flow, habitat fragmentation, and habitat alteration through the spread of invasive plant species; therefore, the proposed action is **likely to adversely affect the vernal pool fairy shrimp** .

For the San Diego fairy shrimp and Riverside fairy shrimp, occurrence data was not available for these species from GBIF and NRM and so the exposure to potential activities in the action area is unknown. However, threats to these two species include habitat loss and indirect effects from development and habitat fragmentation. Roads and timber-related activities could impact the San Diego fairy shrimp and Riverside fairy shrimp resulting in direct mortality, decreased reproduction, decreased gene flow, habitat fragmentation, and habitat alteration through the spread of invasive plant species; therefore, the proposed action is **likely to adversely affect the San Diego fairy shrimp and Riverside fairy shrimp** .

For the big sandy crayfish, the primary impacts to species are from ground-disturbing activities that increase erosion and sedimentation, which degrades the stream habitat required by the species. Under the proposed action, potential in-stream work and sedimentation are expected to be temporary and conditions should return to normal after work is complete. Some features of crustacean habitat may be positively affected by future timber and road activities by increasing sunlight on surface waters, which in turn produce higher abundances of periphyton upon which crayfish feed. However, suitable habitat includes low-silt and unembedded slab boulders; slab boulders and cobble that become highly embedded with sediment deposits are not suitable for this species (USFWS 2025r). Further, females that are reproductively active select slab boulders closer to stream banks in late summer and fall when egg extrusion occurs, typically avoiding higher velocity flows that could dislodge sediments (USFWS 2025r). Depending on the timing and duration, sedimentation from road construction or timber harvest activities could reduce reproductive success of this species. Therefore, even temporary effects from in-stream work due to the proposed action may be **likely to adversely affect the big sandy crayfish** .

For the Big Creek crayfish and St. Francis River crayfish, the impacts to species from potential in-stream work and sedimentation are expected to be temporary and conditions should return to normal after work is complete. Some features of crustacean habitat may be positively affected by future timber and road activities by increasing sunlight on surface waters, which in turn produce higher abundances of periphyton upon which crayfish feed. However, the Big Creek crayfish and St. Francis River crayfish are currently threatened by non-native woodland crayfish species and there is currently no means to slow or stop the spread of this species where they have been introduced (88 FR 25512). The Big Creek crayfish and St. Francis River crayfish have experienced reduced abundances and range contractions where non-native invasive crayfish have established (88 FR 25512). The construction of new roads and potential for increased public access could facilitate the introduction and spread of non-native crayfish into more of the Big Creek crayfish and St. Francis River crayfish ranges and reduce overall viability of these species; therefore, the proposed action is **likely to adversely affect the Big Creek crayfish and St. Francis River crayfish.**

As of 2023, there were only eight isolated populations of Shasta crayfish known to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the land ownership overlapping these populations was identified as private and state parks (USFWS 2023u). However, of the occurrences available in the GBIF and NRM layers one record was documented on NFS lands, but outside of the action area. The Shasta crayfish has experienced population declines and competition due to the proliferation of the signal crayfish. If the Shasta crayfish is present within the action area or close enough to experience downstream effects, the construction of new roads and potential for increased public access could facilitate the introduction and spread of non-native crayfish into more of the Shasta crayfish’s occupied range and reduce overall viability of this species; therefore, the proposed action is **likely to adversely affect the Shasta crayfish.**

## Snails

To assist in analyzing effects to a large number of species, ESA-listed species were grouped taxonomically. The snail group includes 4 total species including 3 endangered freshwater snails, and 1 threatened terrestrial snail (Table 22). Two of the listed species have designated critical habitat, however, no critical habitat for these ESA-listed snails overlaps with the action area. Two species, Anthony’s riversnail and Alamosa springsnail, potentially occur on two National Forest Service units based on IPAC, while the other two listed snails may only occur on one NFS unit (see Appendix A).

Road construction, road reconstruction, road use, and timber harvest can affect snail species by removing habitat, fragmenting habitat leading to a loss of gene flow between populations, creating edge effects that destabilize environmental conditions that support the species, and causing direct mortality through vehicle strikes and right-of-way maintenance equipment. The primary effects of the proposed action on snail species are discussed below and presented in Table 23. A discussion on species protection afforded by land management plans and other documents beyond the protections of the 2001 Roadless Rule is also included.

Three of the ESA-listed snails are freshwater snails, including the Alamosa springsnail, Anthony’s riversnail, and interrupted rocksnail. The Alamosa springsnail occurs in one spring complex on private land with the primary threats to this species including collection, vandalism, and effects of droughts and flood events (USFWS 2018j, USFWS 2023v). Anthony’s riversnail inhabits medium to large rivers with cobble or boulder substrates (USFWS 2023w). Interrupted rocksnail is endemic to the Coosa River drainage and inhabits bedrock, boulders, cobbles, and gravel in slowly moving water (USFWS 2014d). Both the Anthony’s riversnail and interrupted rocksnail are threatened by the degradation of water quality and habitat, and habitat fragmentation (USFWS 2011d, USFWS 2014d).

One of four ESA-listed snails in the action area is a terrestrial snail, the Morro shoulderband snail. This species is endemic to San Luis Obispo County in the central coastal region of California and is associated with sand or sandy soils, slopes not greater than 10 percent, and native coastal dune scrub vegetation (USFWS 2019s). Threats influencing the viability of Morro shoulderband snail populations at the time of listing included in part off-road vehicle activity and invasive species; however, since the time of listing the USFWS determined that these threats, particularly off-road vehicle activity, were no longer affecting the species (USFWS 2019s). The most common threats currently are those associated with land use practices that eliminate, reduce, fragment, and/or modify habitat used by the species (USFWS 2019s).

### Major Stressors

#### _Direct Mortality_

**Terrestrial snails:** Road construction, reconstruction, or maintenance via mowing within the distribution of Morro shoulderband snail can alter habitat characteristics and can result in direct and indirect injury or mortality to snails within both affected and adjacent areas. In addition to direct mechanical injury or mortality, mowing and the construction of roads is likely to increase exposure of this species and therefore increase its vulnerability to desiccation and predation, particularly if these activities occur during the dry season when snails are aestivating (USFWS 2019s).

#### _Habitat Fragmentation and Edge Effects_

**Freshwater snails:** Similar to bivalves, habitat fragmentation impacts freshwater snails by isolating populations, leading to population decline. Improper construction of culverts and other in-stream infrastructure can convert flowing river habitat into non-flowing water features unsuitable for these listed freshwater snails. Additionally, culverts can act as barriers to dispersal of freshwater snails in some cases (Vaughan 2002). This isolation prevents gene flow between populations, leading to reduced genetic diversity, which can diminish fitness and adaptive potential. Consequently, isolated populations are more vulnerable to environmental stochasticity, pollution events, and local extinction (USFWS 2014d). Further, barriers to natural flow can alter the riverbed dynamics, causing sediment retention upstream and scouring of substrates downstream, which degrades essential microhabitats. Although in-stream work has the potential to fragment riverine habitat, the Forest Service designs and installs culverts in a manner to improve streamflow, not restrict it. Fragmentation can still occur during construction but those effects are assumed to be temporary and that surface flows will return to normal, or better than normal, when construction has ended. Short-term fragmentation of aquatic habitat is not expected to have population level effects to listed snails.

**Terrestrial snails:** Road construction, reconstruction, or maintenance via mowing within the distribution of Morro shoulderband snail can alter required habitat characteristics associated with vegetation structure and humidity. Loss of habitat connectivity and reduced ability to disperse between populations can reduce genetic diversity in the long-term (USFWS 2019s). Mechanical

activities associated with road construction, reconstruction, or mowing could increase vulnerability of the Morro shoulderband snail to desiccation and predation, particularly if mowing occurs during the dry season when snails are aestivating (USFWS 2019s).

#### _Sedimentation and Pollution_

**Freshwater snails:** Freshwater snails can be highly sensitive to water and habitat quality (Vaughan 2002). Anthony’s riversnail is threatened by habitat and water quality degradation from activities that cause sedimentation and non-point source pollutants, including timber harvest and road construction (USFWS 2011d). Excess sediment and water pollution from these activities can alter stream channels, reduce riparian vegetation, increase turbidity, degrade water quality, and reduce food availability (USFWS 2011d). However, USFWS noted in the most recent 5-year review for the Anthony’s riversnail that implementation of best management practices can be effective in protecting water quality and instream habitats, which can moderate threats in many instances as is the case with forestry (USFWS 2023w). The interrupted rocksnail requires flowing water, stable stream channels with minimal sediment and algae growth, and adequate water quality (USFWS 2014d). Historical causes of water and habitat degradation in the Coosa River and its tributaries where the interrupted rocksnail occurs included drainage from construction runoff USFWS 2014d).

### Existing Protections

Federally listed threatened, endangered, and proposed species on NFS Lands, including inventoried roadless areas, would continue to be planned for and managed according to the requirements of law, regulation, and policy. All current Forest Service land management plans, through the National Forest Management Act (NFMA) and planning regulations (1982 Planning Rule or 2012 Planning Rule), are required to maintain and contribute to the recovery of threatened and endangered species and conserve proposed species in the plan area (39 CFR 219.9, 2012 Planning Rule; Sec. 219.19, 1982 Planning Rule). Specifically, under the 2012 Planning Rule, federally listed species are maintained in the plan area by providing the ecological conditions necessary to support the persistence of those species. These ecological conditions may include standards or guidelines related to habitat features, condition, or connectivity. It is assumed that under all alternatives, future land management plan revisions or amendments would comply with ESA, NFMA, and planning regulations to meet this requirement to the extent feasible within Forest Service authority and consistent with the inherent capability of the plan area (36 CFR 219.9 and FSH 1909.12).

The 2022 Cibola National Forest land management plan includes plan components for at-risk species, including the Alamosa springsnail (available at USFS 2025a), although the plan notes this species has only been documented in habitat directly adjacent to the Cibola’s boundaries. More specifically, Table 100 of the Cibola National Forest Land Management Plan Final Environmental Impact Statement Volume 2 identifies which plan components alleviate or eliminate key threats to the Alamosa springsnail (USFS 2021). Existing protections identified include, in part, forestwide standards and guidelines to: prevent damage to soil, slope, and watershed conditions from timber harvest; protect stream ecosystems from fragmentation; and locate new roads and trails outside of riparian management zones (USFS 2021). The 2024 Gila National Forest land management plan and associated documents do not contain species-specific protective measures for the Alamosa springsnail or identify this species as one of the ESA-listed species potentially present on the unit (land management plans available at USFS 2025a).

For the Anthony’s riversnail, the 2004 Cherokee National Forest and 2023 Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests (where this species potentially occurs based on IPAC) land management plans and associated documents do not contain species-specific protective measures for this species or identify this species as one of the ESA-listed species potentially present on the unit (land management plans available at USFS 2025a). The Cherokee National Forest land management plan includes forestwide standards for watersheds including a standard that states specifically: “ _Resource management activities that may affect soil and/or water quality will implement Tennessee Best Management Practices (BMPs) as a minimum to achieve soil and water quality objectives. when standards exceed BMPs, standards shall take precedence over Tennessee BMPs_ ”. The Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests land management plan includes a forestwide standards for aquatic systems that states: “ _Management activities shall be designed to avoid, minimize, or mitigate negative impacts on aquatic habitats and species unless the management objective is to protect a native species from encroachment by a non-native species…_ ”. This land management plan also includes forestwide guidelines for aquatic systems including: “ _During forest management activities such as timber harvest or road maintenance, channel-spanning and other passage techniques should be considered to promote passage of aquatic organisms…_ ” and “ _Management activities should follow all applicable North Carolina and National Core Best Management Practices (BMPs) to meet relevant laws, regulations, and policies as described in the streamside zone and water resources sections. Exemptions to regulatory policies may be requested on a case-specific basis where application of the standard policy could result in greater resource damage_ ”.

The interrupted rocksnail was federally listed in 2010 (75 FR 67512). The current land management plan for the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest (where these species potentially occur based on IPAC) land management plan is from 2004 and pre-dates the listing of this species and therefore does not include analysis or plan components specific to this species (land management plan available at USFS 2025a). However, this land management plan does include several forestwide standards protective of aquatic habitats.

For the Morrow shoulderband snail, the 2005 Los Padres National Forest (where this species potentially occurs based on IPAC) land management plan and associated documents do not contain species-specific protective measures for this species or identify this species as one of the ESA-listed species potentially present on the unit (land management plans available at USFS 2025a).

### Critical Habitat

Final critical habitat was designated for the interrupted rocksnail in 2010 (75 FR 67512) and for the Morro shoulderband snail in 2001 (66 FR 9233). There is no overlap of the designated critical habitat for these two species with the action area.

For the Alamosa springsnail, the Cibola National Forest land management plan states that this species has been documented in habitat directly adjacent to the Cibola’s boundaries (land management plan available at USFS 2025a) and the USFWS states that this species is endemic to one spring complex on private land in Socorro County, New Mexico (USFWS 2018j, USFWS 2023v). The Gila National Forest land management plan does not identify this species as potentially present on the unit and this species is unlikely to be present based on USFWS documentation (USFS 2025a, USFWS 2018j, USFWS 2023v). The Cibola National Forest land management plan includes plan components to alleviate or eliminate key threats to the Alamosa springsnail, including from threats related from timber harvest and roads (USFS 2025a). Given that the Alamosa springsnail occurs outside of but adjacent to NFS lands and that the closest Forest Service unit to the species includes protective measures for this species related to timber harvest and roads, the proposed action is **not likely to adversely affect the Alamosa springsnail.**

For the Anthony’s riversnail, occurrence data was not available for this species from GBIF and NRM and so the exposure to potential activities in the action area is unknown. Documented threats to this species include habitat and water quality degradation due to sedimentation and non-point source pollutants associated with timber harvest and road construction (USFWS 2011d). USFWS noted that implementation of best management practices can be effective in protecting water quality and instream habitats (USFWS 2023w). While the Cherokee National Forest and Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests land management plans do not contain species-specific protective measures for the Anthony’s riversnail, they do include forestwide standards and guidelines that require the use of best management practices and protective measures in watersheds and aquatic habitats. However, if this species is exposed activities the response to sedimentation could include mortality and decreased reproductive capability, which could impact individuals and the population as a whole. For this reason, the proposed action is **likely to adversely affect the Anthony’s riversnail.**

For the interrupted rocksnail, occurrence data was not available for this species from GBIF and NRM and so the exposure to potential activities in the action area is unknown. This species requires flowing streams with minimal sediment and algae growth, and adequate water quality (USFWS 2014d). Although the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest land management plan pre-dates the listing of this species, it does include plan components protective of aquatic habitats. However, if this species is exposed to activities the response to sedimentation could include mortality and decreased reproductive capability, which could impact individuals and the population as a whole. For this reason, the proposed action is **likely to adversely affect the interrupted rocksnail.**

For the Morro shoulderband snail, occurrence data was not available for this species from GBIF and NRM and so the exposure to potential activities in the action area is unknown. However, threats to this species include direct mortality, habitat loss, and indirect effects from habitat fragmentation due to road construction, reconstruction, and maintenance activities. Further, this species prefers areas of less than 10 percent slope where timber operability and roads associated with that activity are more likely. If the species is present in the action area, the proposed action could impact the Morro shoulderband snail resulting in direct mechanical injury or mortality, increased desiccation and predation, and decreased gene flow; therefore, the proposed action is **likely to adversely affect the Morro shoulderband snail.**

## Plants

We have identified 130 flowering plant species, two fern species, one lichen species and one conifer species that occur in the action area (Table 24) which we are referring to as the plant taxa group. The plant taxa group includes 134 total species including 74 endangered and 60 threatened plant species. Of these, 38 species have critical habitat designated and critical habitat is proposed for two species. Plant species ranges in the action area vary from extremely small such as Pedate checker-mallow ( _Sidalcea pedata_ ) encompassing less than 20 acres and occurring on just one National Forest to multi-regional in scale such as whitebark pine ( _Pinus albicaulis_ ) which encompasses over 42.9 million acres on US Forest Service lands (USFWS 2021i) over multiple states and multiple National Forests. Most of the plant species in this analysis are found in upland habitats but 41 of the 134 plant species are found in aquatic, wetland or riparian habitats. The plant species in this assessment are found in a variety of habitat types from hardwood and coniferous forests to swamps and bogs to arid deserts to rock crevices and cliffs. Many plant species are specialized, growing on specific geological parent soil types such as serpentine and limestone soils.  Life history of plant species in the action area varies from annual to biennial to very long lived, with some species living multiple centuries (whitebark pine; Arno and Hoff 1989).

Road construction, road use, and timber harvest can affect plants and plant habitats by direct physical damage, habitat loss, soil disturbance, changes in microhabitat conditions (e.g., light, humidity), and changes in hydrology that can degrade the fragile ecosystems where rare plants survive. The presence of roads increases human access and vehicle traffic, which can introduce invasive species, spread pollutants, and compact soils, further stressing native vegetation. Timber harvest intensifies these impacts by removing canopy cover, altering microclimates, and disrupting ecological processes essential for plant survival. Collectively, these activities reduce population sizes, isolate plant communities, and can make recovery more difficult under the Endangered Species Act. The primary effects of the proposed action on conifer, fern, flowering plant, and lichen species are discussed below and presented in Table 27. A discussion on species protection afforded by land management plans and other documents beyond the protections of the 2001 Roadless Rule is also included.

### Major Stressors

#### _Direct Mortality and Habitat Loss_

Road construction and timber harvest physically move or remove vegetation and soil, causing direct mortality of exposed plants in the short term, and reduction, degradation, or elimination of plant populations and habitat, including critical habitat, in the longer term. Even narrow roads can eliminate microhabitats essential for rare species. As seen in the Deconstruction Table (project activities and taxa response, Table 27), trampling is an impact associated with numerous management activities that are part of the proposed action. Severity depends on the intensity, frequency, and duration of disturbance, but trampling can lead to direct mortality or reduced plant size, vigor, and reproductive ability, while more intense disturbances can favor invasive species, decrease species richness, and alter a site's ability to support rare plants.

Heavy machinery and trampling can directly crush plants and seedlings. Activities like trenching and grading can physically move or bury plants. Use of vehicles and heavy machinery in road construction and maintenance, timber harvest, and fire suppression activities, disturb the ground (direct mortality) and lead to soil compaction, which can lead to changes in hydrology, reproduction, and seed dispersal (indirect mortality). Soil disturbance also leads to conditions that favor invasive species (Dixon et al. 2024), which may threaten listed plants and/or habitats.

Roads create favorable conditions for invasive plants by providing light gaps, dispersal corridors, and reduced competition. Vehicles and road maintenance equipment can spread invasive plant seeds, further contributing to their proliferation (Coffin et al. 2021). Off-road or off-highway vehicles (OHVs) are cited as a threat for many threatened and endangered plant species, and OHV use will increase in areas where new roads are built. OHV use leads to continued physical damage to plants, soil disturbance and compaction, and spread of invasive species.

_Ground disturbance and soil compaction_

Soil compaction from road construction and timber harvest may negatively affect threatened and endangered plants by limiting their access to essential resources (water, air, nutrients) and physically impeding their growth, often giving a competitive advantage to more resilient invasive species. Compacted soil has increased bulk density and soil strength, making it difficult for roots to penetrate and expand. Roots may become stunted, thicker, and shallower, unable to form robust taproots or access deeper soil layers for stable water and nutrient sources. Restricted root systems are less efficient at exploring the soil volume and absorbing nutrients, particularly immobile ones like phosphorus (Frene et al. 2024). This can lead to nutrient deficiencies, even if the nutrients are present in the soil in adequate amounts. In addition to impeding growth, soil compaction drastically reduces the vital pore spaces in the soil that hold air. Roots require oxygen for respiration, and low oxygen levels (anaerobic conditions) in compacted soil can suffocate roots and impair their function. Compacted soil exhibits decreased water infiltration, leading to increased surface runoff and erosion (Pandey and Bennett 2024). This also creates a patchy soil moisture environment, where some areas may be waterlogged (leading to root rot) while others remain too dry and hard for plants to thrive. Beneficial soil organisms, such as earthworms and microbial communities, are highly sensitive to compaction due to reduced pore space and altered aeration. This disruption impairs essential ecosystem services like organic matter decomposition and nutrient cycling, further degrading soil fertility. Soil disturbance or removal also has the potential to degrade or remove the soil seed bank of listed plant species.

Heavy machinery used in salvage operations can compact soil, increase erosion, and disrupt seed banks and seed germination. These changes can be particularly harmful to rare plants with narrow ecological tolerances. Leverkus et al. (2020) conducted a global meta-analysis showing that salvage logging negatively affects ecosystem services which may affect rare plants. PuigGironès et al. (2020) observed slower plant regeneration in post-fire salvage logged areas, which may reduce the availability of resources for rare plant species but may benefit other rare plants that depend on more open and disturbed conditions.

Some species will benefit from ground disturbance, (shorter term, recurrent) as they are disturbance dependent. Examples include Price's Potato-bean ( _Apios priceana_ ), which requires moderate disturbance to maintain open canopies from natural processes and from human created openings including silvicultural activities and road rights-of-way and Brauton’s milkvetch ( _Astragalus brauntonii_ ), a post-disturbance species that requires fire or other ground disturbance for seedling germination and to reduce vegetative competition. Of the 134 plant taxa species, approximately 60 (44.8%) need some level and type of disturbance including fire, ground disturbance, vegetation or canopy removal, and natural hydrological processes (for example, flooding, scouring).

#### _Habitat Fragmentation_

Habitat fragmentation is explicitly identified as a threat to 14 plant species in this analysis and likely is a concern for many more listed species within the action area. Road construction and timber harvest break continuous habitats into smaller, isolated patches, which reduces effective population size and increases genetic isolation for rare plants, raising extinction risk through demographic stochasticity and inbreeding (Hulting et al. 2024). Habitat fragmentation can lead to population isolation—plant populations become separated, which restricts the movement of pollinators, limits gene flow, and reduces genetic diversity (leading to inbreeding and lower vigor). This makes populations less resilient and more susceptible to disease and environmental changes. Smaller, isolated populations have a higher risk of local extinction due to random disturbances or demographic stochasticity (chance events).

Fragmentation effects can vary across a species’ range but often produce measurable declines in endangered plant performance toward patch edges and range margins (Laurance et al. 2007). At edges, microclimatic shifts (higher light, temperature fluctuations, lower humidity) change germination, seedling survival, and adult physiology for shade‑adapted species, while edges also facilitate invasion by nonnative plants and altered herbivore or pathogen dynamics that further depress native recruitment. Fragmentation also alters mutualisms: pollinator and seed‑disperser behavior often changes near edges and in small patches, reducing pollination success and seed set for plants that depend on specialized partners, which compounds demographic declines for already threatened taxa (Laurance et al. 2007). Fungal diversity and networks may decline with land use intensity reducing resiliency (Carneiro de Melo Moura et al. 2025) and fragmentation (Grilli et al. 2017). Fungal associations are especially essential to many of the listed orchid species. Research shows reduced reproductive output, poorer offspring performance, and altered functional traits, from habitat fragmentation pushing many vulnerable species closer to extinction (Hulting et al. 2024).

In general, plant species that reproduce asexually (via rhizomes or roots) are highly susceptible to habitat fragmentation by roads because their populations get physically separated and cannot easily expand across the disturbed ground.

#### _Invasive non-native species_

Roads and soil disturbance from silvicultural activities can be the main facilitator for the introduction, invasion, spread and dominance of invasive and non-native species (Coffin et al. 2021).  Invasive, non-native species are responsible for the decline of the largest number of threatened and endangered species (Prosser and Brain 2024) in the United States, estimated to be 42 percent of listed species (Kurth 2017). Invasive and non-native species causing these declines include plants, animals, fungi, and pathogens. Of the 134 plant taxa in this analysis 81 (60 percent) are threatened by invasive or non-native species. Invasive and non-native plant species compete with rare plants for light, nutrients and space resulting in mortality, loss of vigor, reduced reproduction and loss of suitable habitat. They can also alter soil conditions (tamarisk) and facilitate more frequent fire (downy brome) thus altering fire regimes and affect forest regeneration (Oswalt et al. 2007). Invasive and non-native animals such as feral hogs affect plants through direct mortality and by altering habitat through ground disturbance. Feral hogs are the most frequently identified non-native animal threatening the plant taxa in this analysis. They can cause ground disturbance especially in wetlands, resulting in plant mortality, altering hydrology and facilitating invasive plant species thus making the habitat less suitable for the short and longer term. Under certain conditions silviculture may be used to help prevent and control invasive species (Muzika 2017). The US Forest Service implements BMPs and has a National Strategic Framework for Invasive Species Management that provides consistent direction across forests to prevent, detect, control, manage, restore and rehabilitate areas with invasive species (USFS 2013b). Forest Service Manual 2900 provides policy and direction for the prevention and control of invasive species on National Forest System lands. This policy and direction will help minimize the effects of invasive and non-native species from the proposed action on the plant taxa identified in this analysis.

#### _Herbicides and Pesticides_

Herbicides and other pesticides are used to control invasive, non-native and other non-desirable species along roadsides, disturbed areas and during and after silvicultural activities.  Non-target application, overspray, drift, leaching and volatilization can negatively affect plants resulting in mortality, injury, reduced vigor and reproduction and failure to germinate (Wan et al. 2025; Rinella et al. 2009; Fishel 2011). Applications of herbicides and other pesticides may also negatively affect pollinators (Sánchez-Bayo and Wyckhuys 2019; Straw et al. 2021, Straw et al. 2022; Dicks et al. 2021; Linguadoca et al. 2022; Tamburini et al. 2021) resulting in decline of plant pollinated species (Pan et al. 2024; Biesmeijer et al.2006). Herbicides and pesticides were found to be a threat to 25 (18.5 percent) of the 135 plant taxa in this analysis.

The USDA and USDOI developed best management practices to enhance pollinator habitat on federal lands (USDA and USDI 2015). Forest Service Manual Chapter 2150 outlines the Forest Service policy and direction for the safe and effective use of pesticides. Prior to application of pesticides, forests are required to complete a Pesticide Use Proposal (PUP) that is then reviewed for safety and effectiveness. Sensitive areas, including areas where threatened, endangered or proposed plants are located, will be identified during the PUP process. In addition, individual project consultation that includes pesticide use will include design criteria and measures to minimize pesticide impacts to rare plants. As such, the effects of herbicides and pesticides are not considered further in this analysis.

#### _Loss of Pollinators_

As discussed elsewhere in this document, the proposed action is likely to adversely affect some insects, some of which serve as essential pollinators for threatened and endangered plant species. Loss of pollinators disrupts specialized plant–pollinator mutualisms, causing reduced fruit and seed set, lower genetic diversity, and heightened extinction risk for already small and fragmented populations of threatened and endangered plants. Global declines in bees, butterflies, bats, and other pollinators—driven primarily by habitat loss, pesticide exposure, and long-term alteration of weather patterns—undermine reproduction for most angiosperms, as animal pollinators are vital for the reproduction of over 75% of flowering plants. Recent assessments indicate that more than 22% of native North American pollinators face elevated extinction risk (Cornelisse et al. 2025), with native bees particularly imperiled, amplifying reproductive failure and demographic collapse in plant species reliant on these partners. The cascading effects extend beyond individual species, degrading ecosystem functions and resilience as pollinator-dependent plants falter, further threatening biodiversity and ecological stability (Artamendi et al. 2025).

#### _Pollutants_

Roads, mining and silvicultural operations produce pollutants that can harm plants both through air deposition on plants and soil and through runoff, vehicle exhaust and spray and through application of dust abatements and snow deicers. Pollutants include dust particulates, nitrogen oxide, sulfur oxides, metals and salts (Neher et al. 2013). Plants can uptake these pollutants through the air and the soil. Roads and some mining and silvicultural activity produce dust, which deposits on leaves resulting in reduced photosynthesis and clogged stomata affecting efficient respiration and transpiration. Pollutants deposited by air, road surface runoff and vehicle spray are found on foliage and in soil resulting in toxicity to plants and change in pH (Mullerova et al. 2011, Neher et al. 2013). Some nutrient deposition from roads can benefit plants by acting as a fertilizer or changing soil pH. Effects on plants can occur more than 30 m from roads (Hao et al. 2025). The spray zone where road pollutants are deposited are 15 ft or greater from roadsides (Gould 2013).

Lichens can be especially sensitive to air pollution along roadsides from vehicle exhaust. Air pollution affects lichen physiology including photosynthesis, respiration, and cell membranes (St. Clair 1987). In addition, the habitat for lichens may also be affected by air pollution from sulfur dioxide emitted by vehicles (USFWS 2020k). Air pollution is considered to affect some lichen species including Rock gnome lichen ( _Gymnoderma lineare_ ) (USFWS 2020k).

Pollutants were found to be a threat to five (3.7 percent) of the 134 plant taxa in this analysis. Pollutants from roads are expected to mostly negatively affect the plant taxa in this analysis although a few species may benefit.

#### _Runoff, Erosion, and Sedimentation_

Erosion from roads and other disturbed areas can be from wind or water that carries sediment from roads, roadsides, open pits or other disturbed areas creating sheets, gullies, rills or landslides. Topography, soil type, road type and amount of traffic affect the amount and type of erosion. Erosion and sedimentation occur both constantly and in large pulses during weather and/or use events. Erosion which removes and redeposits sediment can result in burying, bending or uprooting plants, wholly or in part. Depending on the amount of erosion this can affect individual plants or whole occurrences. Effects to rare plants from erosion and runoff include mortality, reduced vigor, damage to all parts of the plant, and reduction of population.  Some plants need and benefit from natural erosional and depositional disturbance processes (such as Ute ladies'-tresses, _Spiranthes diluvialis,_ in wetland and riparian areas) whereas others are threatened by this process.

#### _Altered hydrology_

Roads and associated transportation support (bridges, culverts, ditches, etc.) can alter hydrology (Coffin et al. 2021; Jones et al. 2000) in rare plant habitat. Of the 134 plant species in this analysis 45 (33.3 percent) have been identified as being threatened by hydrological alteration. Altered hydrology can affect plants by changing the hydroregime such as the timing, duration, frequency and quantity of water (Cassanova and Brock 2000; Raulings et al. 2010; Nielson et al. 2013) in rare plant habitat. Changes in hydroregimes can change habitat conditions and result in habitat conversion that no longer supports rare plants (Cantu de Leija and King 2023, De Jager 2012; Raulings et al. 2010). Changes include flooding, draining, altered hydroperiods both in length of time and seasonality of water retention or drying, and scouring. These changes can affect the physical and chemical soil conditions such as redox potential and oxygen availability and ability for plants to uptake nutrients. The correct amount of water availability is important during life stages such as seedling germination and recruitment and reproduction. Drying conditions can result in plant mortality, reduced vigor and reproduction, and failure to germinate or recruit. Plants can be buried by water or sediment or uprooted either wholly or in part by flooding resulting in mortality. Some plants need flooding or scouring to create and maintain suitable habitat such as the Santa Ana River wooly star ( _Eriastrum densifolium_ ssp. _sanctorum_ ) and altering that process reduces suitable habitat. Alterations to hydrology from the proposed action are most likely to result in negative effects to most of the plant species in the action area, especially those that are threatened by altered hydrology although some plants may benefit by increasing water availability.

#### _Light environment and Temperature_

Construction and maintenance of roads and mines and silvicultural activities reduce or remove vegetation creating areas with more open canopies. These areas with reduced or removed vegetation and more open canopies create a change in both temperature and light conditions for plants. Surfaces of roads and cleared areas can absorb heat and radiate that heat to the adjacent environment, creating heat islands along roadsides. These higher surface and air temperatures can negatively impact plants by reducing soil water availability, increasing transpiration, creating water stress resulting in plant mortality, reduced growth and vigor. Plants that are adapted to arid conditions may benefit from an increase in heat and aridity.

Likewise open canopies can transmit more light into cleared areas. This can be beneficial to plants adapted to high light conditions but be detrimental to plants that grow in partial or full shade under tree canopies. Old growth forests are important for providing habitat for many species (Franklin et al. 1981). Threatened, endangered and proposed plants whose habitat includes stable closed or partial canopy light environment and are subjected to rapidly changed light and temperature environment are likely to react negatively resulting in mortality and reduced vigor. These openings may make habitat for some threatened, endangered and proposed species unsuitable.  Some threatened, endangered and proposed species that are dependent on fire or other disturbances may respond positively to periodic vegetation removal from silvicultural activities and repeatedly disturbed roadside environments that increase both light availability and temperature.

#### _Fuels management and succession_

One of the purposes for the proposed action is to help manage areas with elevated wildfire risk due to years of fire suppression leading to overgrowth or large stands of dead or diseased vegetation. Addressing wildfire risk through prescribed fire or vegetation management may be beneficial to a number of threatened and endangered plant species that require occasional fire or other disturbance to clear away competing vegetation. Lack of fire or succession that occurs due to fire suppression is a threat to 35 (26 percent) of the 134 plant species in this analysis, so the proposed action may benefit these species and their habitats.

### Critical Habitat

For critical habitat analyses, we consider the effects of the proposed action on the physical and biological features (PBFs) of the habitat described in the Final critical habitat listing rule to determine the level of impact. Of the 134 total species included in this flowering plant, fern, lichen, and conifer analysis, 38 have critical habitat designated and two have critical habitat proposed. Of the 38 species, 14 have critical habitat that overlaps the action area. Of these, nine species have critical habitat that exceeds 2% overlap with the action area, and of these nine, 5 species exceed 5% critical habitat overlap with the action area. The amount of critical habitat by species overlapping the action area is found in Table 24. The main PBFs for listed threatened and endangered plant species generally fall into categories relating to their essential habitat needs and interactions with their environment. These include:

- **Suitable Plant Community and Habitat:** The specific native plant communities and physical landscapes (e.g., forests, wetlands, specific soil types) required for the plant's survival, growth, and reproduction. This often includes maintaining appropriate plantplant interactions and overall ecosystem resilience.

- **Appropriate Soil Conditions:** The presence of specific soil types, nutrient levels, and moisture regimes (e.g., adequate water quality and flow regimes) that the plant species requires.

- **Pollination and Seed Dispersal Mechanisms:** The conditions and presence of necessary pollinators or dispersal agents (e.g., insects, birds, specific wind patterns) that allow the plant to reproduce effectively.

- **Protection from Threats:** Features that ensure the plant community is protected from significant threats, such as:

- **Invasive species:** Mechanisms to resist the introduction and proliferation of nonnative species that compete for resources.

- **Altered fire regimes:** Maintaining a natural fire frequency/intensity or protecting areas where fire regimes have been altered.

- **Overutilization:** Regulatory mechanisms or physical protections against overharvesting for commercial, recreational, or scientific purposes.

- **Disease and Predation:** Defense against specific diseases or predators that pose a significant risk (e.g., fungal diseases).

- **Weather Impacts:** Habitat features that confer resilience to the effects of longterm alteration of weather patterns, such as changes in temperature or precipitation.

- **Genetic Diversity:** The maintenance of sufficient genetic variation within populations to ensure long-term adaptability and reduce risks associated with inbreeding depression.

These features are specific to each species and are detailed in relevant recovery plans and federal register documents.

For one species, Heliotrope milk-vetch ( _Astragalus montii_ ), 100 percent of its critical habitat overlaps with the action area. Likewise, a significant portion of critical habitat for San Bernardino Mountains bladderpod ( _Lesquerella kingii_ ssp. _bernardina_ ) occurs in the action areas (36.34 percent). The San Bernadino National Forest Plan includes protections for San Bernardino Mountains bladderpod (Table 26) that will help to reduce or avoid impacts to the species’ critical habitat. In the case of Heliotrope milk-vetch, where the proposed action will not benefit the species or its habitat and for the other plant species whose critical habitat overlaps the action area, individual forests will consult on specific projects that may impact critical habitat and develop protective measures to minimize impacts to critical habitat. However, the FS cannot discount some adverse effects may occur, thus the FS has determined the proposed action is likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for Heliotrope milk-vetch and San Bernardino Mountains bladderpod and any plant species with critical habitat overlap with the action area of more than 1% (Table 24).

Other species with critical habitat overlapping the proposed action area include Cushenbury milk-vetch ( _Astragalus albens_ ), Ash-grey paintbrush ( _Castilleja cinerea_ ), Cushenbury buckwheat ( _Eriogonum ovalifolium_ var. _vineum_ ), Parish's daisy ( _Erigeron parishii_ ), Cushenbury oxytheca ( _Oxytheca parishii_ var. _goodmaniana_ ), and California taraxacum ( _Taraxacum californicum_ ), all of which are part of the carbonate, montane meadow, or pebble plain habitats of the San Bernadino Mountains. Species and habitat protections are described in the Existing Protections table below (Table 26).

Given the small amount of overlap with designated critical habitat, that most vegetation impacts will be temporary, and that some effects may be positive, the proposed action is not likely to adversely affect designated critical habitat for plant species with overlapping critical habitat of less than 1% (Table 24). In the event activities occur in designated critical habitat, the effects to physical and biological features will be minimized or avoided as dictated by local conditions.

### Existing Protections

Due to the large number of plant species, the assessment of species-specific existing protections focuses on species with critical habitat overlapping the action area and/or species that were identified as having a high exposure level based on percent of Inventoried Roadless Area (IRA) occurrences in operable or potentially operable but complex areas. These species are listed in Table 26 with existing protections.

The determinations for each species as shown in Table 24 are based on the amount of known occurrences and critical habitat that overlaps the operable or potentially operable action area, the protections that are in place in individual Forest Plans (Table 26), and that before any project will be able to be implemented it will need to be consulted on separately under ESA.  Although we analyzed the extent of the proposed action in the action area, we do not expect that the entire action area will be affected by the proposed action. In addition, some of the proposed actions will benefit certain listed species, such as actions to reduce vegetation succession, which will address a primary threat to 35 of 134 (26.1 percent) species. ## Cumulative Effects

Under the ESA, cumulative effects are the consequences of future State, Tribal, local, and private activities that are reasonably certain to occur within the action area. The action area for rescission of the Roadless Rule is owned and managed by the US Forest Service. As such, nearly all activities that will occur in the action area will require ESA consultation, with the FS as the lead agency for those consultations. Although private activities may occur within proximity to currently inventoried roadless areas, there are no reasonably certain private activities that overlap the time and scale of this consultation. Cumulative effects will be considered more thoroughly during project level consultation.

# PROJECT-LEVEL CONSULTATION

The proposed action described below is a “framework programmatic action” as defined in 50 CFR 402.02, where the framework programmatic action only establishes a framework for the development of specific future action(s) but does not authorize any future action(s). The effects to listed species and designated critical habitat of future actions that are subsequently authorized, funded, or carried out under this program will be addressed in subsequent section 7

consultations, as appropriate. The Forest Service proposes to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule. This action does not affect state-level roadless rules that may exist, nor does it preclude the development of state-led roadless efforts. Rescinding the Roadless Rule does not authorize, fund, or carry out future forest management activities that could occur in these areas. Rescinding the Roadless Rule does not constrain or alter the statutory requirement of sections 7(a)(1) through section 7(a)(4) of the Endangered Species Act. All future activities in currently inventoried roadless areas will require compliance with the ESA prior to implementation.  Rescinding the Roadless Rule does not alter the protections afforded to designated wilderness areas or areas protected by other law, regulation, or policy.

Although rescinding the Roadless Rule does not dictate or prescribe forest management in previously inventoried roadless areas, it is reasonably certain that active forest management and road construction will increase in these areas. However, currently the Forest Service does not have a reliable method to identify, describe, or analyze the likelihood and location of any future projects that may be proposed for currently inventoried roadless areas.

Future projects in current inventoried roadless areas will require compliance environmental laws and regulations, including the Endangered Species Act. As is typical, future project designs in these areas will avoid and minimize adverse effects to ESA-listed resources to the greatest extent feasible. All projects must be consistent with the land management plan that governs management for their geographic location.

Adverse effects to ESA-listed resources from road construction and timber projects in roadless areas may include, but are not limited to: behavioral avoidance, increased energy expenditure, reduction in fitness, abandonment, degradation of unique critical habitat features, and even mortality. However, these effects will be fully explored during project-level compliance efforts, including consultation under section 7(a)(2) of the Endangered Species Act.

The Forest Service has determined that rescinding the Roadless Rule will have no direct effect on ESA-listed resources because it does not authorize, fund, or carry out future forest management activities in areas currently identified as inventoried roadless areas. However, after rescinding the Roadless Rule, future forest management may occur in inventoried roadless areas that result in road construction and timber harvest activities. These future activities may affect ESA-listed resources. Future activities in current inventoried roadless areas will comply with the ESA through project-level consultation, when details about the project are known.  The Forest Service shall consult with the Services on any future projects in currently inventoried roadless areas that may affect ESA -listed resources.

# CONCLUSION

Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule will increase the likelihood of road construction and timber harvests occurring in locations previously considered inventoried roadless areas.  In many cases the Forest Service anticipates this increased activity to adversely affect some ESA-listed species and their designated critical habitats. However, all future projects in these areas will be required to comply with environmental law, regulation, and policy, including the Endangered Species Act.  Projects that are determined that they “may affect” ESA-listed species or designated critical habitats will undergo consultation under section 7(a)(2) of the ESA. Through consultation with the Services at the project-level, jeopardizing listed species or adversely modifying critical habitat should be avoided.

#### **Appendix B: Best Management Practices**

Forest Service policy and guidance are described in several different Forest Service publications. The Forest Service Directives System is a series of manuals and handbooks used by Forest Service personnel to guide the agency and manage national forests and grasslands. Forest Service manuals contain legal authorities, objectives, policies, responsibilities, instructions, and guidance regularly used by agency employees to do their work. Forest Service handbooks provide specialized guidance and instruction for carrying out the directions in the manuals. Field issuances are localized supplements to the national manuals and handbooks.

Primary references are available in FS directives such as Forest Service Handbook (FSH) 7709.56 Chapter 60 for typical road maintenance, FSH 2409.15 Chapter 50 for timber related road maintenance, and FSH 7709.56 Chapter 40 for development and construction requirements.
